title: 70 Up review – a deeply moving conclusion for the 63-year-long TV experiment | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegaic, thoughtful outing ever
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegaic, thoughtful outing ever
Content: ‘100% the most important thing’ … Symon (centre) with some of his family in 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘100% the most important thing’ … Symon (centre) with some of his family in 70 Up.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockTV reviewTelevision & radioReview70 Up review – a deeply moving conclusion for the 63-year-long TV experimentThe landmark documentary series looked like it was done for good – until one participant was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Asif Kapadia takes the helm for its most elegaic, thoughtful outing everLucy ManganTue 15 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd so the great experiment begun by GranadaTelevisionin 1964 is over. That year, Seven Up! introduced the viewing public to 14 primary school children – 10 boys and four girls from a range of backgrounds – who would become part of an ongoing documentary project that returned to film them at regular intervals and interrogate the truth of the Jesuitical motto “Give me the child for the first seven years and I will give you the man”.Seven Up!, part of ITV’s flagship World in Action series, was directed by Paul Almond but thereafter the enterprise became synonymous with Michael Apted, who originally helped find the children and took over the making of the programmes. Hedied in 2021, two years after completing 63 Up. It had been thought the series would end there but when one of the participants,Nick Hitchon– a Yorkshire farmer’s son who grew up to be a nuclear scientist – called one of the team to say that he had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and wanted to give one last interview, a final episode was commissioned.Directed by Asif Kapadia, it has a more reflective and elegiac tone than in previous years. Lynn, who spent most of her life as a devoted children’s librarian – council funds and cuts permitting – died in 2013. Almost everyone else is retired. Everyone is looking back. Jackie speaks with great relief of the calm and relative solitude in which she now lives, having moved away from the family that – reading between the lines – she clearly loves but required much from her. The three prep school boys, John, Charles and Andrew, first seen perched on the sofa in their headteacher’s study and talking with disarming sweetness about futures at Charterhouse, the Dragon and Oxbridge, have had the lives of privilege and ease that they expected and that we expected for them. Andrew wishes he had spent more time with his family. “School plays,” he says. “Sports days.” There are shades of similar regret from some of the other men, too. But the Up series has always had to sacrifice the interrogation of such detail for breadth of coverage, and this is one of the many potentially fruitful paths you wish had been travelled further down.Tony, the self-described “Little Artful Dodger” and would-be jockey turned cab driver remains as irrepressible as ever, though he notes his biggest mistake was deciding not to commit to the former career after his mentor warned him that he would struggle to meet the necessary weight all his life.Brucehas retired from teaching and now sings in the local choir, walks his dog on the beach and volunteers with the local branch of the RNLI. The thoughtful, gentle, Christian boy has become a thoughtful, gentle, Christian man.Symon, the terribly sad-eyed boy brought up in a children’s home (“What you don’t have, you don’t miss,” he said at 14, and it was so nakedly untrue that you still have to look away when they show this moving scene again here) has fostered more than 100 children with his second wife over the last 20 years. He looks happier now. The children are welcomed back for visits all the time. Paul, Symon’s companion in the children’s home, has built himself a good life in Australia. He is a grandfather now. “Family is 100% the main thing.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m probably as happy as I can be’ … Neil.Photograph: ITV/Nick Wall/ShutterstockNeil– the perky, bright Liverpudlian schoolboy who dreamed of Oxford but has struggled with depression all his life, and experienced periods of homelessness in between being a local councillor and lay minister and, briefly, a husband – now lives alone in France. The perkiness left long ago but he is as thoughtful, articulate and unassuming as ever. He is clearly still vulnerable in many ways and his existence precarious, but he has found a way of being that brings him contentment enough. Yes, he says, he is sometimes lonely. “But that is a characteristic of the age … I’m probably as happy as I can be, given my life.”‘It’s the Bayeux tapestry of TV!’ After six decades, the seminal series bows out with 70 UpRead moreThere is, especially in the second instalment of this final film, something of a meta-narrative too, as the participants give their thoughts about the series and about Apted. We also hear archive footage of Apted reflecting on what he learned over the years. Jackie was perhaps his earliest and most vocal combatant, challenging him over various questions – largely about marriage and sex – that she said he only dared ask the women, and she pulls him up on his class bias too. John describes him as having “a sneering and somewhat supercilious manner” and, in essence, painting the privileged as bogeymen. Apted himself said he was judgmental at the beginning, and gradually taught himself to stay out of things as much as possible. But it remains clear, 60-odd years on, that this was not a rigorous or objective journalistic venture but a series profoundly shaped by one man’s vision, background and baked-in assumptions. Acknowledging this, as Kapadia does, is the best thing to do with it now. The achievement has become an artefact to be admired, still, but questioned too.70 Up aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now in the UK and on SBS and SBS on Demand in Australia on 7 October.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionDocumentaryMichael AptedreviewsShareReuse this content

title: AI on course to kill us all within 10 years? Donald Trump says: ‘Hold my Coke’ | John Crace | The Guardian
description: US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel
Author: John Crace
Headline: US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel
Content: ‘Donald Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence.’Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence.’Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchAI (artificial intelligence)AI on course to kill us all within 10 years? Donald Trump says: ‘Hold my Coke’John CraceUS president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheelTue 15 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTShareWe can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account,Donald Trumphas declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart.All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind.You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best.Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass theTuring test. Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference.double quotation mark‘No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one’Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us.It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die.You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking.Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis.And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary,Jonathan Reynolds, had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid.“There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years.People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one.And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion.And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated.So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak.There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that. They would much rather keep their competitive edge, notch up obscene profits in the next few years and take their chances when their machines turned against them.By now, Webb was unable to suppress his rising panic. He had always believed himself to be one of the immortals: now the existential threat was right in front of him. “But humanity will be obliterated,” he sobbed. Reynolds tried to calm him down. There was nothing personal about this. It was just AI being AI.But Justin was now beyond help. “What about a kill switch?” he shrieked. Johnny wasn’t really listening. He wasn’t even sure how that would work. Who would get to control it? Please not Trump. Only one thing for it. “Always look on the bright si-ide of life.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The politics sketchDonald TrumpJonathan ReynoldscommentShareReuse this content

title: No Big Deal review – is this how AI ends humanity … with a sitcom so bad it bores you to death? | Television | The Guardian
description: The characters are dead-eyed waxworks which speak with all the nuance of a satnav. But this AI-created workplace comedy is so bad that even the greatest actors alive couldn’t stop it being unwatchable
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The characters are dead-eyed waxworks which speak with all the nuance of a satnav. But this AI-created workplace comedy is so bad that even the greatest actors alive couldn’t stop it being unwatchable
Content: Truly deathly … an AI actor in No Big Deal, a comedy billed as ‘The Office meets Dragons’ Den’.Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenTruly deathly … an AI actor in No Big Deal, a comedy billed as ‘The Office meets Dragons’ Den’.Photograph: YouTubeTV reviewTelevisionReviewNo Big Deal review – is this how AI ends humanity … with a sitcom so bad it bores you to death?The characters are dead-eyed waxworks which speak with all the nuance of a satnav. But this AI-created workplace comedy is so bad that even the greatest actors alive couldn’t stop it being unwatchableStuart HeritageTue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs you will no doubt be aware, one Anthropic researcher claimed there is a greater than one in 10 chance thatAI will end all of humanityas we know it within the next decade. However, now that I’ve given it some thought, I think this statistic might actually be a little conservative. This is because I have just watched an episode of a sitcom created by AI, and if I ever have to do it again I’m genuinely going to die of boredom.The show is No Big Deal, and it premiered on YouTube on Friday. I was apparently only the 376th person to watch it. This is by no means a recommendation that you become the 377th, more a warning to avoid it if your algorithm ever decides it hates you enough to suggest this.No Big Deal bills itself as “The Office meets Dragons’ Den”, in that it is a workplace comedy about a group of angel investors who have to listen to various product pitches. In the first episode, the products include a toilet that analyses your poo and a sofa you can have sex on. The investors are nightmarish waxworks who speak with all the nuance and cadence of a satnav telling you that you just missed a turning.If you’ve watched any AI-generated content recently, you’ll know the faults it has, and they are all present here. Shot-to-shot continuity is essentially nonexistent, with characters changing positions every time the camera cuts to a new angle. Background noise either is or isn’t there, seemingly on a whim. The characters – who all fitfully look enough like real-life actors to make the whole thing seem icky and exploitative – move around with not a trace of life behind their eyes. It remains completely impossible to care about anyone once you know they’ve been made by AI.View image in fullscreen‘I really cannot overstate how terrible this thing is to look at’ … Andrew Dickinson’s AI sitcom No Big Deal.Photograph: YouTubePerhaps the most depressing thing about No Big Deal is the fact that it was purportedly written by a human. Although all the characters, locations and scenes were churned out by a machine, the show was apparently written by Andrew Dickinson. Dickinson, once himself an angel investor, originally intended for the show to be made as a traditional television production. When he realised that this would be slow and expensive, he turned to AI.To some degree, this makes sense. It is extraordinarily hard to get a television programme on the air. You can spend years grinding away on an idea, only to see it wither up and die when none of the eight commissioners currently working like the sound of it. Wouldn’t it be better to just seize control of the means of production and make the AI version?On this evidence, absolutely not. This is not a funny show. It’s one-note and bawdy, and none of the jokes land. It seems as though, by rushing straight to AI, Dickinson has bypassed the development process that actually makes something good. You could cast the greatest human actors of their generation to perform this script and it would still be unwatchable.Then again, even if by some miracle Dickinson had written the most hilarious sitcom of all time, it still would have turned to ash the moment he let it loose on these AI abominations. I really cannot overstate how terrible this thing is to look at. While the technology has improved to an extent that, should you pause a scene at just the right moment, the characters are photorealistic, there’s something truly deathly about watching them move.The Guardian has only ever published 18 zero-star reviews. Here they all areRead moreTheir lips don’t line up with dialogue. There’s a creepy smoothness to their movements. Sometimes, when they don’t have anything to do in a scene, they just sit there completely still like a powered-down robot. Their voices bark on monotonously like Siri reading out a pasta recipe. Even something as simple as a fist shake (a fist shake! In a sitcom! In 2026!) gets mauled beyond all recognition here, causing the shaker to judder and glitch as if they just stepped on an uninsulated wire.The most tragic thing of all is that nobody involved can see that this is just a stepping stone to the endgame. Dickinson thinks he can get away without human actors or crew, but we are a nanosecond away from the technology deciding that it doesn’t need human writers, either. By capitulating even a jot to AI-created content, all Dickinson is doing is nudging himself further towards extinction.And me, too, because if this is the future of entertainment then I’d rather die than write about it. If we really do only have a decade left, every second should be precious. Please don’t spend any of it watching crap like this.No Big Deal is on YouTube nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewAI (artificial intelligence)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: When is an ebike not an ebike? When it has a powerful, illegal engine. Get this menace off our roads | Peter Walker | The Guardian
description: As a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the law, says the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: As a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the law, says the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker
Content: Illegally modified bikes and e-scooters are crushed at an automotive recycling centre in Southampton, England, 2 July 2025.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllegally modified bikes and e-scooters are crushed at an automotive recycling centre in Southampton, England, 2 July 2025.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesOpinionEbikesWhen is an ebike not an ebike? When it has a powerful, illegal engine. Get this menace off our roadsPeter WalkerAs a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the lawTue 15 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTShareOne of the curiosities of debates about cycling in the UK is that almost all of them centre on the place with the greatest concentration of not only bikes but also politicians and journalists: innerLondon. Inevitably this is just a small part of the story.Much of the current focus is on so-called share bikes operated by companies such as Lime and Forest – nippy electric-assist machines that can be picked up and left on pavements. On Saturday, a Guardian investigation revealed that councils in the capital have so far this year seized3,393 dangerously parked or abandoned ebikes, a number 23% higher than the total for the whole of last year.Depending on your view, ebikes are either a gamechanging boon to short-distance urban transport or, if we heed the testimonies of those who have been menaced or injured, adangerousand lawless scourge.But even this misses the point. Outside the handful of urban areas where Lime and their competitors operate, the ebikes that exist are privately owned. And many of these are not, at least under the law, ebikes at all.This can sound complex, but bear with me. To be classed as an ebike, a machine must have a powered speed limit of 15.5mph and a motor that only kicks in when you pedal, not via a throttle.Wander around pretty much any UK town or city for long enough and you will see contraptions that very much do not meet these criteria. They might look broadly like a bike, with pedals and a chain. But they are often throttle-powered and can travel much, much faster than 15mph.These are not ebikes. They are illegal electric motorbikes. This is a vital distinction to make before you start discussing ebikes, and whether they are, indeed, a brand new peril on our streets.Now that we know where we are, how much, if at all, of the media scare stories about ebikes or their illegal cousins have a basis in fact? Again, it’s slightly more complex than it might seem.If you hang around central London, it won’t take too long to see someone on a Lime bike sail serenely through a red light, sometimes weaving awkwardly through gaggles of pedestrians.This is, of course, illegal, and for all that some cyclists try to justify such behaviour on self-preservation grounds, I’d also argue that it is selfish and intimidating. People should be able to cross the road at a green pedestrian signal without having to first scan the horizon for a beefy twentysomething called Josh on a Lime bike who is running late for his post-work five-a-side game.View image in fullscreenAbandoned ebikes block the pavement in central London, 29 April 2026.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockBut is there any need to panic? Not really. Cyclists are no different from drivers in that quite a few break the law if they think they can get away with it. One issue for cycling PR is that two-wheeled offences are often just more visible.Government statistics show that when the traffic is flowing freely,fully three-quarters of drivers speed in 20mph zones. This is harder to spot, but the difference is that this sort of behaviour has a realistic chance of killing someone.Very serious or fatal pedestrian casualties with legal bikes and ebikes do happen, but they are vanishingly rare, unlike incidents with motor vehicles. This is not a matter of morals, just physics – more specifically the way kinetic energy increases so rapidly as the inputs of mass and velocity change.Some argue that riders of Lime-type bikes are disproportionately likely to flout the rules, in part because they are paying for the transport by the minute. I’m not sure that’s the case.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEither way, it’s undeniable that, overall, share ebikes – in fact all legal ebikes – are a good thing. They make cycling available to demographics that would not normally consider using a bike, especially people without anywhere safe to store their own machine. Despite the occasional annoyance of the Josh contingent, I welcome them to the bike lanes.Thousands of ebikes seized by London councils as anger rises over blocked pathsRead moreIt is a very different case for the illegal variants. These are often heavier – some are designed to look like motorbikes – and can go at significant speed. It’s not uncommon for me to be overtaken by a silent, moped-weight gizmo doing 30mph or more. I am, it is fair to say, not a fan of this.This is, however, not a cycling problem. It’s a law-enforcement problem. It’s therefore also a political problem, not least whether or not any ministers are willing to crack down on a food-delivery industryheavily reliant on riders using illegal bikes.But the repeated conflation of these two issues has ramifications for cycling. In part it is a call for restrictions on cycling because of offences by those speeding on illegal machines. And because illegal bikes often have vast, poorly made batteries with a tendency to catch fire, some rail companies are pondering bans on all ebikes.The cycling world is changing quickly. And it is perfectly OK to be annoyed with the Lime bike buffoons. But do remember – they’re not the problem here.Peter Walker is the Guardian’s senior political correspondentExplore more on these topicsEbikesOpinionCycle hire schemesCyclingLondonTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spy | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: She has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: She has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?
Content: ‘I played one match for Wales then thought: I’ve done that’ … Aimee-Ffion Edwards.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I played one match for Wales then thought: I’ve done that’ … Aimee-Ffion Edwards.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTelevision & radioInterview‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spyDonna FergusonShe has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a moment, just before Aimee-Ffion Edwards jumped off a nightclub balcony inSlow Horses, when she had to lie to herself about what she was about to do. “It was quite hard,” says the actor. “You basically tell yourself, ‘You’re not jumping.’ Obviously, you know you’re harnessed in, but you’re also going, ‘This is mad! This is mad! This is mad!’”She laughs. “I couldn’t feel my fingers for a second. I was like, ‘Huwwaah!’” She sucks in her breath, then says: “But there were 200 people stood there watching. You’re like, ‘Well, I gotta do it.’”In the scene that we see, though, Shirley Dander – the tough, traumatised, cocaine-snorting MI5 agent Edwards plays – does not hesitate, leaping from the balcony to land on a suspect. That collision (on a stuntman) was no soft landing either and, at 38, Edwards knew she’d feel it the next day. And yet she jumped off the balcony “five or six times” during filming. “I played rugby in a boys’ team,” she explains, “and I think I have a fearlessness that comes from that. It’s quite instinctive.”double quotation markMy biggest achievement? I was an answer on Pointless!Edwards is wearing an elegant sleeveless blouse, smart navy trousers and gold hoop earrings. She does not, as she sits there sipping a flat white in London’s Soho Hotel, look much like a rugby player. Yet, with some pride, she reveals that her childhood dream was to play rugby forWales, where she was born and raised. “That was all I cared about. And I did! I played one match for Wales. Then I was like, ‘I’ve done that. I think I’m going to do some acting.’”View image in fullscreen‘There’s so much to play’ … with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/Apple TV+Edwards, a fluent Welsh speaker, still lives in Newport. She had a paper round there until she was 19 and grew up the middle child of five. “I have a strong sense of being part of a pack,” she says. The actor regularly commutes to London (“it’s so close – an hour and 35 minutes on a good train”) and finds it refreshing to be able to play a British spy with her authentic Welsh accent, pleased Shirley’s Welshness is not a talking point in the hit show.“Nobody ever mentions it,” she says. “And I think that’s really important. It’s good to normalise it. We hear northern and other accents all the time, but Welsh accents have been underrepresented.” Except, she adds, in comedy roles. “Like there’s a novelty aspect to being Welsh – like it’s some sort of kooky thing. It’s really not.”Before Slow Horses, which follows a ragtag bunch of reject MI5 agents who are presumed to be inept despite usually saving the day, Edwards had to fake a Brummie accent as the opportunistic criminal Esme Shelby inPeaky Blinders, and adopt a southern one as manipulative Elizabeth Barton, the “Holy Maid of Kent” in Wolf Hall.But as Shirley, and especially as Richard Burton’s older sister Cis in the 2025 film Mr Burton, she has increasingly been able to lean into her Welsh identity. And now she is voicing Princess Leia in the first-ever Welsh language-dub of 1977 blockbuster Star Wars. Due to be broadcast in Wales on Christmas Day, its Han Solo will be voiced by Matthew Rhys. So is she a fan? “Oh my God, I was pinching myself. That was so surreal, being in a booth, watching the film and lip-syncing I was going, ‘I don’t know how I got here, but I’m here – and I’mherefor it.’ It was amazing. And it’s brilliant the Welsh language dub is happening. I’d be excited even if I wasn’t in it.”View image in fullscreenLooking for contradictions … as Esme Shelby in Peaky Blinders.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/BBC/Caryn Mandabach Productions Ltd.In season six of Slow Horses, about to launch on Apple TV, Shirley’s anger and grief about the death of her colleague Marcus, played by Kadiff Kirwan, keeps bubbling to the surface. This grief is, to some extent, genuine: “I found it really hard when Marcus died, especially coming in for season five, because it was quite a lonely experience.”She and Kirwan were “partners in crime”, she says. “That unique relationship between Shirley and Marcus – it was purely platonic, but with a lot of love, a lot of frustration, a lot of projecting each other’s nonsense back at each other.” At the same time, his death has helped her to develop Shirley’s character emotionally. “There’s so much to play.”As a strong, dangerous woman whose physical bravery and moral courage is undermined by her emotional cowardice, explosive temper and penchant for violence, Shirley is “liberating” to play. “I love that she’s scrappy,” says Edwards. “There’s so much negative energy in her and she doesn’t know what to do with it. She can’t communicate it properly.”View image in fullscreen‘I love making things with wood’ … if she ever gave up acting, Edwards would get a dog and become a carpenter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianEdwards – whose first major role was as Sketch, the stalker in teen dramaSkins– looks for contradictions in the women she plays, which may explain why she is so good at humanising liars, criminals and sneaks. “I’m fascinated by people’s strengths,” she says, “and the mechanisms we have to protect ourselves when we feel vulnerable.” Shirley, she says, gives off a “stench” of “Try it – come and get it” when she walks into a room. “But I understand why she is like she is. I keep trying to pick at those threads, to expose them a little bit.”Gary Oldman, who plays the chain-smoking, whisky-drinking, rarely washing boss Jackson Lamb, is the joker of the cast. “He loves making people laugh. He’s always got an anecdote, a tale to tell. He’s very silly and funny – a fun father figure.”In her spare time, Edwards exercises a lot, mainly swimming and running, because team sports are a problem. “The nature of this work means you can’t commit,” she says, adding that she also enjoys making furniture in her garage. If she ever gave up acting and working far from home, she’d like to get a dog and become a carpenter. “I love making things with wood.”Social media doesn’t interest her much. “I’m here for YouTube videos about carpentry, but I don’t know why anyone would ever be interested in what I had for breakfast.” She prefers to keep her personal life private, to protect her family and those she loves. And perhaps as a result, even though strangers often smile at her like they know her, they rarely identify who she is, even in Newport. “They think we went to school together or I work in the corner shop, rather than know me off the telly.”This suits her. No actor, she says, ever regrets someone appreciating their work. “If they do, they should quit.” But she feels lucky she gets to live “a normal life” in her home town, where no one bothers her. “I’ll tell you what my biggest achievement is: so many people messaged me one day, because I was once an answer on Pointless.”The question on the TV quizshow was: name a famous Edwards. “Which is ironic, because nobody knew who I was.” She beams. “What a contradiction.”Slow Horses series six launches on Apple TV tomorrow.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTelevisionSlow HorsesPeaky BlindersDramaTV crime dramaThrillersinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant women | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: ICE says it has no updated information on the number of miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Lawmakers, advocates and immigration attorneys have raised alarms that pregnant detainees are not receiving basic prenatal care and screenings
Author: Maanvi Singh
Headline: ICE says it has no updated information on the number of miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Lawmakers, advocates and immigration attorneys have raised alarms that pregnant detainees are not receiving basic prenatal care and screenings
Content: ICE recorded 18 miscarriages in its detention centers during the first nine months of Trump’s second administration.Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenICE recorded 18 miscarriages in its detention centers during the first nine months of Trump’s second administration.Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesDeleted dataICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Revealed: ICE lost count of miscarriages, while detaining a record number of pregnant womenICE says it has no updated information on the number of miscarriages after 3 October 2025. Lawmakers, advocates and immigration attorneys have raised alarms that pregnant detainees are not receiving basic prenatal care and screeningsMaanvi Singh,Amy Qin,Will CraftandFlávio PessoaTue 15 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTShareICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers – placing them in detention centers where they say it can be exceedingly difficult to access medical care. At the same time, the agency appears to have lost count of how many suffered a miscarriage.Government documents obtained by the Guardian show that theTrump administrationplaced more pregnant immigrants in detention last fall and winter than at any time over the previous year.ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration, the documents show, but the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.Meanwhile, detained pregnant women report that they are struggling to access routine and emergency medical care. In interviews with the Guardian and in testimonies shared by their attorneys, women who miscarried or were hospitalized for pregnancy complications said they did not receive follow-up care, despite experiencing ongoing pain and symptoms.Anabell, 35, said she didn’t know she was pregnant until she was arrested and told to take a pregnancy test during a medical examination at the Campbell county detention center in Kentucky. A month later, she started bleeding heavily – soaking through a new menstrual pad every 30 minutes. Chained to a hospital bed at a local ER, she was told she wasn’t pregnant anymore.Laura, 21, was in the second trimester of a high-risk pregnancy when she was sent to the Dilley detention center in Texas. Now, still detained and approaching her third trimester,she’s experiencing persistent abdominal pain and bleeding – and says she hasn’t been allowed to see an OB-GYN.Angie, 26, learned she was pregnant a few weeks after she was booked into the Mesa Verde detention center in California. A few weeks after that, she woke up to large amounts of brown fluid excreting from her body. The medical staff at the detention center told her the miscarriage wasn’t her fault, she said.View image in fullscreenCopies of several meal stickers affixed to Anabell’s food throughout March, shared by her lawyer, show that ICE was offering a modified diet.Photograph: National Immigrant Justice CenterAlthough it is difficult to pinpoint the cause of a miscarriage, or to attribute a miscarriage solely to the conditions in detention, it is clear that detained women aren’t getting the medical care they need when they experience miscarriage symptoms, said Deborah Ottenheimer, an obstetrician-gynecologist and medical expert with Physicians for Human Rights.Women who miscarry and don’t receive proper treatment, including an ultrasound and other tests to ensure that their pregnancy tissue has been vacated from their body, could experience infection and other severe complications, Ottenheimer said.“These incarcerated women are not getting the prenatal visits that they’re supposed to get. They’re not getting high-risk prenatal visits if they need them. And if they do miscarry, the medical care they receive is minimal to none,” Ottenheimer said.Christina Davidson, the chief medical officer of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists,saidin July that “placing and holding pregnant patients in detention poses serious medical and mental health risks for both the pregnant patient and fetus”. Lapses in care at detention facilities, she added, could escalate treatable conditions into life-threatening emergencies.The Guardian filed a Freedom of Information Act request and then filed suit in collaboration with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press to obtain data on the number of pregnant people in ICE detention. Eventually,ICE shared records tracking the number of pregnant, postpartum and nursing women who were in detention from October 2024 through mid-January 2026, but only provided data on miscarriages up to 3 October 2025. In internal documents provided to the Guardian, the agency said it did not have miscarriage data for subsequent months because of a change in its medical accounting system.In response to follow up questions about its tracking practices after 3 October 2025, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, first said that the agency was tracking miscarriages in monthly reports. But later, the spokesperson confirmed what was in its internal documents – it does not have data on miscarriages from October 2025 through June 2026.DHS has never before acknowledged that it had lost count of miscarriages – not even when US senators asked the agency for the data.It is convenient for the administration that ICE cannot report how many women in its custody had miscarriages, said Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-chief executive of Raíces, a Texas-based humanitarian aid and immigration services non-profit. “When you don’t track something of that magnitude, then you don’t have to be confronted with the reality of what your policies have yielded.”Bar charts showing the increase of pregnant people in detention and miscarriages in detention, since January 2026To Anabell – an asylum seeker from Nicaragua who has birthed three children and miscarried once before – hardly anything about her last pregnancy had gone as normal.She was wondering why her period hadn’t come yet when she turned up for her mandated ICE check-in appointment on 25 February, she said. The visit went as normal until she was about to leave and an officer told her she couldn’t.The next few hours were a blur. She was taken to the Campbell county detention center in Newport, Kentucky. She underwent a medical examination, and was given one pregnancy test. Then another test. They both came back positive. “It was a surprise,” she said, speaking from the detention center on the phone. “All I could do was cry.”She wasn’t given a blood test to confirm a healthy pregnancy or prenatal vitamins, she said. Nor was she scheduled for an ultrasound. She did receive a special meal, labeled with a sticker that read: “Medical Diet - Pregnancy High Protein w/ PM Snack.” Usually, this meant an extra peanut butter sandwich and a small carton of milk.Over the next weeks, she was often nauseous and could hardly eat or sleep. She’d wake up to the cries and screams of the other detainees, or to the sound of officers yelling.About a month after she was arrested, she began to bleed – first a little, then a lot. “I told them I need to see a doctor,” she said, but an officer told her she’d have to wait. In an emergency medical request, she wrote, in Spanish: “This is URGENT, please. I am pregnant and have been bleeding since yesterday … I am scared for the baby.”Fellow detainees noticed she looked unnaturally pale and tried to get her help as well, she said. A day later, she was rushed to the ER. Shackled to a hospital bed and under the watch of three immigration officers, she was told she wasn’t pregnant anymore through a Spanish interpreter on the phone.ICE has repeatedly declined to release Anabell’s medical records to her and her lawyer. She didn’t even know which hospital she had been taken to, so her lawyer hunted down her hospital record by calling nearby medical facilities. The doctor’s notes said her pregnancy hormone levels were low, suggesting that she may have lost her pregnancy even before she started bleeding heavily.Still at Campbell, Anabell has continued to bleed, vomit and lose her hair in chunks. She has lost about 30lbs, and her skin is tender with rashes, she said. In hospital records she shared with the Guardian, the ER doctor wrote that she should return to the hospital if she experiences any new symptoms and that she should receive follow-up care at a women’s health clinic – but the medics at Campbell haven’t offered any check-ups.“I don’t know what is going to happen to me,” she said.Anabell said she met two other pregnant women in detention – including another who seemingly miscarried.The data ICE released to the Guardian shows that the agency has been increasingly detaining pregnant people sinceDonald Trumptook office in January 2025. Amid high-profile, militarized immigration raids in Minneapolis, Chicago and other cities last autumn and winter – ICE held more pregnant individuals in detention than at any time over the previous year, according to the agency’s records. In October, there were at least 87 pregnant women and adolescents in detention and in November, there were 101.Most women of reproductive age who enter immigration detention receive pregnancy tests during an initial medical assessment, but not all of them do. Some detained women have said they were unable to access pregnancy tests, so ICE’s numbers could be an undercount.Records from ICE show that at least 18 women miscarried while in custody from January 2025 through September 2025. This is also very likely an undercount, according to experts on healthcare within the immigration system. Some women who experience miscarriages, especially early in pregnancy, don’t notice significant physical symptoms and therefore don’t seek or receive emergency medical care – so their pregnancy loss may not be tracked in ICE’s records.There are no updated data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025, ICE noted in internal agency documents, because the agency had ended its contract with the Veterans Affairs Financial Services Center (VA-FSC), which had been handling medical billing for the agency.Acentra Health, a private Virginia-based company, was contracted to replace the VA-FSC starting in October 2025 – but ICE’s medical claims processing has been delayedfor months.Immigration attorneys and former DHS officials told the Guardian it was odd that ICE was only keeping track of miscarriages via its medical billing provider.Chart showing the number of recorded miscarriages at five ICE detention/processing centers.Federal policy, outlined in a 2021 directive, instructs ICE to wholly avoid detaining pregnant, postpartum and nursing immigrants “unless release is prohibited by law or exceptional circumstances exist”. If ICE does detain a pregnant individual, the directive obligates officers to consistently monitor and document their health. Agents or contractors at detention centers are to send monthly updates on these detainees to the executive associate director of enforcement and removal operations. The ICE health service corps, which oversees healthcare in detention, is to continuously evaluate whether it is medically advisable to keep them detained.“In the very limited circumstances in which detention is necessary and appropriate, ICE must monitor individuals known to be pregnant, postpartum, or nursing detained in ICE custody for general health and wellbeing, including regular custody and medical reevaluation, to ensure appropriate pre- and/or postnatal and other medical and mental health care,” the directive states.A spokesperson for DHS said the agency is still adhering to the directive. “The 2021 directive is still in place,” said spokesperson Chandler Rebel. “Pregnant women receive regular prenatal visits, mental health services, nutritional support, and accommodations aligned with community standards of care.” He did not engage with the Guardian’s questions about reports that women were not receiving essential prenatal, postpartum and miscarriage care.Acentra did not respond directly to questions about whether it was keeping track of miscarriages on behalf of ICE. Instead, it directed the Guardian to a statement clarifying that there were delays in implementing ICE’s new claims processing due to government shutdowns.Court records as well as interviews with US congress members, immigration attorneys and pregnant detainees indicate that the administration has all but abandoned adherence to the directive.The Guardian reviewed case details of eight pregnant women and teens who complained of medical neglect at the Dilley detention center in Texas – the country’s only ICE facility that holds families as well as single adults. Several of them alleged that language barriers made it difficult to access medical care. One woman who was four months pregnant stopped trusting the medical staff after a nurse shouted at her because she couldn’t speak English, according to Raíces. A woman who was pregnant with severe anemia and asthma was unable to get prescribed treatment. A woman who was six months pregnant with a high viral load of hepatitis B was unable to access the antiviral medications she needed to lower the risk of transmitting the infection to her baby.View image in fullscreenA protest against ICE detaining five-year-old Liam Ramos, on 28 January 2026 in Dilley, Texas.Photograph: Joel Angel Juarez/Getty ImagesLaura, the 21-year-old who remains detained at Dilley along with her two-year-old son, said she has a history of miscarriages. Two days before she was detained at a mandated ICE appointment, she had gone to the ER with symptoms of miscarriage and was diagnosed with a high-risk obstetric condition. After arriving at Dilley, a physician at the facility evaluated her and told her her condition requires a specialist. “Despite this clinical determination, facility administration has failed to approve or schedule the consultation for me,” she stated in a legal declaration that Raíces shared with the Guardian.She and her son should never have been detained in the first place, said Al-Juburi of Raíces. She was certified for a special visa for the victims of crime after a stray bullet struck her and her son last year.The 2021 directive instructs ICE to avoid detaining pregnant people “except in exceptional circumstances”. But in more than a dozen cases reviewed by the Guardian, attorneys said they did not receive any clear explanation from ICE officers or from the DHS as to how they met the criteria of “exceptional circumstances”. Many were asylum-seekers with scheduled immigration hearings, and dutifully attended mandated ICE appointments – showing that they posed no flight risk.“I have yet to encounter a pregnant or postpartum person who I believe meets the definition of extraordinary circumstances, as it’s used in other areas of the law,” said Sarah Decker, a senior attorney at the Robert and Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. Many of her clients are detained at the South Louisiana processing center in Basile, an all-women detention center with the highest number of pregnant detainees in the county, according to ICE data.Decker also raised doubts that ICE was unaware of how many women in its custody had experienced pregnancy complications or miscarried.“Many of the pregnant women that we’ve met at Basile have told us that they disclosed their pregnancy to ICE officers, that they had to advocate for access to prenatal care and access to a gynecologist, that they needed emergency care for complications,” she said. “So ICE is clearly aware and I think their desire to kind of obfuscate the access that people have to this data is intended to cover up the level of life-threatening medical neglect that’s happening in these facilities.”The Guardian is not using full names for the pregnant women in this story to protect their privacy and safety.Quick GuideHow the Guardian reported on the conditions of pregnant women in ICE detentionShowOur findings are based on interviews with pregnant people in immigration detention, lawyers and medical professionals, as well as data and documents released to the Guardian through a public records lawsuit with the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press.The Guardian filed a records request with ICE for data and documents on all pregnant, postpartum and nursing women in immigration detention. In response to our lawsuit, the government released spreadsheets of the number of pregnant and nursing women per facility through January 2026 and the number of miscarriages per facility per month through September 2025. The documents with information on miscarriages released to the Guardian said that ICE had no updated data after 3 October 2025.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.

title: Ministers vow sweeping NHS changes after ‘devastating’ report on Lucy Letby hospital | Lucy Letby | The Guardian
description: Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurse
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurse
Content: Screen grab taken from body-worn camera footage issued by Cheshire constabulary of the arrest of Lucy Letby on 3 July 2018.Photograph: Cheshire Constabulary/PAView image in fullscreenScreen grab taken from body-worn camera footage issued by Cheshire constabulary of the arrest of Lucy Letby on 3 July 2018.Photograph: Cheshire Constabulary/PALucy LetbyMinisters vow sweeping NHS changes after ‘devastating’ report on Lucy Letby hospitalLady Justice Thirlwall’s report concludes three babies might have survived if hospital had acted on concerns about nurseJosh HallidayNorth of England editorTue 15 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters have promised sweeping changes to the NHS after a “devastating” official review concluded that three babies might have survived if hospital bosses and doctors had acted on concerns about the nurseLucy Letby.A public inquiry found a “complete failure” to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.In a series of findings, the inquiry chair, Lady Justice Thirlwall, said two newborn twins would not have died and five others would not have been harmed if Letby had been removed from the unit sooner.Thirlwall said a third baby who died, a two-month-old girl, and two others who suffered unexplained collapses might have been protected if a doctor had detected an earlier insulin poisoning on the unit. One of those infants, now aged 11, suffered a lifelong brain injury and needs 24-hour care.Yvette Cooper,the health secretary, said she was “profoundly sorry” for the “devastating” failures revealed in the report, telling MPs: “This must be a turning point for theNHS.” She said she had asked officials to urgently take forward plans for “cot cam” monitors for neonatal units in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation.However, Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald, told the Guardian the government had “moved with too much haste” and acted before the outcome of her challenge to her convictions was known.Thirlwall report: what did it say about Lucy Letby case and what does it recommend?Read moreLetby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life prison terms after being convicted of the murder of seven babies and attempted murder of seven other newborns at the hospital in the year to June 2016.The former neonatal nurse is fighting to overturn her convictions, which have been described by the senior Conservative MP David Davis as a “clear miscarriage of justice”.The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which investigates potential miscarriages of justice, is reviewing a dossier of evidence submitted by experts on her behalf before deciding whether to refer the case back to the court of appeal, which has twice rejected her legal challenges.Deliveringher reportat Liverpool town hall on Tuesday, where families of some of the babies had gathered, Thirlwall said: “My report describes dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding.“There was a complete failure to protect babies on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. This was because no one seems to have understood that safeguarding action is required when a member of staff is suspected of causing deliberate harm and does not require colleagues to be sure of guilt.”View image in fullscreenBosses at the Countess of Chester hospital did not contact police until nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths.Photograph: Brian Hickey/AlamyFamilies of the babies who died or were injured said the report painted a “damning picture of what happens when concerns over patient safety are not listened to and acted on”.Tamlin Bolton, a solicitor at Irwin Mitchell representing seven of the families, urged ministers and the NHS to act on the report’s recommendations, saying: “It cannot be the end of the matter.”Richard Scorer, of the law firm Slater and Gordon, which represents three of the families, said: “Far too often public inquiry recommendations are left to gather dust. This cannot be allowed to happen again.”In her 822-page report, Thirlwall said it was “inexcusable” that successive governments had failed to act on reforms proposed by other public inquiries into NHS scandals stretching back 30 years.13:01Damning Lucy Letby inquiry finds ‘complete failure to protect babies’ - The LatestThirlwall is said to believe that “cot cams” – allowing parents to monitor their newborn around-the-clock – could have prevented all seven of the deaths as medics would know they were being monitored.Samantha Dixon, the Labour MP for Chester North and Neston, whose constituency includes the hospital, said the inquiry revealed a “truly appalling state of affairs” that needed “the firmest response possible from government”.Ministers are working on the urgent introduction of other CCTV in hospital neonatal units as well as cot cams, in line with Thirlwall’s recommendation, and stricter rules on the storage of insulin.Hospital executives who are found to have failed in their responsibilities will be prevented from working again in the NHS under new regulation to stop managers being transferred to another part of the country.And they will roll out a single tracker to monitor the delivery of recommendations made by inquiries into maternity and neonatal scandals.View image in fullscreenLucy Letby’s lawyer, Mark McDonald, said the government had ‘moved with too much haste’.Photograph: Marissa Davison/ReutersMcDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “The government has moved with too much haste. They have made the same mistake as Thirlwall not to pause and wait for the new evidence to be considered.”However, others said the inquiry’s findings and recommendations must be taken seriously irrespective of Letby’s legal challenge.Dr Tom Dolphin, the chair of the British Medical Association, said it stemmed from “system reform” within the NHS and that it required “major reforms” to the culture of the health service.Leaders of NHS trusts and other bodies said the inquiry had shone a light on the “upheaval caused by successive reorganisations, the complex regulatory landscape, staff shortages, unacceptable ‘revolving door’ appointments and the inadequacies of underfunded NHS IT systems”.Letby was first linked to baby deaths in June 2015. That month, three newborns died in unexplained circumstances within two weeks – the number usually expected on the neonatal unit in a year.Senior doctors became concerned about Letby’s connection to the unusual rise in deaths and serious incidents over the following months and raised their fears with executives. However, the inquiry found that senior nurses effectively dismissed the concerns about Letby and that there was a “prolonged delay” in calling the police.Rather than being believed, Thirlwall said, clinicians were themselves made the subject of investigation in a “deplorable” grievance process brought by Letby when she was finally removed from the neonatal unit in July 2016.Parents were “kept in the dark” for years about what happened to their babies and the concerns they may have been deliberately harmed, the inquiry found. Thirlwall described their treatment as “reprehensible”.The inquiry chair accused hospital executives of overseeing “an exercise in spin” by downplaying the rise in deaths to the board of directors. Their failure to contact police before April 2017 – nearly two years after the unexplained increase in deaths – suggested that protecting the hospital’s reputation was “prized more highly” than the doctors’ concerns, she found.View image in fullscreenThe Thirlwall inquiry’s 822-page report was published on Tuesday.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesThree hospital executives, who have not been named, were arrested last year on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter. Cheshire police said its investigation into the former bosses, and a parallel investigation into corporate manslaughter, was ongoing.Thirlwall, a court of appeal judge, said it was “clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier”. She said the precise number of deaths that might have been prevented would never be known for sure.However, the inquiry concluded that if Letby had been removed from duties in October 2015 – when senior managers were made aware of the concerns – then the twin boys known as babies O and P would not have died in June 2016 and five further babies would not have suffered harm.Thirlwall said it was possible that three newborns would not have died and seven others would have been protected if a senior doctor had not “disregarded” an insulin result for a week-old baby boy in August 2015, whom Letby was later convicted of attempting to murder by poisoning him.Explore more on these topicsLucy LetbyNursingHospitalsHealthNHSDoctorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Search under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playground | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss
Content: Noah is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey.Photograph: Family Handout/Suffolk Police/PAView image in fullscreenNoah is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey.Photograph: Family Handout/Suffolk Police/PASuffolkSearch under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playgroundMore than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing lossYassin El-MouddenTue 15 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a three-year-old boy who went missing on Tuesday during a visit to a playground near the Suffolk-Essex border.The boy, named Noah, was last seen at 3pm in Merriam Close in Brantham, near Manningtree, before being separated from a relative. Officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah was reported to have run down an alleyway near the playground towards a housing estate.He is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey. Police also confirmed that Noah is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss.The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined in the search efforts by Tuesday evening and that train services between Manningtree and Ipswich were running at reduced speed while searches continued.Police have cordoned off the alleyway and there were reports of door-to-door inquiries in the area.A spokesperson for Suffolk constabulary said late on Tuesday: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches. Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”A coastguard helicopter was also seen circling the village, which is near the estuary of the River Stour, and there were reports of sightings of drones flying overhead.Anyone who believes that they have seen Noah is being asked tocontact Suffolk police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.Explore more on these topicsSuffolknewsShareReuse this content

title: Thirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigation | Metropolitan police | The Guardian
description: PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station
Content: Panorama’s investigation followed seven months of undercover filming.Photograph: Mark Thomas/AlamyView image in fullscreenPanorama’s investigation followed seven months of undercover filming.Photograph: Mark Thomas/AlamyMetropolitan policeThirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigationPC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police stationYassin El-MouddenTue 15 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 13th servingMetropolitan policeofficer has been dismissed in relation to an undercover BBC investigation into misogyny and racism at Charing Cross police station.PC Mason O’Connor was found to have committed discreditable conduct and breached professional behaviour standards, linked to a comment he made towards a female colleague, according to the Met.ThePanorama investigation aired in October 2025and followed seven months of undercover filming. It included footage of officers calling for immigrants to be shot and boasting about using violence against suspects.On Tuesday, a disciplinary panel heard that O’Connor told a female colleague in October 2024 that he “hope[d] you get raped on your way to Waterloo”, while he was off-duty in a pub.The incident was reported as part of a witness appeal and “proactive wider investigation” launched after the broadcast of the Panorama film.At the time, the Met police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said the footage was “vile to watch” and featured “incontrovertible evidence” that would enable the fast-tracking of misconduct hearings.O’Connor’s sacking comes a few weeks after the dismissal of PC Lloyd Hunter, who was found to have made comments that trivialised the use of force and suggested that he would enjoy using force against members of the public. Hunter also said he “hated” homeless people.Commander Simon Messinger, from the Met’s professionalism department, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes.“I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation.“We continue to support the ongoing IOPC [Independent Office forPoliceConduct] investigation.”The IOPC confirmed that investigations were continuing against 15 other officers or police staff and that misconduct had been identified from footage provided by theBBCwhich had not been included in the Panorama broadcast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA gross misconduct hearing is scheduled for later this month over comments made by a detention officer regarding the treatment of people being held in police custody.Amanda Rowe, the IOPC’s director of engagement, said: “This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated, and the sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter.”Both O’Connor and Hunter will be barred from rejoining the police force.Explore more on these topicsMetropolitan policeBBCLondonPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Britons of all ethnicities feel racial inequality is worsening, study shows | Race | The Guardian
description: Nearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Nearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year
Content: The British Future poll found that racial or nationality prejudice was most common in public spaces.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe British Future poll found that racial or nationality prejudice was most common in public spaces.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersRaceBritons of all ethnicities feel racial inequality is worsening, study showsNearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past yearGeneva AbdulTue 15 Sep 2026 18.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more common, according to a thinktank study.The report by British Future has found that people across ethnic groups believe racial equality is worsening in Britain. One in six people are from minority ethnic backgrounds.“Most ethnic minorities in Britain feel there was a positive change against racism in our lifetimes yet now fear that progress being reversed,” said the thinktank’s director, Sunder Katwala.The research found nearly half of ethnic minority respondents had faced racial or nationality prejudice over the past year, with the problem notably higher among those aged 18 to 24. Prejudice was most often reported in public spaces, followed by on social media and in the workplace.The research found that 62% of ethnic minority Britons saw racial inequality as a serious problem, a view supported by 57% of the white population.White respondents were less likely to see structural barriers in education, work and public services and more likely to believe minority communities received equal or preferential treatment.The report, part of a three-year study funded by theNuffield Foundation, found a growing polarisation over perceptions that minorities received preferential treatment.Among white respondents, 37% felt ethnic minorities were treated better than white British people, while 33% disagreed. Among ethnic minorities, 23% agreed and 48% disagreed.The report found divisions by age and politics were deeper than those relating to ethnicity. “In both the white and ethnic minority surveys, gaps between rich and poor are seen as the most important divide impacting the UK,” the report said.The research was driven by two online surveys of 2,009 white adults and 3,014 ethnic minority adults between 30 March and 29 April. It was supplemented by information from 12 focus groups.The study noted a difference within ethnic minority attitudes, finding Black respondents were frequently more positive about the UK making progress on racial equality. By contrast, Bangladeshi and Pakistani heritage respondents were found to be more pessimistic, with heightened anxiety seemingly linked to the 2024 riots.“Women, particularly ethnic minority women, are also more pessimistic than men throughout,” the report said.The study found that ethnic minority Britons would like to see more effort to promote equal pay and tackle disparities in essential services and unequal treatment in media reporting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis was brought into “sharp focus”, the report said, by the intense media scrutiny onJason Arday, a Cambridge University professor who died at his London home after allegations of plagiarism.The report, which criticised successive governments for having “rarely held” a sustained focus on race, laid out 10 recommendations for the government, including challenging zero-sum thinking, supporting grassroots activities and pushing the watchdog Ofcom on compliance against online racism.Overall, it found low trust among political parties. While the Green party and Labour led narrowly in terms of treating people of different backgrounds fairly (+15 and +13 in net trust scores respectively), Reform UK had a net score of -31 (16% trust/47% distrust).Katwala said leaders should “counter the sense of a zero-sum contest over race equality: that fairness for ethnic minorities comes at the expense of the white majority, or vice versa”.He added: “The antidote to that is to pursue a broad and proactive fairness agenda – with the confidence and tools to tackle racism and discrimination where it is most needed.”Explore more on these topicsRaceInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers | Carers | The Guardian
description: More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says
Content: The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianCarersAbout 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carersMore than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK saysPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorTue 15 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they try to balance their vulnerable relatives’ growing care needs with declining access to state-funded social care services.Research estimates that more than a million people have left the workplace to look after ageing, ill and disabled loved ones in the past two years, highlighting the social challenges caused by UK’s rapidly changing demographic profile.Unpaid caring is now a “widespread social and economic reality” for UK households, it says, with one in five employees – equivalent to 6.7 million people – facing career and financial sacrifices as they juggle paid work and care for family or friends.Over a fifth of those surveyed (22%) had reduced their job hours to juggle work and care, with over a third (34%) working less than eight hours a week. Around one in 10 carers said they had turned down promotions or taken on lower-paid roles to stay in work.Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy atCarersUK, said: “These figures represent real people who have had to make difficult decisions about their careers, their financial security and their futures due to the pressures of balancing work and care.”Carers UK, which published the report, called on government to strengthen employment rights for unpaid carers, including introducing a statutory entitlement to 10 days’ annual paid carer’s leave for employees.It urged Louise Casey’s independentreview of adult social care, expected to report in the next few months, to recommend policy changes putting carers at the centre of a reformed system, by making it easier for carers to combine work and unpaid care.Midwife Jacqui Hylton, aged 58, gave up her 30-year NHS career to become a full-time carer two years ago when her then 86-year-old mother Winnie’s health took a serious turn for the worse.Hylton moved from Hertfordshire to Leeds to live with Winnie and become her full-time carer. But she is frustrated that her professional skills are going to waste when the NHS faces a midwife shortage.Caring will make it harder for her to return to midwifery as she is unable to work the required number of hours a year to maintain her professional accreditation. Enhanced respite allowance would potentially enable her to keep her hand in at work.“I don’t regret caring for my mum. But financially I’m worse off, my pension will be less than it should have been. It’s lonely at times and its extremely hard work – harder than working in the NHS,” she said.The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Around one in five (20%) of UK adults, equivalent to 11 million people, report unpaid care duties.As well as affecting carers’ finances, careers and wellbeing, the report estimates the doubling in the number of people quitting paid work to care over the past seven years comes at an annual £37bn economic cost to the UK.A government spokesperson said: “Unpaid carers make an extraordinary contribution to families, our communities and the economy, and I would like to personally thank Carers UK for their invaluable work in supporting unpaid carers and championing the issues they face every day.“We want to ensure there are good jobs for carers who want to work alongside managing their caring responsibilities. This is why we are exploring how best to support unpaid carers through our review of employment rights.”Explore more on these topicsCarersnewsShareReuse this content

title: All supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Four openers and live band for Sheeran’s tour depart after removal of Macklemore over ‘free Palestine’ comments
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Four openers and live band for Sheeran’s tour depart after removal of Macklemore over ‘free Palestine’ comments
Content: Finneas, pictured in Los Angeles on 8 April, withdrew from Sheeran’s tour on Tuesday.Photograph: Jordan Strauss/APView image in fullscreenFinneas, pictured in Los Angeles on 8 April, withdrew from Sheeran’s tour on Tuesday.Photograph: Jordan Strauss/APEd SheeranAll supporting acts withdraw from Ed Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with MacklemoreFour openers and live band for Sheeran’s tour depart after removal of Macklemore over ‘free Palestine’ commentsAdrian HortonTue 15 Sep 2026 17.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll four supporting acts for upcoming dates ofEd Sheeran’s Loop tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opening actMacklemore, as backlash grows against his removal from the tour over onstage comments in support ofPalestine.Finneas, the singer who was scheduled to open for Sheeran on six South American dates in November, withdrew from the tour on Tuesday afternoon, hours after Sheeran posted his own lengthy statement to Instagramexplaining pressurefrom venue owners toremove Macklemorefor pro-Palestine comments made during two shows at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.In a two-minute speech on 4 September, theGrammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, along with the words “free Palestine”. The remark prompted apetitioncalling for Macklemore’s removal from the tour from the Israeli American Council and the opposition of some venue owners – including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of theNew England Patriotsand a prominent donor to Israel.“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneaswroteon social media. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran.
