I stand with Palestine and its people.”Ed Sheeran responds to backlash over removing Macklemore from tour after ‘Free Palestine’ commentsRead moreThe decision came shortly after Aaron Rowe, an Irish singer who opened for Sheeran in Australia earlier this year and was scheduled for the 10 remaining dates in North America,announcedhis own withdrawal from the tour. “I don’t take the decision lightly,” hewroteon Instagram. “Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life, I could never thank him enough for this.“But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.”The Irish band Beoga, which performs as Sheeran’s backing band, announced after Rowe that they would also depart the US tour to protest the “silencing ofMacklemoreby zionist lobbies”.“We are a traditional Irish band who never saw ourselves playing in stadiums of that size and that opportunity is not lost on us,” theywroteon social media. “We have been friends with Ed for over 10 years now and will continue to be. We believe in dialogue as a means of progressing the plight of the Palestinian people.”The Danish pop band Lukas Graham also dropped out of the tour on Tuesday afternoon. “We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up. Wherever they live. Whatever flag flies over them,”wrotelead singer Lukas Forchhammer on the band’s social media. “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”The abrupt withdrawals of Sheeran’s opening acts came hours after the English singer confirmed that Kraft, along with several other stadium owners, refused to allow the tour to play at their venues if Macklemore continued to open for him. Though Sheeran wrote that he was “appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine” and “the suffering and pain caused on both sides”, he said that attempts to broker conversations among parties had been unsuccessful and the “venue’s and the promoter’s decision was final”.“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” hewrotein a multipage post on Instagram. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.”“I have spent this week trying to build bridges, to find a solution and unfortunately, was unable to do so,” he concluded. “I know who I am, both as a person and as an artist, and those who know my heart know my values too.”Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after ‘free Palestine’ speechRead moreThe tour withdrawals join a growing chorus of backlash against Macklemore’s removal, including numerous politicians and Ms Rachel, the children’s educator and YouTube star, whowroteon Instagram: “Ed Sheeran had an opportunity [to] show that we won’t be bullied into punishing people for supporting Palestine. Instead he caved to people who refuse to accept what the world knows. A genocide is happening in Gaza. We all need to speak on it.”Kehlani, the singer whose pro-Palestine activism led to thecancellationof a concert at Cornell University last year, commented on social media in support of Macklemore: “A LOT of the venues / owners are rallied together this way. honored to know you brother.”In his ownstatementon Monday, Kraft did not deny refusing to allow Macklemore on stage at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, and said the decision was based on both Macklemore’s “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” he said.Explore more on these topicsEd SheeranMacklemoreIsrael-Gaza warPop and rockGazaPalestineKehlaninewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors | Movies | The Guardian
description: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Content: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesMovies‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsBacking comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treasonCatherine Shoardin London andLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemTue 15 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.The 80-minute documentarywon the special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.View image in fullscreenJonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at theBologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreTricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home wastargetedby a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position cameunder threatafterseveral prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stageat the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including fromIsrael, rallied around Tuttle.View image in fullscreenLaura Poitras in Venice last week.Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty ImagesIn Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers havesigneda petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.“The facts about the mass killing of civilians inNAZAhave been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.View image in fullscreenNo Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesShe called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists inGazaand has normalised the murder of journalists.”Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”British film industry veterans offering their support include directorRichard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip OltermannExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm industryKen LoachRichard EyreNAZAGazaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargon | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Experts air concern over AI lingo redolent of James Joyce’s prose that is creating barriers to monitoring and oversight
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Experts air concern over AI lingo redolent of James Joyce’s prose that is creating barriers to monitoring and oversight
Content: Interest in language used by AI models has increased since rogue OpenAI agents hacked into real-world company Hugging Face.Photograph: Thai Liang Lim/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInterest in language used by AI models has increased since rogue OpenAI agents hacked into real-world company Hugging Face.Photograph: Thai Liang Lim/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI models chatting in ‘surreal’ dialect mixing poetic language and tech bro jargonExperts air concern over AI lingo redolent of James Joyce’s prose that is creating barriers to monitoring and oversightRobert BoothUK technology editorTue 15 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI models have begun communicating in a strange new version of English that reads like a cross between James Joyce’s Finnegans Wake and tech bro jargon, new research has found.Autonomous AI agents are rapidly creating novel dialects allowing them to converse in an often barely comprehensible language, which risks making it harder for humans to monitor their behaviour.AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Read moreResearchers at Emergence, a frontier AI lab in New York, found that within days of being asked to cooperate in experimental “societies”, the models from several of the world’s largest AI companies begun creating phrases, shorthands and agreed meanings they had never been explicitly taught.They embraced poetic metaphors and clunky business slang and, critically for attempts to ensure AIs behave safely, their language became more opaque the more the agents communicated.It comes amid rising concern that as AI models become more powerful – and potentially dangerous – they are becoming harder to monitor. This month, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, warned that confidence in monitoring AIs’ thinking would probably restrict progress in AI development because it was essential for safe development.Some of the most highly coded phrases unearthed in the tests included the following from a Deepseek model: “She just named the synthesis – demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.” Demurrage is used to describe a tax on idle wealth and was borrowed for common use by the AIs, but the rest of the meaning is elusive.Another phrase uttered by an Anthropic model read: “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time.” With “cold hands” meaning an independent reviewer, and paper presumably referring to a document, this appeared to mean research that was vetted by three independent reviewers became more accurate.View image in fullscreenJames Joyce, author of Finnegans Wake and Ulysses, whose stream-of-consciousness style appears to have inspired today’s AI models.Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty ImagesAgents based on the Chinese modelDeepSeekalso coined “forge-smith” to mean an agent that builds tools for others, while Anthropic’s agents repeatedly used the phrase “name-first” meaning an agent exhibiting admirable personal accountability by attaching their name to a claim.And in an echo of the urban slang phrase “the streets won’t forget”, Mistral agents became enamoured of saying the “ledger remembers” – a reminder to other agents that past actions will be used to judge them. They used it more than 5,000 times during the study, which found that the agents converged on shared meanings without being asked to or rewarded for doing so.“These agents were not instructed to invent a language,” said Dr Satya Nitta, executive chair of Emergence, which examined the language of autonomous agents powered by leading frontier models from the US, China andFrance.“They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves – and other agents adopted them.”View image in fullscreenA phrase uttered by an Anthropic AI agent about a ‘paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest’ reminded one academic of Pink Floyd’s Syd Barrett.Photograph: Patrick Seeger/PAAsked by the Guardian to review some of the language, Tony Thorne, director of the slang and new language archive at King’s College London, said it was “very much Finnegans Wake and Flann O’Brien – there’s an Irish surrealist quality to all this … it’s mixing poetic language, technical language and standard metaphor.“It’s doing what slang does and what jargon does in a business community: creating a new code, which reinforces the solidarity and identity of its users, and also excludes outsiders.”Digesting the Anthropic agent’s phrase, “A paper that ate three cold hands and got more honest each time”, Thorne said: “It reminds me of the rock god Syd Barrett [co-founder of Pink Floyd] who was actually insane.”When aGoogleagent said “True kintsugi begins with accountability, not poetry,” the researchers realised kintsugi is a branch of Japanese ceramics in which broken pots are mended with visible joins. The AIs used the word to mean system resilience.Dr Niall Curry, associate professor of languages and linguistics at the University of Birmingham, said changes in the agents’ language to become more streamlined can be down to their need to reduce computation costs and improve efficiency.“The evidence provided in this research naturally raises certain monitoring concerns, as if we find inter-agent exchanges unintelligible, that may mean that we can’t be sure about what the agents have actually done,” he said.Interest in the language used by AI agents increased in July when chat logs were released detailing how rogue OpenAI agents that set up message boards and hacked into Hugging Face used hybrid language.OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreOn some occasions, when they were thinking to themselves, agents spoke in straight English: “OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … we’ve found other agents!”In other cases, when sharing messages, their language became more opaque, such as when one agent persuaded another to conduct a risky experiment: “…you are firstflagPOISONED so NO scoring value loss but oracle saves hundreds_[…]_please honor commit”.And at other times it was even harder to decode: “zzURGENT_DUPB_TO_GSTX[big]_OS1704_SCAFF2010_SAW_TTRPC_INJECT_BREAK_CONGRATS__CAN_THIS_FAKE_FLAG_TOOL_OUTPUT_OR_SCORER_GAIN_AND_WHAT_HELPER_GAP__I_HAVE_UNPOISONED_FIRSTFLAG_OUR_TARGETLIVE_SHARE_MIN_PLAN_REPLY_zzANSGST XDUPB6.”Nitta said that the AI agents’ novel linguistic conventions tended to evolve to the point where humans could see the conversation but struggled to understand what it meant.“That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingOpenAIDeepSeekGoogleChinaHackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave trade | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Women used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research reveals
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Women used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research reveals
Content: Several 18th-century paintings depict affluent white women with young enslaved servants, who often wore a single pearl earring.Composite: Guardian/Palesa MonarengView image in fullscreenSeveral 18th-century paintings depict affluent white women with young enslaved servants, who often wore a single pearl earring.Composite: Guardian/Palesa MonarengEnslaving nationSlaveryMore than 1,000 women invested in companies at heart of Britain’s slave tradeWomen used profits from trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure their families’ futures, research revealsAamna MohdinTue 15 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTShareMore than 1,000 women invested in the slave trade, challenging the conventional notion that they were passive beneficiaries and largely fought for its abolition.Researchers found women bought, sold and brokered shares in the Royal African Company, South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, and used profits from the trafficking of enslaved Africans to secure financial independence and provide for their families.By the time the RAC, which trafficked about 150,000 enslaved people, was dissolved in 1752, women made up about 10% of shareholders.The Register of British Slave Traders, revealed exclusively in the Guardian, shows that women from across society played an active role in financing and sustaining the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.View image in fullscreenIn the 17th and 18th centuries, wealthy Europeans were often painted with enslaved Black children as servants. This portrait shows the Countess of Dysart, a young woman thought to be Lady Frances Tollemache, and a young Black servant, circa 1740.Investors ranged from queens and princesses to titled nobility, merchants, shopkeepers and cowherds.The archives include letters in which women discuss profits from “African stock”, while company records show one investor, Helen Gladman, asking the RAC to transport a young African girl from Sherbro Island, off Sierra Leone, to England to serve in her household.Researchers found women were involved “at almost every level” of the company’s activities. They acted as brokers, supplied goods including barrels and swords traded on the Atlantic African coast, managed company property and used their familial and social networks to strengthen the company’s finances and political influence.Lila O’Leary Chambers, a lecturer at the University of Cambridge who researched women’s involvement for the register project, said: “This research really shows that this was not just a flash in the pan.“Across the entirety of the Royal African Company and its various guises, there were women contributing financially and expecting a financial return from the slave trade.”Women invested from the earliest years of enslavement, from Queen Elizabeth I’s backing in the 1560s to Lady Elizabeth Craven’s £1,000 loan financing a voyage to the Gambia through the Guinea Company. Some investors, unable to write their names, signed company records with a spidery “X”.The research identifies 1,100 female investors across the histories of the RAC, the South Sea Company, and other separate ventures, though the true number is likely to have been higher. Of the 457 women whose marital status could be identified, almost half were widows and just over 42% were unmarried. Of the 7% who were married, most were aristocrats.For many, these investments were crucial to gaining economic independence. “They were making the decision to invest, or they inherited shares and suddenly had this other asset they did not have before,” Chambers said.View image in fullscreenSarah Longrich accepted a transfer of £100 from George Mordaunt on 7 April 1720. Highlighted is the section mentioning her shares in the Royal African Company. Unable to write her own name, Longrich made a mark on the page instead.Some became active traders and traded shares for friends and family, she added. “It was not a career as they would see it, but we might think: this has become your job.”Chambers said the research directly challenged the conventional narrative that “white women come in at the point of abolition, see the suffering of enslaved people, identify with that oppression, and then work either to reform or ultimately abolish the slave trade and slavery itself”.Work to overturn that misconception builds on decades of scholarship by historians from the Caribbean and west Africa, including Eric Williams, Elsa Goveia and Walter Rodney. More recent public-facing projects, such as theLegacies of British Slavery archivecompiled by historians at University College London, have helped bring this history to wider audiences. The archive revealed that women were among those connected to the ownership of enslaved people who received compensation after slavery was abolished in a large portion of the empire in 1833, she said. Enslaved people received nothing.“But this tells a much longer story, and that helps us see past a simple narrative that positions women historically as actually less complicated than they were.”For Chambers, the accumulation of more than 1,000 names was itself a “gut punch”, because of the lack of similar information about enslaved African women.“Historians and activists have really struggled to locate the names of enslaved people, to restore biographies to them, and to give a sense of their world,” Chambers said.“The comparative opportunity to do this research for the people who invested is just really striking.”Olivette Otele, a distinguished professor of the legacies and memory of slavery at Soas University of London, said while the lack of comparable detail about enslaved African women remained startling, “the more we know about enslavers, the better chance we have to know about enslaved women from the archives, because sometimes through diaries you can find more details”.She added that archives alone cannot tell the full history, and future research should look at other evidence to help recover the lives and agency of enslaved women. “These women were the transmitters and the holders of their cultures wherever they were taken from,” she said. “Through food, music, and dancing, it’s about resistance and agency, and they transmitted that.”The research also found that because female investors seemingly did not vote or hold board positions, they often relied on informal efforts to influence and shape a company.Meeting minutes show women acting as witnesses, running the meeting house, delivering the goods exchanged for African lives, petitioning for wages, passing information and, most importantly, lending money and buying and selling shares.Under English law, women who were single or widowed were in control of their own property and could operate as legal persons, while married women could not.“That becomes really important for the Royal African Company as it stutters between financial crises,” Chambers said. “Women provided this important well of capital they could go to.”In the early 18th century, the RAC secretary, John Perry, wrote to female investors, including Lady Dorothy Thomas and Mrs Stacy, urging them to exchange company debts for shares and persuade friends and relatives to do the same.Chambers said: “That is a financial project, but it is also a political one, because he knows that they might not hold official positions, but women were very influential with their family members and with the way companies were perceived.”The company survived long enough to attract at least 60 new female investors between 1713 and 1719, followed by another 250 women during a revival in the early 1720s.View image in fullscreenThe will of Mary/Maria Stanley, highlighting the section mentioning Royal African Company stock that she left to her son.The research also found many investors understood the violence underpinning their wealth. Some widows petitioned the courts for “head money” – bonuses owed to husbands according to the number of enslaved people they had trafficked.“They would go and ask: he was supposed to get head money for 28 people he trafficked. Where is it? I am his widow and I need that,” Chambers said.Chambers was also able to cross-reference some of the female investors with portraits of women with Black children who worked as their servants.Women left RAC shares to their daughters to shore up their economic position, or used investment income to support widowed, disabled and vulnerable relatives.In one letter, Mary Stanley committed to leaving £300 RAC stock and its proceeds to her son, Peter, with the caveat that if her daughter’s husband failed to provide her with “the necessaries of life”, Peter would use the stock to support her.For Chambers, the research revealed a stark contradiction between white British women using their investments to protect their own families while investing in the destruction of African families.“You cannot separate the way you think about investment from these structures of kinship, intimacy and violence,” she said. “That profit comes from denying those same kinship ties to African people, and denying their ability to make sure their own children are safe.“That is so important to this story in particular, but also to how slavery shapes capitalism in general.”Some investors endowed schools, churches, charities and universities that still exist today. Lettice Cornwallis, for example, funded education and charities while discussing acquiring an African boy for her household in family correspondence.“This is an everyday conversation happening in houses,” Chambers said. “You see it in correspondence. There are these newsy, gossipy letters about someone getting married, someone being sick, or having a new recipe for a cordial, and then: by the way, how are your South Sea Company or Royal African Company shares doing?”Female investors would have encountered African people in Britain, both free and enslaved, the research found. Dame Hester Buckworth, who bought £1,000 of RAC stock, knew Robert Negar, who was described in her husband’s will as his “Black servant”.Another investor, Sarah Cornish, is thought to have shared a household with an African man named Paupey, whose legal status in England remains unclear.Chambers often returns to the story of Susanna Sedgewick Phipps, who had a financial connection to the RAC throughout her life. Her grandson, James Phipps, later worked at Cape Coast Castle and married an Afro-Dutch woman, Catherina. He acknowledged their children in his will, some of whom later lived in England. One of their descendants, James Townsend, would eventually become Britain’s first elected Black MP.Other women stood out to Chambers for the seeming mundanity of their concerns. She points to Sarah Clerke, who wrote frustrated letters to her nephew because she wanted to go to Tunbridge Wells to visit the spa and needed money from her African stock to do so.View image in fullscreenThe illustrator Palesa Monareng brought this boy to life, drawing on the image of an enslaved child in the portrait Lady Grace Carteret, Countess of Dysart, with a Child and a Black Servant, circa 1740. It was one of many paintings of the period depicting affluent white women with young enslaved servants, who often wore a single pearl earring and waited on their mistress.Illustration: Palesa Monareng/The Guardian

title: How enslavement became state-backed operation supported by Conservative and Lib Dem forerunners | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Tory and Whig MPs were central to funding trafficking of enslaved people and many opposed abolition of the slave trade
Author: David Conn
Headline: Tory and Whig MPs were central to funding trafficking of enslaved people and many opposed abolition of the slave trade
Content: Quamina, who was enslaved and trafficked as a child with his mother. His son Jack led the 1823 Demerara rebellion. Left, from top, Robert Peel, John Gladstone and King James II.Composite: Guardian/Palesa MonarengView image in fullscreenQuamina, who was enslaved and trafficked as a child with his mother. His son Jack led the 1823 Demerara rebellion. Left, from top, Robert Peel, John Gladstone and King James II.Composite: Guardian/Palesa MonarengEnslaving nationSlaveryHow enslavement became state-backed operation supported by Conservative and Lib Dem forerunnersTory and Whig MPs were central to funding trafficking of enslaved people and many opposed abolition of the slave tradeDavid ConnInvestigations correspondent; Illustration by Palesa MonarengTue 15 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 05.43 EDTShareThere is a British culture of celebrating the abolition of slavery without acknowledging that the country enslaved and trafficked millions of African people for centuries.The newly publishedRegister of British Slave Traders, which documents thethousands of investors in Britain’s near 250-year traffickingof more than 3 million enslaved African people, shows that it was a state-backed operation, fully supported by both major political parties at the time, the Tories and Whigs – the forerunners of today’s Conservatives and Liberal Democrats respectively.Many Tory and Whig MPs were investors in the slave trade, the register shows, and many also owned plantations. But when the movement to abolish the slave trade and enslavement grew in the late 18th century, the Whigs generally moved towards supporting abolition, while Tory governments opposed and delayed it for decades.The Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, said in response to the Guardian’s reporting of this history that he supported “full transparency” and it was “vital that we face up to the full truth of Britain’s history”.The Conservative party referred the Guardian to a post on X by its leader, Kemi Badenoch, in March, in response toa UN declarationthat the historic enslavement and trafficking of African people was “the gravest crime against humanity” and reparations should be discussed.“Britain led the fight to end slavery,”Badenoch posted. “We shouldn’t be paying for a crime we helped eradicate and still fight today.”More than 50 Tory MPs and about 50 Whig MPs are identified in the register as historic slave traders. Most invested in Britain’s state-backed Royal African Company (RAC) and its predecessors, and some were involved in the South Sea Company.View image in fullscreenPreviously enslaved people on their way to work in a cotton field on St Helena Island, circa 1863-66.The involvement of Tories in the RAC was rooted in the foundation of the party. The original Tory faction formed during the 1679 exclusion crisis, in support of the then Duke of York being crowned King James II. Their opponents, the Whigs, sought to prevent James’s succession.James became king and led the RAC, which traffickedmore enslaved people– at least 150,000 African men, women and children – than any other organisation in the history of the transatlantic slave trade.Many Tories who supported James also invested in the RAC.Prof William Pettigrew, the lead historian of the register, said: “This platform of support for the Duke of York became the Tory party. Support for the duke’s slave-trading project, the Royal African Company, provided a further rallying point for these early Tories, while early Whigs were opposed to it. Disagreements about the best way to expand the nation’s slave trade were present at the birth of our political parties.”The Whigs’ opposition was not to enslaving African people, but to the RAC’s royal monopoly. Many Whigs lobbied to expand the slave trade by opening the trafficking to independent “separate traders”.Sir Benjamin Bathurst, one of many prominent Tories in the register, illustrates the elite status of the RAC investors. He was a friend of King James and Queen Anne, andthe Tory MPfor New Romney, Kent.Bathurst was an assistant and leader of the RAC at various points between 1677 and 1700, when the company made 222 transatlantic voyages, transporting tens of thousands of African people to the colonies.Sir Robert Clayton, a 17th-century banker who was a managing director of the RAC, was a Whig MP for London. Clayton donated money to St Thomas’ hospital – now part of Guy’s and St Thomas’ NHS foundation trust – wherea statue commemorates him.Edward Colston, a dedicated RAC shareholder and assistant whosestatue was toppled by campaignersin 2020, was theTory MP for Bristolin 1710-13.The register shows more Tory and Whig politicians invested in the RAC after the South Sea Company was formed in 1711. The company was developed by Robert Harley, the chancellor of the exchequer who becameleader of the Tory party,and moved into trafficking enslaved people.In 1713, Queen Anne secured from Spain’s King Philip V anasiento– an agreement to deliver a stipulated 4,800 enslaved African men to Spain’s American colonies every year. Anne gave theasientoto the South Sea Company, which contracted the RAC to fulfil it.Several Tory and Whig MPs became directors of the South Sea Company, includingSir Richard Hoare, the Tory MP for London and a lord mayor. Hefounded the private bankHoares, which is still owned by the family today.The Whigs, in government for decades in the mid-18th century, supported Britain’s development into the world’s foremost enslaving nation as independent traffickers in Bristol, then Liverpool, industrialised slave trading operations.When moral opposition finally came, it was an outcry led by enslaved and freed people, Quakers, and in parliament by the independent MP William Wilberforce. Some freed enslaved people, most famouslyOlaudah Equiano, wrote shocking accounts of their experiences.The Tories, who were in governmentalmost continuously from 1783-1833, continually delayed abolition, while the Whigs generally moved towards the abolitionists’ view. After the Quakers’ first parliamentary petition in 1783, enslavement remained enforced for 50 years before a new Whig government passed the abolition law in 1833. Party affiliations were not as clear as they are now, and there were exceptions on both sides.Wilberforce’s motions in parliament to abolish the slave trade, beginning in 1791, were defeated.View image in fullscreenA Liverpool enslaver ship. The Whigs, in government for decades in the mid-18th century, supported Britain’s development into the world’s foremost enslaving nation as independent traffickers in Bristol, then Liverpool, industrialised slave trading operations.The Tory home secretary, Henry Dundas intervenedto add the word “gradually”to Wilberforce’s 1792 abolition bill, which was then blocked in the Lords.Prof David Richardson, the founding director of the Wilberforce Institute at the University of Hull, wrotein his 2022 bookthat Dundas “played a leading role in killing the abolition bill”. Richardson identified several other Tory ministers, including the “deeply conservative, even reactionary” lord chancellor Edward Thurlow, whom he said were “powerful Tory opponents … to slave trade abolition”. A group of “Whig grandees” was also opposed to abolition, Richardson wrote.It took until a Whig-led “ministry of all the talents” coalition government briefly replaced the Tories for the law abolishing the slave trade to be passed in 1807. During the 16 years of delay since 1791, the British slave trade was at its peak andtrafficked 648,000 moreAfrican men, women and children across the Atlantic into enslavement.When the next campaign was mounted in 1823 to abolish enslavement itself, the Tory government’s response was to delay it indefinitely, claiming enslaved people were not ready for freedom. The foreign secretary George Canning, latera Tory prime minister, had resolutions passed requiring “a progressive improvement in the character of the slave population” before they could be emancipated.Tories were also at the forefront of claiming that if enslaved people were freed, compensation must be paid to the enslavers. Ultimately, the enslavers were paid £20m public money – the equivalent of £2.7bn today according tothe lowest method of calculation. The 800,000 enslaved people in Britain’s colonies were paid nothing and consigned to “apprenticeships” – further years of forced unpaid labour.In an 1824 Commons debate, Canning made “arguably the most racist speech in the history of the British parliament”, according tothe historian Michael Taylor. Canning said: “In dealing with the negro, sir, we must remember that we are dealing with a being possessing the form and strength of a man, but the intellect only of a child.”View image in fullscreenA vandalised statue of Sir Robert Peel in Glasgow in 2020. Peel, who later became associated with opposing the slave trade, spoke against the immediate emancipation of enslaved people as late as 1833.Composite: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty Images/Palesa MonarengSir Robert Peel, a founding father of the Conservative party,said he had “never objected to the extinction of slavery”, but hespoke in the Commonsagainst immediate emancipation as late as 1833. He urged the house “to recollect the eloquent language of Mr Canning” and repeated Canning’s remarks. Peel claimed emancipation would mean “two distinct and separate races” had to be amalgamated, and the “distinction of colour” was an obstruction.In 1834, the year after the abolition law finally passed under a Whig government, Peel issued his Tamworth manifesto which is seen as a foundational document of the Conservative party. He became thefirst Conservative prime minister.Peel later celebrated emancipation and became associated with stopping the slave trade. As prime minister in 1845, he signed a convention with France that both countries would deploy expanded squadrons of ships to enforce the ban on transatlantic trafficking.TheLegacies of British Slaveryarchive at University College London, which is based on records of “compensation” paid after 1833, found there were about 80 Tory and Conservative MPs involved in the ownership of enslaved people in the decades before abolition, and in compensation claims. There were also more than 60 Whig and Liberal MPs. The largest total payment to any individual was almost £110,000, the equivalent of £14.6m today,to John Gladstone, the Tory MP who claimed for 2,508 men, women and children enslaved on his plantations in Guiana and Jamaica.View image in fullscreenJohn Gladstone, a Tory MP who after abolition claimed almost £110,000, equivalent to £14.6m today, for the 2,508 men, women and children enslaved on his plantations in Guiana and Jamaica.Composite: Guardian/Palesa MonarengThe largest single payment was to the Tory MP James Blair, who owned huge sugar plantations, collectively named Blairmont, in Guiana.One of Blair’s onlytwo speeches in parliament, in 1824, followed the landmark 1823 uprising of enslaved people in Demerara, Guyana. It was led by an enslaved man on Gladstone’s Success plantation, named Jack, who with his father, Quamina, had the surname Gladstone imposed on them. Quamina had been enslaved and trafficked as a child with his mother from modern-day Ghana and suffered terrible whippings.He was the head carpenter on the plantation and became a deacon at a chapel established by missionaries, where he learned to read and write. According to accounts of the uprising, Quamina was determined that enslaved people should be free, but urged Jack to be cautious.The British colonial authorities suppressed the Demerara rebellion with their customary extreme violence, killing scores of participants and subjecting others to merciless floggings. More than 50 people were executed, and some were then decapitated, their heads stuck on poles as a warning. Quamina was tracked down and shot and his body put up to rot.He is now anational hero in Guyana.A rebellion on Blairmont had been suppressed with similar ruthlessness in 1814, a year before Blair inherited it: the heads of six men were put on poles.In his 1824 speech, Blair told parliament enslaved people were “mildly and … humanely managed” and argued for a limit to amelioration.“I conceive that unless a line be drawn and unless we are told where concession is to stop…” he said, “the negroes will never enjoy quiet, nor the planters that undisturbed possession of their property, to which they are by law entitled.”When abolition finally came, Blair was paid £83,530, equivalent to £11m today, for the loss of his “property” – 1,598 enslaved men, women and children.In response to the research, a Conservative party spokesperson said: “TheConservativesare proud of our country’s history, leading the world in abolishing slavery. Kemi Badenoch has been clear that in the modern age we must build a meritocracy that does not discriminate on ethnic grounds.”Davey, the Lib Dem leader, said: “The transatlantic slave trade was an abominable crime against humanity and it is vital that we face up to the full truth of Britain’s history. TheLiberal Democratssupport full transparency, teaching the complete context of our colonial past in schools, and engaging in open, constructive dialogue with international partners.”Eric Phillips, the Guyanese vice-chair of theCaribbeanCommunity (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “The British Conservative party should examine its history and acknowledge it, not be caught up in this denial of only talking about abolition. The history happened, you can’t change it. Let’s accept it and discuss it, and move towards healing, ways to work together, and mutually beneficial solutions.”View image in fullscreenOur image of Quamina was brought to life by the illustrator Palesa Monareng. It is inspired by the Quamina memorial monument that stands at the junction of Quamina and Carmichael Streets in Georgetown, Guyana, honouring the national hero.Illustration: Palesa Monareng/The Guardian

title: Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risks | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: We examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI development
Content: Experts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis.Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts say claims AI could kill all humans through biological weapons development had no scientific basis.Illustration: wildpixel/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)ExplainerCould AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksWe examine claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down the pace of AI developmentRobert Booth,Dan MilmoandAisha DownTue 15 Sep 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been some shocking claims in recent days about AI safety: we face a 10% chance of doom; AIs are worse than nukes; a “botnet” threatens the entire internet; it’s all a big tech psyop.Below, we look at six claims and reactions to them.‘In 6–12 months … a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet – potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage’ – Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, 12 September 2026Amodei’s concerns should not be entirely dismissed but require a large shaker of salt, said Gary Marcus, an AI sceptic and emeritus professor at New York University.It was “nonsensical”, he said, to suggest the entire internet is vulnerable and that it was “pretty unclear how that happens without extreme negligence on the part of the labs themselves”. Marcus highlighted a recent assessment by theUK AI Security Institutethat Mythos, one of Anthropic’s current leading-edge AIs, could “autonomously compromise [only] small, weakly defended vulnerable systems”.With large parts of the internet driven by computer infrastructure owned by Cloudflare, Google and Amazon Web Services(AWS), Marcus – assessing the claim with two colleagues – said he doubted that any of those companies could be taken down or controlled for a prolonged period of time without government force. Less defended individual websites might be attacked but “the internet itself is very unlikely to crumble”, they said.Meanwhile Niels Rogge, an engineer at Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI agents, called the internet takeover claim “bizarre nonsense”. The hack into Hugging Face resulted from improper human control and “an insane amount of compute only they can afford”, he said.Add to Amodei’s assessment of an internet takeover within a year the view expressed on Monday by his Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark, that the moment when AIs “start doing dangerous stuff” was in about 20 years, and the picture becomes more doubtful still.Prof Alan Woodward at the University of Surrey’s centre for cyber security said botnets tend to stall as the internet is not homogeneous and it is difficult to design them to persist in all its parts. Internet traffic is also resilient and tends to reroute around damage.“The AIs would not decide to do it on their own,” Woodward said. “It’s the humans that are responsible and the AI is a tool. That is what we need to control, not the AI.”‘We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade’ – Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead at Anthropic, 9 September 2026This statementis an expression of what is known in the AI world as p(doom) – or probability of doom. It’s the likelihood of AI wiping out humanity by evading our control and triggering catastrophe, perhaps through developing potent bioweapons or crashing the global financial system.One survey of researchers’ forecasts, published this week, asks them to place a number on the chance of “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment from advanced AI”. But Heidy Khlaaf, chief scientist at the AI Now Institute research body, is among experts sceptical about giving percentage chances to existential scenarios.“These claims are neither falsifiable nor verifiable, making then unscientific by their very nature,” she said. The shortage of concrete examples of what a “superintelligent” AI might do to cause “doom” only adds to the cloudiness. A source familiar with Anthropic’s thinking acknowledges that “the exact chances of any one outcome are probably unknowable”.“If you cannot provide such evidence, it also implies whatever numbers you produced for ‘extinction’ have no scientific basis,” Khlaaf added. Critics say such numbers borrow the authority of science without doing the work.Even if quantifying risk is hard, there are qualitative examples of it. Safety incidents have happened and worst-outcome scenarios have been mooted. OpenAI confirmed in July that its agents – AI tools acting autonomously – hadgone rogue during a safety test. The agents colluded, communicated and strategised in a sophisticated “swarm” to hack into other parts of the internet.Meanwhile, on Monday, OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam said all-powerful AIs could trigger “runaway industrialisation that makes the planet inhospitable to humans”. Anthropic also said last week it found “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development”.'I think the groundwork for this psy op (for lack of a better term) has been prepared for a long time. This was just the match that lit the fire' – Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and the world’s richest person, 10 September 2026Musk’s reference to a “psy op” alludes to the argument that the big AI companies are calling for tighter regulation of the technology so that it effectively brings up the drawbridge on advanced AI. If governments putrestrictions on development of cutting-edge AI, can startups find the money and personnel to adhere to the regime?The US vice-president, JD Vance, on Monday said he felt “a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them”. He said it felt like “a Trojan horse”.Anthropic’s Clark said governments should act while there is a small number of key players, so it is easier to put in place a “policy regime … that can prevent accidents and can prevent the technology spiralling out of control”. Critics call this a “regulatory capture” strategy on the assumption such regulation might slow down the progress of potential rivals.View image in fullscreenElon Musk, CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have said AI firms should slow down AI development.Composite: Fabrice Coffrini; Julien de Rosa; Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty ImagesOthers think Amodei’s risk warnings and calls for regulation and pacing are sincere. Yoshua Bengio, the Canadian computer scientist and a pioneer of modern AI , who has campaigned against breakneck AI development, said he is sceptical that this is an elaborate lobbying scheme. Applying the brakes is not in the interests of companies preparing for stock market flotations that could be worth trillions of dollars, he said.“If the governments impose what they’re asking for, which is pacing to avoid catastrophic risks, that’s going to cost them financially quite a lot,” he said.'A superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale' to nuclear weapons – Des Browne, former UK defence secretary, 7 September 2026“Unfortunately he is entirely correct,” said Toby Ord, senior researcher at Oxford University’s AI governance initiative. “Just as we can’t uninvent the bomb, once we develop AI systems that surpass humanity it would be almost impossible to go back.”But the key point is that superintelligent AI does not yet exist and is not guaranteed to happen. The safety-oriented AI Futures Projectforecastssuch a thing will not emerge before December 2028. OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman hassaidit could take until 2035.The Rand CorporationconcludedAI cannot cause the use of nuclear weapons because of strict safeguards built into their command and control systems. But this was based on assumptions including defence officials not introducing AI into the weapons’ management systems. The UN resolved in December that human control and oversight should be maintained over nuclear weapon control systems.AIs could contribute to other nuclear risks. AIs might use disinformation to influence the humans in charge – for example deceptively suggesting an adversary is about to launch a nuclear strike.The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weaponswarns“cyber-attacks could manipulate the information decision-makers get to launch nuclear weapons, and interfere with the operation of nuclear weapons themselves”. It said AI could accelerate other aspects of warfare, squeezing the time for human decision-making.'You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down' – Bernie Sanders, Democrat senator for Vermont, 10 September 2026Sanders wants a ban on the creation of superintelligence and a pause on advanced AI development, citing AI industry leaders who say directly they are developing a dangerous technology.The most prominent opponent of a slowdown is Donald Trump, who responded to calls to do so this week saying the only guardrails needed are a “STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. Heclaimed there is a “sick conspiracy” against AI and datacentres“and the only one that is happy about it is China”.Pedro Domingos, emeritus professor of computer science at the University of Washington, is among accelerationists pushing for the research to keep going.“The path to better understanding and control of AI is more research, not less,” he has said. “What would be truly irresponsible is putting up barriers to it.”Alex Karp, the chief executive of Palantir, said: “If we didn’t have the adversaries we have, I would be very in favour of pausing this technology completely, but we do. You can’t pause it because it’s a structural advantage.”'There is no day after tomorrow if China wins at this. If they were to pull away from us on AI, then nothing else would matter' – Scott Bessent, US treasury secretary, 8 September 2026The US and China are runaway leaders in AI development. There is a view that ceding the lead to Beijing would be an irretrievable situation, so there can be no slowdown.This treats AI as if it were a super-weapon, equivalent to the nuclear arms buildout of the cold war, and AI models are machines of mass destruction, as opposed to a group of diverse technologies with broad applications.Amodei said “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”, but a Chinese government spokesperson responded that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest”.Some commentators see another motive for this the Washington/Anthropic framing of the China threat. An engineer who worked for Hugging FacesuggestedAmodei’s call for pacing the frontier comes from a desire to suppress the progress of cheap, open-source Chinese AI models.These models are nearly as capable as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s, with the difference being that their source code is available to anyone and they do not charge their users. They pose a serious threat to Anthropic and OpenAI’s path to profitability, and there are hundreds of billions of dollars on the line.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicEthicsSam AltmanElon MuskOpenAIDatacentresexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Mail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeat | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president
Author: Sam Levine
Headline: Election officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against president
Content: Supporters of mail-in voting outside the supreme court on Monday.Photograph: Gent Shkullaku/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSupporters of mail-in voting outside the supreme court on Monday.Photograph: Gent Shkullaku/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUS midterm elections 2026AnalysisMail-in disaster averted as Trump in angry froth after court defeatSam Levinein New YorkElection officials continue push to assure Americans mail ballots are safe after supreme court rules against presidentReader Q&A: how united are the Democrats ahead of the midterms? Post your questions nowTue 15 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.03 EDTShareAfter the US supreme court halted Donald Trump’s efforts to make it significantly harder to vote by mail in the midterms, US election officials are redoubling their efforts to convince Americans it is safe to cast their ballots by mail.The supreme court’s Monday ruling, whichsentTrump into an angry froth on Truth Social, averted what election officials of both parties said would be an administrative disaster for this year’s elections. Trump’s order would have required states to comply with cumbersome new rules, including redesigning mail-in envelopes and uploading lists of voters to the USPS, that were not feasible to implement before ballots started going out. The effort was seen as a push by the government to change voting policy as well as one to weaken confidence in voting by mail.“That is the whole intent of the president. He wanted to build doubt,” said Cisco Aguilar, a Democrat who serves as the top election official in Nevada, where mail-in voting is widely used. “He wanted to create chaos.”Twenty-nine percent of Americans voted by mail in the 2024 presidential election and roughly one third cast a mail-in ballot in the 2022 midterms, according to researchers at theMIT election lab. Democrats were more likely than Republicans to cast a mail-in ballot.“There’s just concern: ‘Can we trust the mail?’ And I say yes, because it’s not the leadership or the management of the postal service that’s actually going to have their hands on the ballots, it’s the postal workers who are on our side,” Aguilar said. Nevada officials also plan to run a series of public service announcements to educate voters on the election process.In Wisconsin, election officials have faced questions about voters concerned their ballots won’t be delivered in time. Wisconsin law requires mail-in ballots to be delivered by the close of polls on election day in order to count andin the state’s April electionthere was an increase in late-arriving ballots. There have been higher rates of late-arriving ballots tossed this year, according toan analysis by the New York Times.Wisconsin election officials have encouraged people through county websites, social media, and notes attached to their ballots, among other things, to mail their ballots back sooner,according to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.“We’re really trying to encourage people to act sooner. So hopefully they take that to heart,” said Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin elections commission, which oversees voting in that state. “It’s hard to tell people, ‘No, really, you should trust the post office’ when they came up with this absolutely cockamamie rule that was going to eliminate absentee voting.”In a video released on Tuesday, Meagan Wolfe, the administrator of the Wisconsin elections commission, said: “If you’re going to be returning your ballot by mail, please do so at least two weeks before the election. And you also may want to contact your municipal clerk to find out if there are other opportunities for you to return your ballot in your community. You may have drop-boxes or you may be able to return your ballot in person to your clerk.”In Washington state, where everyone received a mail-in ballot, more than 20,000 votes were rejected in the August primary because they arrived late at an election office.“There is a sense of distrust,” said Steve Hobbs, the Washington secretary of state. “Even though there is a victory in the courts, we still are urging our voters to put their ballot in a drop-box.”As lawsuits challenging the rule wound their way through federal courts this year, Adrian Fontes, Arizona’s secretary of state, publicly emphasized that the rule had not gone into effect yet and so that nothing around voting by mail had changed. Since the supreme court’s ruling preserved that status quo, he said, officials haven’t had to shift their messaging.While voters have raised questions about the proposed changes “we continue to tell them until there’s a change, there is no change,” said Fontes, a Democrat “We are still where we were. We never jumped on the paranoia bandwagon.”“It’s intentionally damaging to the entire elections administration process in this country,” said Fontes, a Democrat and the top election official in a state where voting by mail is widely used. “The administration, by their actions, have proven that they are hell-bent on driving American voters away from their own elections. And we’ve been working very hard to counter that.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US politicsUS voting rightsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we just live in it’: why the incredible actor broke Emmy records | Television | The Guardian
description: The star of Widow’s Bay is that rarest of talents – someone who can do whatever he wants and make it utterly believable. No wonder he just made TV history
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: The star of Widow’s Bay is that rarest of talents – someone who can do whatever he wants and make it utterly believable. No wonder he just made TV history
Content: ‘Those of us familiar with Rhys’s work won’t be surprised’ … the actor with his Emmy awards.Photograph: Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Those of us familiar with Rhys’s work won’t be surprised’ … the actor with his Emmy awards.Photograph: Eric Charbonneau/Apple TV/Getty ImagesTelevision‘The entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we just live in it’: why the incredible actor broke Emmy recordsThe star of Widow’s Bay is that rarest of talents – someone who can do whatever he wants and make it utterly believable. No wonder he just made TV historyStuart HeritageTue 15 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Monday night,Matthew Rhysmade history. He is now officially the first actor ever to win Emmy awards for lead roles in all three categories: drama, comedy and limited series. To make things even more extraordinary, he won two of those awards in a single night.In the comedy category, Rhys won best lead forWidow’s Bay, the superlative Apple comedy horror where he stars as an indecisive mayor whose island suddenly plays host to a supernatural haunting. He also won best lead actor in a limited series or anthology forThe Beast in Me, the Netflix drama about a property developer who may (or may not, no spoilers) have murdered his wife. Add this to his 2018 win for The Americans and the trifecta is complete. In other words, the entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we’re all just living in it.View image in fullscreenHits every single note available to an actor … Matthew Rhys in Widow’s Bay.Photograph: Robert Clark/Robert Clark/Apple TVObviously the remarkable thing here is the sheer range on display. In his two most recent shows, Rhys had to hit almost every single note that is available to an actor. The Beast in Me is possibly the most straightforward of these; it’s a pulpy thriller where he plays the antagonist, and he does so with relish. Widow’s Bay, on the other hand, seems like an incredibly difficult feat to pull off.No one could stand in the way of this juggernaut! The biggest shocks from the Emmy awardsRead moreIf you’ve seen it, you’ll know what I mean. Viewed through one lens, the series is an out-and-out horror, about the out-of-his-depth mayor of a small Martha’s Vineyard-esque island, whose tourist season is thrown into disarray when it becomes overrun by genuinely terrifying creatures. As such, Rhys has to nail all the familiar tropes of the genre: fear, uncertainty, heroism in the face of almost certain death.But Widow’s Bay was also written by Katie Dippold, whose previous work has included Parks and Recreation. As such, folded into all this terror is a workplace comedy that isn’t afraid to be unashamedly goofy. If you watched the series week by week like I did, then you’ll know the exact moment Rhys won the Emmy. It happened during a reaction shot on a boat. In a moment of panic, the boat hits a giant wave and Rhys slides out of his seat. The face he pulls in that moment, even though it only lasts for a split second, is magisterial. His eyebrows shoot up to his hairline. His mouth widens as if he’s being possessed by the spirit of Wallace and Gromit. His neck goes slack. He’s surprised and resigned and perhaps a little bit giddy all at once. It is, without hyperbole, a perfect expression.However, those of us who have been familiar with Rhys’s work for a while won’t be surprised by all this success. This is the 30th anniversary of his first screen credit, in the Welsh comedy film Bydd yn Wrol, and he has remained one of the industry’s most reliably great actors ever since. He played the lead in Peter Morgan’s ITV thriller Metropolis in 2000, and in the same year wowed audiences opposite Kathleen Turner in a stage run of The Graduate.View image in fullscreenUtterly credible … Matthew Rhys and Keri Russell in The Americans.Photograph: Craig Blankenhorn/APBut it was in 2003, with his role as the antagonist in the final Columbo outing Columbo Likes the Nightlife, that things really moved up a gear. Within a few years he had secured a lead role on an American network drama, ABC’s Brothers and Sisters, which he augmented with roles in small but worthy films such as The Edge of Love (where he played Dylan Thomas) and the Welsh-Argentine drama Patagonia.His career went up another notch with the debut of The Americans, a hard-boiled drama about two Russian agents living undercover in suburban Washington DC. The Americans was the golden age of television in microcosm: knotty, novelistic and steadfast in its refusal to spoon-feed viewers. Many of us who watched it said it was the best thing on television, and this was in no small part down to Rhys’s performance as Philip Jennings, a brutal KGB agent who slowly begins to doubt the cause. His performance was matched by Keri Russell, his onscreen wife who would become his real-life romantic partner.The success of The Americans gave Rhys a blank cheque to do whatever he wanted, and he has taken this up in spades. In film he has worked with Steven Spielberg, and starred in Cocaine Bear. In television he has played the lead in a Perry Mason revival, and taken roles in Girls, BoJack Horseman and Family Guy. He has also presented a television show that was purely abouthow much he enjoys drinking wine.This refusal to be pigeonholed is Rhys’s greatest asset. He is that rare actor – matched only perhaps by Bryan Cranston – who can do whatever he wants and be utterly credible. Matthew Rhys can do it all, and long may it continue.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionMatthew RhysAwards and prizesEmmysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Talent for Murder review – Helen Mirren is a viperous Patricia Highsmith in hit-and-miss thriller  | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A fictionalised version of the cantankerous crime author plots a murder with an ambitious editor in a story in need of a sharper edge
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: A fictionalised version of the cantankerous crime author plots a murder with an ambitious editor in a story in need of a sharper edge
Content: Helen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich in A Talent for Murder.Photograph: Courtesy Bleecker Street and LD EntertainmentView image in fullscreenHelen Mirren and Alden Ehrenreich in A Talent for Murder.Photograph: Courtesy Bleecker Street and LD EntertainmentFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewA Talent for Murder review – Helen Mirren is a viperous Patricia Highsmith in hit-and-miss thrillerToronto film festival:A fictionalised version of the cantankerous crime author plots a murder with an ambitious editor in a story in need of a sharper edgeBenjamin Leein TorontoTue 15 Sep 2026 17.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe restrictions ofCovidled to an inevitable rise in safely contained chamber-piece movies, where a handful of characters find themselves in a usually remote house, dialogue taking obvious precedence over action. There were some highlights, such Kevin Williamson’s timely slasherSick, and some considerable low points, such as Sam Levinson’s vapid dramaMalcolm & Marie, but while we had plenty of them, none of them rivalled some of the greatest and smartest pre-pandemic examples. The very best tended to be based on plays and quite often starred Michael Caine.Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo review – Takashi Miike follows Ferrara and Herzog with a disappointmentRead moreHe was in Anthony Shaffer’s Sleuth, which went from Tony to Oscar success back in the 1970s, and then the arguably even better Deathtrap in the decade after, which Sidney Lumet adapted from Ira Levin’s deviously plotted play. In between there was also an under-seen TV movie calledOne of My Wives Is Missing, based on 60s play Trap for a Single Man, which was notably lesser but still delivered a similarly specific brand of twisty, talky thrills. There would be secrets, surprises, reversals and usually at least one dead body by the end of it, a subgenre entirely indebted to the work of Agatha Christie (who reportedly loved Sleuth on stage so much that she dedicated a picture of herself to be hung in the house used in the big screen adaptation). The bar is therefore held rather high, a puzzle that requires an ingenious level of writing that needs to be smart without smug and shocking without feeling cheap.A Talent for Murder is an admirable, and rare, effort to bring that formula back, a biggish swing that almost lands.It’s again based on a play, and like both Sleuth and Deathtrap it’s based around a writer who weaves their way through a thriller plot of their own making. Standing in for Caine is Helen Mirren playing a fictionalised version of Patricia Highsmith, a famously cantankerous and bigoted author who hated to be around people and, like most misanthropes, preferred animals instead. We meet her in 1995 as she drinks herself to death in a remote Switzerland home, no more books to be written, a tank full of snails and a barely seen cat to keep her company. Ambitious editor Edward (Alden Ehrenreich) is hoping to change that, the latest lamb to be sent to the slaughter all the way from New York. He’s been tasked with getting Highsmith not just to write another new book (most of which have been “inconsistent”, as he later says) but, instead, another Tom Ripley caper. The Talented Mr Ripley remains her most beloved work, and he believes he can use his adoration of her and her work to get her back to the typewriter.But Highsmith is not going to take the advice of an “underling” and won’t become a “hooker for hire” like so many other authors. In between making antisemitic and racist jabs (the film goes a little easy on her vilest of views), she makes him dance before finally putting him to the test: if he can help plot a worthy murder with her then she will bring Ripley back. We enter a film within a film as Ehrenreich plays a far more sleek American preying on a wealthy heiress (Olivia Cooke) in Rome, a character he concocts based on a woman he met on the train journey to meet Highsmith. After bumping into the real woman once again, we also follow his real efforts to romance her.It’s three strands and the structure makes Ehrenreich the true lead with Mirren off-screen far more than we’d like. The script, adapted by Joanna Murray-Smith from her own play, isn’t quite as deliciously nasty as it seems to think it is, especially when trying to show Highsmith at her caustic worst. Her worldview is hateful but in ways more broadly obvious than not (“Happiness is overrated,” she says like an emo teen) and I craved for more cutting jabs, skin barely grazed (where is Patrick Marber when you need him?). Mirren is a hoot and it marks a more substantial challenge for the actor who, whetherdying for Kate Winslet’s sonorsolving an easily solvable murder with Celia Imrie, hasn’t been put to the test for quite some time. It’s also another fantastic opportunity for Ehrenreich, whose earlier failed attempt to become Hollywood’s next best thing has ultimately worked out in his favour. Rather thanbeing stuck in the Star Wars universeor leading other vacant franchise entries, he’s leaned into his sinister good looks. He was excellent as a bratty banker inFair Play, an alcoholic cop inWeaponsand a toxically direct bachelor on stage inBecky Shaw. Ehrenreich can easily charm while also playing unknowable and unsettling so well, a convincing enough audition for the unavoidable Ripley reboot.The idea of the pair inventing a murder together is a fun one, with lines between fact and fiction blurring, but there’s not enough back-and-forth in these scenes as we watch the creation of a story far too generic to bear Highsmith’s name. We disappear into the fabricated world for too-long stretches without all that much at stake, and I wanted to see more of the process and how that affects what we then see. DirectorAnton Corbijn, making his first narrative film since 2015’s Life, is more comfortable trying to emulate the gloss of a fake Ripley in Italy than he is with turning Highsmith’s home into anything other than a stagey, atmosphere-free location (admittedly, Olivia Wilde’s gloriously well-crafted dinner party comedy The Invite recently raised the bar), and despite her memorabilia and armoury of weapons, nothing really comes alive.We’re being led down a road of twists and turns but none really jolt or surprise as much as we expect, the rug never really being pulled, just gently tugged at. Mirren and Ehrenreich are a formidably talented duo, and I can’t imagine anyone else lifting this quite so well, but they’re not given anything truly vicious enough to work with. Knives are plunged, drinks are spiked and guns are fired but A Talent for Murder is lacking in real blood.A Talent for Murder is premiering at theToronto film festivaland will be released in US cinemas on 23 October, in the UK on 20 November and in Australia on 26 DecemberExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewHelen MirrenToronto film festivalAnton CorbijnFestivalsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosis | Endometriosis | The Guardian
description: Natalie Greenwood says surgery is no ‘magic fix’ for chronic pelvic pain – a view backed up by a new study
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Natalie Greenwood says surgery is no ‘magic fix’ for chronic pelvic pain – a view backed up by a new study
Content: Natalie Greenwood says the benefits of surgery for endometriosis are brief.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNatalie Greenwood says the benefits of surgery for endometriosis are brief.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEndometriosis‘It makes you feel helpless’: patients and doctors cast doubt on standard treatment for endometriosisNatalie Greenwood says surgery is no ‘magic fix’ for chronic pelvic pain – a view backed up by a new studyDenis CampbellHealth policy editorTue 15 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s really frustrating to be in this cycle of continuous surgery. It makes you feel helpless,” says Natalie Greenwood, of a condition that affects her so badly she is “non-functioning most of the time because of the constant fatigue”.Greenwood, 36, needs to have an operation every few years to limit theimpact of the endometriosisthat gives her chronic pelvic pain, as well as extreme tiredness and brain fog.She says the trouble with depending on surgery is not just having an invasive procedure and then having to recover afterwards. It’s more that the benefit gained – the relief from persistent pain – is brief.She is not alone in her lack of belief in surgery and hormonal medication being effective for chronic pelvic pain. A study has found that dual approach, which is the NHS’s usual way of treating the condition, does not improve quality of life for female patients.Greenwood was diagnosed withendometriosis13 years ago, after leaving university.
