It is a condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus – the endometrium – is found outside the uterus, most commonly in the pelvic cavity, and can cause inflammation and pain.View image in fullscreenGreenwood, 36, was diagnosed with endometriosis 13 years ago and has a ‘pain management toolkit’, including a Tens machine, to help with the condition.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianGreenwood, who is a languages teacher in West Yorkshire, has already had surgery three times: when she was 23, 28 and 32. In the first two operations sheunderwent ablation, in which the endometriosis is removed using heat or cold. The last procedureinvolved excision, in which the surgeon cuts out the endometriosis.“The surgery is effective in that it can keep the pain at bay for a few more years. But I’ve never come out of it feeling better,” she said. “And in between surgeries I’ve still had to have hormone treatments, like a hormonal coil, or been put into chemical menopause. That keeps the endometriosis at bay by shutting down the hormones that cause it. But the endometriosis keeps growing. So you might feel better for a while but it’s always there in the background.”Even after surgery, Greenwood has still needed what she calls her “pain management toolkit” – Tens machines, peppermint teabags, cooling patches, hot-water bottles and CBD oil.Endometriosis is one of the main causes of chronic pelvic pain, a condition that affects between 6% and 27% of women worldwide. Others include vulvodynia andbladder pain syndrome.“The surgery has never been a magic fix for me,” said Greenwood. “I don’t think it’s a magic fix for many people. You don’t just suddenly feel completely better. A life of surgery every five years is just not something you want to do. It’s not sustainable. It’s like a constant rut.”Greenwood has a boy of five and is keen to have another child. But endometriosis has affected her fertility so much that she will soon start a course of IVF.Whatever the outcome of that treatment, she is sure of one thing: “I won’t have surgery again. It’s not manageable to keep having surgery every five years. Whatever happens with the IVF, after it I’m going to have a hysterectomy and my ovaries removed because that might give me some relief from endometriosis.”Dr Jasmine Hearn, a reader in health psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University who co-led the research in the new study, said: “Sadly patients are often left struggling due to current pain management strategies not sufficiently alleviating pain.“Chronic pelvic pain is often invisible but its impact can be profound. Our findings highlight that women with pelvic pain report poorer quality of life when they’ve had surgery and hormonal medication for pelvic pain and better quality of life when psychological support is part of treatment.”The 147 women in the study, who were aged 18 to 66, all reported that their pelvic pain had a major impact on both their physical and psychological quality of life and ability to function normally.Surgery was found to be associated with lower physical quality of life while painkillers were associated with women having poorer physical, psychological and environmental quality of life.In contrast, women who received psychological help as part of their treatment to help them manage their pain said their quality of life was better. The evidence for its effectiveness was so great that all those who suffer pelvic pain should be offered it, Hearn added.Dr Lucy Whitaker, a researcher with the charity Wellbeing of Women and a clinical lecturer in obstetrics and gynaecology at the University of Edinburgh, agreed. She said the same suggestion was made in 2020 by Westminster’s all-party parliamentary group on endometriosis and by aconfidential national inquiryinto the condition in 2024.Whitaker added: “Chronic pelvic pain conditions like endometriosis carry a well-documented psychological burden and integrating psychological support alongside medical management reflects a more holistic approach to a condition that has long been under-resourced.”A spokesperson for NHS England said: “Chronic pelvic pain can have a significant impact on women’s lives and mental health. That’s why psychological professionals provide specialist pain-management support as part of wider physical health services – including for chronic pelvic pain – while women can also self-refer to NHS talking therapies for support with long-term physical health conditions.”Explore more on these topicsEndometriosisHealthNHSWomen's healthHealth policynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favourites | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print cover
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: From a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print cover
Content: Cover stars … clockwise from top left: Cosmopolitan, Frieze, Colors, Bloomberg Businesssweek, S&M Sniper, the Cornhill MagazineView image in fullscreenCover stars … clockwise from top left: Cosmopolitan, Frieze, Colors, Bloomberg Businesssweek, S&M Sniper, the Cornhill MagazineArt and design‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favouritesFrom a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print coverDaniel Dylan WrayTue 15 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘We need to rethink what a successful magazine looks like,” says Steve Watson, founder of the subscription magazine club Stack. “It doesn’t make sense to compare the magazines of today to those of the 1960s when many people still didn’t have colour televisions. Print magazines are no longer the best way of reaching lots of people quickly and cheaply but they are still really great at engaging deeply with readers, providing an opportunity to slow down and absorb information. They provide us with an alternative way of seeing the world.”Watson, along with a group of editors, publishers, designers, historians and academics, will be discussing the varying roles and functions that magazines have played over the years duringa one-day event at the forthcoming London design festival. In contrast to the doom and gloom we often hear about the print industry, he remains upbeat about the humble mag’s future. “The truth is there are brilliant new magazines launching all the time,” he says.And with every new title comes new opportunities for bold, innovative and eye-popping cover design. Here, industry experts – including many taking part in theLondon design festivalevent – pick out their favourite magazine cover designs and tell us why they find them so enduring …Photograph: Wyndham Lewis Memorial TrustBlast, issue 1,1914Scott King, ex-art director for i-D magazine and former creative director for SleazenationBlast was published a month before Britain entered the first world war. It was an anti-petit-bourgeois rant against the professional classes. It features lines such as “Curse abysmal inexcusable middle class” and “The britannic aesthete – cream of the snobbish earth”. It was – for want of a less gratuitous expression, given when it was published – a call to arms. It was punk 60 years before punk was invented. In fact, Blast often reads exactly like a Fall song [the band’s singer Mark E Smith was a huge fan], with the artist and editor Wyndham Lewis piecing together phrases into a collage of barely focused loathing: “Blast the amateur, sciolast, art-pimp, journalist, self man, no-organ man.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Million PublishingS&M Sniper, issue 5, 1984Meara Sharma, senior editor of ElasticThis is a fetish magazine but it does what I think every magazine cover needs to do: seduce. It’s luring a reader in, tickling the senses, giving a flavour of what’s inside, but also tantalising whoever’s passing by. This does a great job of fulfilling that mandate of seduction. The art itself is this incredible photorealistic airbrushed painting by Yosuke Onishi, an amazing Japanese artist who featured in every issue. So the artist gets to play, but you get this lovely consistency and distinct look, and it becomes unmistakably that magazine. It’s so lush, visceral and delicious. The lips are dripping and they feel like they’re bursting out of the page.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Benetton GroupColors,issue 90, 2014Steve Watson, founder of StackmagazinesThis is the last issue of Colors ever published and it was edited by Patrick Waterhouse, who I think is a genius. This was the year of the World Cup in Brazil, so they did a survival guide to football but they took a completely different view. There’s stuff in here about refugee and amputee teams and artists who change the shape of the football pitch to explore what it would do to the game. It’s full of of nice little symmetries and links: it’s issue 90 and a football match is 90 minutes long, and the cover has got this gold foil on it that references football cards. It’s loads of fun, but also really clever.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Retro AdArchives/Hearst/AlamyCosmopolitan debut UK issue, 1972Dr Sharon Maxwell Magnus, media historian and principal lecturer inmasscommunications at the University of HertfordshireCosmopolitan was different from anything that went before it. Other women’s magazines in the UK, at the time, focused on domestic life, family, cooking, recipes, and were very homely. This was for women not bound by marriage and children, and who can, and are, having sex before or outside marriages. The cover is a brilliant partnership between design and words. It’s daring but not so daring that newsagents aren’t going to stock it. It was a revolutionary moment for the magazine industry and it sold 350,000 copies by lunchtime on its first day.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Life Magazine/The Life Picture CollectionLifemagazine: Faces of the American Dead in Vietnam, 1969Jaap Biemans, art director at VolkskrantmagazineThis cover is like a slap in the face. You have the image of a face, just like you see on thousands of covers, but when you read the headline you get goosebumps everywhere. It’s the maximum of emotion with minimal elements. It’s a great execution by cropping the face and, design-wise, it’s the most simple cover you can make but it’s got such an impact. When you look at normal covers about war, you see heroic poses, grieving people, flags, explosions, battlefields. But on this one, you don’t see any of that, but it fires into your mind and heart like an arrow.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Smith, Elder & CoCornhill, December 1865Tony Quinn, magazine historian and founder of MagforumThe people behind this cover were all working at the top of their trade. It was edited by William Makepeace Thackeray and engraved by WJ Linton, while designer Godfrey Sykes was working at the time on the architectural decoration for the V&A Museum. Cornhill was named after a street that had a market where they brought in agricultural products, so Sykes interprets Cornhill via the manufacturing of corn: each roundel shows a stage of making it. Everything about this cover has a story behind it. It also changed the way that names were invented for magazines – within about 40 years there were dozens of magazines named after streets in London, from Pall Mall to the Strand.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: BloombergBloomberg Businessweek, 2 May, 2016Alice Sherwin and Harry Bennett, founders of Studio Ground FloorDesigner Tracy Ma’s run for Bloomberg Businessweek was unbelievable – as her work continues to be. For us, this is a particular standout, because it both embodies her editorial approach to the periodical and taps into something we love in design: everyday visual language. Typographically, systematically and spatially, Tracy draws on familiar visual cues, the design that comes to exist without designer’s involvement, and subverts them. That way, people are drawn in and then shown something surprisingly new. In this case, it’s super self-aware. Kitsch and boring. It’s sublime design and a capsule for the time, helping its audience better understand the issue at hand through creative choices.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: New York MediaNew Yorkmagazine, Lindsay Lohan as Marilyn Monroe, 2008Charlie Baker,editor of the FenceI was 19, living in New York, and remember being struck by this. I think this was the last era when you could do a cover that would be a little bit daring, bold, and put it out into the ecosystem as a way of getting readers to buy it. It was like a last great show of what covers can do. I think it’s good for tasteful erotic things to be in mainstream culture but I don’t think you could do something like that now.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Frieze PublishingFrieze, issue 134, 2010Frith Kerr, art director at Studio FrithI love this. It’s an instinctive, joyful response to something poetic made from the very ordinary: a sock, a foot and a logotype. The image is so concise that the magazine becomes an artwork – an egalitarian one that you can afford.Artshould not only be for the super-rich.The scale is important, as is the sharp yellow of the logotype. The graphic simplicity poses a question. It is a visual idea. Questions are much more potent than answers as they engage and form relationships. Visual communication is all about creating relationships. A good magazine cover, like this, will instantly do that.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Crystal Ball MediaInterviewmagazine, Lana Del Rey, 2023Jeremy Leslie, founder of magCultureThis cover really struck a chord. The photoshoot by Nadia Lee Cohen is timeless, this could have been the 1950s or 70s. It’s a fabulous portrait of a woman that was really of that moment. It sold out and became hugely in demand. I visit universities for talks and there’s a box of magazines I take with me and my copy of that went missing at one. It’s easy to go back and find classic covers from, say, the 1960s but that was a different time. It’s interesting seeing how today a cover can still punch above its weight and deliver something that’s an iconic cultural moment.Reading Magazines: 300 Years of Magazine Evolutionis at London design festival, 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designLondon design festivalDesignArtMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bridesmaid proposals: a sweet gesture – or another way to make weddings ludicrously expensive? | Weddings | The Guardian
description: Being a bridesmaid is a big commitment. Now, asking prospective candidates is becoming an event in itself, sometimes with a heavy price tag
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Being a bridesmaid is a big commitment. Now, asking prospective candidates is becoming an event in itself, sometimes with a heavy price tag
Content: We do!Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenWe do!Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoPass notesWeddingsBridesmaid proposals: a sweet gesture – or another way to make weddings ludicrously expensive?Being a bridesmaid is a big commitment. Now, asking prospective candidates is becoming an event in itself, sometimes with a heavy price tagTue 15 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Bridesmaid proposals.Age:Relatively new.Relative to what?To marriage proposals.I’mconfused.Is it when the groom realises he’s made a terrible mistake, and he really loves one of the bridesmaids?So he pops the question to her, maybe during the actual ceremony (but hopefully before the vows)?Er … nope.Go on then, enlighten me.What it says on the tin really: asking someone to be your bridesmaid.What’s with the proposal though, can’t you just ask?It’s a big ask, and a big commitment on the part of the bridesmaid.Not as big an ask as“Will you spend the rest of your life with me?”Where are these bridesmaid proposals taking place?Well, they’re becoming a bit of a thing on social media …I knew it!For example,an Instagram postby Darcy McQueeny is causing something of a stir.What’s Darcy doing?She’s got everything laid out neatly …Like what?Six pink wheelie suitcases, blankets, pyjamas, bikinis, cosmetics. They’re all customised, monogrammed, embroidered and personalised with the names of the prospective bridesmaids. Plus there are handwritten letters, asking the question. “I hope they say yes,” she says, putting her hands together like a prayer emoji.That sounds like an expensive proposal.One of the commenters estimates $1,700 for each bundle, or a little over $10,000 for the lot. Although it’s possible that Darcy didn’t fork out for it all.How does that work then?Well, she’s a content creator with 2.3m followers on TikTok, which means she probably gets stuff sent to her from brands.We’re not all content creators though.True, and weddings aren’t just pricey for the bride and groom – it costs a lot to be a bridesmaid, too.Why’s that then?Increasingly extravagant hen dos, travel, spa hotels, dresses, alterations ... One expert toldthe Washington Postthat the average cost of being a bridesmaid was about $3,000.That’s going to rule out extravagant bridesmaid proposals for average folks then?Not at all. The Brides website says a bridesmaid proposal doesn’t have to be fancy, and hassome suggestionsfor low-key and cheaper ideas for how to do it.Such as?You could schedule a candle making class.Nice, but a bit sedate. How about hosting a fake book club?What, now we’ve discussed the symbolism in the novel, will you be my bridesmaids?Or you could throw a boozy brunch?Now you’re talking!Done! High fives!Do say:“Yes! We do!”Don’t say:“And if you could post about it on social media, that would be even more special.”Explore more on these topicsWeddingsPass notesMarriageRelationshipsFriendshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Polling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no good | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: Surely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graph, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Surely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graph, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: ‘Polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game’.Photograph: Sky NewsView image in fullscreen‘Polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game’.Photograph: Sky NewsOpinionOpinion pollsPolling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no goodJonathan LiewSurely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graphTue 15 Sep 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.07 EDTShareSolemn faces all round. We will listen. We will learn. We will hone and improve. Yes, it’s time for the latest bout of profound soul-searching in the UK polling industry following the allegations raised by the recent Channel 4 investigation that a polling firmreportedly failed to declarethat three polls it published before the local elections in May were commissioned by Reform. By now these reckonings are becoming a regular occurrence in the wake of big elections: pollsters gather in a room, nibble biscuits, ritually self-flagellate, and pledge to learn all the right lessons from the electorate they’ve just catastrophically misread.Yet for all its very public ignominies, political polling is one of those rare and precious industries that somehow manages to keep failing upwards. You might think that afterbotching the 2015and2017 general elections, the2016 Brexit voteand the 2021 London mayoral poll, we might have learned better than to trust in the mystical magic graph. In this parallel universe Keir Starmer is now sitting on a colossal 318-seat majority, as forecast by Survation in itsfinal MRP pollon the eve of the 2024 general election, overstating the actual result by a mere 144 parliamentary seats.I am, of course, being slightly unfair. Most of the reputable pollsters enjoy just as many hits as misses – and are, by and large, staffed by smart and diligent people who genuinely care about their craft. Doubtless many among their number would object to any suggestion that the apparent misbehaviour of one firm – JL Partners, who were secretly filmed agreeing to carry out a poll favourable to Reform without disclosing who was commissioning it – can somehow be extrapolated to the wider profession as a whole. To which the only reasonable response is: well, let’s see how you like it.And rest assured, I’ve read the Substacks. I’ve signed up to (the free version of) the newsletters. I’ve talked to polling experts. I’ve swished a curious finger up and down the interactive graphics. I’ve sat through interminable briefings in which a very nice man explains why he decided to carve up the voting public into 16 distinct blocs with catchy but absurd names: Flag Shaggers, Jealous Judies, Digital Wombats. And because Westminster is basically like the inside of a very small conch, these terms quickly pass into common parlance. “As you can see,” some wonk on the radio will opine, “the Tories are down eight points among the Angry Trevors, a whopping 13 with Disconsolate Flexitarians. But they are at least holding firm with Be At One Mums.”But my problem has virtually nothing to do with methodology and almost everything to do with volume. There’s simply too much of this stuff, and people are taking it too seriously, investing too much predictive power. The British Polling Council (BPC) has swollen to 39 member organisations, many of them new and completely untested. In the first two weeks of September alone there have been 10 separate voting intention surveys issued by seven separate companies. We are all fatally beholden to the cult of Big Poll.There are plenty of noble and legitimate defences of polls. They help to shape and test policy. They allow voters to make their choice with the fullest possible information. Perhaps they even function as a kind of check on an unfair electoral system, signposting to potential tactical switchers where their vote might profitably be spent. But even these defences highlight a paradox: this is a method of measuring and reflecting public opinion – and of subtly influencing it. Which is why so many lobbyists, PR firms and corporate interests are desperate to get involved.Pollsters are not doing this out of some great altruistic duty to democracy. This is a business like any other, often using techniques borrowed wholesale from the market research and advertising sectors, and preying on a resource-starved, click-hungry media desperate for high-impact, low-cost content. “You aren’t going to pay for polling unless you are confident they can deliver the answer you want,” one public affairs executivetold Politico last week. Or as George Gallup, one of the pioneers of modern-day polling, put it: “If it works for toothpaste, why not for politics?”And so what started out as a small table in the newspaper every month has essentially become a biddable political actor in its own right, and there is a cosy symbiotic relationship between the people who conduct the polls, the people who pay for the polls and the people who publish the polls. This is how Reform can be treated like a government in waiting when they have eight MPs. This is how Starmer ends up as a lame duck within two years of his own landslide. In his 2018 memoir, the former FBI director James Comey admitted that his decision toreopen the investigationinto Hillary Clinton’s emails may have been affected by the fact that she was well ahead of Donald Trump in the polls.Beyond this, polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game, a permanent rolling market ticker, in which the aim is not to improve the lives of human beings but to master the line on the graph, where winning elections is the end rather than the means. The BPC, with no fixed office and no full-time staff, was never going to fix this. In reality it is more of a trade body than a regulator, self-run and concerned less with ethics than trust and marketability.And so JL Partners and the industry it belongs to are not the sole culprits here. In reality, the problem is the messenger: the people who consume and regurgitate politics for an audience, seduced by the idea that there is some all-seeing eye, a soup of numbers that will tell us all the answers. As someone whose very job deals in opinion, I know its fragility and malleability, the ridiculousness of treating it like a sacred stone tablet, or – I dunno – basing an entire generation of foreign and economic policy on how 635,000 people felt when they woke up on a Thursday in June 2016.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWest Germany banned the death penalty in 1949 even though 77% of people were in favour of it. By 2000 that had fallen to 23%. Explanation, exemplar, persuasion, principle: these are the real tools of politics, at least a politics that seeks not to chase or triangulate public opinion but to mould and shape it. But if your entire existence is tied to a little line on a graph, then you’re never even going to try.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsOpinion pollsOpinionReform UKNigel FarageKeir StarmercommentShareReuse this content

title: There are two kinds of people in this world: hosts or guests. Nobody can be both | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: My hosting persona is an edgier version of Manuel from Fawlty Towers. Invite me to yours, however, and I am a nonstop delight, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: My hosting persona is an edgier version of Manuel from Fawlty Towers. Invite me to yours, however, and I am a nonstop delight, writes Polly Hudson
Content: A world divided … a pleasant dinner party.Photograph: Maskot/Getty Images (posed by models)View image in fullscreenA world divided … a pleasant dinner party.Photograph: Maskot/Getty Images (posed by models)OpinionFoodThere are two kinds of people in this world: hosts or guests. Nobody can be bothPolly HudsonMy hosting persona is an edgier version of Manuel from Fawlty Towers. Invite me to yours, however, and I am a nonstop delightTue 15 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTShareMy epiphany came between the starter and the main. At a friend’s place for dinner, I sat in awe as she put on a kind of magic show – the first course plates were cleared, but I never noticed her doing it. Delicious food was repeatedly produced with no lengthy disappearing act preceding it, no fuss, no panic. The candles on the table flickered invitingly, the background music was unobtrusive but atmospheric, the wine and chat flowed effortlessly. If I had later discovered she secretly had a full staff – planning, preparing, cooking, cleaning – it would have made perfect sense. But no, it was all her. And then I realised, the world is divided into people who are hosts, and people who are guests. You’re either one, or the other – nobody is both, apart from maybe the Duchess of Sussex. If you aren’t sure which camp you fall into, ask someone close to you if you’re a good host. If they pause for longer than 0.2 seconds before answering, you’re a guest.Simple menu, minimal stress, banging playlist: top chefs’ tips for a dinner party even the host will enjoyRead moreAs alluded to above, I am a terrible host. When welcoming people into your home, your mood sets the tone for what follows: if you’re relaxed, calm and smiley, they will be too. I am uptight, edgy – and very, very clearly on my last nerve as I open the door to let them in. I’m probably grimacing, I might be close to tears. I will then be so extremely laser focused on them having a nice time, that it will ensure they most definitely do not. I run from room to room. I yelp. I don’t engage in conversation, because even if I can briefly get it together enough to appear to be listening, I’m really thinking about whether I set the oven to the right temperature, and realising I forgot to look at the clock when I put the food in it. I am neither present nor absent, but an infuriating combination of the two. I loiter. I lurk. My energy is that of a surgeon dashing to the operating room, who has just noticed that they’ve forgotten everything they learned at medical school. Or perhaps it’s Manuel from Fawlty Towers. When it comes to hosting, I am a mess.But as a guest? Sorry, but I’m a freaking delight. Ishine. Now the pressure is off, I will be the warm-up support act the headliner host never knew they needed. I’ll arrive seven minutes late – enough to give you extra time for 11th-hour problems, but not so long you worry no one’s coming because they all hate you. I’ll bring a carefully thought-out gift, but not flowers, because that creates an extra job – putting them in water, finding a vase – at the very moment you least need another thing to do. I will take responsibility for keeping the conversation going, and ensure that everybody is included within it, like my life depends on it. I’ll oooh and ahhh at whatever you serve – non-cooks are always the best people to feed, because we’re impressed with anything beyond our repertoire (toast and cereal, thanks for asking). I’ll help clear the table in an unobtrusive, non-martyr-y way. I won’t leave too early or stay too long. When it comes to guesting, I am the dream.The problem now is payback. Post epiphany, I only want to be the guest star and never host again. But is it OK for all of us to stay in our lanes, play only to our strengths? Obviously, that’s the logical solution, which would be better and more enjoyable for everybody. But if one party repeatedly doles out invites while the other accepts but never returns the favour, will it lead to resentment? I suppose only the hosts among us can answer that. Which is worse? Feeling like you’re being taken advantage of? Or having to come to my house for dinner?Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Bonnie Blue’s baby outrage – and the dangers of our extreme attention economy | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The porn performer and new mother has posted a video of herself holding a baby, while promoting sexual content. It exposes something horrifying about our era, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The porn performer and new mother has posted a video of herself holding a baby, while promoting sexual content. It exposes something horrifying about our era, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Enrage to engage … Bonnie Blue.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnrage to engage … Bonnie Blue.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesOpinionPornographyBonnie Blue’s baby outrage – and the dangers of our extreme attention economyArwa MahdawiThe porn performer and new mother has posted a video of herself holding a baby, while promoting sexual content. It exposes something horrifying about our eraTue 15 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTShareBonnie Blue has mademillions of poundsby having sex with thousands of men. I suppose that last part isn’t particularly unusual for a sex worker; it’s basically the job description. But Blue has reached an unusual level of fame for the profession through grotesque stunts such as having sex with 1,057 men in 12 hours and preying on young men with “barely legal” content and university “bang bus” tours. She’s notorious enough that she was the subject of aChannel 4 documentarylast year.In short, Blue (real name: Tia Billinger), possesses two of the most important qualities for financial success in the modern world: shamelessness and a keen understanding that you’ve often got to go to extremes to cut through in today’s attention economy. She is exploiting the idea that it is profitable to “enrage to engage”: the business model baked into every social media algorithm.Now it seems that Blue,who gave birthto her first child (father unconfirmed) last month, is carrying that enrage-to-engage ethos into motherhood. She has been sharing postpartum content with her subscribers and recently escalated to posting a video where she is holding a baby and is surrounded by men in balaclavas while promoting her sexual content. It is unclear if it’s actually her baby or a doll in the video but, either way, it’s disturbing. So much so that it’s even got me agreeing with the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, for perhaps the first time ever. Speaking to Sky News last week, Badenoch said that the video was a “safeguarding issue”. She added that while it is tempting to ignore the whole disgusting affair, doing so risks “normalising babies in porn adverts”.In response, Blue sent Sky News a statement insisting “my baby is loved, protected, and incredibly well cared for”. Blue may love her baby but there is obviously nothing protective about using your child to entice people to watch you perform sexual acts. Clearly there should be an investigation into this child’s welfare.While she has taken it to a dangerous extreme, Blue isn’t the only parent to be recklessly using their child as a prop on social media to make a buck. There are endless family influencers who share intimate details of their kids’ lives and splash their images all over the internet without theirinformed consent. Then there are all the budding “momagers” who run Instagram accounts for their young girls, hoping it will lead to a modelling or influencer career down the line. In 2024, theNew York Timesanalysed 5,000 mum-run accounts of young girls and found that while “men accounted for about 35% of the audience overall”, many large accounts with “more than 100,000 followers had a male audience of over 75%”.The NYT also documented many instances of grown men sending explicit messages to these underage accounts or reposting pictures, with “even some egregious violations [leading] to no action by Meta”. Which isn’t surprising when you look at the company’s history. In aJuly 2020 internal chat, which was made public in court documents, one employee asked what the company was doing about child grooming. Another replied: “Child safety is an explicit non-goal this half.” Gotta concentrate on ramping up profits so Mark Zuckerberg can build a bigger bunker! Instagram has since instituted more content guardrails for child safety but still faces questions aboutwhether it could do more.Blue is obviously incredibly problematic. But the broader problem here is that the digital economy, with its warped incentive structures, rewards this sort of depraved and extreme behaviour. And while shamelessness can now be a lucrative career path, the traditional route to a comfortable middle-class life has been destroyed. The UK has seen more than a decade ofwage stagnationwhile house prices and the cost of living have rocketed.The job market is grim, particularly for new graduates. AI, if it doesn’t kill us all, is going to make everything worse. It’s no wonder so many people want to be influencers, and no wonder so many people will chase online fame no matter how low they have to stoop to achieve it. Blue’s latest stunt is obscene, but so too is this brave new world the tech bros have forged. It feels as if we’re all screwed.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Are you outraged by Sydney Sweeney – again? More fool you | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Today it’s a silly sports betting ad, but I can’t see anything she’s done that’s worth this ire. She’s in her 20s: she does dumb things. Enjoy! says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Today it’s a silly sports betting ad, but I can’t see anything she’s done that’s worth this ire. She’s in her 20s: she does dumb things. Enjoy! says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Sydney Sweeney at Variety’s Power of Women event at the Beverly Hills hotel, Los Angeles, 29 October 2025.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney at Variety’s Power of Women event at the Beverly Hills hotel, Los Angeles, 29 October 2025.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesOpinionSydney SweeneyAre you outraged by Sydney Sweeney – again? More fool youMarina HydeToday it’s a silly sports betting ad, but I can’t see anything she’s done that’s worth this ire. She’s in her 20s: she does dumb things. Enjoy!Tue 15 Sep 2026 05.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTShareWould it be insanely unfashionable to defend Sydney Sweeney? You may or may not have heard that the Euphoria star has done anad for a sports betting site. Sorry, I think we still have to call them “sports prediction markets” in the United States, which only recently popped its legalised sports betting cherry, and is behaving like a complete teenage boy about the whole thing. Anyway, among other poses, the ad features a naked Sydney holding a couple of American footballs over her breasts, which are – and I feel she would want us to acknowledge this – seriously among the very best in Hollywood. Maybe THE best. Listen, it is what it is. Life would be very boring if we couldn’t say so with a twinkle.Forgive me. Life is, in fact, very, very boring, because yet another Sydney Sweeney-advertising-centred firestorm has been ignited by this ad. (Last year, some lunatic genuinely suggested her “good jeans”American Eagle adwas something to do with white supremacy and eugenics.) Her latest product endorsement has drawn the ire of acascade of female athletes, who have described it variously as demeaning women’s sport, sexualised representation of athletes, and “a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, [and] every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”.Come on. With respect, I just don’t think it’s a kick in the face for any of those things. Not to be a crazed optimist, but the great thing about where women’s sport has got to today is that it feels a whole lot bigger and stronger and more compelling than whetherSydney Sweeneydid or didn’t get her tits out for a gambling ad. I can’t help feeling it would have been cooler for women’s sport to simply not even mention the naked gambling ad at all. And, if it had to, maybe focus on the gambling bit rather than the woman advertising it. I haven’t definitively run the numbers on this, but instinct tells me that gambling wrecks a lot more lives than Sydney Sweeney.Honestly, not everyone has to be the same and on-message, and I could not be more convinced that Sweeney adds to the gaiety of the nations. I love it that she’s out there in the culture, pissing off reflexively judgmental people who ignore so many bigger issues but have really strong views on sexy ad campaigns. And even slightly sexist ones. I truly loved it when, after one controversy or another a couple of years ago, Sydneyposted a picture of herselfin a sweatshirt reading: “SORRY FOR HAVING GREAT TITS AND CORRECT OPINIONS”. (Would also like to know where you buy this sweatshirt, etc.)View image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney and Scooter Braun in Venice for the Venice film festival, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Stefano Mazzola/GC ImagesThat she has emerged as such a frequent culture wars punching bag says so much more about the predictable, playable nature of her serial detractors than it does about her. Why can’t they just face it – Sydney’s gonna Sweeney. None of it feels like that big of a deal in the grand scheme of things.Or rather, it does to some. After another ad campaign last year, some fashion analystgasped to the New York Times: “It seems like she’s not embarrassed or ashamed promoting all of these different projects.” Hmm. Always great to see women implying other women should be feeling shame for hideous crimes like being a face of both Miu Miu AND Armani Beauty. The previous year, a columnist had described Sydney as “problematic yet unashamed”, which, ironically, I found somewhat problematic. Have to say, I’m a big fan of women not being made to feel shame unless whatever they’ve done is really quite bad.Indeed, it was after a veteran female producer and film studies professorpublicly dismissed heras not pretty and bad at acting that Sweeney gave a reactive interview in whichshe observed of Hollywood: “This entire industry, all people say is ‘women empowering other women’. None of it’s happening. All of it is fake and a front for all the other shit that they say behind everyone’s back.” Amazing. Because where’s the lie? Inevitably, it was her who got branded unsisterly for saying it.A few months later, non-insult was added to non-injury once it emerged that Sydney was dating the considerably older former Taylor Swift foe/Justin Bieber manager Scooter Braun, who’s a sort of music industry vampire but not in a hot way. I saw someone who obviously fancied Sweeney lamenting this romance as “like a 19-year-old wonderkid signing for Al-Nassr”, which is a fun joke and about the level of seriousness with which we should treat other people’s dating choices. Don’t worry about it, guys! It’s not likeyouhave to have sex with Scooter Braun. She’s doing it for you – relax.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUltimately, I always feel somewhat compelled to defend Sydney’s right to do whatever stupid things she feels like in her 20s, safe – if not sound – in the knowledge that she will be forced to spend her entire 30s and probably her entire 40s atoning for every single one of them in every single interview, where every single reporter will just really want her to express shame and/or personal growth. It’s all such an endlessly dreary bore. There must be less repressed and joyless things to do with our time. While we spend far too long figuring those out, I do hope Sweeney finds a way to continue apparently not giving a shit – and that everyone else considers they might have more fun if they took a leaf out of her book from time to time.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship | Carolin Würfel | The Guardian
description: Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too, says writer Carolin Würfel
Author: Carolin Würfel
Headline: Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too, says writer Carolin Würfel
Content: A far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) rally in Magdeburg, Germany, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenA far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) rally in Magdeburg, Germany, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersOpinionGermanyI know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorshipCarolin WürfelGrievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer tooTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 04.22 EDTShareThe fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, thefar-right, anti-immigrant, pro-KremlinAlternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era.The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff?I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union(CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.”By 2004, a year before I graduated, thefar-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliamentfor the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise.Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadilyin easternGermanyever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going.But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany.A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave aninterviewto the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.”The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions.You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask.The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD. It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow?I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish?View image in fullscreenPeople from East and West Berlin climbing on the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, Germany in 1989.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyIt’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around.In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was theTreuhand– the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification,94% of East German companieswere taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximatelytwo million jobswere eliminated in the east.In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless,as unemployment in the east skyrocketed.Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?”In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund poses for pictures with a supporter as he campaigns in Saxony-Anhalt, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersOne of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy.Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic | Jörg LauRead moreWhat many have not realised yetis that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote.And for now, that was what counted most.Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen.A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it.In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know.Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Opposition to Mamdani’s 9/11 remembrance was painful to witness | Francine Prose | The Guardian
description: A petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacks
Author: Francine Prose
Headline: A petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacks
Content: ‘Mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.’Photograph: Hiroko Masuike/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.’Photograph: Hiroko Masuike/ReutersOpinionSeptember 11 2001Opposition to Mamdani’s 9/11 remembrance was painful to witnessFrancine ProseA petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacksTue 15 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTShareEveryone who was inNew Yorkon 11 September 2001 has their 9/11 story. My husband and I were at JFK, boarding a plane to San Francisco. Our two sons were home in lower Manhattan, a block away from my 85-year-old mother. They watched the towers fall from our corner. The weather was radiantly beautiful.For a long time, the faces of the missing were everywhere. Their eyes seemed to follow us from the makeshift shrine outside St Vincent’s hospital to the window of our local bodega. We cried at random moments. We slept badly.No one who lived downtown could possibly be surprised by the recently released report about thetoxicity of the airduring those weeks and months. We inhaled it with every breath. Nothing else has ever smelled like that. I never want to smell that again.But I also recall the powerful sense that New Yorkers were in this together. Every firehouse was a memorial. We brought flowers, awkwardly expressed our gratitude, paid our respects. Taxis with passengers in them slowed down and gave people rides. People asked strangers if they were OK when they obviously weren’t OK. It was a kind of a joke: if, weeks after the towers fell, you still remained too scared to be in a crowd or an elevator or to take the subway, it meant that the terrorists had won. But like so many jokes, it had a serious undercurrent.The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans | Nesrine MalikRead moreI know that those days weren’t the same for everyone. South Asian and Middle Eastern kids were isolated and bullied at school, their families harassed on the street. A Sikh gas station owner was shot by a gunman who thought he was Muslim. But mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.That’s why I found it so painful to read, over the last few weeks, that more than 100,000 people had signed a petition designed to prevent the New York mayor,Zohran Mamdani, from attending the official 9/11 commemoration ceremony. Among the reasons offered by rightwing politicians and by the families of some victims was the claim that the mayor should be barred from participating because of “public positions, associations and responses to rhetoric”.The flimsiness, vagueness and illogic of these charges only reveals the obvious. In the eyes of some, the reason why the mayor’s presence would dishonor the dead is not about anything he did. It’s about the fact that, like the men who flew their planes into the towers, Zohran Mamdani is Muslim.Doesn’t it matter that Mamdani was nine years old at the time of the attack on the World Trade Center? Doesn’t it matter that he has never advocated state-sponsored terrorism? Doesn’t it matter that during the election and while in office he promised and has subsequently tried to make life more livable for every New Yorker, regardless of faith, race and ethnicity? Doesn’t it matter that the mayor of New York belongs at an event commemorating something historic that happened in his city?double quotation markIt’s not that hard to understand the roots of so much bitterness and frustration. But it’s dispiriting to see it so misdirectedTo blame all Muslims for the crimes of a very small faction is like blaming every Christian for the evils of Hitler, Stalin and Ted Bundy, like blaming every Jew for the illicit activities of the mob boss Meyer Lansky, like holding writer Arundhati Roy responsible for India’s periodic anti-Muslim riots.On September 11, Mayor Mamdani, who had spent the previous days visiting firehouses, talking with victims’ families, hearing about the persistent health problems of first responders and people who lived near Ground Zero, and releasing the long-secret air quality report, attended the solemn ceremony. There he did what he always does. He radiated human decency, grace, honesty and kindness, qualities in notably short supply among our current politicians. Rudy Giuliani had condemned Mamdani’s attendance,telling Newsmax: “All of the Muslims he supports are murderers” – but Mamdani shook his hand, a gesture of dignity, fellowship and forgiveness, virtues honored by every religion.9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreAny chance that the openness with which the mayor rose above his critics and greeted his opponents might serve as an inspiring example of maturity and reconciliation, any expectation that his presence might heal the wound being deepened by anti-Muslim agitators was more or less dashed (at least for me) when a disturbing video appeared on my phone. It documented a recent anti-Mamdani protest in Manhattan, which turned violent.Given our troubled economy, given the loss of so many jobs, the sacrifice of so many lives to the opioid crisis, it’s not that hard to understand the roots of so much bitterness and frustration. But it’s dispiriting to see it so misdirected. And it’s scary that the anti-Muslim bigotry and propaganda seem destined to persist beyond this latest round of demonstrations.The good news is that approximately three-quarters of New Yorkers supported Mamdani’s presence at the memorial ceremony. Perhaps some of them remember that day, as do I. I like to imagine they share my sense that those whose who died and those who survived would not want their experience used to fuel the vitriolic bigotry that, in one video clip, prompts a furious protester to spit on a reporter. The reporter is only trying to do his job, to film a response to a catastrophe in which we lost so many of every religion, every color, every age, so many innocent people who believed that they were simply going to work on a gorgeous but otherwise ordinary September morning.Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and SciencesExplore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001OpinionZohran MamdaniRudy GiulianiNew YorkIslamophobiaReligionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Lucy Letby: Thirlwall should have waited for the pending case review | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Important recommendations for neonatal care are shadowed by doubts about the nurse’s convictions
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Important recommendations for neonatal care are shadowed by doubts about the nurse’s convictions
Content: ‘As previous inquiries have also found, there are serious problems around accountability, openness and safeguarding in the NHS.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘As previous inquiries have also found, there are serious problems around accountability, openness and safeguarding in the NHS.’Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionLucy LetbyThe Guardian view on Lucy Letby: Thirlwall should have waited for the pending case reviewEditorialImportant recommendations for neonatal care are shadowed by doubts about the nurse’s convictionsTue 15 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.59 EDTShareWhen sherejected calls to pause the public inquiryinto the Countess of Chester hospital, where Lucy Letby was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more, Lady Justice Thirlwall said that questions surrounding Letby’s guilt lay outside her terms of reference. The inquiry, she said, would focus on the hospital and its staff, not the convictions. Eighteen months later, with the822-page reportin the public domain, her decision to press on while Letby’s guilt was in the process of being formally challenged looks like a mistake.The report’srecommendations, based on many months of hearings, include strengthened oversight of hospitals by the Care Quality Commission, more support for whistleblowers from the health ombudsman, and clearer monitoring and reporting on the deaths of children. As previous inquiries have also found, there are serious problems around accountability, openness and safeguarding in the NHS. Lady Thirlwall’s conclusions about service improvements should be added to the roster of outstanding actions.View image in fullscreenLady Justice Thirlwall.Photograph: The Thirlwall Inquiry/Getty ImagesThe report’s description of “dysfunctional management and governance; a gulf between hospital leadership and clinicians; and failure to understand the fundamentals of safeguarding” will resonate far beyond the Countess of Chester’s catchment, with families who have been let down by NHS hospitals in other areas. Poor leadership, toxic cultures and resource and workforce pressures are familiar themes, and Yvette Cooper presented her response to the report as part of a wider reset ofmaternity and neonatal services. Proposals for video monitors in neonatal wards are already being developed, she told MPs, along with plans to bar poorly performing managers.No one doubts that this general reset is needed. The report’s analysis of the policies needed to underpin it should be welcomed. But in the case of the Countess of Chester, it is impossible to set aside questions about Letby herself, as Lady Thirlwall sought to do – no doubt partly influenced by the bereaved families’ wish to proceed. The report takes Letby’s guilt, and the risks she posed to newborn babies, as a given; hence the headline finding thatthree babies might have survivedand seven others could have been protected if hospital bosses had taken earlier action over warnings.Two attempts by Letby to appeal against her convictions have beenrejected by judges. But the legal process has not yet run its course, and a decision by the Criminal Cases Review Commission on whether to refer the case to the court of appeal, as a suspected miscarriage of justice, is expected soon. The appeal, if it goes ahead, will rest on a dossier ofmedical evidencerelated to the air injections that Letby was found to have used to kill babies, and insulin that she was found to have used to poison them.Until that decision is made, doubts will continue to swirl over the inquiry’s findings. If any of Letby’s convictions for murder and attempted murder were to be ruled unsafe, then the whole basis of the report would be undermined. For that reason alone, ministers should have intervened when Lady Thirlwall decided against a delay. An inquiry that has so far cost more than £18m, and which is calling for significant changes to NHS services upon which millions of people rely, should not have gone ahead until the criminal justice process was exhausted.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountability | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Quantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly control
Content: ‘Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects.’Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects.’Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesOpinionBank of EnglandThe Guardian view on the Bank of England’s £120bn bill: power without accountabilityEditorialQuantitative tightening has blurred the line between monetary and fiscal policy, leaving ministers accountable for decisions they cannot directly controlTue 15 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.58 EDTShareWhen Labour made the Bank of Englandindependentin 1997, the idea was that the Bank set interest rates while the Treasury taxed and spent. Monetary policy was in Threadneedle Street, fiscal policy in Whitehall. But in August the Bank of England quietly slipped out that its key policy could cost the Treasury£120bn. That policy –quantitative tightening(QT) – clearly ought to be rethought and the policy of the Treasury indemnifying the Bank for its lossesended. Last year, ministers paid the Bank£17bnto cover these arguably notional losses – an amount considerably larger than the budget of the Ministry of Justice, which is dealing with a real prisons crisis.Bank independence was constructed for a world in which monetary policy decisions had predictable and indirect fiscal effects. The financial crisis, Covid, war and fractious trade disputes have contributed to ending that world. The Bank bought up government bonds to support the economy via its quantitative easing (QE) programme. But the constitutional settlement – of an independent central bank working out on its own what to do with those bonds – has not caught up. The game is surely up when a former Bank deputy governor,Charlie Bean, acknowledges that independence cannot justify effectively giving power to an unelected monetary policy committee (MPC) over decisions with great consequences for public spending.View image in fullscreenGeorge Osborne.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAThe Treasury standsbehindthe losses – and gains – made by the bonds bought during QE and held in a Bank of England subsidiary, called theAsset Purchase Facility. The losses are being produced in three ways. First, the Bank is selling these gilts at current market prices. Because their yields are higher than when QE was operating, the gilts are worth less than the APF paid for them. Second, the APF generates a loss because the £500bn bonds on its balance sheet generate less income than the repayments, charged at the base rate, on the “loan” it took to buy them. Third, gilts bought above their value are booked as a loss when they mature.Labour created the indemnity after the 2009 crash. But it wasGeorge Osbornewho turned it into a quarterlycash machinein 2012. When rates were low, the Treasury profited to the tune of £124bn. Once rates rose, the same mechanism went into reverse – and because it is an uncapped indemnity, even when the windfall has been repaid the Treasury carries on paying the Bank.Ministers should end this arrangement. No other majorcentral bankcarries on in this way. Whatever one thinks of the losses, making the Treasury settle them immediately turns monetary choices into fiscal interventions. Areportthis week says that the Bank and Treasury are drawing up changes to QT to reduce pressure on raising interest rates. Independence seems to have been discarded in favour of quiet coordination. The MPC’s decisions cannot be beyond challenge.Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, calls the overall cost of QT “neutral” – but only, as the economist Patricia Pinopointsout, when assessed over six decades. In fact, billions in cash demands fall within a parliament. Governments do not set budgets, fight elections or run public services over 60 years. It is unsustainable for the Bank to make decisions and have ministers face voters for the political consequences.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The sinister influence of crypto billionaires on our politics | Cryptocurrencies | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the news that Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from Ben Delo
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the news that Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from Ben Delo
Content: ‘When the gravitational pull of crypto wealth begins shaping political parties, we must ask whose interests are being served.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘When the gravitational pull of crypto wealth begins shaping political parties, we must ask whose interests are being served.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianCryptocurrenciesLettersThe sinister influence of crypto billionaires on our politicsReaders respond to the news that Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from Ben DeloTue 15 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTShareCryptocurrency is often sold as decentralised and democratic, yet its real behaviour resembles gravity: wealth is pulled inexorably into a few vast centres while draining from everyone else (Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo, 12 September). Early adopters, insiders and whales acquire huge holdings at negligible cost. Their size then shapes the market, drawing in ordinary investors whose money ultimately fuels those already at the top.Because crypto generates no cash flow and produces little real economic output, it becomes structurally zero‑sum. One person’s gain is another’s loss, and the system relies on a continual inflow of participants whose contributions sustain the fortunes of a minority.It is troubling that some of the biggest beneficiaries of this system have become major donors toReform UK. The party presents itself as a champion of ordinary people, yet it is being funded by individuals whose wealth largely comes from mechanisms that disadvantage those very people. Their interest in Reform is not altruistic; it reflects a desire for deregulation, reduced oversight and a political environment favourable to speculative wealth and offshore structures.The danger is not only financial, but democratic. When the gravitational pull of crypto wealth begins shaping political parties, we must ask whose interests are being served: those of the public, or those of the black holes at the centre of the crypto universe?Colin CharltonMacclesfield, CheshireYour report on Christopher Harborne’s £36m donation to Reform UK contains an irony worth exploring. Reform presents itself as an insurgent, grassroots movement, with stopping the small boats at the centre of its politics. Yet its new financial power now comes partly from a billionaire who owns about12% of Tether, issuer of USDT — the dominant “stablecoin” (payment) of the offshore cryptocurrency economy.This matters because money laundering is not a victimless financial offence, andEuropol has warnedthat cryptocurrencies are increasingly used by human traffickers to receive payments, pay facilitators and launder their profits.There is an uncomfortable question for Reform voters. How does a party built around opposition to irregular migration feel about becoming increasingly dependent on fortunes generated within a financial ecosystem that has also proved useful to the criminal networks facilitating and profiting from irregular migration?Dr Neil SmithBuckfastleigh, DevonThe £72m given to Reform by two crypto billionaires has revealed an abysmal failure to properly regulate party financing. A cap on national party spending in the year before a general election was introduced in 2000, but there is no cap on party spending in any of the years in between general elections. Nor is there any cap on the size of donations that can be made by a single individual. The new £100,000 cap proposed by the government (Will the £72m of donations to Reform UK be allowed?, 14 September)will only apply to UK citizens living overseas.In 2023, the last Conservative government raised the national cap for spending in election years from £20m to £36m. The spending of the £72m donations could legally be targeted at 72 seats, spent over two years, with a total of national spending of £1m in each of them. If parties did not think that financial resources won seats, then they would not try so hard to raise funds to win them. Unless the rules change our democracy is for sale.ChrisRennardLiberal Democrat, House of LordsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Social media is promoting harmful attitudes towards sun exposure | Skin cancer | The Guardian
description: Letter: An awareness campaign isn’t enough. The UK should ban commercial sunbeds, writes Dr Amy Perkins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: An awareness campaign isn’t enough. The UK should ban commercial sunbeds, writes Dr Amy Perkins
Content: ‘UV radiation from sunbeds is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization’s cancer agency.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘UV radiation from sunbeds is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the World Health Organization’s cancer agency.’Photograph: Andrew Fox/AlamySkin cancerLettersSocial media is promoting harmful attitudes towards sun exposureAn awareness campaign isn’t enough. The UK should ban commercial sunbeds, writesDr Amy PerkinsTue 15 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTShareRising melanoma rates demand more than another awareness campaign (Editorial, 7 August). As a consultant dermatologist with a special interest in the health impacts of social media, I see how digital platforms are normalising harmful attitudes towards sun exposure, while the sunbed industry thrives.Social media algorithms reward content that provokes strong reactions. Extreme tanning routines, dramatic before-and-after images andmisleading health claimscan therefore travel further than balanced medical advice. I have previously raised the alarm about irresponsible sunbed advertising, including claims that sunbeds offer a net health benefit. Such promotion is indefensible: UV radiation from sunbeds is classified as aGroup 1 carcinogenby the World Health Organization’s cancer agency.This is also a health-equity issue. Sunbed outlets are more densely concentrated in deprived communities. Although people with lighter skin tones face the greatest skin-cancer risk, no skin tone is immune. This matters increasingly as climate change and warmer weather alter patterns of outdoor behaviour and UV exposure.The government should place a national skin-cancer prevention strategy at the heart of itsnational cancer plan. We should combine practical behaviour-change programmes, community-led education and better support for early detection.Australia, Brazil and Iran have banned commercial sunbeds;the UK should follow. It is easy to dismiss their example as relevant only to traditionally hotter countries; in a warming world,that argument no longer holds.Prevention must begin in childhood.Schools can register withSun Safe Schools, run by the skin cancer charity Skcin, to embed sun-safe habits early. This should be paired with digital literacy that teaches children to question online health claims, recognise commercial influence and understand how algorithms shape their feeds.Awareness matters, but we need safer environments, responsible regulation and lasting cultural change to help shape our futures.Dr Amy PerkinsConsultant dermatologist, GlasgowHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t decide the BBC’s fate behind closed doors | BBC | The Guardian
description: Letter: The details of the BBC charter renewal are too important to be negotiated in secret, writes Phil Harding, a former controller of the corporation’s editorial policy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The details of the BBC charter renewal are too important to be negotiated in secret, writes Phil Harding, a former controller of the corporation’s editorial policy
Content: To what extent should the BBC eschew ratings and stick only to the cultural Olympian heights?Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenTo what extent should the BBC eschew ratings and stick only to the cultural Olympian heights?Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersBBCLettersDon’t decide the BBC’s fate behind closed doorsThe details of the BBC charter renewal are too important to be negotiated in secret, writesPhil Harding,a former controller of the corporation’s editorial policyTue 15 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTShareThe Guardian is right to bring the future of the BBC and its funding back into the spotlight (‘A completely unique opportunity’: the secretive process that will decide the BBC’s future, 10 September). This is too important an issue and the BBC is too important an institution for this to be decided behind the closed doors of Whitehall.Many things have been altered radically by the recent drastic changes in communications technology, but others still have a very familiar feel to them. Chief among these is the extent to which the BBC should eschew ratings and stick only to the cultural Olympian heights. This dilemma was best summed up by the BBC’s former director of programmes, Huw Wheldon, whenhe saidthat it was the job of the BBC “to make the popular good and make the good popular”. It still stands today.Phil HardingFormer editor, Today programme, and former controller of BBC editorial policyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
