title: Music education is powerful, yet its provision is frail | Music | The Guardian
description: Letters: Elizabeth Williams and Luke Madams respond to an article by Robert Ames in which he argues that doors are closing for working-class musicians
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Elizabeth Williams and Luke Madams respond to an article by Robert Ames in which he argues that doors are closing for working-class musicians
Content: ‘The educational and developmental benefits of learning an instrument are well documented.’Photograph: Jose Luis Pelaez Inc/GettyView image in fullscreen‘The educational and developmental benefits of learning an instrument are well documented.’Photograph: Jose Luis Pelaez Inc/GettyMusicLettersMusic education is powerful, yet its provision is frailElizabeth WilliamsandLuke Madamsrespond to an article by Robert Ames in which he argues that doors are closing for working-class musiciansTue 15 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTShareFurther to Robert Ames’s article (I co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musicians, 9 September), I have seen first-hand both the transformative power of music education and the fragility of its provision.I am the chair of trustees ofMaking Music, Changing Lives(MMCL), a Cardiff-based charity established in 2009 to provide musical opportunities for children and young people in the low-income communities of Ely and Caerau. Around 40 young people are loaned instruments for free and they receive free or heavily subsidised weekly tuition from highly-qualified teachers, and the opportunity to play and perform in an orchestra. We also organise school holiday projects, concerts for local schools, and free tickets to professional concerts.The educational and developmental benefits of learning an instrument are well documented. MMCL has now been running long enough for former participants to have progressed to university, studying subjects including medicine, computer science and mathematics. Even more importantly, we hope that our young people leave us with a lifelong joy of music-making.However, despite its success, MMCL survives hand to mouth. We are fortunate to benefit from affordable premises provided by the diocese of Llandaff and from the dedication of staff and volunteers, yet we receive no regular support from either the Welsh government or the local authority. Our future depends on grants and donations that are never guaranteed.Charities such as MMCL can make a difference in their local areas, but they cannot provide a consistent, nationwide solution. As music education continues to decline in many schools, we risk creating a future in which opportunities like those that enabled Ames’s own musical journey become increasingly unavailable to children from less affluent backgrounds.Elizabeth WilliamsCardiffRobert Ames is right that classical music’s economics, not just its outreach programmes, is the bigger barrier. I love composing music and am building a life doing it. I have a postgraduate degree in composition, which I obtained by commuting to London by coach, I’ve worked in theatre, had music on the radio, spoken at conferences and funded and directed my own learning, but it’s not close to being my main source of income. Without financial support, this is something you can only do because you can’t imagine yourself doing anything else.To record a new solo piano project to a standard fit for licensing and broadcast, I recently applied to a funding body to cover the costs of a studio session and travel. This is a few hundred pounds in total for a big career step, but saving money from my admin and teaching work to fund it and mixing and mastering costs, as I’ve done previously, means the process takes longer. It is also money I can’t afford to waste. This is the same “margin for error” issue that Ames describes, just smaller and quieter. It shows up in whether a finished piece of music ever gets recorded at all, long before anyone judges it on its merits.I suspect there are far more people than most realise simply getting on with this quietly, teaching, temping, assembling whatever patchwork of work lets them keep composing or performing, without much fuss made of it. I’m somebody who is irritated by “is classical music dying?” articles, but if the culture only hears the work of people who can absorb costs like these without a second thought, insularity is its endpoint.Luke MadamsCanterburyExplore more on these topicsMusicClassical musicWaleslettersShareReuse this content

title: Szoboszlai screamer seals Liverpool’s progress as De Zerbi’s Spurs woes grow | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Liverpool won the Carabao Cup third-round tie 3-1 against Tottenham via impressive strikes from Alexis Mac Allister, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool won the Carabao Cup third-round tie 3-1 against Tottenham via impressive strikes from Alexis Mac Allister, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai
Content: Dominik Szoboszlai salutes Anfield after his strike gave Liverpool a 3-1 lead in stoppage time.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai salutes Anfield after his strike gave Liverpool a 3-1 lead in stoppage time.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersCarabao CupSzoboszlai screamer seals Liverpool’s progress as De Zerbi’s Spurs woes growAndy Hunterat AnfieldTue 15 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham scored and Roberto De Zerbi eulogised the quality at his disposal, yet try telling Spurs’ suffering away support there was consolation to be found at Anfield.Liverpooltoyed with De Zerbi by advancing into round four with a quality of finishing that he can only dream of.While the Spurs head coach talked a good game and his players played a pretty one in harmless areas, Liverpool produced the only effective one. Alexis Mac Allister promoted his claims for a new contract forthe second midweek in successionwith an excellent strike and Cody Gakpo continued his fine early season form with a smart second plus an assist. But both were overshadowed by Dominik Szoboszlai’s stupendous 25-yard finish in stoppage time.Max Dowman doubles up for Arsenal’s back-ups to beat Ipswich in Carabao CupRead more“It was a worldie,” said Liverpool’s head coach, Andoni Iraola, whose changes injected energy and bite into the home display. “The thing with Dom is you trust him to score before he shoots. With others you might think it’s too far out, but not with him.”Spurs caused a few anxieties when Conor Gallagher headed home after Giorgi Mamardashvili’s failure to deal with a Mateus Fernandes corner. But the Liverpool stand-in keeper atoned with several impressive stops, the best from Omar Marmoush, and the visitors’ wastefulness would prove another factor in their downfall. Defeat was deserved, despite De ­Zerbi’s claims to the contrary.“We have to shoot more, we have to shoot better and we have to finish better the clear situations,” said the Spurs head coach. “But we are sorry for the result, disappointed, frustrated. I think it is unfair but we have to be stronger in these unlucky moments. In these five or six games we have not been lucky. We have to improve a lot of things but we are in the right way. I have big confidence and a big opinion of my players.”View image in fullscreenGiorgi Mamardashvili clutches the ball as Destiny Udogie runs by.Photograph: Jon Super/APDe Zerbi made eight changes fromSaturday’s stalemate with Everton, Iraola made 10 from a similarlydrab draw against Fulham. It was new faces but a similar story for Spurs as, for the second successive game against Merseyside opposition, they seized control from the start but failed to capitalise when in the ascendancy. Lucas Bergvall and Mohammed Kudus both should have scored from left-wing crosses by Destiny Udogie. The former allowed Mamardashvili to make an ­important, improvised save when he had the entire goal to aim for. The latter volleyed over from four yards out.Liverpool turned the tide thanks to impressive contributions from the young quartet of Lewis Koumas, James McConnell, Trey Nyoni and Rio Ngumoha. Koumas led the line with an aggression and work rate that Iraola wants from all of his forwards, regardless of their price tags.Mac Allister opened the scoring when Udogie’s attempt to halt Ngumoha’s weaving run across the area put the ball on a plate for the incoming midfielder. Opening his body, Mac Allister went for power and placement and swept a shot into Martin Dubravka’s top left-hand corner.View image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Alexis Mac Allister fires past Martin Dubravka to open the scoring.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersMac Allister’s opener arrived between Spurs’ two missed chances from Bergvall and Kudus. Another fine Liverpool move and emphatic finish punished the visitors a second time nine minutes after the restart. McConnell and Ngumoha were heavily involved before Milos Kerkez picked out Mac Allister in space, prompting groans from the Kop over the full-back’s refusal to shoot. They were quickly silenced as the Argentina international’s first-time pass found Gakpo, who stepped inside a nonexistent challenge from Archie Gray and beat Dubravka with an angled drive.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll hope appeared to have been lost for Spurs, not that their finishing offered much in the first place, but the stoic backing of their admirable away support indicated ­otherwise. The visitors were handed a lifeline when Mamardashvili and Jeremie Frimpong failed to deal with a Fernandes corner. The goalkeeper missed his attempt to punch clear and Gallagher, left alone at the back post by Frimpong, had the simple task of heading in from close range.Quick GuideRoundup: Bass and Jones Peterborough's shootout heroesShowPeterboroughmoved into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup for the first time since 2009 thanks to a 7-6 penalty shootout victory overBarnsleythat followed a thrilling 3-3 draw between the two League One sides.Barnsley were handed the lead after 61 seconds when a clearance by the Peterborough goalkeeper, Alex Bass, was charged down by Cameron McGeehan, with the Tykes captain nodding in after the ball had come off the bar.Peterborough equalised in the 19th minute when Lucca Mendonca’s cross was pushed out by the Barnsley goalkeeper, Kieran Flavell, as far as Harry Leonard, who prodded in.The hosts then completed the turnaround after 27 minutes when Harley Mills’ free-kick was headed in by the unmarked Danny Ormerod. But the Tykes were level five minutes before half-time when Reyes Cleary beat Mendonca with ease down the left before placing his shot into the bottom corner.The visitors looked to have won it when Cleary bent in his second in the 74th minute, but Ormerod sent the tie to penalties with by heading in Mills’ cross with just two minutes remaining.After 12 successful spot-kicks, a tame effort from Barnsley’s Luke Alker was saved by Bass, giving Harrison Jones the chance to send the hosts through, which he dispatched.Brentfordemerged from a tense finish againstReadingto book their place in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a 2-1 victory. Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho were on target in the first half as the Premier League club showed a clinical touch against League One opposition, who produced a number of chances but lacked the firepower to finish them off. Paudie O’Connor eventually pulled one back to revive Reading’s challenge and Brentford could not rest easy in the remaining 18 minutes, although the substitute Igor Thiago was among those who should have killed the match off.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Mamardashvili made amends in superb style to deny Marmoush an equaliser when the forward’s shot took a slight deflection off ­Ronald Araújo. At the other end Tosin Adarabioyo escaped twice: first with a wayward pass that led to a gilt-edged chance for Szoboszlai, saved by Dubravka, and when Alexander Isak’s cross struck his arm. There was no video assistant referee in operation to correct the decision.Spurs would not escape a third time. In stoppage time, Szoboszlai let Gakpo’s flick roll off his chest before thumping a fabulous shot beyond Dubravka from long range. He celebrated by pointing to his ear, perhaps in response to the criticism his display against Fulham had attracted. The Liverpool vice-captain’s concerns pale in comparison to De Zerbi’s and his toothless team.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupLiverpoolTottenham Hotspurmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Max Dowman doubles up for Arsenal’s back-ups to beat Ipswich in Carabao Cup | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Two mesmerising goals in a man-of-the-match display from Max Dowman underlined why the 16-year-old has been compared to a certain Lionel Messi by his manager, Mikel Arteta, as Ipswich were swatted aside with ease
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Two mesmerising goals in a man-of-the-match display from Max Dowman underlined why the 16-year-old has been compared to a certain Lionel Messi by his manager, Mikel Arteta, as Ipswich were swatted aside with ease
Content: Max Dowman (right) scores Arsenal’s third goal – his second – at Ipswich.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAView image in fullscreenMax Dowman (right) scores Arsenal’s third goal – his second – at Ipswich.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PACarabao CupMax Dowman doubles up for Arsenal’s back-ups to beat Ipswich in Carabao CupEd Aaronsat Portman RoadTue 15 Sep 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bad news for everyone else is that Arsenal’s next generation is already here. Two mesmerising goals and an assist in a man-of-the-match display from Max Dowman underlined why the 16-year-old has been compared to a certain Lionel Messi by his manager, Mikel Arteta, as Ipswich were swatted aside with ease. Almost as impressive was the performance of the 17-year-old Marli Salmon, who oozed class in central defence on only the second senior start of his career.Ipswich won here the lasttime these two sides met in this competition, in 2011, but were beaten 3-0 in the second leg of the semi-final at the Emirates beforeArsenal infam­ously lost to Birminghamin the final. ­Fifteen years on, Gary O’Neil’s heavily rotated side stood no chance against last year’s runners up after Dowman’s brilliant opening goal. Noni Madueke and the stand-in skipper Mikel Merino were also on target as Arsenal made it seven wins out of seven to start the new campaign. Having finally ended their long wait for silverware in style, this team are hungry for more and know they can now rely on one of the most exciting talents ever to have emerged from their Hale End academy.Szoboszlai screamer seals Liverpool’s progress as De Zerbi’s Spurs woes growRead more“He can deliver those actions effortlessly. That’s his biggest quality,” said Arteta of the delightful shimmy that preceded Dowman’s first goal. “It’s a joy to have him. But what we have to do is look after him. He’s 16 years old, you don’t see that in this league. In other leagues in Europe, that’s a totally different context. We really need to make sure every time we throw him in, he’s in the right context with the right ­preparation. That’s what we are ­trying to do.”Both managers made their prior­ities clear as there were a combined 19 changes from their sides’ wins in the Premier League at the weekend. After a summer of heavy spending, many of those who helped Ipswich bounce straight back from the Championship last season were given an opportunity to stake a claim but largely failed to do so. “It’s the most extreme test that you can face,” admitted O’Neil. “Every time we made a mistake we were punished.”Dowman’s most recent first-team appearance was in the final game of last season when Arsenal were crowned champions, and he has since completed his GCSEs before spending a week in New York during the World Cup where he rubbed shoulders with Paul Pogba.Arteta said beforehand he would have “earn his minutes” like anyone else and it only took seven of them for Dowman to seize his opportunity. Ipswich’s fans were taunting their Arsenal counterparts about never being crowned European champions when he muscled Santiago Núñez off the ball on the halfway line and set off towards the penalty area. The imposing figure of Cédric Kipré – all 6ft 3in of him – was all that stood in Dowman’s way but he went past the Ivory Coast defender in a flurry of feet before cooly dispatching a shot into the corner and performing a Thierry Henry knee slide for good measure.Quick GuideRoundup: Bass and Jones Peterborough's shootout heroesShowPeterboroughmoved into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup for the first time since 2009 thanks to a 7-6 penalty shootout victory overBarnsleythat followed a thrilling 3-3 draw between the two League One sides.Barnsley were handed the lead after 61 seconds when a clearance by the Peterborough goalkeeper, Alex Bass, was charged down by Cameron McGeehan, with the Tykes captain nodding in after the ball had come off the bar.Peterborough equalised in the 19th minute when Lucca Mendonca’s cross was pushed out by the Barnsley goalkeeper, Kieran Flavell, as far as Harry Leonard, who prodded in.The hosts then completed the turnaround after 27 minutes when Harley Mills’ free-kick was headed in by the unmarked Danny Ormerod. But the Tykes were level five minutes before half-time when Reyes Cleary beat Mendonca with ease down the left before placing his shot into the bottom corner.The visitors looked to have won it when Cleary bent in his second in the 74th minute, but Ormerod sent the tie to penalties with by heading in Mills’ cross with just two minutes remaining.After 12 successful spot-kicks, a tame effort from Barnsley’s Luke Alker was saved by Bass, giving Harrison Jones the chance to send the hosts through, which he dispatched.Brentfordemerged from a tense finish againstReadingto book their place in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a 2-1 victory. Callum Wilson and Fabio Carvalho were on target in the first half as the Premier League club showed a clinical touch against League One opposition, who produced a number of chances but lacked the firepower to finish them off. Paudie O’Connor eventually pulled one back to revive Reading’s challenge and Brentford could not rest easy in the remaining 18 minutes, although the substitute Igor Thiago was among those who should have killed the match off.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Ipswich’s mission got even harder when Madueke hammered in after Bruno Guimarães and Merino had combined to set him up after Dowman had started the press. Barely a quarter of an hour had been played. To their credit, the hosts rallied and it needed a clearance off the line from Salmon to deny Zian Flemming. Not to be outdone by Dowman, Salmon – who signed his professional contact when he turned 17 last month having also played in the Champions League and FA Cup last season – set out on a slaloming run just before half-time after calmly turning his way out of trouble under pressure from Flemming, drawing a round of applause from the Arsenal bench.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe former Arsenal player Chuba Akpom scores Ipswich’s second goal.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesIpswich’s hopes of mounting a comeback were extinguished within two minutes of the restart when Dowman struck again. Martín Zubimendi’s pass found him on the edge of the six-yard box and the finish was caressed into the far corner. Merino then curled home off the post from Dowman’s touch to put the result beyond any doubt, although the biggest roar of the evening came when Ipswich hit back through Anis Mehmeti after he was set up by the substitute Jack Clarke.Including Myles Lewis-Skelly – a relative veteran these days at 19 and surely in line for an England recall this week after an excellent start to the season – Arsenal had four teenagers on the pitch at the end after the 18-year-old Theo Julienne came on at right-back. Even Ipswich had a Hale End grad­uate in their ranks by then as Chuba Akpom grabbed another consolation in injury time via a deflection. But, not for the last time one suspects, it was Dowman’s name that was on everyone’s lips at the end.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupIpswich TownArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Raheem Sterling could face prison for reckless driving while using nitrous oxide | Raheem Sterling | The Guardian
description: Ex-England footballer pleads guilty and admits to failing to provide a specimen as he appears in court
Author: Sam Cunningham
Headline: Ex-England footballer pleads guilty and admits to failing to provide a specimen as he appears in court
Content: 1:50Bodycam footage shows Raheem Sterling's arrest for dangerous driving – videoRaheem SterlingRaheem Sterling could face prison for reckless driving while using nitrous oxideEx-England footballer pleads guilty and admits to failing to provide a specimen as he appears in courtSam CunninghamTue 15 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaheem Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and could be sent to prison after driving his ­Lamborghini for more than an hour on motorways during rush hour while inhaling nitrous oxide.The former Chelsea and Manchester City forward stood in the dock to accept three charges before­Basingstoke magistrates court heard how he embarked on a ­prolonged period of reckless driving on the M25 and M3, inhaling nitrous oxide ­balloons, before crashing his £270,000 car. Sterling was disqualified from driving and bailed until 25 November, when his sentence will either be determined or referred to the crown court.Sterling also admitted possession of nitrous oxide and refusing to ­provide a specimen.The maximum term for Sterling would be two years in prison, although a sentence of 12 to 18 months is considered more likely and, with mitigation, that could be suspended.Simon Jones, prosecuting, told the court one witness had “genuine concerns the driver might kill someone” and described Sterling’s driving as “absolutely horrendous”.“As she moved past the vehicle she thought the airbag had been deployed, it was a large white deflated balloon,” Jones said. “She had no idea if the driver could see ahead.”View image in fullscreenRaheem Sterling (centre) arriving at Basingstoke magistrates court on Tuesday.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PABetween 7.45am and 8.52am on 28 May, police received multiple calls reporting dangerous driving – shortly after Sterling had returned to England after a loan at Feyenoord, where he had attempted to revive his career.Dashcam footage provided to police by one witness showed Sterling’s car swerving between lanes and almost colliding with the central reservation. Witnesses reported seeing the driver inhaling balloons while driving.After leaving the M3, the Lamborghini veered off the carriageway on the A327 near the Minley interchange in Hampshire. All four tyres blew out and there was damage to the bodywork. Body-worn footage from officers attending the scene, played in court, showed Sterling, 31, sitting in the passenger seat with two canisters on his lap before confirming he had been driving.Jones said Sterling appeared keen to move a deflated balloon from beside him on to the back seat. His saliva was tested and no presence of cannabis or cocaine was found, but he later refused to provide a blood sample to test for other substances.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Another witness told police they had seen the Lamborghini driving erratically at 1.10am. They reported it entering a drive-through at “alarming speed”, Jones said, and saw the driver holding an inflated balloon.After his arrest, Sterling was taken to Basingstoke investigation centre. “During the process he had disclosed to staff that he had a problem with nitrous oxide,” Jones said.Sterling failed a series of impairment tests, including walking in a straight line without swaying and placing his fingertip on the end of his nose. He was also asked to judge 30 seconds with his eyes closed but recorded 52.Jones said Sterling “appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting” during the tests. “His eyelids were drooping, consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.”The former England international, who won 82 caps between 2012 and 2022 and played in five major tournaments, was taken to a medical room where he refused to provide a blood sample without providing a reasonable excuse and despite repeated and clear warnings.At 5.13pm, Sterling was interviewed with a legal representative present. A signed, prepared statement was read out in which he said he had not slept all night and was tired and confused. He then answered “no comment” to officers’ questions.Jason Bartfield KC for the defence did not dispute this was a top-category case, given the prolonged driving and clear serious impairment. Bartfield cautioned, however, that there would have been “short periods” of “serious impairment”, compared with consuming cannabis or alcohol.View image in fullscreenRaheem Sterling after being stopped by police in May.Photograph: Crown Prosecution Service/PABartfield did not accept the car damage was serious, describing it as “relatively superficial” and “minor scratching” alongside the blown tyres. He also argued that the fact there were two canisters in Sterling’s lap when police arrived showed “this was very much not a case of trying to conceal anything from them”.The court was not told the full mitigating circumstances, but ­Bartfield said: “Clearly there is extensive ­personal mitigation. Voluntary steps have been taken to address them. I hope this has weight with the court.”District judge Kirsty Allman ordered a pre-sentence report and adjourned the hearing. She said she had not decided whether to retain jurisdiction or commit sentencing to the crown court. A magistrates court cannot impose a sentence of more than 12 months.“I’m going to release you on unconditional bail,” she said. “If you don’t attend, a warrant will be issued for your arrest. I’m going to disqualify you from driving as of today. You must not drive a motor vehicle on the road as of today. I will determine the period if I sentence you, otherwise it will be for the crown court. You must not drive while disqualified – if you drive while disqualified you will be committing a prisonable offence.”Explore more on these topicsRaheem SterlingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United shocked as talented youngster JJ Gabriel asks to leave | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: The highly regarded 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave a day before he was to be included in Manchester United’s squad to face Brighton
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: The highly regarded 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave a day before he was to be included in Manchester United’s squad to face Brighton
Content: JJ Gabriel training with Manchester United’s first team this month.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJJ Gabriel training with Manchester United’s first team this month.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedManchester United shocked as talented youngster JJ Gabriel asks to leave15-year-old wants his registration to be cancelledHe was to be in squad to face Brighton on WednesdayDominic BoothTue 15 Sep 2026 10.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United have been left confused and shocked by the news that the talented 15-year-old player JJ Gabriel has asked to leave the club, a day before he was to be included in the first-team squad to face Brighton.Gabriel could have become United’s youngest player in the Carabao Cup third-round tie at Old Trafford on Wednesday. But the Guardian understands he has asked for his registration to be cancelled.Are Manchester United as poor as the early Premier League table suggests?Read moreUnited are unsure what has prompted this decision and believe they have done everything they can to show Gabriel and his family there is a pathway to the first team. Those efforts have included meetings with Ruben Amorim, when the Portuguese was head coach, and Sir Alex Ferguson.United believe the situation, first reported bythe Telegraph, is rectifiable given the time remaining on Gabriel’s contract. Club officials say the player has a deal to the end of the season and cannot be deregistered despite his request. The north London-born Gabriel cannot sign a professional contract until he turns 17 in October next year, but can sign a scholarship agreement when he turns 16.Gabriel, who has been with United since the age of 11, has emerged as one of the most exciting prospects at Carrington in years, scoring a hatful of goals for the youth teams, most recently a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut against Sabah last week. He regularly plays for older age groups at United, scoring 26 goals in 29 games last season, and has made two appearances for England Under-17s. Gabriel is also the most recent, and youngest, winner of United’s prestigious Jimmy Murphy young player of the year award. He has regularly trained with the first team.Quick GuideCarrick say VAR blunder will fuel UnitedShowMichael Carrick believes Manchester United will have an edge against Brighton in the Carabao Cup owing to the wrong video assistant referee decision that allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s defeat by Manchester City.United host Fabian Hürzeler’s side on Wednesday aiming to bounce back after Haaland’s 60th-minute strike was judged to be legal by the VAR, who ruled that Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup. Pro Ref admitted the goal should not have been allowed and that Matt Donohue, the VAR, had made the wrong decision. He has been stood down for this weekend's Premier League action.Carrick, speaking before Pro Ref’s statement, was asked whether his players would have an edge against Brighton owing to their annoyance at ruling.“It does give you something, when something like that happens, to use moving forward," the manager said. "The players have got an edge. They've shown that to me since I've been here. We've had setbacks, and they've bounced back particularly well and had some really good performances and good results."United have taken  four points from their first four games. “We've got to move on [from City loss]; we've got to win games,” said Carrick. “We have done – we've won a lot of games, and we need to continue to do that. I understand it's a new season, and the points tally right now is not what we want it to be. I'm not hiding from that, but it's more of about getting back to winning games, that feeling, getting the habit. It's easier said than done, but we're capable of it.”Luke Shaw may be available after a knock.Jamie JacksonWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Speaking after that 5-0 win against Sabah, Adam Lawrence, United’s lead under-21 coach, said: “JJ is surrounded by people that really, really believe in him from the top of the club right the way through. He’s been at the club for so long. He’s got real good relationships with the players, with the staff, so I think over the course of time obviously that helps as well.“At the moment, just in terms of his game, his games programme, his training programme, it’s about making sure that he’s getting the right exposure across different levels. We’re obviously not perfect but it’s definitely something we put a lot of thought into.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBarcelona and Manchester City have been linked previously with Gabriel, after reports emerged last year suggesting the player’s family would be planning to move him.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: England thrash Sri Lanka after Harry Brook rejects rest to blast brilliant century | Twenty20 | The Guardian
description: Harry Brook smashed 114 off 49 balls before England bowled out Sri Lanka to record an emphatic win by 119 runs in the first T20
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Harry Brook smashed 114 off 49 balls before England bowled out Sri Lanka to record an emphatic win by 119 runs in the first T20
Content: Harry Brook celebrates his hundred, which he took only 42 balls to reach.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Brook celebrates his hundred, which he took only 42 balls to reach.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesTwenty20England thrash Sri Lanka after Harry Brook rejects rest to blast brilliant centuryEngland captain hits unbeaten 114 off 49 balls in first T20Sonny Baker claims three wickets in 119-run victorySimon Burntonat the Utilita BowlTue 15 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs he nears the end of a hectic summer, Harry Brook was offered the chance to rest rather than play this series and how Sri Lanka must wish Pakistan’s red-ball side had extended him enough to force a layoff. As it turned out, the 27-year-old could hardly have looked fresher as he inspired his side to an overwhelming win over emphatically outclassed opponents, a brilliant century powering England to a 19th victory in 22 completed games since he took over the captaincy, secured by the margin of 119 runs.Maiden Matt Renshaw ODI century sets up Australia win in ZimbabweRead moreBrook cavorted to triple figures off 42 balls, of which precisely a third were dispatched to the boundary, six of them beyond it, and ended unbeaten on 114 as England posted 254. But as much as his power his running impressed, using the size of the ground and manipulation of angles to maximum advantage, aided occasionally by the tourists’ imperfection in the field, as he scurried a succession of twos.“I’ve been feeling there or thereabouts all summer, in all three formats,” Brook said. “I feel I’ve let myself down a couple of times, I’ve had opportunities to get a big score, and thankfully I didn’t give that opportunity up today.”These teams have already met nine times this year, with potentially six more encounters to come between now and Halloween. Having been left punch-drunk here, if Sri Lanka fail to recover their senses and create a plan to counter Brook in particular they are in for a miserable few weeks.This was the 27-year-old’s second international T20 century, the other coming in Sri Lanka, against Pakistan during the World Cup earlier this year, the first time that he batted for his country at No 3. He has now done so eight times , scoring in addition to those two tons two unbeaten half-centuries and compiling an average of 95.2 at a ludicrous strike rate of 200.84.View image in fullscreenHarry Brook hits out during his unbeaten 114 for England against Sri Lanka, watched by the wicketkeeper, Kamil Mishara.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesBen Stokes,posting on Xin the moments after England’s innings concluded, described him as “an absolute freak” who “not even the genius of KP could come close to talent-wise”, referencing Kevin Pietersen, the new batting mentor. The same may well be true of Jos Buttler, by general acclaim England’s greatest white-ball batter, who scored a 44-ball 80 – aided by being dropped on 45 – but languished in deep shade opposite his successor as both captain and inspiration.Aneurin Donald, at 29 England’s oldest debutant since Dawid Malan in 2017, started strongly, hitting Maheesh Theekshana for a six and a four off the final two balls of the first over, but the next one he faced, the opening delivery of the third over and Dunith Wellalage’s first of the night, was skewed into the air, straight down the ground, and easily caught.Encouraged by an over that brought a wicket and just five runs, Wellalage – who would return to top score for Sri Lanka from No 8 – stayed on for a second, off which Brook flayed three sixes and as many fours, and from there England never let up.England, put in to bat, had the best of the conditions but Sri Lanka’s innings featured nearly three times as many dot balls as theirs, and just over half as many boundaries. After six overs England had 90 for the loss of one wicket; the tourists at the same stage had 32 and had lost three, their task already far beyond forlorn.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSonny Baker, on his home ground, took three wickets as England never let Sri Lanka threaten the target.Photograph: John Walton/PAIt did not help that Sonny Baker, expensive against Ireland on T20 debut almost exactly a year ago, looked a player transformed on his second appearance, his four overs bringing three wickets and just 12 runs.There were a few brief moments of fun as Dasun Shanaka hit Adil Rashid for successive sixes, struck with enormous power either side of long-off, but the next ball found his edge and Buttler’s gloves, and Wellalage’s cameo was the only succour for the tourists thereafter. They were eventually bowled out for 135, with an over unbowled. As Charith Asalanka, the Sri Lanka captain, put it: “It was a tough day for us. Positives-wise, it didn’t have anything.”England seem to have taken a liking to the Rose Bowl, and in their last three appearances here havethrashed South Africa by 342 runsin a record-breaking one-day international, comfortably beaten India in a T20, and now this.So perhaps giving Southampton an Ashes Test is not such a bad idea after all.Explore more on these topicsTwenty20England cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Howard Webb says accidental handball law ‘a nonsense’ and calls for reform | Laws of football | The Guardian
description: Howard Webb said he wants to stop ‘ridiculous situations’ and that the VAR officials in the Manchester derby had ‘tunnel vision’ over Erling Haaland’s goal
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Howard Webb said he wants to stop ‘ridiculous situations’ and that the VAR officials in the Manchester derby had ‘tunnel vision’ over Erling Haaland’s goal
Content: Harry Maguire handled the ball and then his off-target shot was deflected in by Jacob Greaves, meaning it counted as an own goal.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarView image in fullscreenHarry Maguire handled the ball and then his off-target shot was deflected in by Jacob Greaves, meaning it counted as an own goal.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/AllstarLaws of footballHoward Webb says accidental handball law ‘a nonsense’ and calls for reformWebb wants to stop ‘ridiculous situations’Says VAR officials in United v City had ‘tunnel vision’Paul MacInnesTue 15 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHoward Webb has described the law around accidental handball as “a bit of a nonsense” and called for its reform to stop referees being drawn into “ridiculous situations”.The chief refereeing officer for English football made his remarks on Tuesday, when he also fronted up over the error that allowed Manchester City to win Sunday’s Manchester derby. Webb said he was “really disappointed” with the video assistant referee call that failed to spot Enzo Fernández interfering with play from an offside position beforeErling Haaland scored the only goal.VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood downRead moreSpeaking on Match Officials Mic’d Up, Webb reviewed a number of controversial incidents from the Premier League season. He said the buildup to an Ipswich own goal at Manchester United, where the ball hit Harry Maguire’s hand before he took a shot thatdeflected off Jacob Greaves and into the net, highlighted problems with the handball law.“It’s a bit of a nonsense, isn’t it?” Webb said. “If [Maguire] strikes the ball beautifully into the top corner, then the goal gets disallowed. [But] he skews his shot, it becomes an own goal, and it’s awarded.”The handball law says it is an offence “if a player scores in the opponent’s goal directly from their hand/arm [or] immediately after the ball has touched their hand/arm, even if accidental”. If another player touches the ball before it goes in, however, only a deliberate handball would lead to play being brought back. Webb said he believed this was the wrong approach.“The law should change away from that idea,” he said. “We’re in this ridiculous situation whereby the goal is allowed to stand because it’s an own goal. You also get officials having to work out: was the shot on target, was it not on target? The worst-case scenario for us is that the officials decide that the ball is going wide and it’s an own goal, but then later on the goal is attributed to the player that scored, whose arm it hit. So, I think we ought to look at this and just allow the officials to determine whether it’s a normal handball offence. Did he make himself bigger? Did he deliberately handle the ball? And I don’t think [Maguire] does those things in this situation.”Webb, who has promised greater transparency from Pro Ref, is increasingly expected to give a public verdict on controversial decisions and it was not a surprise to find Match Officials Mic’d Up scheduled for TV 48 hours after the farrago in the Manchester derby.View image in fullscreenErling Haaland celebrates after his goal in the derby was cleared to stand.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesThe VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus were stood down from their duties on Monday, after Pro Ref acknowledged “an error of judgment” in assessing City’s winning goal. Donohue was called on to check the decision to disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute strike for offside. Using semi-automated offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that the striker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Fernández had influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWebb said it was “important” this error had been acknowledged. “I was really disappointed with this outcome, we all are, none more so than the officials themselves,” he said. “They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they’re obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation. They’ll not be officiating again until after the international break.”Webb said that Donohue had got “tunnel vision” while assessing the lead-up to the goal, concentrating on Haaland and not Fernández, because the on-field decision was against Haaland. “Donohue doesn’t truly evaluate the full impact of Fernández’s position,” Webb said. “He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score. He doesn’t touch the ball, but he doesn’t truly evaluate other elements of offside. In that moment, he gets tunnel vision. He gets focused on Haaland, and it’s down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn’t happen.”Explore more on these topicsLaws of footballHoward WebbRefereesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top golfers to get no favours for PGA Tour return after LIV bankruptcy | Golf | The Guardian
description: Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour’s commissioner, said: ‘The Tour is built on meritocracy,’ with Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton likely to start back on the DP World Tour
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour’s commissioner, said: ‘The Tour is built on meritocracy,’ with Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton likely to start back on the DP World Tour
Content: Tyrrell Hatton, one of those LIV golfers who may seek a return to the PGA Tour, at Wentworth for the PGA Championship, which starts on Thursday.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAView image in fullscreenTyrrell Hatton, one of those LIV golfers who may seek a return to the PGA Tour, at Wentworth for the PGA Championship, which starts on Thursday.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAGolfTop golfers to get no favours for PGA Tour return after LIV bankruptcyPGA commissioner: ‘The Tour is built on meritocracy’Rahm and Hatton likely to start back on DP World TourEwan Murrayat WentworthTue 15 Sep 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of thePGA Tourhas insisted there will be no favours offered to golfers looking to return to the ­platform after LIV’s bankruptcy filing last week.The increasing likelihood is players such as Jon Rahm, Cameron Smith and Tyrrell Hatton will have to play their way back on to the PGA Tour through performances in Europe in 2027 in what would represent a boost to the DP World Tour.LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’Read moreThe removal of LIV’s Saudi Arabian funding beyond this year has left the business seeking to launch a 2.0 version. Huge deals with players such as Rahm and Smith will no longer be sustainable. Yet, technically, these golfers are still LIV employees.Rahm said at Wentworth on Tuesday that “there is a long legal process they have to go through before a lot of things fall into place”. Golfers are, for now, at the mercy of courts and bankruptcy proceedings. Whenever that is complete, the expectation is of a mass exodus back to the PGA Tour.Brian Rolapp, the PGA Tour’s commissioner, says his organisation has no plans to reintroduce the sort of scheme Brooks Koepka took advantage of when returning from LIV at the start of this year. Koepka was reintroducedin return for sporting and financial sacrifices. Others opted not to take that opportunity.“As I said a few weeks ago in Atlanta, there are really three things when it comes to anyone who wants to compete on the PGA Tour,” Rolapp said. “One, the PGA Tour is built on meritocracy. Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place. Two, we are a membership organisation; we have rules and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced.“Which brings me to No 3, accountability and discipline. These are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA Tour and the sport. It’s what holds the Tour together. Those are guiding principles for us. In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning-member programme like the one you saw in January.”The PGA Tour is trying to determine how cards can be earned from the DP World Tour in future. Tiers of competition will soon be created on the PGA Tour. Also at Wentworth,Rory McIlroysaid those progressing from Europe should feed into the top-level Championship Series in the US.“I don’t see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the [second tier] Challenger Series,” McIlroy said. “I don’t see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move. So it would just be: OK, how many cards is reasonable to give to the DP World Tour for the Championship Series? I would imagine that is what the ongoing discussions are.”On that specific topic, Rolapp said: “We have not determined what the DP World Tour cards will be, as of yet. That’s under discussion. I don’t see any scenarios where there’s no Championship Series cards.”Explore more on these topicsGolfRory McIlroyLIV Golf SeriesPGA TourEuropean TournewsShareReuse this content

title: London snubbed in favour of Nairobi for 2029 World Athletics Championships | World Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: London’s bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships has ended in failure after it lost out a ‘groundbreaking’ pitch from Nairobi
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: London’s bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships has ended in failure after it lost out a ‘groundbreaking’ pitch from Nairobi
Content: Athletes clear the water jump in the women's 3,000m steeplechase at the most recent World Athletics Championships in London, in 2017.Photograph: Matthias Hangst/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAthletes clear the water jump in the women's 3,000m steeplechase at the most recent World Athletics Championships in London, in 2017.Photograph: Matthias Hangst/Getty ImagesWorld Athletics ChampionshipsLondon snubbed in favour of Nairobi for 2029 World Athletics ChampionshipsMunich selected for 2031, president Seb Coe announcesSource in British bid ‘gutted’ at double disappointmentSean IngleTue 15 Sep 2026 05.45 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 05.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon’s bid for the 2029 World ­Athletics Championships has ended in failure after it lost out to Nairobi, the Kenyan capital which will now become the first African city to host the global championships.Speaking at a press conference in Budapest theWorld Athleticspresident, Sebastian Coe, said the decision to go to Nairobi was historic and promised that it would stage a “­groundbreaking championships”.Hunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist?Read moreWhile eyebrows will also be raised given that 318 elite Kenyan stars have been banned for violating anti-doping rules since the Athletics Integrity Unit was set up in 2017, a World Athletics spokesperson defended the decision, pointing out the Kenyan government had committed $5m (£3.7m) annually to anti-doping efforts.“Kenya is much improved in this area, and we believe Nairobi hosting the world championships can act as a powerful catalyst in the Kenyan government’s continued fight against doping,” the spokesperson said. “It will put a spotlight on clean sport and galvanise the nation behind compliance.”As Nairobi and Munich, which was awarded the 2031 championships, celebrated, London was left licking its wounds.One senior source in the London team, which had been seen widely as the frontrunner for 2029, told the Guardian they were “totally gutted”.Only over the weekend did some start to fear that their £45m bid, made up of £35m from the government and £10m from the mayor’s office, might not get over the line. London believed it had a strong case , and the sight of around 60,000 fans watching track and field every night for a week was a compelling proposition.Jack Buckner, the chief executive of UK Athletics, said: “We are deeply disappointed. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.“Although today’s announcement hasn’t gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world’s athletes love competing here and we’ll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.”View image in fullscreenSebastian Coe says that the decision to award the 2029 World Championships in Nairobi is grounded in ‘serious analysis’.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAIn hindsight, the lengthy public battle with West Ham to get permission to use the stadium in September 2029 – which was settled only on the eve of the bid being submitted – was not ideal. The sparse crowds on the opening days of last month’s European Athletics Championships in Birmingham perhaps did not help either.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, the London 2027 team believed those factors were irrelevant, and it simply came down to a thirst in World Athletics for Kenya to host the championships, and the size of Nairobi’s bid.Lord Coe, though, stressed that there had been a range of factors at play. “Yes, of course, we see the historical, groundbreaking nature of taking theWorld Athletics Championshipsto Africa, but that alone is not the basis upon the decision,” he said. “It was made across budgets, it was made across financial government guarantees, it was made across the growth potential of the sport. It was also grounded in some really serious analysis.”Coe also pushed back when he was reminded that going to Kenya would mean that Europe, which has the biggest fanbase for track and field, will have only staged one World ­Athletics Championships between one championship, in Budapest in 2023, between 2017 and 2031.“Look, Europe is a heartland, and we openly accept that,” he said. “It is in large part the breadbasket of our sport. But we do also have a responsibility to make sure that an international governing federation made up of well over 200 federations has the opportunity to be able to take our championships into areas that strategically we think will actually grow the footprint of our sport.“And Munich 2031 is a European city. What it does allow us to do in the next three editions is to have our World Athletics Championships globally based: in Africa, in obviously Europe, and of course our next ­edition in Asia in 2027 [Beijing] next year.”Explore more on these topicsWorld Athletics ChampionshipsSebastian CoeWorld AthleticsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hyrox changes rules and apologises for allowing Australian athlete who soiled herself to continue | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: Organisers of the global indoor fitness competition have pledged immediate rule changes following widespread backlash to an incident involving Australian Joanna Wietrzyk
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: Organisers of the global indoor fitness competition have pledged immediate rule changes following widespread backlash to an incident involving Australian Joanna Wietrzyk
Content: Joanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in HYROX Beijing 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes in HYROX Beijing 2026.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAustralia sportHyrox changes rules and apologises for allowing Australian athlete who soiled herself to continueAustralian Joanna Wietrzyk went on to win fitness race in BeijingHyrox admits making mistake by ‘not reacting immediately’Ima CaldwellMon 14 Sep 2026 22.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrganisers of the global indoor fitness competition Hyrox have apologised and pledged immediate rule changes after an Australian athlete was allowed to finish and win an event in Beijing despite soiling herself mid-race.Footage of world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk competing on Saturday showed her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment, with faecal matter visibly running down her legs. The incident went viral on social media and triggered debate about Hyrox’s health and safety standards, and athlete responsibility.How to enjoy Hyrox: I tried the gruelling, thrilling, hugely popular race – and discovered 11 ways to tackle itRead moreHyrox, an increasingly popular fitness competition launched in Germany in 2017, is now held in locations across the world. It debuted in mainland China in late 2024.In each race, participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.Prior to the weekend’s incident, official event rules already penalised athletes for minor infractions such as littering on the course, or spitting or clearing their nose on the floor. It contained no immediate protocol for faecal matter.Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologised in astatementon Instagram to everyone affected “directly or indirectly” by the incident. “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race. In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents – and I did not,” Fürste said.He added that Hyrox has made “rulebook changes immediately”.“As of this moment, there are new rules and procedures in place to prevent situations like this from happening again.”View image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk of Australia competes at Hyrox Beijing 2026 at National Speed Skating Oval.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesIn statements released by Hyrox China and Hyrox World, organisers confirmed that affected lanes were isolated for deep cleaning overnight, contaminated equipment was removed and venue carpet was replaced overnight before competition resumed the following day.“After the incident, the organising committee immediately closed off and isolated the affected area and track, and completed comprehensive disinfection,” Hyrox China organisers said.Hyrox World said that it has clear bio-contaminant and medical procedures in place: “Protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood.”Wietrzyk, the world record holder in the Hyrox women’s solo event, was invited to compete at the Beijing event. She posted and then deleted a selfie to her Instagram story from what appeared to be a hospital bed, with the text: “Go hard or go home … a win is a win. In all seriousness, thank you for all the support. I’ll be back soon x.”It is not uncommon for athletes to soil themselves while competing in high endurance sports, particularly marathons. British athlete Paula Radcliffe won the 2005 London marathon after suffering from “runner’s diarrhoea” and having to stop at the 22-mile mark to relieve herself, in full view of cameras.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSocial media users and other athletes at the event questioned the response and why Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the race, while impacting the health and safety of fellow competitors.Joe Ho, a male competitor in Beijing, said that fellow athletes — who generally pay a fee to take part in Hyrox races — had been failed.“For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences,” Ho wrote in an Instagram post.“I paid Hyrox to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with Hyrox.“If the organisation accepts that something went wrong, why not offer affected participants refunds, credits, or some meaningful form of compensation?”Following online vitriol directed at Wietrzyk after her identity was shared, organisers warned that anyone sending abuse or threats of violence towards the athlete would be banned from all future events.Guardian Australia reached out to Wietrzyk and Hyrox for comment.Explore more on these topicsAustralia sportFitnessnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bank | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Britain is understood to have been formally invited to become founding member of multilateral lender
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: Britain is understood to have been formally invited to become founding member of multilateral lender
Content: John Healey, centre, pictured last year when he was defence secretary, talking to British soldiers.Photograph: Leon Neal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey, centre, pictured last year when he was defence secretary, talking to British soldiers.Photograph: Leon Neal/AFP/Getty ImagesDefence policyJohn Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bankExclusive: Britain is understood to have been formally invited to become founding member of multilateral lenderPippa CrerarPolitical editorTue 15 Sep 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey is in talks with the Canadian government about joining a new global defence bank intended to help allies rearm to counter mounting security threats, just weeks afterRachel Reevesrejected the move.The chancellor is understood to be actively considering a bid to join the proposed Canada-led defence, security and resilience bank (DSRB), which proponents say could help the UK fund defence projects at lower cost, before planned talks with his Canadian counterpart this week.When he was defence secretary, Healey was understood to have been a strong advocate for keeping UK observers present at Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney’s, defence bank talks, despite resistance from the Treasury, which wanted to shut off those international discussions.Reeves, his predecessor as chancellor, was concerned the bank would not address the UK’s defence procurement issues and was more focused on lending to smaller defence firms in nations with lower credit ratings. The UK has had a AA credit rating since 2016.Healey, who has long been a proponent of multilateral funding mechanisms, met the Canadian finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, twice at a G20 summit in North Carolina two weeks ago.They are due to meet again in the UK this week, when the two men are – according to sources – likely to discuss the defence bank, and both are expected to be at EU finance minister talks in Dublin later this week.Canada is understood to have already formally invited the UK to become a founding member of the bank, along with eight other countries including Ukraine and Turkey.Healeyresigned as defence secretaryin June, accusing Keir Starmer and his chancellor, Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk because the defence spending package fell £13bn short of what he argued was required.As chancellor, he is expected to avoid setting a target date for reaching 3% defence spending in next month’s budget and instead is planning to set out a pathway to reaching the goal at the 2027 spending review.The DSRB could play a role in this by using financial leverage, separate from the balance sheets of ​already indebted nations, to boost defence investment. But it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments to become a major player.Reeves announced at the Nato summit in Ankara in July that the UK would join the Netherlands, Finland and Poland to launch a new lender called the Multilateral Defence Mechanism.She said the MDM would help the UK with procurement – saving the UK as much as 20% – and stockpiling, which would give taxpayers better value for money while allowing government to borrow at a low rate to fund defence. The UK has committed an initial £600m to the new lender.The former chancellor had called for the two rival international defence financing schemes to merge, arguing that it made sense for countries to only fund one institution that could work for all nations.In addition to overlaps with existing initiatives, there were also understood to be concerns in the Treasury over the amount of capital that countries would need to commit while public finances are strained. The UK’s initial capital contribution would be between £1bn and £2bn over three years.The DSRB has ​been seeking to raise around €100bn, which it would use to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers.A government spokesperson said: “We are fully committed to working alongside our international partners to scale defence industrial capacity.“We are working closely with our Canadian allies on ensuring the Multilateral Defence Mechanism and Defence Security Resilience Bank are complementary.”Explore more on these topicsDefence policyJohn HealeyRachel ReevesMilitaryCanadaAmericasEconomic policyShareReuse this content

title: Air pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggests | Air pollution | The Guardian
description: Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide
Content: Researchers at Queen’s University Belfast say environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies.Photograph: Tomasz Trybus/AlamyView image in fullscreenResearchers at Queen’s University Belfast say environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies.Photograph: Tomasz Trybus/AlamyAir pollutionAir pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggestsAnalysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxideAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAir pollution is associated with anincreased risk of suicideand suicidal thoughts, according to research.Environmental pollution is known to beassociated with poorer mental healthbut its role in suicide risk is less well understood. Scientists at Queen’s University Belfast examined whether air, noise, light, and water pollution could influence the risk of death by suicide and suicidal behaviours.Their meta analysis of 29 studies found that exposure to airborne small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide were linked to a heightened risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.Narrative analysis of a further 16 studies suggested that some other air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone, as well as noise pollution, were also associated with a higher suicide risk. However, evidence for light and water pollution was inconclusive.The authors said the findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and CommunityHealth, suggested that environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies and that suicide prevention should also be viewed as a public health issue.“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they said.“Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing.”Air pollution from ships may be more harmful than road traffic emissions, port study findsRead moreBut other experts expressed caution about the findings. Dr Jess Moody, the senior research and evidence manager at Samaritans, said: “While the reasons for suicide are complex, evidence shows that a variety of factors can impact suicide risk and we must not ignore the environments we live in, particularly inequalities around living conditions. Samaritans welcomes research that helps awareness of how suicide links to wider public health concerns.”Dr Jon Van Niekerk, the chair of the general adult faculty at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said the research suggested some forms of air pollution may be associated with a small increase in suicidal behaviour but it did not establish that air pollution itself caused suicidal thoughts or attempts.He added: “Air pollution is closely associated with other factors which we know can influence mental health, including socioeconomic deprivation, urban living, physical health and housing.“The study provides further population-level support for reducing harmful air pollution, though the findings should not be seen as supporting individual suicide risk prediction or suggesting that pollution reduction alone could be a suicide prevention measure.”Dr Rosie Cornish, a senior research fellow in epidemiology and health data science at the University of Bristol, said there were many factors associated with higher levels of air pollution as well as increased risk of suicide.“If air pollution is not actually a cause of increased risk of suicide then reducing pollution will not help to prevent suicide. The authors do not acknowledge this when drawing their conclusions.”Dr Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge, said: “This study confuses two fundamentally different concepts: causation and association.“There are many other factors that could potentially explain the associations observed. For example, areas with higher levels of pollution may differ in other ways that affect suicide risk.“This research finds factors that are associated with increased suicide risk, but further research is needed to claim that the factors identified are causes of increased risk.”More than 720,000 people globallydie by suicide each year. It is the third leading cause of death among 15– to 29-year-olds, according to the World Health Organization.In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAir pollutionMental healthHealthMedical researchnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK paying £56,000 for each person returned to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Home secretary defends cost, saying it is about the same or cheaper than putting someone up in a hotel for a year
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Home secretary defends cost, saying it is about the same or cheaper than putting someone up in a hotel for a year
Content: The UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is shown a drone used by French police trained in stopping migrants boarding small boats, at Zuydcoote beach in northern France.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenThe UK home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is shown a drone used by French police trained in stopping migrants boarding small boats, at Zuydcoote beach in northern France.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAImmigration and asylumUK paying £56,000 for each person returned to France under ‘one in one out’ schemeHome secretary defends cost, saying it is about the same or cheaper than putting someone up in a hotel for a yearRajeev SyalHome affairs editorTue 15 Sep 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government’s “one in, one out” deal is costing about £56,000 for every person sent back to France,Shabana Mahmoodhas told MPs.The home secretary disclosed the figure as she was questioned by the home affairs select committee over whether the scheme was delivering value for taxpayers.About 1,400 people have been removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some havesubsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats.Asked how much each return had cost, Mahmood said: “I’ll need to write to the committee on the most recent figures.“I think it’s per person for the numbers that have been returned so far, it’s about £56,000.”She later defended the cost, saying it was “still cheaper, or just about the same as supporting someone in a hotel for a year”.Under the deal, the UK sends a person who arrives by small boats back toFrancein exchange for taking an asylum seeker applying through a legal route.The pilot has already been extended once and is now due to run into October, with its long-term future still to be decided.France wants the bilateral arrangement to be eventually replaced by a wider EU-UK returns deal.An EU-wide returns deal known as the Dublin agreement existed before the UK left the EU. Attempts to continue the returns deal post-Brexit have been rejected by EU leaders.Mahmood dismissed suggestions an EU-wide system would be a “silver bullet” for the Channel crisis.She said the deal had already returned more migrants than Britain ever managed under the EU’s old Dublin arrangements.“It is a real mistake to think that that pact is the future. And if we were in that, this problem would go away because I promise you, it would not,” she said.She said the government’s scheme had struggled to scale up to larger numbers of returns, adding that it had been “operationally difficult” to increase removals because of constraints such as detention space.“It’s not been without its challenges. Obviously, the numbers are still relatively small,” she said.Laurent Nuñez, the French interior minister, has told Mahmood that he wants to end the scheme, it emerged earlier this week.In June, Nuñez told a French parliamentary inquiry: “For our part, we want to move away from this bilateral relationship with the UK. We consider that France should not have to carry it alone, and that it would be better to integrate it into an agreement between the EU and UK.“So I have already clearly told my counterpart that this pilot agreement, which we signed in August 2025, was not intended to be renewed beyond October 1, 2026.”Mahmood told the committee only “relatively small numbers” of rejected asylum-seeking families had taken up a separate pilot offering them as much as £40,000 to voluntarily leave Britain.She said: “If you’re a failed asylum-seeking family, what you’re trading off is an offer of £40,000, which will help you resettle back in your country of origin, versus, you know, access to free healthcare and education for your children.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumMigrationShabana MahmoodRefugeesEuropean UnionFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates
Content: André Mendonça and Alexandre de Moraes in Brasília, Brazil, on 2 September.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APView image in fullscreenAndré Mendonça and Alexandre de Moraes in Brasília, Brazil, on 2 September.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APBrazilFerocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential electionScandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidatesTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroTue 15 Sep 2026 15.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pitsMoraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former presidentJair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealedan explosive police dossierrelating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. Inone text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct.
