Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands of sea turtles reach Mexico in yearly migration threatened by climate crisis – video | Marine life | The Guardian
description: More than 330,000 sea turtles arrived in southern Mexico in a mass nesting phenomenon
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than 330,000 sea turtles arrived in southern Mexico in a mass nesting phenomenon
Content: 1:05Marine lifeThousands of sea turtles reach Mexico in yearly migration threatened by climate crisis – videoMore than 330,000 sea turtles arrived in southern Mexico in a mass nesting phenomenon known as an ‘arribada’.The sixth arribada of the season, which began in March, brought thousands of turtles to the beach in less than 48 hours to lay their eggs, according to officials at La Escobilla beach sanctuary in Oaxaca, Mexico.The olive ridley turtle plays a fundamental role in marine and coastal ecosystems by contributing nutrients to beach-dune systems and regulating populations of jellyfish and sponges, according to Mexico's federal attorney for environmental protection, but the climate crisis is now threatening their survivalSource: ReutersTue 15 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsMarine lifeWildlifeMexicoReptilesOceansAmericas

title: ‘It’s really taking off’: hedge revival as farmers rediscover ancient tools | Farming | The Guardian
description: Grant applications in England surge as interest grows in habitat that captures carbon and helps reduce flood risk
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Grant applications in England surge as interest grows in habitat that captures carbon and helps reduce flood risk
Content: Emma and Robert Rose, who look after Rosewood Farm in Ellerton, have been experimenting with hedge laying techniques for years.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEmma and Robert Rose, who look after Rosewood Farm in Ellerton, have been experimenting with hedge laying techniques for years.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianFarming‘It’s really taking off’: hedge revival as farmers rediscover ancient toolsGrant applications in England surge as interest grows in habitat that captures carbon and helps reduce flood riskSandra LavilleTue 15 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ancient craft of hedge laying is experiencing a strong revival as farmers use techniques that peaked in the 18th and 19th centuries to boost wildlife, capture carbon and help tackle flooding.Hedge laying, which restores and revives mature hedges to keep them fresh, was among the four most popular categories of capital grants selected by farmers out of a total pot of £225m provided by the government this year to support practical environmental improvements on farms and across the countryside.The 2,500 farmers across England who applied for grants to restore and maintain their mature hedgerows using a craft that dates back thousands of years, will – if the grants are approved – lay 1,300km (800 miles) of mature hedgerows, enough to stretch from Land’s End to Hadrian’s Wall and back.View image in fullscreenThe craft of hedge laying fell out of favour after the second world war.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMegan Gimber, the key habitats officer for the People’s Trust for Endangered Species, said hedge laying was one of the most effective tools farmers had to respond to the climate crisis. “Hedge laying really stopped after the war, so it has been over a generation since it was a normal part of farm management and we have seen a huge decline in hedgerows as a result,” she said.“These grants will give 1,300km of potentially ancient hedges a new lease of life, to help plug the gap, and it is fantastic that it is such a popular grant application.”Mature, maintained hedgerows are a carbon sink, capturing more carbon in every hectare than forests. They support thousands of species, provide shade for livestock, reduce soil erosion and slow down, absorb and store vast amounts of rainwater to help reduce flooding.“They are massively important,” said Stephen Budding, the chair of the National Hedgelaying Society. “The greatest biodiversity gain is from hedge laying older hedges.“Our members are seeing quite a surge in work, but I don’t think this would be happening without the government grants available.”View image in fullscreenMature hedgerows are a valuable carbon sink and an important habitat for wildlife.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHedge laying involves cutting through the hedge stems almost completely, then laying them at an angle to the ground. Laying the branches down invigorates growth at the point where they have been cut, filling gaps in the hedges and restoring youth and freshness. It is done by hand by skilled layers – many of whom will compete next month at theNational Hedgelaying Championshipsin Chipping Norton.Robert Rose, who farms 220 acres of grassland for beef cattle and arable fields at Rosewood Farm in Ellerton in Yorkshire’s Lower Derwent valley, is waiting for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) to approve his application for a grant to lay old blackthorn, newer hawthorn and ash and willow hedges across his farm.“We lay the hedges in a modern conservation style that retains more of the bushy growth for the benefit of nesting birds as well as stock proofing,” said Rose, who farms with his brother and wife.View image in fullscreenRobert Rose says he has noticed a real surge in interest online in time honoured hedge laying practices.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe trio planted new hedges 20 years ago, but maintaining them is vital to keep them working to store carbon, support wildlife and retain water. “We taught ourselves how to do the laying, which was a bit of trial and error,” he said. “It is only recently that we have noticed how much other farmers are talking about hedge laying online, in community groups, it really seems to be taking off.”The grant Rose has applied for will help him lay about 50 metres of hedges as well as planting new hedgerows and coppicing others.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPeak hedge laying season starts in October and ends in February so farmers like Rose are hoping for quick decisions from Defra. “There are so many benefits with hedge laying for wildlife, for livestock, for conservation. We see a lot more birds using the hedges and a lot more small mammals around the bottom of mature managed hedges,” said Rose.“I think hedge laying is, if you like, a bit of a gateway drug into more conservation. It spreads around the communities to other farmers, the talk about it is everywhere. So this grant scheme is exactly what is needed.”View image in fullscreenRobert Rose is enthusiastic about the opportunities provided by Defra’s grant scheme.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAs well as grant requests for hedge laying, about 5,000 applications are for planting new hedges – representing approximately 2,500km of new hedgerows, roughly equivalent to the distance from Newcastle to Naples. But without management, the new hedges will not survive.‘Spraying should be the last option’: how farmers are exploring alternatives to pesticidesRead moreFigures from theUK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology in 2023showed the country is still losing hedges despite record planting efforts through over-trimming and undermanagement. The centre also discovered that 61% of the newly planted hedges surveyed existed as hedges in their 2007 survey, but had since been lost and required replanting.“Hedgerows are succession habitats, made up of trees and shrubby woody species, that naturally change over time,” said Gimber. “They require management to maintain the valuable mid-succession stage of bushy, low growth and prevent them developing into lines of trees.”A Defra spokesperson said: “This government is putting its full weight behind farmers – giving them the funding, tools and opportunities they need to succeed.“In July, we opened a new round of environmental land management capital grants with increased funding of up to £225m available to support investment in infrastructure that boosts productivity, strengthens resilience and supports environmental outcomes, which has now closed following strong uptake.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingClimate crisisWildlifeRural affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The love of her life died at sea hunting shipwrecks. Now she’s taking the helm | Oceans | The Guardian
description: After Jennifer Sellitti lost her partner Joe Mazraani, she thought everything was over. Then she inherited his ship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After Jennifer Sellitti lost her partner Joe Mazraani, she thought everything was over. Then she inherited his ship
Content: Jennifer Sellitti and Joe Mazraani at sea.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Atlantic Wreck SalvageView image in fullscreenJennifer Sellitti and Joe Mazraani at sea.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Atlantic Wreck SalvageOceansThe love of her life died at sea hunting shipwrecks. Now she’s taking the helmAfter Jennifer Sellitti lost her partner Joe Mazraani, she thought everything was over. Then she inherited his shipAJ McDougallTue 15 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTShareAfter Joe died, Jennifer Sellitti felt as though she were living underwater.Other people became murky, their words muffled. She slept constantly; unconsciousness was a blessing. On the worst days, memories bowled her over.“It was flashbacks, constantly,” she said. “I’d be having a conversation with you and look completely normal, but I’d really not be paying any attention because I’d be seeing these horrible images over and over again.”Her brain replayed a grim carousel of intrusive memories from the morning of 29 July 2025. Pulling Joe out of the water, his limp body swinging from the hydraulic winch they normally used for retrieving deep-sea treasures.Her, kneeling over Joe on the back of his boat, trying desperately to revive him. The death-mask look settling on his face as the life drained out of it. The two moles under his right eye, the ones she liked to kiss when she said goodbye.She knuckled down, found tricks to stem the torrent. She had always been good at packing uncomfortable feelings into boxes; her job as New Jersey’s top public defender demanded it. But the problem with doing that, she knew, was the potential for those boxes to explode.One night in early September, six weeks after his death, she stopped off at the dock to check on Joe’s boat – there had been a problem plugging into the shore power grid the day before. It was after a work event, and Jenn was in a ballgown and heels. She stepped aboard and immediately felt like someone had taken a baseball bat to her stomach.“I don’t think I’d cried that hard since it happened,” she said. She lay down in Joe’s bunk. When she got up, somehow two hours had passed. “It was suddenly midnight and I’m on this boat, and it was like, what next?”Joe Mazraani had died on a dive, seeking to identify a shipwreck the couple had discovered with their crew the previous summer. Both criminal defense lawyers by day, Joe and Jenn spent every waking hour outside the office plotting their next voyage, triangulating their next quarry. “We’re pirates,” Jenn likes to say.More specifically, Joe and the crew of Tenacious were technical wreck divers, part salty sea dogs and part maritime detectives. Jenn managed the research and expeditions. She also ran point on hauling their discoveries into the light – not just organizing public appearances and liaising with museums, but connecting with the families of victims and survivors. Making sure their stories were told.Their company, Atlantic Wreck Salvage, regularly madenational headlineswith their finds; as members of the crew will tell you, NBC’s Brian Williams interrupted the broadcast of an Olympic opening ceremony to announce they had discovered the last missing German submarine sunk off the coast of Nantucket during the second world war.View image in fullscreenThe Tenacious crew.Photograph: Atlantic Wreck SalvageBoth Joe and Jenn were load-bearing pillars of the operation, but she would be the first to tell you that Joe was the undisputed captain. He had built Tenacioushimself, bolt by bolt; his knowledge of the boat had no backup.So with his death, at 47, his crew, held together largely by his appetite for risk, love of adventure and force of will, was suddenly without an anchor. They drifted away, to other dive boats or towards retirement. Everyone assumed the boat would be sold to a man.But Jenn had her captain’s license, too. Joe had given her Tenaciousin his will. Even amid the grief, a plan was beginning to take hold in her mind. It was probably crazy. No, it wasdefinitelycrazy. But it might just ensure their survival.“The way I see it, I have no other choice,” she said.The popular image of a shipwreck hunter – a swashbuckler armed with a leather map and a bottle of rum – does not survive much contact with the actual thing. Ditto the shipwrecks themselves.“Everybody thinks of a big pirate ship just sitting on the bottom of the ocean, perfectly preserved,” said Mike Dudas, a technical diver active since 1988. “It’s more like diving a junkyard.”The linings of the east coast, particularly on the approach into New York Harbor, are littered with wrecks. These sites, each an alien world unto themselves, are far from hospitable to human intruders. Twisted steel and rotting timbers lie half-buried in a fine gray silt, rusted over or studded with anemones, pecked at by schools of fish, dragged about the sea floor by hapless fishers dropping their nets. It’s gloomy and still until a current materializes without warning, threatening to rip divers away from the debris field. The hulls have been rearranging their interiors for decades: collapsed passageways, fallen bulkheads, rooms you can no longer enter.“A lot of times, you’re taking your bottles off, pushing them in front of you, and tearing your suit on the way in,” said Chris Ogden, a younger member of the Tenacious crew, “and just hoping you can get out the same way.”Real shipwreck hunting is similarly unromantic. The vast majority of the process is made up of painstaking research, poring over historical charts, survivor accounts and archival clippings. Then comes the actual search itself, which largely constitutes arguing about sonar data. This phase involves towing a torpedo-shaped device called a towfish behind the boat on an armored cable, at three to five knots, sweeping back and forth across a predetermined search grid for hours on end. Divers call it “mowing the lawn”. If you’re lucky, out of the endless stream of acoustic images of the ocean floor, an anomaly will emerge.Then you get in the water.Recreational divers work to a limit of about 120ft (37 metres); technical divers like those aboard Tenacious regularly descend to 300, sometimes pushing toward 400 – squarely in what veteran diver Eric Takakjian calls the “don’t-try-this-at-home category”. That far down, the light disappears fast. Packer heard Simon and Garfunkel in his head every time he traversed an anchor line. Hello, darkness, my old friend.The math also changes. A diver gets roughly 25 minutes of bottom time, followed by two to three hours of mind-numbing ascent to dissipate the nitrogen that’s accumulated in their blood and tissue. Ascend too quickly and that nitrogen can form bubbles inside the body, causing paralysis, brain damage or death.The technical diving community of the eastern seaboard is small enough that everyone, at most, knows someone who knows someone who’s died on a dive. The Andrea Doria, a once gorgeous luxury liner, has claimed the lives of nearly two dozen divers since its sinking in 1956. The toll is accepted as the price of admission.“Call it passion, maybe, but it’s more like a sickness,” Ogden said.Jenn was standing with her back to the door, studying her bookcase, when she sensed someone was watching her.It was 2014 and she had been in her new office for three or four days. Her bosses at the public defender’s office had sent her to take over a trial region that had grown, in their estimation, sloppy. The space reflected it, with jumbled records everywhere.She turned around. A man she had never seen before looked back at her.“How did you get in here?” Jenn demanded.“I’m Joe Mazraani.” He seemed amused.“That’s not what I asked.”Her secretary materialized in the doorway, flustered – “no, no, he’s OK, he’s a pool attorney, I wanted you to meet him”– and Sellitti turned back to the stranger. He was looking her up and down with a frank appraisal. His eyes landed on her shoes.“Are those Louboutins?”“Yes.”A beat.“Are you going to shake things up around here,” he said, “or is it going to be status quo?”Jenn stared at him. “I’m going to shake things up around here.”He nodded once and walked out of her office.They became friends not long after, the way two trial animals usually do, working a case together. They had similar philosophies – push, fight, do not make peace with the state on its terms.View image in fullscreenJoe Mazraani and Jennifer Sellitti.Photograph: Atlantic Wreck SalvageTheir first date was in early 2015 at a place called Rat’s Restaurant in central Jersey. The maître d’ assumed Joe was Jenn’s professor. Joe, four years younger than Jenn, found this hilarious.He had never been married, he told her. Every previous relationship had buckled under the weight of the same rival. “There was always the other woman,” Jenn said. Tenacious– the 45-ft fiberglass fishing boat Joe had bought in Maryland on a bitterly cold winter’s day in 2010. He had been diving for far longer, but the boat gave him what he had been missing: the ability to go where he wanted, when he wanted, for as long as the work required.Joe Mazraani grew up in Beirut in the 1980s. He would tell anyone who asked, and plenty who didn’t, that he was Phoenician. “Our people are sea people,” he would tell Jenn. The Phoenicians were the great maritime civilization of the ancient world, the ones who first charted the Mediterranean, who had pushed past the Pillars of Hercules into open ocean. If you were going to be obsessed with the sea, you may as well have the blood for it.He was 15 when his family sent him to America. He lived with relatives in New Jersey, then Florida. He went to college on Staten Island, where he lived for a time in a Lebanese church. He was 19, when he took his first dive class.In the meticulous logs of his first 197 dives, which Jenn found only after his death – Joe had sworn up and down he hadn’t kept any such logs, he had never had the patience – he excitedly recorded horseshoe crab sightings and expressed fears about low visibility. The little PADI (Professional Association of Diving Instructors) booklet had a section for personal information. UnderDistinguishing scars/marks, Joe had written: “I AM AN ASSHOLE!”Allergic to: “Idiots”.Medications I must have: “Knowledge”.He became a lawyer primarily as a means of paying for his habit; an older diver had told him that only the law or medicine could support a serious diving hobby. Doctors, Joe thought, spent too much time on land.Jenn understood this in a way his previous partners hadn’t: she was the same. The daughter of educators, she had spent years ice climbing, a pastime that involves clambering up frozen waterfalls at altitude. She was familiar with the patterns of being unable to commit to plans more than a day in advance; waiting all week for the temperature to plunge; checking forecasts obsessively; deciding on a dime to drop everything and drive three hours to New Hampshire. She knew what it was like to be in the grip of something that looked, from the outside, like a pathology.Their first New Year’s together, Joe decanted wine into a barnacle-crusted vase he had raised from the SS Choapa, a Chilean freighter that sank off the Jersey Shore in 1944. They danced beside the kitchen table while Édith Piaf crooned La Vie en Rose. He whispered to her that he loved her, over and over again.For Jenn, who had been married once before, “love” didn’t do it justice. “What we had was more intense than that,” she said. “It was like looking at another person and finally, fully understanding who you are.” It felt more like the two of them burned together.Tom Packer, a veteran diver on the east coast scene who had known Joe for years, had taken to teasing him about the burgeoning romance. “When are you going to marry this girl? My God,” he remembered thinking. Joe and Jenn had already decided that marriage and kids weren’t for them, but in a few years’ time they would move out to a small Raritan Valley farm, filling it with marine artifacts at the expense of basic furniture.View image in fullscreenMazraani and Sellitti.Photograph: Atlantic Wreck SalvageHis friends could see it plainly enough – the way Joe looked at Jenn, the way she and the boat both fit perfectly into his life. “I was so happy for him,” Packer said. “We all were.”The first time Jenn set foot on Tenacious was 18 June 2015. She didn’t have her diver’s certification yet, but there was no shortage of things to do on a working boat. She cooked. She led yoga sessions on deck. She learned the service support routines. She logged a daily 20,000 steps on a vessel she could cross in 30 paces.By then, Joe had already built something of a professional reputation for himself. He was a world-class grump and could be fiendishly uncommunicative, particularly when it came to what he had planned for his next conquest. But he was also known to be one of the most capable and accomplished wreck divers in the region.His was the crew that had recovered the auxiliary stern helm of the SS Ayuruoca, a Brazilian freighter that belches oil and lies in a deep, silty offshoot of the Hudson River aptly nicknamed the Mudhole. They had raised telegraphs and foghorns, portholes and bells, crockery and silverware and bathroom tiles, the instruments and ornaments of ships that were, in their time, the finest things men could make.The crew was a rotating cast of around 20 regulars, handpicked by Joe and recruited through reputation and word-of-mouth, trips coordinated through a text chain and the occasional email. Among them was a diver called Tim Whitehead, who readily sold his 2003 Cobra Mustang to buy the right equipment for their expeditions.“Anybody that dives in Jersey wants to dive on Tenacious,” Whitehead said.Her first year, Jenn stuck to day trips. In 2016 she did one offshore run – the Andrea Doria, for the wreck’s 60th anniversary. She got her open water certification in 2017, her advanced certification two years later. But what bound her to Tenaciouswasn’t the diving; it was the stories. The more she learned about the people on these ships – who they were, why they were there, what became of them – the less she could stop.One ship in particular ensnared her imagination.Le Lyonnais was a transatlantic passenger steamship that collided with an American sailing vessel in heavy fog off the coast of Nantucket five years before the outbreak of the civil war. The American ship, the Adriatic, left the damaged liner to sink and its survivors to fend for themselves. After a week at sea beset by storms and freezing temperatures, just 18 of 132 souls aboard survived. The Adriatic’s captain was put on trial, only for the proceedings to be swept aside by the onslaught of war. The victims’ families never received justice, and for more than a century and a half Le Lyonnais’s final resting place remained unknown.It took eight years for Jenn to find the ship. By the time she was done, she had literallywritten the bookon the subject.She fell in love with Le Lyonnais in 2016, when a friend and shipwreck detective named Eric Takakjian mentioned its existence to her. “It quickly became my dream to find it,” Jenn remembered. “Every year, I would collect a binder full of the information I’d found and drive up to Eric’s house in Fairhaven, where we compared notes.” They called it, for reasons unclear, Project Mayonnaise.By 2019, they had narrowed down the ship’s probable location to part of a rugged, uncharted underwater plateau called Georges Bank. Jenn’s hopes sank. Tenacious, plucky though she was, didn’t have nearly the horsepower required to motor all the way from the Jersey Shore to the bank, which lay 200 miles offshore of Fairhaven.The nearest Coast Guard station may as well have been on another planet. And then there were the conditions. “Everything is just wilder there,” a sea captain once told Jenn. A popular route from America to England in its time, the Bank was a veritable graveyard of ships – but knowledge, even anecdotal, about dive conditions was virtually zilch.Joe went silent on the matter. Jenn figured it was a lost cause. Then he came back with a plan. New engine. Double the fuel capacity. Side-scan sonar. Give him the winter of 2021 to upgrade Tenacious, he said, and maybe they could find Le Lyonnais.The crew motored out to Georges Bank for the first time the next summer, “mowing the lawn” and taking measurements of anomalies they didn’t have the conditions to investigate further. In August 2024, they finally identified one of these blips as their culprit, diving down and matching a part of her rigging and engine cylinder to Le Lyonnais’s recorded specifications.“Being able to find this ship, I felt like I was giving closure to the people who suffered there,” Jenn toldthe New York Times.Their celebration was purposefully short-lived, however. “We never rested on our laurels,” Packer noted. “As soon as we’d accomplished something, it was behind us and we were on to the next thing.”“The problem is how quickly the moment fades,” Jenn said. “The only way to get it back is to find something else. The search never ends.”View image in fullscreenHunting for Le Lyonnais.Photograph: Atlantic Wreck SalvageThe Times’s report noted the crew had one false start on that expedition, first diving down to a “completely different wreck” they suspected might be Le Lyonnais. This Jane Doe ship they dubbed the Big Engine Steamer. They vowed to return and identify her the next year.It would be Joe’s last dive.Joe died on a Tuesday. The night before, he and Jenn had stood on the back of Tenaciousand talked about how far they had come as the light faded around them. The ocean around them felt like it was all theirs – it would be their playground for the next 10 years, at least. She would retire first, maybe work part-time at his firm. He put his arm around her.“We were very much in this moment,” Jenn said, “on the edge of everything that we had dreamed of. Truly.”Jenn didn’t tell Joe, but she had been trying to stifle an uneasy feeling since Thursday, the night before they had struck out for the Bank. Their Portuguese water dog, Pirate, had laid down in the driveway and didn’t get up. Pirate had been old and sick, long since retired from sea life, but his death still came as a shock.“Joe was really upset,” Jenn recalled, but delaying the trip was out of the question. “He was also a good compartmentalizer,” she said. “Once he got his head in the game, that was it.”Between her own waves of grief, Jenn tried not to think of Pirate’s death as an ill omen. But her apprehension didn’t abate as they drove up to Nantucket and pulled out to sea. The sky over the ocean looked ominous and foreboding in a way it never had before.Keeping watch and listening to music on Monday night, she couldn’t ignore it any more; she looked up at the stars and asked for a sign. The next song that started playing was I Am Disappeared by Frank Turner, which is about open seas and pirate ships and people “wrapped up tight in the things that will kill them”. Jenn ripped her headphone jack out so hard that she almost lost her phone overboard.She tried to tell herself it was only the approaching storm. There is little room for superstition or doubt on a 45-ft boat. Fear is contagious in an environment that small. You keep your worries to yourself.Joe was in a good mood that next morning, which for him meant garden-variety grumbling instead of barking out rapid-fire orders. Jenn always told him the same thing before he splashed: “Have fun.”Never: “Be careful.” You don’t speak like that on the water. But on 29 July 2025, at 10 in the morning, she kissed him and said: “Be careful.”He looked at her strangely.“Of course,” he said, and dropped out of sight.View image in fullscreenMazraani aboard Tenacious.Photograph: Atlantic Wreck SalvageSeventy-five minutes later, Jenn was pacing the deck, watching the clock, waiting to feel the tell-tale sensation of their hook being freed from the wreck. Four divers, including Joe, were below, and they were behind on schedule, which she remarked on to Eric Takakjian, who was working calmly in the galley at his laptop.That’s when she spotted Joe’s fins, breaking the surface behind Tenacious’s transom.He wasn’t supposed to surface for another hour and a half. The nitrogen he had accumulated at depth was still in his body, expanding faster than his body could expel it, a potentially lethal state.Jenn screamed. Joe, disoriented but conscious, seemed to moan and reach for the equipment line. Takakjian was in the chase boat before Jenn could move. He grabbed Joe, flipped him on to his back. Joe made one more sound and then went still as Takakjian started slicing his gear off. Jenn was half in the water, tugging at his equipment from underneath as Takakjian cut above.Somewhere in those seconds she understood: it was already too late. There was no getting Joe back down deep enough for the decompression he would need to survive.They got him onboard with the hydraulic winch and started performing CPR until Jenn said: “Eric. If you’re doing this because you think I don’t know he’s dead, you can stop.” Takakjian took his hands off Joe’s chest. They looked at each other. They were both crying.It took hours for the three other divers – Packer and two longtime Tenacious crewmates named Andrew Donn and Rick Simon – to surface.Only Simon had seen anything wrong underwater.He had run into Joe while ascending, 50ft down, his eyes closed and his tether unclipped from the anchor line. Simon grabbed Joe and performed the standard first move for an unresponsive or distressed diver at depth, hitting his bailout valve, a mouthpiece switch that pulls a diver off the recycled gas loop he has been breathing and on to a shot of open-circuit gas from a dedicated emergency tank.Joe’s eyes opened. It wasn’t clear if he was fully conscious, but he shot up toward the surface, too quickly for Simon to safely follow. Simon lost sight of Joe in the murky water overhead, but figured he might be heading for the emergency oxygen bottle they had hung at 20ft.Back on the boat, they radioed the Coast Guard, who told them to bring Joe’s body in. There was no point in sending officers out if he was already gone. “In that moment,” Jenn said, “that felt like the worst thing in the world.”The crew put Joe in a sleeping bag and zipped it up. The 200-mile return journey was 16 hours of tortuous silence, punctuated only by the sounds of someone breaking out in sobs. At some point, Jenn crawled into the top bunk, unable to bear her usual berth, which faced Joe’s empty one.It’s over, she remembered thinking.It’s all over.Jenn spent years learning how to find what was lost. She hadn’t yet learned how to be one of the people left behind.As she moved through life underwater, the rest of the crew was undone in their own ways. Packer, 67 years old this summer, found himself unable to move for days at a time. He would get dressed to work out, sit down to put his sneakers on, and find himself unable to rise again, let alone walk the 10ft to his basement gym.Whitehead was ready to sell his rebreather and give up technical diving entirely. Ogden, who had pushed through his grief by immediately getting back in the water, told him to stop being stupid. “I was like this insane cheerleader for three months,” he said.An autopsy report ruled Joe’s cause of death as barometric trauma: the bends. What actually caused him to go into paroxysms underwater, before he shot to the surface, will probably never be known. The Coast Guard investigation, which stretches on, found that his equipment hadn’t failed. “I’m a nervous diver, so Joe always used to tell me, ‘If you can breathe, you can think,’” Jenn said. “I saw him calm and collected underwater in the most catastrophic situations. So the only conclusion I can draw is that he couldn’t breathe.”But she could breathe. She could think. She started seeing a therapist for the first time in her life. She was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, which, yeah, that felt about right.Her plan began to take shape in the weeks after she collapsed aboard Tenaciousin her ballgown and heels. Two trusted friends in the diving world, Dudas and Harold Moyers, came over to install a television at the farm one night, and she decided to lay it all out for them then and there. It was an exacting 10-year plan to rebuild the operation to what it had been, this time with Jenn at the helm, culminating in the scattering of Joe’s ashes on the U-550, the sub whose discovery had interrupted the Olympics on NBC.Moyers, a captain himself, got a funny look on his face. She waited for him to tell her she was insane, advise her to sell Tenacious.“I don’t think it’s going to take that long,” he said instead.In early October, they held a memorial at a friend’s restaurant called the Shipwreck Grill. They sounded the foghorn of the Andrea Doria, one of Joe’s most prized treasures. In front of the crew, colleagues, friends, and Joe’s family, including his parents, who had flown out from Lebanon, Jenn gathered herself to tell them about the dive they had done the previous weekend, their first expedition since Joe’s death.“The weather was rough. We learned the other boats had turned back …” she said. “It was scary. And just then I heard a voice. It was the first time I really felt him. The first time he had really talked to me since he died. That voice whispered one word: ‘Forward.’ So I put the throttle down, and it wound up being a beautiful day.”Though she didn’t say it at the memorial, what they had accomplished on that single dive – retrieving the anchor of the Maurice Tracy – had been her plan for the entire fall. As soon as Ogden surfaced with the anchor and the lift bag, he looked to Jenn. So did the rest of the crew.What next?They went diving again the next day.In January, the crew of Tenacious held an all-hands muster at her house – still without furniture – and unanimously voted her their captain.“You just inherited a huge, huge family of brothers,” Takakjian told her, “who are going to help you for ever.”She told them how it would work with her in charge. She would make the calls on things she was certain about but, unlike Joe, she wanted their input. They would all carry on Joe’s legacy together.This summer, the plan revolves around the Carolina– Joe’s favorite wreck. No one has found her bell yet. Jenn has a good feeling about it.“All I know is,” she said, “that the further from shore I am, the closer I am to him.”

title: Indonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in Borneo | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Critically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blaze
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: Critically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blaze
Content: An orangutan named Sampurna receives emergency treatment in the village of Kuala Satong after being rescued from wildfires in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn orangutan named Sampurna receives emergency treatment in the village of Kuala Satong after being rescued from wildfires in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersThe age of extinctionWildlifeIndonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in BorneoCritically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blazeThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentGloria DickieTue 15 Sep 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWildfires in Indonesiaare sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes.In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park.Hundreds of Bornean orangutans(Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, withmore than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered.“Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years.In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns –has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall.View image in fullscreenField assistants fight fires near the Rangkong research station.Photograph: Jessica LamanScientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said.But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said.“[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an orangutan research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.”In a desperate effort to save Rangkong research station, a team of more than 40 people – mostly field assistants, staff and local villagers – are fighting day and night to stave off the encroaching inferno. Recently, they constructed a firebreak and an improvised sprinkler system using a punctured hose line around the station to saturate the surrounding peat.View image in fullscreenBurnt forest near Palangka Raya, in Central Kalimantan province this week.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersOnce fire reaches a peat swamp, it can smoulder underground for months – even after surface flames have been extinguished. Keeping the peat wet is therefore a key defence.“The issue has surpassed any local organisation’s capacity,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung orangutan conservation programme. “We need large-scale water bombing and skilled firefighters.”Even if they manage to save the research station, it may be for nothing if the orangutans lose their home.“The orangutans need the forest,” Knott said. “If all we have left is the building, what are we studying if the orangutans are all gone, and the food they have is all gone? They can’t survive without that forest.”As solitary animals, orangutans require large ranges and live at low population densities. “You can’t just shove them all together in what remains of the forest,” Knott said.View image in fullscreenRescue workers prepare to transport a mother and baby orangutan named Raya and Rayu who were rescued from wildfires in East Kotawaringin, Central Kalimantan province.Photograph: Reina/AFP/Getty ImagesThose leading the on-the-ground fire response have already witnessed the impact on the apes. “Five orangutans from our long-term study population were observed fleeing the fire, some only metres from the flames,” said Wahyu Susanto, research director for Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian NGO that protects Bornean orangutans. “These are individuals that we have followed and studied for years.”Indonesian meteorologists predict an intense fire season persisting through October as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño.“The hotspots are everywhere,” O’Connell said. “I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that what we thought couldn’t burn could actually completely disappear if we’re looking at these dry conditions going on for months.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeThe age of extinctionIndonesiaEndangered speciesMammalsWildfiresAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Leader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assault | UK news | The Guardian
description: Dan Thomas, elected in May, says he does not wish to be a ‘distraction’ on same day Reform MS defects to Plaid Cymru
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Dan Thomas, elected in May, says he does not wish to be a ‘distraction’ on same day Reform MS defects to Plaid Cymru
Content: Dan Thomas is the former leader of Barnet council in north London, but is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDan Thomas is the former leader of Barnet council in north London, but is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesUK newsLeader of Reform UK in Wales stands down after arrest on suspicion of assaultDan Thomas, elected in May, says he does not wish to be a ‘distraction’ on same day Reform MS defects to Plaid CymruBen QuinnandBethan McKernanTue 15 Sep 2026 14.26 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leader of Reform UK in Wales is standing down after he was arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.Dan Thomas, a former Tory councillor, had only been announced as Reform’s Welsh leader by Nigel Farage in February.He was elected as leader of the opposition in May’s election to the Welsh parliament, when Reform UK became the second largest party.However, it emerged on Tuesday that Thomas would not be taking part in the first plenary session of the new Senedd term and questions for the first minister on Tuesday afternoon. Reform said he was absent for “personal reasons”.In a statement later on Tuesday afternoon, Thomas said: “Over the weekend, I was reported to the police and was released without charge. I stress that I have done nothing wrong, but I do not want the coming headlines to be a distraction from the fantastic work our Senedd team is doing in holding this government to account.”View image in fullscreenDan Thomas, left, and Nigel Farage at the Reform Wales manifesto launch in March.Photograph: Jon Rowley/Getty ImagesGwent police said: “On Sunday 13 September, a 45-year-old man, from the Aberbargoed area, was arrested on suspicion of assault and engaging in controlling/coercive behaviour.He has been bailed pending further inquiries.”Thomas, a former Conservative leader of Barnet council in north London, is originally from Blackwood, Caerphilly.Eyebrows had been raised on Monday when Thomas was notably quiet when it came to commenting on the meeting of the nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, who called on Westminster to prepare for independence referendums.His resignation comes as a big blow to Reform, which has poured significant resources into Wales, where it believes further inroads could be made in traditional Labour strongholds.However, the perception of Thomas as a figure who was parachuted in by Reform headquarters has caused tensions.It is believed Farage chose an outsider to the Welsh branch of the party in an effort to distance from its former Welsh leader, Nathan Gill, who was jailed for accepting bribes to make pro-Russia statements in the European parliament.Since the new Senedd opened in May, there have been frequent reports of infighting in the Reform group, and its performance in the Siambr so far has been notable for unparliamentary conduct.Thomas led Barnet council between 2019 and 2022, when the north London council was seized by Labour, and defected to Reform last summer.He stood down in December as a councillor in Finchley – long synonymous with Margaret Thatcher – to move back to his south Wales valleys home town.In May, Reform won 34 seats at the expense of Labour and the Conservatives in the Welsh parliament’s newly expanded 96-seat chamber, behind Plaid Cymru’s 43.Reform had been aiming to become Wales’s biggest party, Thomas said, but it still performed better than any Welsh Conservative result on record and managed to increase its vote share from 1% in 2021 to 29% in 2026. With more than a third of the seats, the Senedd is the biggest political platform Reform has had to date.At almost exactly the same time Thomas announced his resignation, the Reform MS Sarah Cooper-Lesadd said she was defecting to Plaid Cymru – a party nearly on the opposite end of the political spectrum.View image in fullscreenSarah Cooper-Lesadd accused her former party of not being serious about governing in Wales.Photograph: SeneddShe said in a statement: “[Reform UK] … are not serious about governing Wales. They are far more interested in division, opposition and headlines than in finding solutions.”The defection of Cooper-Lesadd coincided with more bad news elsewhere for Reform as three of its councillors resigned from the party on one of its flagship county councils, Durham, after allegations of bullying.Ken Skates, the leader of the Labour Senedd group, said: “Nigel Farage chose to make Nathan Gill his leader in Wales and he turned out to be a Russian asset. He chose to take £5m from a crypto billionaire that triggered an investigation.“He chose to meet two men in a pub in Clacton to discuss breaching electoral law. And he chose to make Dan Thomas his leader in Wales, who has now quit suddenly.”The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said on X that “people are innocent until proven guilty” but added that there was “a pattern” in terms of Conservatives who had defected to Nigel Farage’s party.“He took a large number of very problematic people from the Conservatives. Reform is where they belong,” she said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK retirees with no other income will not pay tax on new £13,000 state pension, No 10 says | Economics | The Guardian
description: Average wages rose by 3.9% in three months to July, signalling pensioners will receive uplift of same percentage in 2027 under triple lock
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Average wages rose by 3.9% in three months to July, signalling pensioners will receive uplift of same percentage in 2027 under triple lock
Content: With the tax-free personal allowance frozen at £12,570, experts had said retirees were in line for paying income tax on the new state pension for the first time.Photograph: Bill Cheyrou/AlamyView image in fullscreenWith the tax-free personal allowance frozen at £12,570, experts had said retirees were in line for paying income tax on the new state pension for the first time.Photograph: Bill Cheyrou/AlamyEconomicsUK retirees with no other income will not pay tax on new £13,000 state pension, No 10 saysAverage wages rose by 3.9% in three months to July, signalling pensioners will receive uplift of same percentage in 2027 under triple lockRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has promised retirees they will be excluded from paying tax on the full new state pension after official figures paved the way for an inflation-beating increase above the tax-free personal allowance.Figures published on Tuesday showed that average UK wages rose by 3.9% in the three months to July, signalling that pensioners will receive an uplift of the same percentage next year underthe triple lock.This implies the full new state pension will rise from £241.30 a week (about £12,500 a year) to £250.70 a week (about £13,000 a year) from next April. For the two-thirds of pensioners who reached qualifying age before April 2016 in receipt of the old basic state pension, it will mean a rise to £192.10 a week (about £9,990 a year).With the tax-free personal allowance frozen at £12,570 – under a policy introduced by the previous Conservative government and extended by Labour until 2031 – experts warned that retirees were in line for paying income tax on the new state pension for the first time.However, ministers moved to reassure pensioners with no other income this would not happen as the government faced the prospect of a political backlash, in a development that will add to the challenges facing the chancellor, John Healey, at next month’s budget.Torsten Bell, the pensions minister, said: “In line with thecommitment made at budget 2025, pensioners who only just the exceed the personal allowance will not have the administrative burden of paying small amounts of tax in this parliament.“The chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the budget.”Under the triple lock, the state pension rises by whichever is highest out of inflation, average earnings growth or 2.5%. Forecasters do not currently anticipate a rise in inflation in September – the key month for the policy – above the 3.9% rate of wage growth in July.Graph showing pay growth in Great Britain from 2022 to 2026There are, however, growingcalls for an overhaul of the policy, which was first introduced by George Osborne in 2011, amid rising pressure on the public finances and demands to refocus state support on younger generations.In the latest intervention, the British Chambers of Commerce hascalled for the policy to be scrapped, and the money saved to be put towards tackling the youth unemployment crisis.The development comes despite a slowdown in wage growth from a rate of 4.1% in the three months to June, in a renewed squeeze on workers as theBank of Englandprepares to set interest rates on Thursday.Reflecting a cooling jobs market, the Office for National Statistics said the number of workers on company payrolls continued to edge down, driven by a decline in jobs in the retail and hospitality sectors. Job vacancies in the three months to August fell to 702,000 from 706,000 in the previous month.The headline rate of unemployment remained steady at 4.9%, confounding expectations for a modest rise to 5%.It comes as the Bank considers its response to the rise in global energy prices triggered by the Middle East conflict before a crunch meeting on Thursday that will take place against a darkening global backdrop.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity investors expect Threadneedle Street will keep the base rate on hold at the current level of 3.75%. Financial markets anticipate at least four increases to 4.75% before the end of next year.The Bank has signalled that a weaker backdrop in the labour market could help limit the capacity for stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched in the economy. However, oil prices have risen above $107 a barrel and British consumers have faced a jump in petrol and diesel prices.‘Costing billions’: is the pensions triple lock a lifeline or simply unaffordable?Read morePat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said the figures showed the jobs market had remained resilient. “But we know there is more work to do, particularly to ensure young people gain the skills, experience and confidence needed to succeed,” he added.Official figures due on Wednesday are expected to show the headline rate of UK inflation rose above 3% in August, adding to the pressure on households that have faced years of fast-rising prices after the lifting of pandemic lockdowns and the Russian invasion of Ukraine prompted a cost of living crisis. The Bank of England targets 2% inflation.Jake Finney, a senior economist at PwC UK, said: “This presents a dilemma for the Bank of England. With the jobs market remaining weak, it is difficult to see the case for raising interest rates. But the external backdrop is deteriorating again.“Oil prices are now above $100 a barrel, close to the most adverse of the three scenarios the Bank outlined in July, raising the risk of renewed inflation pressures.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsState pensionsInterest ratesTaxUK unemployment and employment statisticsBank of EnglandUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Army officers ‘let down’ soldier over sexual assault claim before she killed herself, court martial told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Court hears that two officers did not deal properly with allegation Jaysley Beck made against a superior
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Court hears that two officers did not deal properly with allegation Jaysley Beck made against a superior
Content: Jaysley Beck, a Royal Artillery gunner, was assaulted during a training exercise in Hampshire in July 2021, when she was 19, and killed herself five months later.Photograph: Family handout/PAView image in fullscreenJaysley Beck, a Royal Artillery gunner, was assaulted during a training exercise in Hampshire in July 2021, when she was 19, and killed herself five months later.Photograph: Family handout/PAUK newsArmy officers ‘let down’ soldier over sexual assault claim before she killed herself, court martial toldCourt hears that two officers did not deal properly with allegation Jaysley Beck made against a superiorSteven MorrisTue 15 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo army officers “let down” a teenage soldier who went on to kill herself when they did not deal properly with a sexual assault allegation she made against a superior, a court martial has heard.Jaysley Beck, 19, told Col Samantha Shepherd that she had been touched on the leg by a warrant officer during a social event at an adventure training exercise, the court was told.But Shepherd allegedly misrepresented what Beck had told her when she reported the claim, falsely saying there had not been physical contact.The second officer, Maj James Hook, failed to take the incident seriously and was sceptical of what Beck had reported, believing she wanted to leave the training package, the court heard.Shepherd and Hook deny “conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline”. Shepherd is accused of misreporting what she had been told by Beck while Hook allegedly did not treat information passed to him in a manner “consistent with its seriousness”.At the start of the trial, the assistant judge advocate general Edward Legard said he expected the board hearing the case – an RAF air commodore, navy captain and army colonel – almost certainly knew of the Beck case.He told them she had taken her own life and there had been significant press interest but they should put anything they had heard about it to one side.Legard also instructed them not to be influenced by anyone’s views – including their chain of command – on the subject of unacceptable sexual behaviour in the armed forces.Cdr Paul Patterson, for the crown, said Beck was taking part in the training package in Hampshire in July 2021. Hook was running the exercise while Shepherd was the regimental colonel.Following a social function, Beck was found distressed and sleeping in her car early in the morning by a colleague, L/Cpl Drew Tudor. She told him there had been an incident the night before with a warrant officer, Michael Webber, who was senior in rank to her.Hook was alerted and Beck expressed concern over what would happen if she made a complaint. He gave her until noon to decide what she wanted to do.The court was told he was sceptical as Beck was not enjoying the adventure package and he thought she may be wanting to leave.Patterson said rather than empowering her, Hook could be seen as “leaning on her”. He said an issue for the board to consider was if Hook knew he was dealing with a potential sexual assault.Shepherd was told of the incident later. She went for a walk with Beck, who told her Webber had touched her leg and tried to kiss her, the court heard.Patterson said when she went to speak to an adjutant, whose role includes advising on discipline, about the incident, Shepherd was asked if there had been physical contact and allegedly replied that there had not been.The prosecutor said that the colonel “edited the information” when she “should have told the truth”. He told the court it was the crown’s case that Shepherd deliberately tried to suppress the detail about touching, knowing that if she did report this it would go to service police.Patterson said Beck told each of the officers enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted and she had been let down by them.Tudor became emotional as he gave his evidence. He said when he found Beck in her car she was distressed and told him that Webber had “tried something on with her”. He said he could not now remember Beck’s exact words but added: “I was concerned enough to want to report it.”The adjutant, Maj Mae King, told the court Shepherd had told her Webber had attempted to kiss Beck but Beck had leant away. She said: “My understanding was no physical contact had been made.”King said incidents such as this were “relatively normal” and it was not the most serious she had dealt with.King told the court that Webber’s wife worked in the same building as her and there was concern about her welfare. She said she did not know if the wife knew about what had allegedly happened during the adventure package. “It wasn’t our business to tell her,” King said.Beck’s mother, Leighann McCready, from Cumbria, sat in the front row of the public gallery, holding her daughter’s army cap.The trial at Catterick in North Yorkshire continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bristol becomes first British city to ban advertisements for fast fashion | Bristol | The Guardian
description: Green-run council also curbing ads for airlines, cruises, fossil fuels and SUVs on its billboards and bus shelters
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Green-run council also curbing ads for airlines, cruises, fossil fuels and SUVs on its billboards and bus shelters
Content: The policy reflects political trends in the city, which elected the Green party’s Carla Denyer as MP in 2024.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenThe policy reflects political trends in the city, which elected the Green party’s Carla Denyer as MP in 2024.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PABristolBristol becomes first British city to ban advertisements for fast fashionGreen-run council also curbing ads for airlines, cruises, fossil fuels and SUVs on its billboards and bus sheltersDamien GayleEnvironment correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBristol has become the first British city to impose a ban on the advertising of fast fashion, in new restrictions that will also curb ads for SUVs and airlines.The ban is part of moves by the West Country city, known for itsradical political scene, to impose sweeping bans on advertising for polluting industries.Restrictions have also been placed on advertising SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on advertising sites owned by the Green-run council.“We don’t want Bristol to be a billboard for polluters while we’re working hard to improve health, air quality and nature in the city,” said Heather Mack, Bristol city council’s deputy leader.“We’re proud to be thinking holistically about the changes we need to keep Bristol green and thriving.”Bristol council’s strategy and resources committee passed the new advertising and sponsorship policy by an eight to one vote on Monday. It updates a policy passed in 2021 which made Bristol the first council outside London to ban junk food ads.Tech companies know everything about me – so why do they try to sell me so much rubbish? | Joel SnapeRead moreThe policy will apply to all council-owned advertising space, including billboards, bus stop shelters, print and online.Bristol joins more than 20 UK councils that already have restrictions on ads for polluting products and services. But none has previously ibanned advertising for fast fashion products.The change in policy reflects political trends in the city, which elected the Green party’s Carla Denyer as MP in 2024, the same year that voters made the Green party the largest party in the council chamber. In Bristol,83% of residentsare concerned about climate change, according to a recent council survey.Denyer said: “I am so pleased that the council has now taken this much-needed next step and added high-carbon products and services to the list of things that will not be advertised on council-owned space.“Our Green-led council is making huge strides on Bristol’s climate and sustainability commitments, working on public transport infrastructure, home heating and community energy.“It makes no sense for these efforts to be running alongside advertisements for things like oil and gas companies, SUVs or fast fashion which do not align with our community values.”Cardiff, Edinburgh, Portsmouth and Sheffield are among the cities that have imposed restrictions on climate-harming products.The restrictions came after campaigning by Adfree Cities, a network of campaign groups, which is calling for local bans on climate-harming promotions to be made national.The group has also lobbied London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, to curb ads for fossil fuels and other polluting products on Transport for London, which has one of the largest advertising estates in the world.Nicola Wilks, co-founder and co-director at Adfree Cities, said: “We know ad bans are a catalyst for healthy change. Removing tobacco ads saved lives by reducing levels of smoking.“As a Bristol resident who cares deeply about climate change and air pollution, I am proud that Bristol has gone even further than other UK councils in curbing polluting ads; it feels like common sense.“Now we need to scale up bold local action to national tobacco-style bans on polluter advertising, to break the toxic influence of polluting companies, and support meaningful action for climate and clean air.”Explore more on these topicsBristolAdvertisingAirline emissionsClimate crisisPollutionGreen partyFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait
Content: Displaced Yemenis at a shelter north of Aden in southern Yemen. Thousands have been forced to flee their homes as fighting in the country intensifies.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemenis at a shelter north of Aden in southern Yemen. Thousands have been forced to flee their homes as fighting in the country intensifies.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in YemenEstimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab straitPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorTue 15 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting acrossYemenled the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced.As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel,Qatarwarned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign thatIranis still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute.The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict betweenSaudi Arabiaand the Houthis.Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port ​of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrel.Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest ​crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌closed its East-West ‌pipelinedue to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the ​Yanbu terminal since the start of theUS-Israel war on Iranin late February.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from a Houthi video released earlier this week purporting to show militants on an armoured personnel carrier during an offensive near Yemen’s Red Sea city of Mocha.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPAQatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthi attacks on Saudi cities.The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” againstKing Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia.The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke withOman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran.View image in fullscreenA shipping vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Qatar has warned a blockade of the waterway could have a significant impact on world trade.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe prospect of the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe.The Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”.The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships.So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive theHouthisback north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions.The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations.Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs and expatriates said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.”Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen.A map of Yemen annotated with details of locations of military actions that have taken place in September 2026.Houthi forces have been advancing in recent days amid a new offensive.But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Center thinktank said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.”She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures.“This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.”Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area.Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen.Explore more on these topicsYemenSaudi ArabiaStrait of HormuzQatarMiddle East and north AfricaUnited NationsHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nick Reiner will not face death penalty if convicted of killing parents, LA district attorney says | California | The Guardian
description: Reiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, in their home in December 2025
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Reiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, in their home in December 2025
Content: Nick Reiner appears during his arraignment on murder charges for the killing of his parents on 23 February 2026, in Los Angeles.Photograph: Chris Torres/Pool EPA/APView image in fullscreenNick Reiner appears during his arraignment on murder charges for the killing of his parents on 23 February 2026, in Los Angeles.Photograph: Chris Torres/Pool EPA/APCaliforniaNick Reiner will not face death penalty if convicted of killing parents, LA district attorney saysReiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, in their home in December 2025Dani AnguianoTue 15 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNick Reiner will not face the death penalty if convicted of the killings of his parents, Rob and Michele Singer Reiner, theLos Angelescounty district attorney’s office announced.Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles DA, said on Tuesday that his office will not pursue the death penalty in the case. He told reporters gathered outside a Los Angeles courthouse ahead of a pretrial hearing that the prosecutors had considered the wishes of Reiner family members and mitigating factors in making their decision.While the death penalty is legal inCalifornia, Gavin Newsom put a moratorium on the practice in 2019, and the last execution took place in 2006.Reiner is accused of fatally stabbing his parents in their Los Angeles home in December 2025. The deaths of Rob, 78, a celebrated director and actor, and Michele, 70, sent shockwaves through Hollywood.The 33-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two charges of first degree murder. The charges include a special circumstance of multiple murders, and a special allegation for the use of a dangerous weapon. Agrand juryindicted Reiner last month on two counts of first degree murder with an additional special circumstance of lying in wait.The maximum penalty he will face, prosecutors said, is life in prison without parole.Reiner had a history of addiction and mental health challenges, family members have said, and collaborated with his father on the filmBeing Charlie, which was reportedly inspired by his experiences. Jake Reiner, the eldest son of Rob and Michele, said in arecent interviewthat his parents “never stopped helping” Nick.Reiner’s former attorney, Alan Jackson, previously said that “pursuant to the laws of California, Nick Reiner is not guilty of murder”.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaRob ReinerCapital punishmentLos AngelesUS crimeUS justice systemWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestiality | FBI | The Guardian
description: Senators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestiality
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Senators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestiality
Content: Kash Patel speaks during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on the FBI at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKash Patel speaks during a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing on the FBI at the US Capitol in Washington DC on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockFBIKash Patel defends FBI hiring policy on applicants who have engaged in bestialitySenators question FBI chief on move to cut restrictions on agent applicants who have engaged in bestialityUS politics live – latest updatesAriana BaioTue 15 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe FBI director,Kash Patel, defended his agency’s decision to roll back restrictions on agent applicants who have previously engaged in bestiality, arguing the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” by automatically disqualifying them.The unusual topic of bestiality emerged during aSenate judiciary committee oversight hearing on Tuesdayafter Democrat Dick Durbin and Republican John Kennedy questioned Patel’s decision to remove barriers that previously prevented applicants who engaged in prostitution and bestiality from being qualified for a job at the FBI.“I’m trying to understand why you did this,” Kennedy told Patel. “We’re having a tough time attracting agents, good quality agents we all can trust … Why would you even get into bestiality?”3:13Kash Patel defends changes in FBI hiring policy regarding bestiality – videoFBI no longer banning all applicants who have had sexual encounters with sex workersRead morePatel said the change was recommended to him after he saw various “cases” in which qualifiedFBIapplicants were denied consideration because they had been forced into bestiality as a result of human trafficking.“I say this with respect to the person who recommended it, why didn’t you just say: ‘What planet did you parachute in from?’” Kennedy replied.It is unclear how many FBI applicants have fallen into this category. The FBI did not respond to a question about the data to support Patel’s assertion.In a statement, an FBI spokesperson insisted the bureau was “not relaxing hiring standards” and that the change allows it to consider “the whole of person” in certain circumstances.
