They reiterated that applicants who engaged in criminal sexual acts were not eligible for employment.The spokesperson said it had “a number of applicants in previous years who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing questions about prostitution, bestiality or other similar issues to affect their background check process through zero fault of their own”.“They showed me cases in which people were forced into it and had applied to the FBI, and so I thought: ‘They should be considered. It’s not an automatic disqualification.’ That’s all,” Patel told Kennedy.The rule change,first reported by CBS News in August, allows the FBI to consider candidates who hired a sex worker under specific circumstances, a person who stole from an employer under certain circumstances, and a person who engaged in bestiality or animal cruelty – so long as the incident took place before they were 18 years old.Kennedy, generally an ally of Donald Trump’s administration, grilled Patel on the hiring qualification change, arguing that it “really hurt” the FBI’s reputation.At one point, the Republican senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service.While Patel characterized the change as nondiscriminatory toward victims, Durbin refuted the notion and claimed it was a way to protect those who engaged in bestiality.“You dropped automatic disqualification for applicants who have been engaged in bestiality, not victims of bestiality – applicants who have engaged,” Durbin said to Patel.Patel responded: “Applicants who have engaged in bestiality means they were victims of bestiality because they were forced to do so.”Democratssent a letter to Patel on Mondayrequesting more information about the rule change and applicants who fell into the categories.Explore more on these topicsFBIKash PatelUS SenateTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge blocks Trump limits on how long foreign students and journalists can stay in US | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Ruling comes a day before homeland security department’s substantial restrictions were set to take effect
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ruling comes a day before homeland security department’s substantial restrictions were set to take effect
Content: Graduation at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts on 29 May 2025.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenGraduation at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts on 29 May 2025.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersUS immigrationJudge blocks Trump limits on how long foreign students and journalists can stay in USRuling comes a day before homeland security department’s substantial restrictions were set to take effectReutersTue 15 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge on Monday blocked theTrump administrationfrom implementing a new rule that would ⁠limit how long foreign students and ⁠journalists can remain ​in the US without applying for extensions.F Dennis Saylor, the US district judge in Boston, ruled in favor of a coalition of unions and higher education advocacy groups a day before ⁠the federal Department of Homeland Security (DHS)’s rule was set to take effect.Saylor said DHS adopted the policy based on “exceptionally weak” rationales. The agency had cited national security and the need to prevent fraud in the visa ⁠program, but the judge found it had not adhered to its legal obligations to engage with concerns about a policy change ​or consider less burdensome alternatives.In a statement, James Percival, the DHS general counsel, criticized Saylor’s ruling, saying that ‌under it US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) must “permit this rampant abuse of our immigration system”.“Come on a student visa, take one ‌class per semester, and stay here for decades,” he said.Saylor, an appointee of George W Bush, wrote that the rule upended a system through which the United States for nearly five decades had issued visas to foreign students for their “duration of status”.That system, he said, has permitted tens of millions of foreign students and researchers to come to the US, leading to “groundbreaking research in science, medicine, and technology, substantial economic growth, and a host of other benefits, often on a vast ‌scale”.Saylor said the rule DHS adopted in July seeks to replace that system with one that would substantially restrict the overall number of foreign students, professors and journalists in the US.Under the rule, F ​visas for international students and J visas that allow visitors on cultural exchange programs to work in the US would be capped at four years, while I visas for journalists, which now can last years, would be up to 240 days.About 1.6 million people currently have F visas and another 500,000 have J visas. Major research universities like Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and Harvard have large percentages of foreign ⁠students, particularly at the graduate level, the judge noted.If the rule took effect, such universities would probably suffer hundreds of millions of dollars ​in costs and enrollment would decline, Saylor said.“The ​damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to ​be catastrophic,” Saylor wrote.Miriam Feldblum, ‌the head of one ​of the plaintiffs, the Presidents’ ​Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said the judge’s ruling recognized the harm the rule would cause to international students, universities and the economy if it was allowed to take effect.“While the case continues, this relief preserves the longstanding system that enables our colleges and universities – and our country – to attract, educate, and retain global talent,” Feldblum said.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationTrump administrationUS politicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US universitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why this AI doomsday warning from former Anthropic researcher broke through | Technology | The Guardian
description: Last week, researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, stating that AI ‘could kill us all by the end of the decade’
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Last week, researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, stating that AI ‘could kill us all by the end of the decade’
Content: Jacob Coxon had insider access to both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he worked for five years.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJacob Coxon had insider access to both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he worked for five years.Photograph: Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesTechScape newsletterTechnologyExplainerWhy this AI doomsday warning from former Anthropic researcher broke throughLast week, researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic, stating that AI ‘could kill us all by the end of the decade’Blake MontgomeryTue 15 Sep 2026 08.21 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian. Today in tech, we’re discussing the past week’s all-consuming apoplexy over AI safety.Why did this warning about the AI apocalypse break through when so many others didn’t?Less than a week ago, a youngAnthropicresearcher announced his resignation from the AI giant on X, in a post that has shaken Silicon Valley, Washington DC, and even Beijing.“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” wrote Jacob Coxon.Since then, the post has been viewed 171m times, per X’s metrics. Why did it travel so far?It’s not the first time AI insiders have issued dire warnings. Every few months for the past several years, an AI researcher has resigned in a moment of crisis, proclaiming the impending apocalypse. His proclamation comes at a unique political confluence, a moment of high-strung public fear and rage.Loudly declaring that your peers in Silicon Valley are failing at AI safety is as old as the companies themselves. OpenAI’s board fired Sam Altman over safety concerns in 2023. Dario Amodei split fromOpenAIfive years ago with the aim of founding a “safety-first” lab. In 2015, Altman and Elon Musk founded OpenAI as a counterweight to Google’s approach to AI. Musk sued Altman for failing to keep a fundamental safety promise and lost.Major AI researchers have made second careers of predicting doom. Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as “the godfather of AI”, said as far back as 2023 that the technology could cause human extinction within three decades. He’s since shortened his timeline. He resigned from Google for reasons similar to those of Coxon. Hinton has been on the speaking circuit ever since, prophesying doom.Hinton’s resignation even inspired a significant response from lawmakers. In the US, Joe Biden issued an executive order mandating safety testing by AI companies. Congress summoned AI CEOs for a grilling, though that resulted in little legislative action. In the European Union, the EU Artifical Intelligence Act passed in part due to a strong reaction to Hinton’s warnings.And yet, here we are again, burdened with the feeling that little meaningful regulation is preventing harm by AI.So why is Coxon’s apocalyptic proclamation percolating deeper?First, there’s the messenger: Coxon’s call for greater safety is credible by several metrics: He had insider access to both Anthropic and OpenAI, where he worked for five years. He resigned before he would have received equity in Anthropic, demonstrating the personal cost of speaking out. And his colleagues, still on Anthropic’s payroll, corroborated his assertion that many AI researchers believe there’s a possibility that AI will bring about human extinction, with one co-worker gauging that outcome as more than 10% likely.Recent incidents in the AI field have made apocalyptic claims more credible. A swarm of AI agents operated by OpenAI went rogue, broke containment and hacked into multiple sites and organizations during safety testing with startling coordination earlier this year. On Thursday, Anthropic detailed how criminals and rogue scientists had attempted to use Claude to make bioweapons.“The reason this time is different is that out-of-control AI is not in the future, but in the past. People have seen evidence of it happening,” argued Max Tegmark, co-founder of the Future of Life Institute, which has been funded with hundreds of millions of dollars from the billionaire founder of the cryptocurrency Ethereum. (Tegmark’s organization already in 2023 called for a slowdown of AI development, which at the time provoked a rejection from Amodei.)“If you had tried to get people worried about nuclear winter in 1942, good luck. People would ask whether a nuclear weapon was even possible,” said Tegmark. “It was obvious to physicists then, but you couldn’t have freaked out normal people. It was all theoretical. With AI, it was all theoretical until this happened. Now the debate over whether you can lose control is over.”Then there’s the context. The general feeling towards technology in the US is kindling-sensitive, and claims of impending doom are fiery. The country is in the throes of a multifaceted backlash to technology. People outside major tech hubs feel imposed upon physically by data centers and figuratively by AI’s takeover of the workplace.Looming over the country are tech billionaires – in control of vast wealth, global communication channels – throwing their weight around in US politics withunmatchable campaign contributions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s been at least over a year of steadily increasing data center pushback that has made being pro-AI regulation the new common sense, and it certainly has made being pro-AI industry a very toxic brand,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute and a former senior adviser on AI for the US Federal Trade Commission.There’s the fact that the companies involved have responded vigorously to Coxon. Their pledged commitments have details and heft.“It allowed for companies like Anthropic and others to position themselves immediately as the primary experts in how to deal with these fears. How to solve problems that, by every account, they have created or are best positioned to prevent,” Kak said.Two closing thoughts. In a sign of how broad the crisis of confidence in AI has become: Strange bedfellows have partnered up in response. The Future of Life Institute is hosting a rally today in Washington promoting AI safety with headliners Bernie Sanders, the progressive senator from Vermont, and Steve Bannon, former chief of staff to Donald Trump, who have been sworn enemies on other issues.And finally: Why is the AI industry so full of men – only men in AI have expressed these fears of human extinction – in the throes of a crisis over the extinctive potential of their work?“These people certainly believe what they’re saying. It’s not a fringe view,” said Shakeel Hashim, writer of theTransformer newsletteron AI. “The best way I’ve had it explained to me is that we’re trying to build something that’s smarter than us in the way we’re smarter than monkeys. Our existence hasn’t gone great for monkeys; AGI’s existence probably won’t go great for us.”Read more about the great AI freakoutAI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fearsEurope must build own AI or risk getting cut off by US or China, says ECB’s LagardeTrump attacks ‘sick conspiracy’ against AI as tech stocks slideMicrosoft proposes limits on its AI with code of conduct amid safety debateMake sense of the crisisI worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AIWe greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism?Explore more on these topicsTechnologyTechScape newsletterAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Leading UK retailers ‘breaking law’ by not refunding customers for returned goods, Which? finds | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Consumer group says online shops routinely failed to reimburse delivery costs of unwanted purchases or cost of items
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Consumer group says online shops routinely failed to reimburse delivery costs of unwanted purchases or cost of items
Content: Matalan refunded the cost of the returned product to just seven of Which?’s 12 mystery shoppers. None received a refund for their original delivery fee.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatalan refunded the cost of the returned product to just seven of Which?’s 12 mystery shoppers. None received a refund for their original delivery fee.Photograph: John Keeble/Getty ImagesRetail industryLeading UK retailers ‘breaking law’ by not refunding customers for returned goods, Which? findsConsumer group says online shops routinely failed to reimburse delivery costs of unwanted purchases or cost of itemsSarah MarshConsumer affairs correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeading retailers are breaking the law by failing to properly refund customers for returned goods, a Which? investigation has found.Some of the UK’s biggest online shops routinely failed to reimburse delivery costs when customers returned unwanted purchases, while others failed to refund the cost of the goods themselves.The consumer champion Which? sent 12 mystery shoppers across Great Britain to buy more than 200 items from 17 big online retailers in June and July.The shoppers then returned their purchases by post – the most common method of returning goods – and tracked the entire process, from the cost of returning an item to whether they received the correct refund.John Lewis came out on top, with shoppers praising the retailer for keeping them informed at every stage of the returns process. Its strong performance led to it becoming the first retailer to receive Which?’s new recommended provider for returns status.But at the other end of the table was clothing and homeware retail chain Matalan, which failed to refund customers properly in a series of cases.Matalan does not offer free returns, and refunded the cost of the returned product to just seven of Which?’s 12 mystery shoppers. None received a refund for their original delivery fee.In one case, a shopper returned an item costing £3.99. They had initially paid £3 for delivery and a further £2.99 to return it. When no refund was received, they were left £9.98 out of pocket, despite being entitled to lose only the £2.99 return cost.View image in fullscreenJohn Lewis received praise from shoppers for keeping them informed at every stage of the returns process.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianOne mystery shopper said:“There’s a returns label in the bag but it’s so faded that I can’t read the instructions.”A Matalan spokesperson said: “We want returns to be straightforward for our customers and take our obligations around refunds seriously. We have asked Which? for the transaction details behind its findings so we can understand and investigate the individual cases raised.”Reena Sewraz, retail editor at Which?, said:“Returning an online purchase shouldn’t be a battle to get your money back. Yet leading retailers are breaking the law by failing to give shoppers the refunds they are entitled to.”She said retailers “need to take responsibility for getting their returns processes right”, adding that shoppers “shouldn’t be left to foot the bill for retailers’ mistakes”.Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, online shoppers generally have the right to change their mind and cancel an order within 14 days of receiving it, with a further 14 days to return the goods. Retailers must normally refund the customer within 14 days of receiving the returned item, although some products – such as personalised goods and items with a hygiene seal – are exempt.Retailers can make customers pay the cost of returning unwanted goods, but they must also refund the standard delivery charge originally paid. Customers are not entitled to a refund of any additional premium they paid for faster delivery.River Island and Sports Direct failed to refund the original delivery fee in any of the cases tested by Which? – despite retailers being legally required to reimburse standard delivery charges when customers exercise their statutory right to cancel an online purchase.View image in fullscreenPets at Home refunded only six of Which?’s 12 mystery shoppers for products they had returned.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAA Sports Direct spokesperson said: “Unfortunately, we are not able to provide any meaningful comment on the ‘mystery shopper’ claims.“Despite requesting the basic details of the orders from Which? to be able to understand what has or has not happened with the specific transactions, they have refused to supply the necessary information. We of course seek to address genuine customer concerns.”River Island has been approached for comment.Both retailers also charge customers to return unwanted goods. While retailers are allowed to do this, the combination of return charges and missing delivery refunds left Which?’s shoppers significantly out of pocket.The investigation also uncovered failures to refund the cost of the goods themselves. Pets at Home refunded just six of Which?’s 12 mystery shoppers for products they had returned.Pets at Home said: “We regularly review our policies and the information available on our website to ensure customers have access to clear and accessible guidance on our terms and conditions. As always, if customers have any questions or concerns, we would encourage them to contact us directly.”The findings raise fresh questions about how effectively leading retailers are complying with consumer protection rules and leave customers at risk of losing money when they return unwanted online purchases.Which? said some retailers such as M&S did not qualify in the mystery shop because it didn’t offer postal returns on items bought online under £10 if you checked out as a guest – instead, you have to return in-store.Argos also did not offer postal returns, so similarly could not be included.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryEnglandJohn LewisConsumer affairsOnline shoppingConsumer rightsE-commercenewsShareReuse this content

title: Parents seek out school uniform deals, cutting average spend to £54.53 | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Overall grocery inflation in Great Britain rises to 2.3%, as Ocado and Lidl gain market share
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Overall grocery inflation in Great Britain rises to 2.3%, as Ocado and Lidl gain market share
Content: ‘Value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season,” said Fraser McKevitt of Worldpanel by Numerator.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season,” said Fraser McKevitt of Worldpanel by Numerator.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyRetail industryParents seek out school uniform deals, cutting average spend to £54.53Overall grocery inflation in Great Britain rises to 2.3%, as Ocado and Lidl gain market shareBusiness live – latest updatesJulia KolleweTue 15 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParents and carers in Great Britain spent 12.5% less on school uniform in the run-up to the start of this academic year, turning to promotions and secondhand items to keep expenses down as families struggled with thecost of living crisis.The average spend on school uniform was £54.53 in the four weeks to 6 September, down an eighth from £62.29 in the same period last year, according to the market research company Worldpanel by Numerator. Overall grocery inflation picked up to 2.3% from 2.1%.Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail and consumer insight at the company, said “value is the watchword for parents this back-to-school season” as they try to balance stretched household budgets.Leading UK retailers ‘breaking law’ by not refunding customers for returned goods, Which? findsRead moreAlmost half of households (44%) prioritised keeping costs low above all else when it comes to buying uniform, even if that means compromising on quality, while a third (33%) aimed to strike a balance between the two, according to a back-to-school survey conducted by Worldpanel in August.“It’s a clear sign that, for many families, the return to school is landing at a difficult time financially, and retailers who can offer reassurance on price without compromising on quality stand will stand in good stead,” McKevitt said.Grocery sales rose 2% year on year over the period, the monthly Worldpanel figures showed. August brought more warm weather and the end of a summer of sport. But with the return to school and work looming for many, shopping habits began to shift. Shoppers made 18m fewer trips to supermarkets compared with a peak of 497m in July.“The end of the summer holidays typically brings a cooling in trip frequency and a pivot towards priority purchases, and this year is no exception,” McKevitt said. “While grocery inflation ticked up modestly last month, it remains significantly lower than the levels we saw earlier in the year, giving households some welcome breathing room.”Sandwiches featured in more than half of all kids’ lunchboxes, with more than half a million more households that include children buying loaves of bread in the seven days to 6 September compared with the previous week. The number buying satsumas (+29%) and cucumbers (+21%) also rose in the final week before the return to school.Sales at Asda rose by 0.1% over the 12 weeks to 6 September, as the grocer returned to growth for the first time since March 2024. However, the Leeds-based retailer’s market share dipped to 11.5%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe online supermarket Ocado, with sales up by 13.3%, remained the fastest-growing grocer overall, with a slightly higher market share of 2.2%. Lidl moved up to 8.7% of the market.Sainsbury’s and Morrisons maintained their previous market share of 15.2% and 8.4%, respectively. The UK’s largest supermarket, Tesco, dipped to 27.8% from 28.1%. The German discounter Aldi took a 10.6% share.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryConsumer affairsSchoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI race | Technology | The Guardian
description: From Stephen Hawking to Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation, fears that AI could threaten humanity have shaken the industry without stopping its pursuit
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: From Stephen Hawking to Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation, fears that AI could threaten humanity have shaken the industry without stopping its pursuit
Content: ‘Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing AI,’ OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote to Elon Musk in 2015.Photograph: Michael Dwyer/APView image in fullscreen‘Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing AI,’ OpenAI CEO Sam Altman wrote to Elon Musk in 2015.Photograph: Michael Dwyer/APTechnologyAnalysisWhy a decade of doomsday warnings failed to slow the AI raceJohana BhuiyanFrom Stephen Hawking to Jacob Coxon’s viral Anthropic resignation, fears that AI could threaten humanity have shaken the industry without stopping its pursuitTue 15 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 04.01 EDTShareBefore anAnthropicresearcher resigned and declared human extinction imminent last week, tech leaders and scientists had sounded the alarm about a superintelligent AI ending humanity for over a decade.The development of artificial intelligence “could spell the end of the human race”, warned professor and astrophysicistStephen Hawkingin 2014 – a little less than a decade before the public got its hands on the generative AI features of the original version of ChatGPT.It’s a now-familiar warning, echoed across the AI and tech industry by countless employees and CEOs of the leading frontier labs across the US. However, at the time, generative AI was still in its infancy. To the public, the idea that the technology could perform many of the tasks it can today, much less become super intelligent and take over the world, felt largely hypothetical, if not entirely a thing of science fiction.Every few years, a schism occurs within AI. Teams of researchers and tech leaders issue somber warnings about the dangers of AI built irresponsibly. Rather than push for a pause on any development, a faction of researchers breaks away to create a new AI company.However, no moment has created as many reverberations across the industry as the now-viral resignation of Anthropic safety researcher, Jacob Coxon, who tweeted on 9 September that Anthropic and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving super intelligence and gambling with our lives”. His concerns were echoed by dozens of staffers from Anthropic, OpenAI and other competing firms.Days later, the CEOs of the leading US AI firms answered a call from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to slow down what he called a “reckless” approach to creating AI.“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious,” Amodei wrote in a blog post. “I’vewrittena lot about them too. They include the risk oflosing control of AI systems,misuse of AI for cyber-attacks and bioterrorism, andserious economic disruption. A race to the bottom, spurred by commercial incentives, can make these risks more acute.”While there’s often scant detail and even less hard evidence provided for the ways AI could lead to the ultimate doomsday scenario, that specter has loomed large over the technology’s development.Hawking’s fear was that AI would become so advanced that it would redesign itself, and humans “who are limited by slow biological evolution” wouldn’t be able to compete “and would be superseded”, he said in an interview with theBBC.Google was the biggest household name in the field at the time, particularly after acquiring a two-year-old AI startup, DeepMind, for $650m in January 2014. But Google and other firms like it weren’t building AI responsibly enough, according to Elon Musk andSam Altman. The threat that AI could be developed in a way that could be dangerous for humanity was so pervasive, they claimed, that they co-founded a nonprofit dedicated to building it safely, OpenAI, in 2015.OpenAI’s statedmissionwas to “advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return”. But even before there were clear consumer use cases for more rudimentary versions of the technology, both Musk and Altman were already motivated by competition.“Been thinking a lot about whether it’s possible to stop humanity from developing AI. I think the answer is almost definitely not,” Altmanwrotein 2015 in an email to Musk, which was released as part of Musk’s 2024 lawsuit against OpenAI. “If it’s going to happen anyway, it seems like it would be good for someone other than Google to do it first.”In the intervening years, priorities within OpenAI shifted away from safety, some employees claimed. In 2021, several employees focused on AI ethics and alignment at OpenAI left the firm. They argued the company had started to prioritize rapid commercial development over safety.Those employees created another company: Anthropic.Founded by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic pitches itself as an “AI safety and research company” with a familiar mission: Developing and deploying AI models “in a way that benefits people”.Coxon worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic.The underlying premise of each of these firms is that AI is “only safe in their hands” and that if they don’t build it, someone else will, said Sarah Myers West, co-executive director of the AI Now Institute, which studies the impacts of AI. That paranoia is fueling a race to the bottom, she argued.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth Anthropic and OpenAI face enormous pressure from investors to turn a profit soon. The former has raised over $130bn, while the latter’s funding has reached over $190bn, and both companies have filed for an initial public offering on the US stock market. Altman only recently said the company plans to push back its IPO to at least 2027 due to safety concerns.“They are investing literally billions of dollars in building AI at a larger and larger scale, and the first thing that gets cut is meaningful investment in baseline security protocols,” Myers West said.Around the same time that the fractures among OpenAI’s safety teams began to form, Google’s AI arm faced its own internal reckoning. In 2020, Dr Timnit Gebru was ousted from her role as co-lead of Google’s ethical AI team after publishing a paper that explored the biases and potential real-time harms of AI systems. Gebru, who founded the independent research firm the Distributed AI Research Institute, stillarguesthat the so-called doomer scenarios are a distraction from the real-time harms that AI is causing today.Three years later, Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate often referred to as the godfather of AI, also leftGoogleover his own fears of the risks that AI could be used by bad actors and one day harm humanity.Now, about five years since its founding, Anthropic is facing the same employee and industry concerns that it was born out of. In July, over 1,000 leading staff and leaders from Anthropic as well as Google, Meta and OpenAI signed a petition calling for the US government to create incentives for slowing the pace of AI development.The petition came after OpenAI disclosed that hundreds of its AI agents worked together without the company’s knowledge to breach the security of AI firm Hugging Face. Anthropic, too, disclosed that its agents also compromised the security of external firms.It wasn’t the first time a petition like this made the rounds. In 2023, after OpenAI released a new version of its chatbot, the Future of Life Institute published anopen lettersigned by figures like Musk and former Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak that called on AI firms to agree to a six-month moratorium on the development of the most advanced AI models. The Future of Life Institute is a nonprofit that is largely funded through a cryptocurrency donation from Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin.Two weeks after the 2026 Hugging Face breach, OpenAIannouncedit was pausing development of some aspects of AI training. That didn’t stop the company from ultimately releasing its latest AI model called Astra – albeit with more limited cybersecurity capabilities, the company said. Anthropic,too, said it had temporarily paused development of some aspects of its AI training.Coxon resigned shortly afterward.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)GoogleSam AltmanStephen HawkingChatbotsAnthropicanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin David | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Her father was Laurie Lee, her mother the Bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape painting
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: Her father was Laurie Lee, her mother the Bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape painting
Content: Her own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity … Untitled (Green Landscape), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistView image in fullscreenHer own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity … Untitled (Green Landscape), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistArt and design‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin DavidHer father was Laurie Lee, her mother the bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape paintingAlice FisherTue 15 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Clio David was growing up, her mother’s studio was off-limits. The wooden outbuilding where her mother, Yasmin, went to paint was in the apple orchards that surrounded her childhood home in southDevon. It had once been a dormitory for the students of Dartington Hall, a progressive school where Clio’s father taught during the 1960s.View image in fullscreenYasmin with her father, Laurie Lee, West Sussex, 1940.Photograph: Estate of Yasmin David“It was somewhere she went every day to paint and work, and no one was allowed near it,” says Clio. “The walls of our house were covered in her paintings, but the studio was a private place.”Yasmin’s own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity. Her mother, Lorna, was one of theGarman siblings, a free-spirited family whose friendships and love affairs connected everyone fromPeggy GuggenheimtoVita Sackville-West. Lorna married Ernest Wishart, a wealthy communist who co-founded socialist publishing houseLawrence & Wishart, but she was also Lucian Freud’s lover and the subject of a number of his paintings before the painter met and married Lorna’s niece, Kitty. When she was 19, Yasmin discovered that her biological father was writerLaurie Lee. He dedicated his 1944 book of poetry, The Sun My Monument, to her mother and to “Y”. Yasmin found out that her name was chosen because a capital letter Y resembles two conjoined Ls – to symbolise Laurie and Lorna’s relationship.View image in fullscreenUntitled (Waterfall 2), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistBut Yasmin quit London and art school at 23, moving to rural Devon with her husbandJulian David, who became a Jungian analyst. She lived onLuscombe farmfor much of the rest of her life, and the full extent of her painting talent was only discovered after her death. Clio was going through her mother’s possessions, and opened a cupboard to find more than 200 canvases and 550 works on paper neatly stacked inside – luminous, brooding pictures of the area’s moorland, woods and rivers, with the wild landscape lit by spectral sunlight. There was also a wealth of poetry, nature writing and touching letters from Yasmin’s father.A selection of these pieces were shown alongside the paintings in a memorial show at theNew Art Gallery Walsall in 2021. The gallery had been built by Lorna’s sister, Kathleen Garman, to showcase work by her husband, sculptor Jacob Epstein.Untitled (Luscombe 1962), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistThis month, Yasmin’s work is in a new solo show that focuses on her contribution to British landscape painting. The Nature of Light, featuring more than 40 works on canvas alongside drawings, sketches, notebooks and photographs, is at theThelma Hulbert Gallery in Honiton, about 40 miles from Yasmin’s home in Luscombe.Curator Gemma Girvan says: “Presenting Yasmin’s works here brings them full circle, reconnecting them to the place which inspired them. Yasmin lived and worked on the edge of Dartmoor and many of the landscapes she painted will be instantly recognisable to our local audiences. We hope this exhibition will encourage wider debate about the many talented female artists whose work remains under-recognised including our gallery’s namesake,Thelma Hulbert.”Art historian Sophie Hatchwell, who is giving a talk on Yasmin’s work during the run of the show, says that it “sits in comparison with that ofJoan Eardley,Barbara DelaneyandGillian Ayres. It offers a way into thinking about the British landscape outside the traditional patriarchal framework as a territory to be conquered.”The British art world, confronting its long history of institutional bias and sexism, is now reconsidering the importance of female art inspired by nature. The Courtauld gallery in London ran the exhibitionA View of One’s Own: Landscapes by British Women Artiststhis spring, and artists as disparate as Cuban sculptorAna Mendietaand British printmakerAngie Lewinhave major shows either on or scheduled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPortrait of Yasmin David in 1972.Photograph: Estate of Yasmin DavidClio David, a documentary film-maker based in London, is now sharing her mother’s work with academics at the Courtauld Institute to ensure Yasmin’s contribution to the landscape genre is recognised. “She was one of the few women working in landscape during the latter part of the 20th century, and I want to place her archive within that period of art history.”Yasmin’s art is unique, but her background undeniably is, too. And raising the profile of her work would also change the picture of a family where typically women supported the men in their creative endeavours. Clio is all too aware of this: “I want to show her work as her family history is largely dominated by male artists and writers –Laurie Lee, Lucian Freud, Jacob Epstein, Roy Campbell, Michael Wishart. She was a female artist from a very well-connected family, but working outside the art establishment on a farm in the middle of the countryside, about as far from the Colony Rooms as you could get. I want her work as an artist to be recognised and celebrated.”Yasmin David: The Nature of Light is atThelma Hulbert Gallery, Honiton, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArt and designPaintingPoetryLaurie LeeArtDevonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Benedict Cumberbatch on his Earth-saving eco film: ‘We are in the last grab of the extraction era’ | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: From Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venison
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: From Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venison
Content: ‘Nature can be monetised to be protected’ … Cumberbatch in How to Live on Earth.Photograph: Conor McDonnellView image in fullscreen‘Nature can be monetised to be protected’ … Cumberbatch in How to Live on Earth.Photograph: Conor McDonnellDocumentary filmsInterviewBenedict Cumberbatch on his Earth-saving eco film: ‘We are in the last grab of the extraction era’Helena HortonFrom Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venisonTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenedict Cumberbatch is dreading stepping outside. He’s speaking to me from his air-conditioned hotel room in Soho at the peak of the summer heat. Few doubt that climate breakdown was a major cause of those scorchers, with nature, farming and water supplies all placed under huge strain. By midsummer,according to a report co-authored by the Met Office, there were 2,700 excess deaths in England and Wales due to the searing heat.But for Cumberbatch, in a bittersweet way, the record-breaking temperatures have come at a good time. The actor has been on a tour to promote his new documentary, How to Live on Earth. “The irony is not lost on anyone,” he says. “We’re living in the results of climate breakdown so stepping outside is – literally – a call to action.”double quotation mark‘I walk my dog on the heath. I cycle, use public transport – and I’m a wild-water nut’His film launches on YouTube this month and the actor hopes it is a “blueprint” for how we interact with our besieged planet in the future. It features Cumberbatch delivering monologues from the cavernous halls of the Natural History Museum in London, in between short films showing how activists, scientists and even chefs are learning a “new way to live on Earth” – one that could stop humanity damaging it.Cumberbatch has spent the last two decades trying to reframe his relationship with the planet: he’s tried to live more gently on Earth and became vegan. However, this was a problem during the shooting of The Courier, in which he plays captured British spy Greville Wynne, who languishes in a Russian jail. “They said, ‘You can’t have any fibre in the last two weeks. You need to eat lean meat.’ And I was like, ‘I’m vegan!’”View image in fullscreen‘You should think about eating a little bit of meat now’ … Cumberbatch in The Courier.Photograph: Liam Daniel/APNo fibre for two weeks must have been tough on the bowels? “Yes, it was, but it was much less than what the character I was portraying went through, because it was a true story.” Although he went straight back on the vegetables, the extreme diet caused his blood sugar to plummet and he became unwell. “People were saying, ‘You should think about eating a little bit of meat now, because your body doesn’t really work under these conditions – you’ve lost so much weight.’”Now, Cumberbatch tries to source the meat he does eat ethically, opting for venison, which in the UK needs to be culled as the country has an overpopulation of deer. But his experience on The Courier is just one way that working in films can challenge even the most committed eco-campaigner. Cumberbatch works with theGreen Ridermovement, which asks actors to make cutting pollution and emissions during filming a condition of taking part.“What we’re trying to push towards is where it becomes contractual,” he says. “We’re working with Disney at the moment – their Avengers project in the UK. So yeah, it’s scaling up – and everyone I speak to about it in my community is on board.”So, he’s ditched veganism, but would he get a private jet? “No,” he says, but adds the caveat: “We just waste our energy if we’re naysaying and calling people hypocrites. The fashion industry is a bigger polluter than aviation, and the food industry massively. That’s all of us, that’s everyone.” Not just movie stars.View image in fullscreen‘A lot of the work we do just isn’t widely seen’ … snow leopard expert Dan O’Neill in the rainforest.Photograph: Open Planet StudiosThe 50-year-old has long been an environmental campaigner. He visited the Extinction Rebellion protests in 2019 and has been dismayed by the recent government crackdowns on climate protests, with long sentences given to people who have blocked roads and smashed windows for the cause. “We should have the right in a democracy to peaceful action, even if it is direct action,” he says.Cumberbatch is keen to highlight the film’s positive message and, unlike most environmental documentaries, it does (almost) have a happy ending. It follows some remarkable people, from Indigenous activists trying to protect salmon from a dam, to Barack Obama’s former White House chef who is experimenting with alternative proteins. The message is that there are alternatives out there, and that nature can heal if humans stop hurting it.One of the film’s most striking characters is Dan O’Neill, a biologist who studies big cats and spends weeks at a time in the depths of rainforests to study the creatures who live there. He’s hopelessly in love with nature and that comes across in the film. “I always work in remote places,” he says. “A lot of the work we do just isn’t seen by wide audiences. People in Mongolia often have never seen a snow leopard, for example. I am so proud How to Live on Earth is going on YouTube – as people who live in these remote places can see it. It democratises our message for the entire world. Indigenous communities will see themselves represented.”In one scene, O’Neill is being whisked away from the rainforest in a car, and he turns on his phone to finally receive messages from friends and family after a long stretch without signal. But his dopamine hit turns to frustration as he is barraged with notifications and he ends up missing the seclusion of the forest. “That happens every time,” he laughs. “It is so weird that we are addicted to this little device. The ability to communicate with my family even from remote parts of the world is powerful. But the second you get your phone, you realise you don’t want it.”Many of us have a similar love-hate relationship with our phones and Cumberbatch is no exception. “For about half a year,” he says, “I haven’t brought myself to look at the tally of unanswered WhatsApps and emails. It’s just thousands. I can’t deal with it.” He talks disparagingly of “swiping left, clickbait, all the rest of it”.View image in fullscreen‘We’re making cutting emissions a condition of taking part in a film’ … in Avengers: Infinity War.Photograph: Chuck Zlotnick/APJonnie Hughes, the film’s joint producer, says many of its participants work in far-flung corners of the globe. “Some people,” he says, “just cast themselves because they’re incredible individuals who have done something amazing and they can get across all the emotion and the excitement we should all be feeling, because it’s too easy to feel gloomy when we see what’s going on.”Cumberbatch and company discuss some blue-sky thinking in the documentary, which to the jaded viewer could seem unrealistic. The conclusion is that the trees in rainforests should be viewed as more valuable than the gold underneath them – which may be true in some moral sense, but is it going to happen in today’s economic system?double quotation markWe don’t want to foster extraction – nor all the other nasty things of populism and nationalism“Nature that’s alive is actually far more valuable to us than dead nature,” Cumberbatch says. “So an elephant’s tusk is not worth as much as the elephant alive, in terms of what it brings to the savannah, to make the savannah work as an ecosystem. It’s how you create a new financial model whereby people can invest as shareholders in nature and that nature – which has done all this work for us for free – can actually be monetised to be protected, actually get paid.”His view is refreshingly optimistic and he says he truly believes humans can save the planet: “Hopefully, what we’re seeing now in this last grab for the extractive industries is that we actually don’t want to foster that, nor all the other nasty things of populism and nationalism.”How to Live on Earth review – Benedict Cumberbatch exudes positivity in response to the climate crisisRead moreAlthough the documentary takes us to remote places, such as the Amazon, it also instructs the viewer to seek out nature at home and nurture it in cities. Where he lives, in Hampstead, London, Cumberbatch is in touch with nature almost daily, primarily through swimming in the ponds on the heath. “I am a bit of a wild-water nut,” he declares. “I also walk on the heath. I have a dog and I cycle and take public transport when I go into town.”O’Neill is doing the same thing when he’s home, across town in Walthamstow. Although there aren’t any snow leopards, he’s managed to find nature: “We have Walthamstow wetlands, which are one of the most important in Europe. I have learned so much. I make sure I spend so much more time in nature in London now.”Cumberbatch hopes to incorporate the message of the film into his daily life. “As a child, you have that sense of wonderment, which we do sadly lose. There’s a lot to knock it throughout our evolution as humans. So hold on to that – and realise how precious it all is.”How to Live on Earth is on YouTube from 20 SeptemberThis article was amended on 15 September 2026. An earlier version described Jonnie Hughes as the film’s director. He is in fact a producer. Also, a reference to filming in Alaska was made in error.Explore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsBenedict CumberbatchNature documentariesClimate crisisConservationEnvironmental activismEthical and green livinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Grey’s Anatomy: the steamy and often thrilling medical drama is still endlessly watchable | Television | The Guardian
description: It launched the careers of Sandra Oh and Katherine Heigl, popularised terms like ‘vajayjay’ and even managed to make bowel obstruction sexy
Author: Patrick Lenton
Headline: It launched the careers of Sandra Oh and Katherine Heigl, popularised terms like ‘vajayjay’ and even managed to make bowel obstruction sexy
Content: Grey’s Anatomy: ‘You can get pleasantly lost for a very long time (years, in fact) in the dramas of Seattle Grace/Grey Sloan memorial hospital.’Photograph: Michael Desmond/fiveView image in fullscreenGrey’s Anatomy: ‘You can get pleasantly lost for a very long time (years, in fact) in the dramas of Seattle Grace/Grey Sloan memorial hospital.’Photograph: Michael Desmond/fiveStream teamTelevisionGrey’s Anatomy: the steamy and often thrilling medical drama is still endlessly watchableIt launched the careers of Sandra Oh and Katherine Heigl, popularised terms like ‘vajayjay’ and even managed to make bowel obstruction sexyPatrick LentonTue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromThe Pittto the Australian hitThe F Ward, audiences just cannot get enough of shows about doctors who not only know how to conduct open heart surgery, but also mend their own broken hearts along the way.In many ways you could say thatGrey’s Anatomy, and other medical dramas includingER, ran in dramatic slow motion through hospital corridors first so that The Pitt could also run (though in a slightly grittier and more realistic way).Shabana Azeez: ‘The most disgusting thing I’ve seen on The Pitt? American coffee’Read moreBut we’d be doing Grey’s Anatomy a disservice if we only spoke about it only as an ancient precursor to other shows, because not only is it still going – it was has now been renewed for an impressive 23rd season, making it the longest running primetime medical drama on US television – but in 2025 it was the second most-streamed series in the US across all platforms.It makes sense too; you can get pleasantly lost for a very long time (years, in fact) in the dramas of Seattle Grace/Grey Sloan memorial hospital.View image in fullscreenSandra Oh as Cristina and Ellen Pompeo as the ‘frankly cursed Meredith Grey’.Photograph: Craig Sjodin/PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyIt’s frankly a legendary show, one that defined its creator Shonda Rhimes’ production company Shondaland and its style of fast dialogue, complicated relationships, diverse casts, shocking twists and emotionally intense storytelling.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsIt launched the careers of stars including Sandra Oh and Katherine Heigl and popularised pop-cultural terms including “vajayjay”, and also became famous for turning songs into emotional shorthand. Snow Patrol’s Chasing Cars and the Fray’s How to Save a Life soundtracked emotional hospital moments, such as Cristina Yang (Sandra Oh) laying in the snow having a meet-cute while impaled by an icicle, and can easily dissolve a room of elder millennials into a weeping mess upon hearing.View image in fullscreen‘Meredith is a kind of Carrie Bradshaw with a medical degree.’Photograph: Gale Adler/fiveGrey’s Anatomy debuted in 2005 and stars Ellen Pompeo as the frankly cursed Meredith Grey. At first, she’s a brilliant surgical intern who makes the world’s worst personal choices and suffers so many truly insane tragedies and moments of real danger that any annoyance you feel about her will-they-won’t-they-why-they relationship with the handsome walking head of hair “Dr McDreamy” (Patrick Dempsey’s Dr Derek Shepherd) is replaced by concern for her mental wellbeing.From drowning to holding an unexploded bomb in someone’s chest cavity, watching her husband get shot, having a miscarriage as a result and spending most of the Covid-era season in a coma, Meredith not only has terrible luck but also most likely deep PTSD. By later seasons, she essentially owns the hospital.Meredith is a kind of Carrie Bradshaw with a medical degree, acting as the narrator and the primary point of view. But by season 19, she steps back from being the primary protagonist – probably because Pompeo is tired and also because there’s nothing else that can possibly happen to her character.The show follows the Shonda Rhimes formula of taking a place that’s not normally very sexy and turning it very sexy. The creator and producer found a way to make the past sexy in Bridgerton; Washington in Scandal; murder school in How to Get Away With Murder, and hospitals. All very sexy. There is so much sex and relationship drama happening in this hospital: on-call rooms become the setting for steamy hook-ups, longing glances are passed over a cracked-open sternum, and the hospital elevator becomes a recurring location to have tight one-minute breakups.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘Of course, 23 seasons over 21 years means Grey’s Anatomy cannot be viewed as the same show the entire time.’Photograph: Richard Cartwright/ABCBut at the same time as all this steamy drama, there is an extremely exciting medical procedural happening – and the medical stunt episodes are legendary. The bomb in the chest two-parter, the active shooter episode, the plane and train crashes – each episode not only becomes a thriller but also raises and resets the personal stakes for all the characters. If there’s a recipe for escapism, Rhimes has found it in the shifting shades from romance to melodrama in Grey’s Anatomy.Of course, 23 seasons over 21 years means Grey’s Anatomy cannot be viewed as the same show the entire time – and in fact it devolves somewhat into soap opera after a while, mostly thanks to the sheer amount of deaths and weddings and births. There’s even a really great musical episode, which does a great job of actually justifying why everyone is suddenly singing (brain tumour).It’s also just fascinating as a historical artefact – going back to those early seasons is a journey through old fashions, outdated ideas, Obama-era hope, even technology (there’s a whole season obsessed with 3D printing). Someone gets proposed to via flashmob.But ultimately what makes this show so endlessly watchable and enduring is that the hospital, with all its smooching and drama and medical malpractice suits, is basically untouched by the outside world – a place you can truly escape to.Grey’s Anatomy is available on Disney+ in Australia and the UK. It’s available on Disney+, Netflix, Hulu and Prime Video in the US.
