title: The Debut review – Julianne Moore is a thrill in Jesse Eisenberg’s oddball comedy | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musical
Author: Richard Lawson
Headline: Riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musical
Content: Julianne Moore in a scene from The Debut.Photograph: Matt Infante/A24/APView image in fullscreenJulianne Moore in a scene from The Debut.Photograph: Matt Infante/A24/APFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewThe Debut review – Julianne Moore is a thrill in Jesse Eisenberg’s oddball comedyToronto film festival:riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musicalRichard Lawsonin TorontoTue 15 Sep 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJesse Eisenberg’s last two directorial efforts – the prickly comedyWhen You Finish Saving the Worldand the slightly softerA Real Pain– are small films rooted in the real world. They have their little idiosyncrasies, their bits of cinematic flair, but they keep their feet grounded in the here and now. For his third film, Eisenberg has said goodbye to all that (or most of that) and run headlong at the surreal and the absurd, borrowing from Charlie Kaufman and other oddballs to tell a small story in a big way.Elsinore review – Andrew Scott is astonishing as Ian Charleson in devastating Aids dramaRead moreThe Debut is about a repressed housewife, Mona (Julianne Moore), who decides to audition for a role in a community theater production of a musical called Nosy Neighbors, one of those gassy Manhattan trifles that were so ubiquitous on Broadway a half century ago. Mona’s kids are about to fly the nest, and her husband barely seems to notice her when she’s standing right next to him. So why not have a little creative adventure?From that setup, Eisenberg could have gone to the obvious place, staging a sweet dramedy about a humble act of artistic expression opening Mona’s eyes to all the possibility of life outside her little bubble. He does do that, in part, but he also wants to take things to a darker place. The film gradually morphs into a study of actorly obsession and vanity, as Mona takes the Stanislavksi-esque teachings of the play’s director, Jerry (Paul Giamatti, doing his wearily charming thing), to extremes perhaps not seen since Black Swan. That’s a clever idea: a director watching in horror as the monster he’s created threatens to lay waste to his production.The trouble is, none of this, not the nice story of blossoming passion, nor the acidic satire of pretentious artistes, unfolds in an environment that looks and feels anything like the dimension all of us are currently living in. Eisenberg has unrooted the film in time – there is lots of 1980s decor, but some more modern clothing; we see nary a cellphone, but there is no other specific period detail – and has his characters behave in archly cartoonish fashion.A movie needn’t be situated in plain reality, of course. But Eisenberg is inconsistent in his quirky abstraction. The Debut toggles too frequently between recognizable humanity and the mores and attitudes of whatever other-place Eisenberg has invented. Which undercuts both the parody and the pathos; without a reliable reference point, it’s hard to know what, exactly, we are meant to think and feel about anything happening on screen. Or, rather, it’s hard to connect to the sentiment that, I’m surmising, Eisenberg is trying to get across: a wry and bleary appreciation for the thrill and risk and silliness and beauty of making art.Still, it is fascinating to watch Eisenberg expand his purview like this, taking a swing at the grand and busy techniques of marquee film-makers like Kaufman, like Ari Aster, like Alejandro González Iñárritu. He shows an aptitude for ornate visuals, his camera ceaselessly moving as we are whisked around the theater and down the grimier avenues of Mona’s curious journey outside of herself. Eisenberg sets a quick pace early on and manages to sustain that energy for the duration. By the end of the picture, we really do feel that we’ve traveled somewhere, that all of the film’s relentless motion and noise has given us some kind of full-bodied experience.But I suspect none of that would be possible without the invaluable presence of Julianne Moore, enjoying one of the most substantial, dynamic film roles she’s had in a long time. She attacks each scene with the breakneck vigor that first endeared her to audiences, in 1990s films like Boogie Nights and Magnolia. And she’s often a riot, knowing just how to make Mona’s mounting melodrama and histrionics funny without tipping it all into hammy slapstick. It’s a thrilling performance, even when Eisenberg seems to have lost his hold on the reins. Maybe there’s a kind of accidental tribute in that, a director finding the right leading lady to hold things together until the production rights itself.Oh, and Moore can sing! Which I guess we sort of knew from her turn in the grisly film adaptation of Dear Evan Hansen. She fares far better here. The music in The Debut will be one of its nerdy selling points, for theater geeks eager to kick the tires of this made-up musical and assess whether it’s credible as a show that could have once existed. Eisenberg wrote the songs himself, and I think they mostly pass the test. Though, what does it ultimately matter, when the film takes place nowhere and at no time in particular? Nothing needs to add up, really, because the film is forever inventing its own rules.That does get frustrating as The Debut unfolds; true investment proves difficult when what we’re watching could arbitrarily change shape at any moment. But at least there is Moore to rely on, whipping up a floridly tragicomic storm. She once again reminds us of her boggling range and tenacity, reaching for things that many other actors might timidly think well beyond their grasp. It’s become a trite word to use about acting, but Moore’s work in the film is at times downright fearless. She careens toward embarrassment, courts the wreckage of a bold choice flopping, and somehow comes up shining. Not every actor can do that – but, as any wannabe thespian with a dream can tell you, man is it fun to try.The Debut is screening at theToronto film festivaland will be released in US cinemas on 11 December, in Australia on 25 December and in the UK on 15 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalJulianne MooreJesse EisenbergComedy filmsPaul GiamattiComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: James McNeill Whistler review – painter’s work shines through attention-grabbing life story | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his art
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his art
Content: Proto-modern … Arrangement in Grey and Black No 1, Portrait of the Artist's Mother by James McNeill Whistler.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesView image in fullscreenProto-modern … Arrangement in Grey and Black No 1, Portrait of the Artist's Mother by James McNeill Whistler.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesMoviesReviewJames McNeill Whistler review – painter’s work shines through attention-grabbing life storyThe latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his artAndrew PulverTue 15 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTimed to coincide withTate Britain’s impressive gallery show– which closes at the end of September, so you haven’t long if you’ve missed it so far – this latest from the Exhibition on Screen strand does a fine job in outlining the ins and outs, and ups and downs of this still somewhat divisive artist who, Whistler’s Mother notwithstanding, is still probably most famous for winning a farthing in damagesin his “flinging a pot of paint” libel actionagainst John Ruskin. The film assembles the customary lineup of notables including the Tate’s Carol Jacobi, critic Rachel Campbell-Johnston and art historian Stephen Calloway, the latter of whom’s dandyish attire and Colonel Sanders goatee suggests he has very much bought into the Whistler aesthetic.In fact, as all the interviewees are keen to point out, Whistler’s self-constructed persona, always with an eye to making a splash, is as significant an element of his artistic presence as the art itself – even if, as I can’t be alone in thinking, there’s something fundamentally irritating about his southern-genteel attudinising even at a century and a half’s distance. Be that as it may, the film gets to grips with Whistler’s instinctive brilliance as an artist, his natural flair for boundary-pushing and forward-thinking idealism. The big life episodes – his arrival in London, painting his mother, the brouhaha over thePeacock Room, the court case and subsequent bankruptcy – are recounted, but there is impressive detail on the actual art: from the dynamics behind hisbrooding Wapping pictureto the temper tantrums (not his) that made Harmony in Grey and Green, his portrait of the eight-year-old Cicely Alexander so distinctive. And while Whistler’s dealings with the women in his life wouldn’t exactly pass modern-era scrutiny, his pictures of them are genuinely brilliant, with especial attention given to awonderfully tender sketch of his wife Beatrix, terminally ill in a hotel bedroom.The only downside is that, so delicate and subtle is his work, Whistler’s shimmering proto-modern visions are perhaps let down a little by pointing a camera at them; it’s hardly the film-maker’s fault but they just don’t jump out of the screen as they do in the gallery. Nevertheless, the film itself is an excellent primer to one of the greats, whose richness of artistic achievement appears to be getting the comprehensive attention it deserves.James McNeill Whistler is in UK and Irish cinemas from 15 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The cauldron was already bubbling …’ Green Lung, Druidess and the return of folk horror to British heavy metal | Metal | The Guardian
description: Playing a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of way
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: Playing a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of way
Content: ‘Metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades’ … Green Lung, with Tom Templar centre.Photograph: Andy FordView image in fullscreen‘Metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades’ … Green Lung, with Tom Templar centre.Photograph: Andy FordMetal‘The cauldron was already bubbling …’ Green Lung, Druidess and the return of folk horror to British heavy metalPlaying a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of wayMichael HannTue 15 Sep 2026 06.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBehind Tom Templar’s shoulder as we talk over video call is a poster forThe Wicker Man, the 1973 cult folk-horror film set on a remote Scottish island, whose sunniness conceals – inevitably – a dark secret. It’s fitting, because Templar is the singer of Green Lung, the breakout British metal band who immerse themselves in British mythology. The forthcoming Necropolitan, their fourth album devoted to the folklore of the isles, takes its inspiration from the “Magnificent Seven” London cemeteries built in the 1830s and 40s, and from the Necropolis railway, which transported the dead out of the city. No generic demons here: this is metal in the spirit of Fairport Convention as much as Black Sabbath.“My big thesis is that heavy metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades,” says Templar. “They’re both riff-based, circling around similar tropes, and about reinventing what has gone before.Metaleven feels like a folk movement, in the way it’s full of festivals no one else has heard of. There’s such a thriving ecosystem.” Green Lung have certainly been nourished by it: at this year’s Desertfest in London, their T-shirts felt like an unofficial uniform.UK black metal has experienced this folkloric crossover, with bands such as Old Corpse Road, Winterfylleth and Wodensthrone, and Shonagh Brown, singer of Newcastle folk-horror-metallers Druidess, has also noticed the evolution. “Metal had quite a Hammer horror focus, and that’s great when times are good,” she says. “When people are comfortable they seek escapism in the less comfortable. But people spend so much time in front of screens and want to shift towards the natural world, and the folk traditions connect with that.”View image in fullscreen‘People want to shift towards the natural world’ … Druidess.Photograph: Idene RoozbayaniGreen Lung and Druidess don’t just write about the past; they sound like it. There’s plenty of Black Sabbath in both, but lots moreDeep Purple, especially in the prevalence of organ. It is more hard rock than metal: words are sung to be heard, melody matters. It’s music that reveres its history, both cult and occult. That big, rich sound, Brown, says fits their sense of past. “This kind of music is from an analog time.”Though its sound is rooted in the 70s, the two bands that planted the seed of this microgenre were active in the early 80s, though it would take years for either to be recognised. Hailing from Stourbridge, Witchfinder General released two albums that were best known at the time for their cover images, one of them showing a Page 3 model being “murdered” in a churchyard. Only later were they credited as the birth of UK doom metal. Their folk-horror claim lies largely in a song sharing the band name, one inspired by the 1968 horror film starring Vincent Price, extremely loosely based on the life of Matthew Hopkins in the English civil war. “I’m coming to get you / I’m coming to take you away!” howled singer Zeeb Parkes. “You witches are evil, you worship the devil / So listen to what I say!”They were trying to sound like Sabbath in a world that wanted velocity, guitarist Phil Cope told me in 2020: “Witchfinder tried to keep the music slow and heavy. But it didn’t really work because the majority of people were moving with the times and they liked that fast music, and we got left behind.”The other original totems, south London’s Pagan Altar, are more obscure – even in their own time. All that existed was one self-released set of demos, which was gradually reissued in various forms, though a whole catalogue of songs written during the band’s initial existence were later recorded for the Mythical & Magical album. Dance of the Druids, had it been released first time around, might have spoiled one of Spın̈al Tap’s most famous songs: “This ritual of the druids has been the saviour of mankind / Unknown to them the price was paid by personal sacrifice.”But in the absence of much music to hear, word spread of their legend: that they had built their studio on a site where witches were burned in Brockley in south London; occasional hauntings, including one by a woman in black who disappeared through the floor; and that they allegedly recreated satanic rituals onstage. “Being a strange and uncovered relic heightened their appeal, because it felt like you were discovering something arcane,” says Nick Ruskell of metal bible Kerrang! (who also moonlights as Necroskull, singer/guitarist of folk-horror-adjacent doom band Witchsorrow).It may be those legends that have made Pagan Altar guitarist Alan Jones reluctant to talk, citing bad experiences with the press, until he agreed to answer questions via email.Their interest in the occult came from their singer, Alan’s dad Terry. “I’d been playing in bands with my dad since I was 11, in 1973,” he writes. “All through the 1970s there was a lot of interest in the occult and folk, and my dad’s lyrics reflected the time.”Interestingly, as well as metal bands, Jones cites folk acts Steeleye Span, Renaissance and Pentangle, all of whom summoned English mythology. And it ties with something Fenriz of legendary Norwegian black metal band Darkthrone told me in 2021 about the rise of occultism in early 80s metal: “One had it from the 60s; the cauldron was already bubbling with Coven, Black Widow, Black Sabbath. Combine that with a lot of folk-rock that didn’t exactly feel Christian but pagan as hell – yes, I get an anti-Christian vibe from Steeleye Span. There, I’ve said it – and top it off with some Vincent Price movies.” It’s your one-pot recipe.But that raises the question: given the status of, say, Fairport Convention’s Liege & Lief, and its thematic relation to this stuff, why don’t we get more metal covers of folk music?“It’s funny you mention Liege & Lief,” says Green Lung’s Templar. “My girlfriend’s dad just gave me that record: ‘You’ll like this!’” Templar’s connection to the English past came not from those records, as it had for musicians 30 or more years older. “I grew up in rural Norfolk. There was very little to do in a hamlet of 400 people, and that was good for the imagination. I’d go round secondhand bookshops, looking for books about ufology or folkloric myths and legends. The horror came in at 16, when I started watching Evil Dead and Dawn of the Dead.”He also credits Julian Cope for spurring interest in the ancient. “He was someone who made me think this stuff was cool as a kid growing up in Norfolk, where you live without a musical context – we didn’t have a Sheffield or a Manchester nearby.”Why does he think British bands, and English bands in particular, have not embraced folklore fully, given its role in European metal? Well, he says, there’s the fact that some Nazi bands in Europe have co-opted folklore (Green Lung sell anti-Nazi merch), though he, Ruskell and Brown, all make it plain that they’ve seen no sign of that in the UK. “I don’t see an interest in British folk history as having been colonised by Nazis,” Templar says. “If anything, it’s associated with new-agey, travelling people. Of course, you don’t want to be associated with a Reform vision of Britain, but this is more Glastonbury crystal shop.”There’s also an innately British reason for resisting folklore. “Folk culture in the UK has often been depicted in a very twee way, and there are always going to be moments where it will be cheesy. But you can’t get to the good stuff if you don’t have a bit of bravery around that.”Necropolitan by Green Lung is released via Nuclear Blast on 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMetalPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci review – confessions of an ex-Trumper | Books | The Guardian
description: The president’s former press secretary has learned all the right lessons, but how come it took him so long?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The president’s former press secretary has learned all the right lessons, but how come it took him so long?
Content: Anthony Scaramucci in 2017.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Scaramucci in 2017.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesBooksReviewAll the Wrong Moves by Anthony Scaramucci review – confessions of an ex-TrumperThe president’s former press secretary has learned all the right lessons, but how come it took him so long?Zoe WilliamsTue 15 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe most interesting chapter in Anthony Scaramucci’s All the Wrong Moves is the one where the hedge funder turned podcaster goes to work for Donald Trump. It’s summer 2017, and he’s been given the job of comms director, which he doesn’t know how to do, but he and Trump think it’ll work out because they’re both from New York. Or maybe he took it because he had “Potomac fever”, which afflicts Wall Street financiers who find themselves on the riverfront in Washington DC thinking they know how to run a country just because they’re “full of power and judgmental insight … about to fix everything”.This appointment lasts only 11 days, not even enough time to be truly tainted by Trump’s first term, though it is enough time for Scaramucci to miss the birth of his son. The account is a mea culpa soup, with the author full of regrets for his hubris, his impulsivity, his “pride, egotism and asinine stupidity”, the fact that, despite the clear-sightedness bestowed by his humble beginnings, he’d come to assume the collective biases of the rich people he hung out with.But what he doesn’t address is the fact that it was quite plain by then whoDonald Trumpwas. Scaramucci himself identifies the beginning of Trump’s explicit use of racism and the politics of hatred, not in his first taboo-breaking statement that Mexicans were bringing drugs and rapists into the US (2015), but with the Obama birther conspiracy, which had been going on for years. Irrespective of all his pondering as to whether Trump was symptom or cause of a broken US, Scaramucci knew when he joined the White House that he was reporting to a racist, a chancer, an egomaniac and a liar. Bluntly, a person with decent values would not have joined this administration.That doesn’t invalidate his analysis, but it does flatten it. The US is all about money, he tells us; the founding fathers were actually the investing fathers; anything not obviously a decision motivated by money is the unintended consequence of one. The very United States was “unified – by money”, because that was all Alexander Hamilton was thinking when he created a central bank. The fact that half the English-speaking world could sing the thousand other things Hamilton was thinking in a close harmony hasn’t occurred to the author, who can’t have seen the musical. It makes his potted history of the US a little brutish, and his organising principle – that the rot started to set in from Clinton onwards, when leaders lost their “moral purpose” – contradictory. If there was never any value higher than money, how can Clinton’s purpose have been any less moral than Franklin D Roosevelt’s?All of that is just backdrop to the book’s fatal flaw. Scaramucci details the three “catastrophic” errors that have created the US’s current doldrums, and this is all wisdom he came about the hard way, through wrong moves of his own, in the board room, in the situation room, in Trump’s inner circle. These were: privileging China during the globalisation era; waging war with no corresponding tax hikes, post 9/11; and bailing out the banks.It’s hard to disagree with any of it. If the world’s manufacturing all moves to a place where wages are lower, you correspondingly destroy the employment prospects of your own workforce. But these are arguments that were diligently made at the time; by political insurgents from the right, during the 1992 election; by protest movements on the left, in the so-called Battle of Seattle of 1999, and in anti-globalisation demonstrations around the world subsequently.Scaramucci writes that he should have taken this more seriously, they were right, he was wrong, but never reflects on how it came to be. It turns out that without institutional muscle – peculiar for Scaramucci to tell the entire history of his nation’s economy with only the most fleeting mention of Ronald Reagan’s union-busting – mere logic and reason aren’t enough, until it’s too late. He similarly tells the story of the war in Iraq as a cashflow snafu without considering whether anti-imperialists and pacifists might have a point, sometimes, and the story of the 2008 bailouts with only the swiftest nod towards the Occupy movement which, again, was broadly correct in its analysis.It’s consequently a book of constant catch-up, a man who thought he knew it all, slowly surrendering to more sophisticated analyses when it is too late now anyway: China no longer looks to the US for its place in global markets; American wars are no longer waged with long-term strategic aims if patchy funding streams, but impulsively; and Wall Street no longer calls the shots, techbros do. He nods towards that last reality with a suggestion at the end to break up Silicon Valley monopolies, but never thinks seriously about how far from Kansas the world has actually strayed.It’s nevertheless quite engaging, and no more or less infuriating than it would be if, say, Alastair Campbell (Scaramucci’s UK opposite number – both coming out with hard-boiled political realism on their Rest Is Politics pods) penned an excoriating critique of the war in Iraq. But it’s hard to choke down an argument whose kernel is “sorry, guys, I just wasn’t listening” from someone still stuck on broadcast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: The Rouse by China Miéville review – a mighty achievement from the ‘new weird’ author | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Twenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousness
Author: Stuart Kelly
Headline: Twenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousness
Content: Stylistic bravado … China Miéville.Photograph: Barney CokelissView image in fullscreenStylistic bravado … China Miéville.Photograph: Barney CokelissBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Rouse by China Miéville review – a mighty achievement from the ‘new weird’ authorTwenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousnessStuart KellyTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina Miéville’s epic new novel is presented as being “20 years in the making”. It is quite a testament to how extravagant – even Stakhanovite – his imagination is that during that period he also produced six novels (includingThe City & the CityandThe Book of Elsewhere, co-written with Keanu Reeves), two novellas, two series of graphic novels, a children’s book, a volume of short stories and two works of nonfiction, on theOctober Revolutionand the Communist Manifesto.It does not mean that these works were, as Graham Greene called The Third Man and Our Man in Havana, “entertainments” –Embassytown, to my mind, is the best translation of deconstructionist philosophy into science fiction – but certainly The Rouse is a quantum jump in terms of ambition, moral seriousness and stylistic bravado. It means that rather than classifying Miéville with “the new weird” or “speculative fantasy”, he ought to be compared to Roberto Bolaño or Mircea Cărtărescu. This new novel is equally maximalist, dense, disorienting and discomfiting, reflecting how surreal our reality seems to have become.Readers acquainted with Miéville’s other work might be disconcerted by the first hundred pages: broadly speaking, they are social realism. We are in 1970s London and Maur, short for Maureen, gets pregnant and decides to keep the baby. Ewan grows up reading Rupert Bear and Starlord comics, watching Steptoe and Son and Rentaghost, and having Chinese takeaways with obligatory background racism. It is canny rather than uncanny, with the exception of a cameo from the truly odd 80s comedian Roy Jay doing his “slither-spook” routine, possibly on The Bob Monkhouse Show. (Now an internet meme, it is unforgettable and queasily sinister – and on YouTube.) Eventually Ewan, at a loss in many ways, decides to join the army. Then Miéville drops the bombshell just before the 100th page: Ewan dies, supposedly by suicide, at an army base. “Now everything is codas,” thinks Maur, and in capital letters we get THE END. The novel – all epilogue – now begins, for more than a thousand pages.The descriptions of Maur’s grief are phenomenal. “After a long time she came to believe what she knew, which was that this would never unhappen. So she did the bargaining. Just for a moment. I understand he won’t come back but I need everything to stop for just a second … What I need is I just need a moment when this isn’t all there is. That’s all I’m asking. To have anything else, or nothing, in my head. All I’m asking is just let me have one single minute ever again when he isn’t dead.”Maur, it transpires, is not the only grieving parent with a connection to Shackingham Barracks, and she finds a support network for those who are similarly bereaved. There seems to have been a spate of suicides, rather like theDeepcut controversy; something is being covered up.She falls in with an investigative journalist, Jock; a fellow bereaved parent, Cybill; and eventually a renegade ex-army operative named Stallo. At the very beginning of the book, the young Maur is warned by her father to “stay out of the dead’s business”. She doesn’t understand the import of his words, thinking, comically, he just means not becoming an undertaker.double quotation markThe Rouse is affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frighteningThe Rouse is the name of the army’s bugle call, played to call soldiers to their duties and also after the Last Post. Here it is a code for more than that: the stirrings are supernatural. The scales will fall from Maur’s eyes about the extent of the deep state’s paranormal interests.Her narrative, however, is held in counterpoint to the story of Allardyce, a soldier with a background in the more eldritch side of the armed forces. His experiences are vastly wide-ranging, from Malaya to Kenya, Akhalkalaki and the Falklands; and with both untrustworthy American allies and cabals of USSR and Chinese counterparts. This global reach is not mere exoticism: not only is Miéville concerned with the geopolitical in the broadest sense, here he holds it in parallel with the “radical democracy of death”, the “revolutionarinessof death”. Why is the military concerned with haunting and the afterlife? I don’t want to give away too much, but somehow death and the dead are an exploitable resource and a radical alternative at the same time. This being Miéville, even those “freed” from life and suffering are prey to capitalist forms of commodification and exploitation: the final twist is genius. The links between Allardyce’s schemes and the quest of Maur and increasingly Stallo are seeded cunningly and have a “rightness” in the reveal – notable in a book obsessed with “not rightness”.Linguistically, the novel is a riot. The name of Cybill harks to Sibyl, the Greek prophetess; Maur sounds like the Frenchmort. Miéville’s prose has always been baroque and esoteric, and here it is combined with slang and period detail perfectly. It has its own idiolect – one character, the spiky backrooms scientist Dr Croome, coins “inodus” as an opposite to “exodus”, commenting that “the efficacy of words is wildly overstated, most especially by those who work with them”. She opines that she “always foundgast,gæst, and particularlygōstto be so close to the dread unsayable as to be ridiculous” – but by not giving an obvious infodump of, for example, phenomena the soldiers nickname “lesprys” (derived froml’esprit de corpsbut conjuring something almost fey), the book keeps its corner-of-the-eye shimmer. The prefix “un” is used as a leitmotif: unsee, unwritten, undone, unopened. It is negation on the level of the sentence.In a sly aside, there is praise for John le Carré, whose version of the world of spooks is less paranormal than Miéville’s. Their books share the shabbiness of cold war espionage, and an ambience of regret for the days of simple us v them situations, but also the capacity to keep the reader guessing about the true affiliation and trustworthiness of the characters. That is just the tip of references, with Miéville’s capacious knowledge of the weird canon on display: there can’t be many novels that nod to Lord Kilmarnock’s 1903 Ferelith. Along with the “found texts” and concrete poems at the end of chapters there is enough here to sate the hungriest of readers. The Rouse is affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening. “Life,” as Miéville writes, “is just a prologue to a ghost story.” This is a novel destined for a rich afterlife.The Rouse by China Mieville (Pan Macmillan, £35). title: ‘We were bored of traditional fantasy cliches’: inside Playground Games’ 10-year effort to revive Fable | Role playing games | The Guardian
description: The distinctively British RPG is returning courtesy of the makers of Forza Horizon – with comedy talent such as Richard Ayoade and Natasia Demetriou voicing sweary characters. We had our first play and spoke to its developer
Author: Tom Regan
Headline: The distinctively British RPG is returning courtesy of the makers of Forza Horizon – with comedy talent such as Richard Ayoade and Natasia Demetriou voicing sweary characters. We had our first play and spoke to its developer
Content: ‘It culminates in a choice that really challenges you to think about who you are’ … a screenshot from the forthcoming Fable reboot.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosView image in fullscreen‘It culminates in a choice that really challenges you to think about who you are’ … a screenshot from the forthcoming Fable reboot.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosRole playing games‘We were bored of traditional fantasy cliches’: inside Playground Games’ 10-year effort to revive FableThe distinctively British RPG is returning courtesy of the makers of Forza Horizon – with comedy talent such as Richard Ayoade and Natasia Demetriou voicing sweary characters. We had our first play and spoke to its developerTom ReganTue 15 Sep 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen PlaygroundGameswas founded in 2010, its objective was straightforward: to make the best cars in video games. Operating out of an unassuming white building in Leamington Spa, the studio sought to challenge Gran Turismo with its critically acclaimed British racing alternative: the acclaimed free-roaming Forza Horizon series. Yet as the team grew, so did their ambitions. Now they are making the most intriguing British fantasy game we have seen in many years.For those who have never ventured into Albion,Fableis a quintessentially British role playing game. Created by Lionhead Studios for the original Xbox in 2004, it boasted cheeky charm alongside world-altering player choices, and its droll writing was brought to life in later iterations by national treasures such as Stephen Fry and Simon Pegg. Thanks to its unique blend of farce and fantasy, Fable grew into a globally beloved franchise – before Microsoftunceremoniously shuttered Lionhead in 2016, after mandating that the studio turn its star series into a multiplayer game. The result, Fable Legends, was never released.Fable at 20: a uniquely British video game with a complex legacyRead moreNow, following a 10-year limbo, Playground is resuscitating the dormant series. “As a developer and a player, working on this has made me think about games more deeply than anything else I’ve done,” reflects Ralph Fulton, Playground Games co-founder and Fable’s game director. “I think it will have that same effect on the people who play it.”Whoever picked up Lionhead’s mantle would inevitably face some scepticism. And despite their commercial success, driving games rarely command the same reverence or critical respect as blockbuster narrative games. For Fulton, taking on an action RPG was an opportunity to prove that Playground belong among the world’s best. “I think there was a little bit of pride in proving we could cut it in a different genre,” he says. “It made sense not to fall too far from Horizon. This project definitely wasn’t going to have cars, but open worlds felt like an area where we had transferable skills.” Playground was an independent studio at the time, but given that Xbox was the home of the Forza Horizon series, Microsoft seemed an obvious choice of partner. “When Xbox mentioned Fable, every other opportunity dissolved into the background. It was all we could think about.”After signing the deal in 2017, Playground suddenly needed to build a massive team overnight, and scrambled to merge their talented torque-heads with developers well-versed in Tolkien. “Building a team from scratch is the hardest thing you can do in video games,” Fulton says. “You can hire the people with the best CVs, but if they don’t gel, six to nine months later you’re back in the market. The human cost meant bringing hundreds of people from all over the world, many of whom relocated solely because they were fans of Fable.”double quotation markNatasia Demetriou brought a level of swearing to her character that honestly shocked usAt the Gamescom expo in Germany, I play the result of the studio’s efforts. While I don’t get to explore much of Albion in this demo, as I fight my way through a dungeon, the combat soon dispels any lingering doubts about Playground’s action chops. Thrust into a wraith-ridden mine, my hero faces an ambush of crackling skeletal knights. Every attack lands with tactile weight, from the heavy crunch of a hammer to the crisp thwick of a bowstring, sending skeletons exploding into bone splinters. When floating wraiths descend in the aptly named Wraithmarsh, fireballs and lightning spells land with spectacle. I fell the swamp’s final foe by transforming them into a squawking rooster.View image in fullscreenThe combat has tactile weight and skeletons exploding into bone splinters.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosThe writing is sharp. Between smashing skeletons, I stumble upon a dust-coated love letter penned with authentically British awkwardness, in which a dying miner’s struggle to channel the earnestness needed to say his goodbyes is clear on the page. “We were a bit bored of traditional fantasy cliches and the way characters usually speak in those settings,” says Fulton. “I love media, particularly in period settings, that use a modern tone of voice, idiom, and phrasing … I don’t think we could have gotten Matt King to play a cliched fantasy character.”Peep Show’s Kingstars as the retired former “greatest Hero of Albion” Humphry, who guides me through this haunted mine shaft with signature sarcasm. King is just one of the big names among Fable’s cast: a who’s-who of British comedy talent including Richard Ayoade (The IT Crowd) and Natasia Demetriou (What We Do in the Shadows). “Richard Ayoade virtually improvised a new script for his scenes on the spot. Listening to him conjure that dialogue was one of my favourite days on this project,” smiles Fulton. “Natasia Demetriou brought a level of British swearing to her character that honestly shocked us, but it’s brilliant and we let her run with it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘Open worlds felt like an area where we had transferable skills’ … Fable.Photograph: Xbox Game StudiosBeyond the swears, satire and sorcery, Fulton stresses that the core of the Fable series remains in this reboot: meaningful player choice. For much of the game, Fulton says, the main quest will feel low-stakes enough to keep players feeling comfortable to mess around in Albion. You will only be locked into the main story during its climatic ending.“Most importantly, we stick the landing,” Fulton says. “It’s easy to look at industry metrics saying 100% of people start a game and only 25% finish, and decide not to invest heavily in the finale. But we relentlessly pursued quality here. In great Fable fashion, it culminates in a choice that really challenges you to think about who you are, with a real personal cost to weigh against the outcome.”Playground’s long-gestating project carries immense weight, both for nostalgic fans and for Xbox itself, given that it was Microsoft that killed off the series and its original creator. Since the Fable reboot started production in 2016, the industry has weathered a disastrous pivot to live service games, a global pandemic, andmore than 6,000 layoffsat Playground’s parent company, Xbox.“I genuinely think Fable is an important game.What has protected us over a long development cycle is that so many people within Xbox view Fable as vital to the DNA of the platform,” Fulton says. “I would go a step further and say it’s important to video games as a whole. It offers a combination of elements that simply doesn’t exist anywhere else.”This interview took place at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by Gamescom.Explore more on these topicsRole playing gamesGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: She was the Royal Ballet’s first ‘young choreographer’ – Charlotte Edmonds’ next 10 years show how dance is changing | Dance | The Guardian
description: As a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directions
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: As a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directions
Content: The challenge is ‘making a living while still being creatively intact’ … Charlotte Edmonds.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellView image in fullscreenThe challenge is ‘making a living while still being creatively intact’ … Charlotte Edmonds.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellDanceShe was the Royal Ballet’s first ‘young choreographer’ – Charlotte Edmonds’ next 10 years show how dance is changingAs a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directionsLyndsey WinshipTue 15 Sep 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the age of 18,Charlotte Edmondswas such apromising choreographer(“astonishing”, in the words of the Observer) that the Royal Ballet invented a whole new job for her. As the company’s “young choreographer”, she spent three years learning everything she could at one of the world’s biggest dance institutions. “It’s mad to think that happened,” she says, a decade on.With that kind of start, you’d expect Edmonds’ career to have followed a predictable narrative, choreographing for the big ballet brands, maybe setting up her own company. But that’s not exactly how it’s gone. Her eclectic portfolio reflects how the dance industry has changed and become ever more precarious, but also expanded in uncharted directions. She has indeed made short works for a number of European ballet companies, but she’s spent more time recently making films, music videos and adverts for the likes of Budweiser and Nike, as well as advocating for artists with dyslexia and launching her own video series,Cameo, in which she interviews female and non-binary choreographers to counter a lack of representation.I ask her to tell me about the practical challenges of making a career in choreography. “I would say, ‘Ohh,’” Edmonds laughs. “It’s really fucking tough. It’s really, really hard to get things going. It was hard back then but it feels even tougher now. Because of Covid, funding cuts, cost of living …” She will have conversions with Arts Council England, she says, during which they remark: “‘This is a project that would have been funded 10 years ago.’ And it’s frustrating for them because there’s only a certain amount of resources.” She goes online to apply for smaller grant funds, “and on the website it says, ‘We’re closing our doors for this year and rethinking how to structure our grants.’”Nevertheless, Edmonds says, “When you do something you love, it’s so consuming.” The challenge is “making a living while still being creatively intact. It’s such a juggling act and that can really take a mental toll.” Everyone has had to diversify – some of Edmonds’ colleagues have become intimacy coordinators; Edmonds does movement direction for singers, recently with Lola Young on a TV appearance (there was no dancing; Edmonds’ job was to help Young navigate the set and cameras, hone the “intention” and emotion of the performance, and even to be “a support system” for a jet-lagged singer).There’s a boom in dance online, with brands making arty short films instead of straight ads andold songs going viral with new dance routines. Edmonds has also experimented with digital art. Amid the flush of excitement over NFTs in 2021, she created several works with the artist Brendan Dawes for Sotheby’s. “With that Sotheby’s exhibition, I remember going into the rehearsal room thinking, am I going to suddenly walk out a millionaire? ‘No’ was the answer. But we could all dream,” she smiles. “The making of the NFT itself was really interesting. It was fascinating where choreography could go and how it could be utilised.”Edmonds is endlessly curious, and entrepreneurial. You have to be a hustler in this business, yes? “Yeah, but not in a Wolf of Wall Street way,” she says. “In a really conscious, intentional sense.” Getting an email just offering you a gig is rare (“Oh my gosh, that literally feels like the lottery”), and you have to make your own opportunities. In the early days Edmonds got a £15,000 Arts Council grant to make an ambitious project, the filmSink or Swim, featuring Royal Ballet principal Francesca Hayward in a giant water tank. She raised another £5,000 herself. It took her a year to raise the money and she didn’t pay herself a fee.View image in fullscreenLukas Bjørneboe Braendsrød, Mica Bradbury, Gina Storm-Jensen and Reece Clarke in Meta by Charlotte Edmonds at the Clore Studio, Royal Opera House, in 2016.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThese days, at 29, she has to think more seriously about supporting herself. “There are so many social pressures,” she says. And then she starts two or three different sentences before saying, “You can see I’m whirring away about the conversations I have with myself about sticking to it. People do step away [from dance] to have stability, have a family; all these elements that naturally creep up as you get older.” For those who choose to leave, even when it’s a profession you’ve been training in your whole life, “it’s not a failure”, she says. “It is a choice of what’s right for you in life.”For Edmonds, though, the drive and passion for choreography she had as a teenager is still strong. I watch her in a studio at London Contemporary Dance School where she’s rehearsing a group of students forher new film, Ladette, examining 90s gender roles. (Edmonds was only a baby in the 90s, but the theme is in sync with the current nostalgia for all things pre-smartphone.) A mass of 43 bodies move with a powerful pulse, shifting from sharp, blunt stamps and jutting shoulders to snakey and molten movement. Edmonds works out steps and shapes on her own body and shares them with the dancers, her classical and contemporary training now shot through with street and club dance influences. She’s in her element in the studio, and it’s still her ambition to make major works for large ballet companies. “I really want to make live work in the UK,” she says. “I’ve been planning and writing and curating ideas that are close to my heart and I’d love to see them take off.” Watch this space.Explore more on these topicsDanceRoyal BalletDigital artSocial mediaBalletDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Venice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victory | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive
Content: Mathilde Arcel poses with the Volpi Cup at the awards ceremony on Saturday in Venice.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenMathilde Arcel poses with the Volpi Cup at the awards ceremony on Saturday in Venice.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersVenice film festivalVenice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victoryMathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrivePhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorTue 15 Sep 2026 06.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe winner of this year’s best actress prize at theVenice film festivalhas revealed that she is on unemployment benefits and had to fly to back to Copenhagen to report to the job centre before receiving her award.On Saturday night, Danish actor Mathilde Arcel won the prestigious Volpi Cup for her first leading role in a feature film, May el-Toukhy’s post-second world war drama Woman Unknown, which alsowon the Golden Lion awardfor best film.Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said the judges had been able to relax Venice rules around not awarding more than one prize per film because the vote for Arcel had been unanimous.Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love and NAZARead moreAfter her triumph, the 30-year-old actor revealed in interviews with Danish media that she had returned toDenmarkafter her film’s premiere to sign on at the job centre, as she is on unemployment benefits when not working on films. She then returned to the Lido after being told it would be wise to be present at the awards gala.In the UK, actors’ trade union Equity said in a2023 reportthat 63% of its members have been in receipt of social security at some point in their life.Set in the direct aftermath of the Nazi occupation of Denmark, Woman Unknown tells the story of Marie, a young housemaid and nanny who is about to marry her widowed industrialist employer.But a chance encounter with an old schoolfriend threatens to reveal a shameful secret, exposing Marie to the retributive hounding of female “horizontal collaborators” who had intimate relations with German soldiers.At Venice, Arcel drew wide critical praise for the contained inner anguish she brings to the role of Marie. “Mathilde is going to blow our socks off,” Gyllenhaal said in a press conference after the awards ceremony.The actor said her agent had received several calls with new job offers since she scooped the Volpi Cup, the male version of which went to Hollywood veteran John Malkovich. “There are a lot of calls and a lot of interest from abroad and things like that, and we need to talk about what’s going to happen,” she told Danish broadcaster DR.Speaking in Venice on Saturday night, Arcel joked that her ultimate dream would be to play a part in one long-running British TV detective drama she was particularly fond of. “I really want to keep on working and meet some new artists”, she said. “I’m looking so much forward to what the future will bring, perhaps even a role in Midsomer Murders”.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalUnemploymentAwards and prizesDenmarkEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Llewellyn-Jones obituary | Deafness and hearing loss | The Guardian
description: Pioneer in the teaching of British Sign Language who devoted himself to improving accessibility and opportunity for deaf people
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pioneer in the teaching of British Sign Language who devoted himself to improving accessibility and opportunity for deaf people
Content: Peter Llewellyn-Jones demonstrating British Sign LanguageView image in fullscreenPeter Llewellyn-Jones demonstrating British Sign LanguageDeafness and hearing lossObituaryPeter Llewellyn-Jones obituaryPioneer in the teaching of British Sign Language who devoted himself to improving accessibility and opportunity for deaf peopleGary TippingsTue 15 Sep 2026 04.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeter Llewellyn-Jones, who has died aged 76, was an interpreter and teacher who helped to establish sign language interpreting as a recognised profession in Britain. Throughout his working life, alongside employment as an actor and writer, he devoted himself to improving accessibility and opportunity for deaf people.He became a pioneer in the teaching of British SignLanguageinterpreting and linguistics, and wrote the UK’s first undergraduate degree course in the subject, for the University of Wolverhampton in 1992. Peter was also instrumental in developing sign-language interpreting for British television and in bringing it on to the stage; starting in the early 1980s, he worked on 600 professional theatre productions across the UK.One of the earliest to interpret for Royal Shakespeare Company productions, he worked on RSC main house shows and tours from 1991 to 2000, interpreting alongside Vanessa Redgrave, Kenneth Branagh, Jim Broadbent and Ian McKellen, among others; McKellen later became a prominent champion of interpreted theatre more broadly. In 2004 Peter wrote about interpreting the plays into British Sign Language in a chapter for the bookShakespeare and the Language of Translation, edited by Ton Hoenselaars.View image in fullscreenLlewellyn-Jones with Tiddler in The Riddlers.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockPeter was also an accomplished actor and writer. He co-wrote and co-presented the second series of Insight (1984), a groundbreaking television programme for deaf children, in which he acted and signed with the actor, comedian and presenterVictoria Wood. He also played Mr Grimley, alongside Victoria Williams and two puppet creatures, in the children’s television series The Riddlers, which ran from 1989 to 1998.He was one of the first sign-language interpreters to appear as an additional on-screen element in British television programming, including for See Hear! in 1982, and for the current affairs series Listening Eye (1983-88). He was the presenter of the weekly educational series Our World, for primary schools (1985-94) and also interpreted the news on various ITV channels in the 80s and 90s.Along with the American academic Robert G Lee, Peter developed the “role-space” model, an influential approach to the interpreter’s role and behaviour. It drops the idea of the interpreter as a neutral, invisible “conduit” who simply converts words, and replaces it with the claim that every interpreter already occupies an active three-dimensional space in any interaction, whether they mean to or not. Peter argued interpreters were never really neutral machines, and gave the profession a way to think honestly about the influence they always have.Peter interpreted at events for King (then Prince) Charles, Diana, Princess of Wales, Norman Tebbit and Neil Kinnock, for social services, health and legal settings, and for industry leaders and politicians. In an 1991 interview in the Guardian with the journalist Mary Russell, Peter observed: “Deaf people have the right to be bored by politicians, same as the rest of us.”Born in Wealdstone, Middlesex, to Arthur, a vicar, and Joan (nee Fisher), an occupational therapist, Peter left school at 16 having passed only four O-levels.double quotation markDeaf people have the right to be bored by politicians, same as the rest of usAfter travelling around Europe for a period, he was persuaded by his father to train in St Albans as a missioner and welfare worker to the deaf, and qualified in 1972, leading to his first employment with the St Albans Diocesan Association for the Deaf.He then worked for the British Deaf Association, and for Tyne TeesTelevision, and began lecturing and consulting, developing university teaching curriculums in the field, and working at the universities of Wolverhampton and later Leeds, where he was senior teaching fellow and programme director for the MA in interpreting and translation studies (2003-12).I had first encountered his name at Channel 4, where I had started out working in the postroom. We met 30 years later when we both became regulars at our local pub in Bassingham, Lincolnshire, and became good friends.Fond of coining and swapping malapropisms (“Do they do it on porpoise?”), Peter was intensely interested in language, and would apply his professional learning to everyday communications, delivering mini sermons on the mechanisms of the conversations and encounters that he took part in, enlightening others with his general knowledge and wisdom. He regularly surprised friends (and his local’s crossword puzzle solvers) with his recall and analysis of Shakespeare’s texts.As a young man, Peter competed in high-board diving and motorcycle grass-track racing. In later life he became a member of the Institute of Advanced Motorists. He would regularly roar around the Lincolnshire Wolds on his sophisticated Japanese Yamaha road bike, a far cry from the 50s British Triumph on which he had begun competing in grass-track events during the 60s.The founding chair of the Association of Sign Language Interpreters, in 1987, Peter received its award in 2003 for his outstanding work in the field. He served as president of the European Forum of Sign Language Interpreters from 2013 to 2015.Peter was married first to Miranda Whitfield, with whom he had a daughter, Rachel, and then to Patricia Boxhall, with whom he had three children, Catherine, Thomas and Joseph; both marriages ended in divorce. In 2005 he married Jayne Clarke. She survives him, along with his four children and six grandchildren.Peter Llewellyn-Jones, sign language interpreter and teacher, actor and writer, born 26 February 1950; died 18 August 2026Explore more on these topicsDeafness and hearing lossHealth policyLanguageTelevisionChildren's TVobituariesShareReuse this content

title: No, collagen won’t make your wrinkles disappear - video | Science | The Guardian
description: Collagen powders, gummies and pills have boomed in popularity in recent years boosted by claims that they smooth wrinkles, promote glossy hair and help with joint pain. Amid the noise it can be hard to figure out whether there’s any actual science behind the promise of looking younger for longer. Luckily Dr Xand van Tulleken has spent the past three years writing Make me well: a quest to understand the confusing world of wellness, and his chapter on collagen dives deep into the evidence. He tells Madeleine Finlay what collagen does in the body, how we can get it without splashing out on expensive supplements, and why getting to the truth behind wellness claims can be so hard

title: The pirates arrived with AK-47s. They took us hostage – then the torture began | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Chirag Bahri was working on board a tanker when six men seized it. For almost eight months, he and his colleagues were held captive, an experience that would change his life for ever
Author: Rose George
Headline: Chirag Bahri was working on board a tanker when six men seized it. For almost eight months, he and his colleagues were held captive, an experience that would change his life for ever
Content: ‘I thought, my God, this is the end’ … Chirag Bahri at home this summer in Noida, India.Photograph: Elke Scholiers/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I thought, my God, this is the end’ … Chirag Bahri at home this summer in Noida, India.Photograph: Elke Scholiers/The GuardianHow we surviveLife and styleThe pirates arrived with AK-47s. They took us hostage – then the torture beganChirag Bahri was working on board a tanker when six men seized it. For almost eight months, he and his colleagues were held captive, an experience that would change his life for everRose GeorgeTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was at noon on 8 May 2010 when the pirates came. Chirag Bahri remembers the exact time and date because it marked the start of the seven months and 20 days he was held hostage by a gang of Somali pirates. Bahri was 28 at the time, and working as second engineer on a chemical tanker, Marida Marguerite. It was his 12th journey through the Gulf of Aden in the Indian Ocean. It had been a good job for a young man from landlocked Uttar Pradesh in India, and Bahri was about to be promoted. “But then, piracy,” he says.The ship had been 120 miles off the coast of Oman, partway through a run taking benzene – a raw material used in petrochemicals – from Kandla Port in India to Antwerp in Belgium. The piracy problem in the Indian Ocean was well known; Somalis armed with AK-47s were setting out in fast skiffs and taking ships hostage. Yet commercial vessels, including the Marida Marguerite, remained undefended.Big ships are slow and small skiffs are fast. The Marguerite was doing 13 knots; the pirates could do 25 – and they knew to approach in the shadow cast by the funnel on the water, so they were invisible until the last minute. There was nothing the crew could do to defend the ship anyway. All they had was razor wire and luck.Bahri was in the engine room when he was told that skiffs were approaching. Within 15 minutes they were under attack. Bahri now had a job to do: according to what are called best management practices, ships can deter pirates by zigzagging, so he started pushing the engines to maximum power. But the pirates shot two rocket-propelled grenades at the ship, raised their ladders and scaled the razor wire. They headed for the bridge, the control centre of the ship. The crew had removed ladders to prevent this, but the pirates climbed up pipes. Within minutes, six pirates, hyped up on adrenaline and probably khat – a narcotic plant that is chewed – now held the bridge. The whole crew was summoned: 22 men, comprising 19 Indians, two Bangladeshis and a Ukrainian. Soon after, a helicopter, perhaps answering the captain’s distress calls, flew overhead but it was too late. The pirates just fired into the air. They told the captain to head forSomalia, and he did.View image in fullscreen‘They were such torturous people. They used to have fun with that’ … Chirag Bahri.Photograph: Elke Scholiers/The GuardianWhen Bahri arrived at the bridge, the pirates, carrying AK-47s, shouted at him to sit down. “I was terrified. I thought, my God, this is the end.” The crew were sitting on the floor. Several were crying; others were comforting their crewmates, saying, “No, they won’t kill us. This is business.”And there they stayed. “People were trying to keep their spirits up in the initial days,” says Bahri. “We thought that ours is a good company – they will pay the pirates and we will be out very soon. We were very positive.”About two days later, they reached the coast off Garacad in northern Somalia. The six pirates left but 40 others came aboard, including a man that spoke better English, who began negotiations with the shipping company for a ransom. “He didn’t get any fruitful result. Whenever the company came up with something, he would ask for more. They started off wanting $15m.”double quotation markI will remember that date all my lifeFor 20 days, they were all kept on the bridge, sitting and lying on the hard deck. The engines had to be maintained, so the engineering crew did 12-hour watches in pairs. A guard would escort them to the engine room. “He always suspected that there are so many satellite phone connections on board,” says Bahri. “They thought every intercom phone was a satellite phone.” The watches were a relief, though, giving Bahri something else to do other than sit terrified at the pirates’ feet.The pirates were all ages, young boys to older men. They had one thing in common. “They were totally insane. Brutal always. Always abusing us and each other. They would fight over a piece of mutton.” At first, the crew ate from the supplies they had on board. When those ran out, the pirates brought rice and dal, and they slaughtered goats on the deck. Bahri paid close attention and began to understand the pirates’ behaviour; the evenings, after they had had their khat, was the most dangerous time. “The mood changes. The eyes get red.”View image in fullscreenThe Marida Marguerite, which was transporting benzene to Belgium when it was hijacked in 2010.Photograph: Dietmar Hasenpusch/Picture-alliance/dpa/AP ImagesAfter 20 days, the captain got permission for the crew to move to four cabins. For four months life went on. Very occasionally – “four times in eight months” – Bahri was allowed to phone home. He told the pirates his family didn’t speak English, although they did. So he spoke in Hindi. “It was terrible. My mother couldn’t speak to me; she was simply crying for two minutes. Government officials told my wife only: ‘One day he will come back.’”The pirates doled out slaps here and there, but, three months in, “at the end of August, they started the physical torture.” Bahri blames frustration that the negotiations weren’t going well.On 9 September the worst happened. “I will remember that date all my life. It was like the end of my life.” He was in the engine room at midnight when some pirates arrived and decided he was hiding a satellite phone. “I said, no, they are intercoms, but they said it was a satellite connection and I was using them with passwords to call the navy and my family.“We were taken up on to the deck at about 6 o’clock in the morning and were asked to lie down on our stomachs. Three pirates came and one took my legs and stretched them, and the other pirate pulled my hands so just my tummy was touching the deck.” He was hog-tied. “It was very, very difficult. They tied a nylon rope around my hands and legs. You cannot move even a few millimetres. Even the genitals were tied up with cable ties. They were such torturous people. They used to have fun with that. Lots of the crew had their genitals tied up.” He was in that position, in full sun, for four hours.View image in fullscreenBahri in his early days as a sailor, before he joined the Marida Marguerite.Photograph: Courtesy of Chirag Bahri“When they released me, for five minutes I was still in that position – I couldn’t bring my hands or legs down. Slowly I tried standing up but I was not able to. I was on my knees. My legs and hands were shaking. My left hand was half-paralysed for about a month.”The pirates’ obsession with hidden satellite connections continued and Bahri stopped sleeping from terror of what they might do next. As the captivity continued, Bahri tried to learn some Somali (Hindi and Urdu contain some Somali words). One pirate became friendlier, which helped. But the beatings continued with sticks or fists.By October, the negotiations were back on track. A $5m ransom was agreed, and on 27 December the money was airdropped into the sea. The pirates fetched it with skiffs, and the money was divided up on board. Other pirates arrived from shore to get paid. “They had logbooks and did the accounts,” says Bahri. This was a dangerous time so the crew stayed away from them. After seven hours, the pirates left with bagfuls of money. Bahri got busy preparing the engines for sailing. “I didn’t want to use tugs. I wanted to take the ship on our power.” It was a matter of pride; proof that the pirates had not taken everything from him.Escape was slow. The sea journey back to Salalah in Oman took about a week, says Bahri, “as we were not able to use speed due to excessive fouling of the hull after the ship was at anchor for almost eight months.” From there he flew to Delhi. “At the airport, my brother-in-law told me my mother had died.” He had thought something was “fishy” when, en route back to Oman, his family told him that his mother was away on a pilgrimage. In fact she had died from the stress, they thought. When he should have been relieved to be home, he felt profoundly guilty. “I was extremely broken, shocked. And the first thing that came to my mind was that I should not have come back. I would be happy staying in captivity, not knowing that my mother is no more. I thought: this is all because of me.”View image in fullscreenA defendant (who was not named) appears in court in Osnabrück, Germany, in 2014. He was sentenced to 12 years for his part in the hijacking.Photograph: Carmen Jaspersen/EPA/ShutterstockFor weeks, he was numb. In a further blow, his wife had left him during his captivity and he has never found out why. The physical after-effects were also hard. His back and his head went into spasm; he was unable to sit still for long. He had tests that showed his sperm count was reduced because of the genital trauma. He had sleepless nights and bad dreams when he did sleep. “All those thoughts: ‘What am I going to do, what will happen to me in the future?’”On top of all this, “there was so much constant feedback coming in from people: ‘Oh, your life is ruined.’ ‘What are you going to do?’ I decided to meet only with positive people and not those who are just there to make fun of my situation.”It may seem preposterous that anyone could make light of his ordeal, but Bahri says that even some friends who worked in shipping would joke that he hadn’t had to do any work for eight months, and was being fed after all. There was, he says, a “gap of awareness. People had no idea what the pirates do ... They had no idea what a piracy situation looks like.”Ironically, these negative comments helped him turn a corner. Thanks to them, he realised that no one was talking about what it was like to be in pirate captivity. His friends and neighbours hadn’t known any better because no one understood the brutal reality. So he did two things: he began contacting families whose relatives were being held hostage, and he began to tell his story publicly. He was alone in this – most of his fellow captives had gone back to sea. “A lot of them didn’t have any other livelihood. What are they going to do?”View image in fullscreenSome ships now carry armed guards but Somali piracy is resurging.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/AFP/Getty ImagesBahri made contact with the International Transport Workers’ Federation, which represents seafarers, where a well-respected ITF official called Roy Paul encouraged him to speak out about his experience. Meanwhile, he completed his senior engineer’s exams and later in 2011 went back to sea. Not the Gulf of Aden though: his family wouldn’t have been able to bear that. He found a job on an Indian tanker whose route hugged the Indian coast. He did two months, then was offered a job by Paul with the Maritime Piracy Humanitarian Response Programme (MPHRP), which supports hostages and their families. “I said: ‘I don’t know. What do you mean by humanitarian support? I’ve never heard of this term. I’m not qualified. I’m an engineer; I’m a technical person.’ He told me that I was already doing it.”Today Bahri is still working in this field. In 2012, ships started using armed guards, reducing the threat from the pirates, and the MPHRP amalgamated with the International Seafarers’ Welfare and Assistance Network. But the pirates are still around, and families of captives are often left floundering. “There were cases where families had issues with their gas supply, because the connection was in the husband’s name. Or the account was seized because it was in the seafarer’s name. And the family could not do much because the account had been dormant for one or two years [while the seafarer was held hostage]. On the humanitarian side, we have found families struggling because they have no information.”Recently, Bahri has been working with the families of 11 of the 17 crew members of the oil tankerHonour 25, now in its fifth month of captivity at the hands of Somali pirates. He is also working with seafarers stuck because of the war in Iran. Using his own experience to help others has been healing for him, he says. “It has helped me a lot. Because when I meet seafarers and their family members, I help bring smiles to their faces. I know at least something good has happened. If I didn’t do this work, I would be struggling. I would still be sailing, still blaming myself, and I wouldn’t have understood that it isn’t good to blame yourself. It was the situation that was wrong.”He has remarried, happily, and now has two young children. Given what he’s been through, how would he feel if either of them wanted to work at sea? “It’s still a long way to go,” he says. “But I keep sharing my stories with my son about shipping. If he wanted to [work at sea], I would definitely like that.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleHow we survivePiracy at seaSomaliafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Can you freeze leftover risotto?  | Rice | The Guardian
description: It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if you must, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mush
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if you must, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mush
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect risotto and the not-soggyarancinishe made out of the leftovers.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food styling: Kitty Coles. Prop styling: Jemima Hetherington and Kitty Coles. Food assistant: Jo Jackson. Photo assistant: Liam Desbois.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect risotto and the not-soggyarancinishe made out of the leftovers.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food styling: Kitty Coles. Prop styling: Jemima Hetherington and Kitty Coles. Food assistant: Jo Jackson. Photo assistant: Liam Desbois.Kitchen aideRiceCan you freeze leftover risotto?It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if youmust, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mushAnna BerrillTue 15 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI have tried various ways to reheat risotto after freezing, but it always turns into a gloopy, starchy, unappetising mess. What am I doing wrong?Jill, by email“Freezing risotto will be a bit of a disaster,” says Theo Randall, chef/patron atTheo Randall Cucina Italiana at the Intercontinentalin London, “and it doesn’t really work.” The reason for this is that the cooked rice absorbs all the moisture while it’s defrosting, resulting in, well, Jill’s gloopy mess.It’s also possible her risotto was overcooked to begin with, says Sue Quinn, author ofCheese Please. “Softer grains mean more leached starch, which leaves less leeway for further cooking without it going sticky and pasty.” Then there’s the question of reheating that defrosted rice for too long: “That can over-soften the already-cooked rice,” adds Quinn, so you have to do it “quickly and only until it’s piping hot”.The reality, however, is that “freezing, thawing and reheating rice will make it squishier whatever you do”, Quinn says, but “if that’s the way Jill rolls”, her best bet is to get that defrosted risotto in the microwave, sprinkle it with a little water or stock, cover loosely, then reheat on high in one-minute intervals, stirring in between, until it’s hot all the way through. “To do this on the hob, put the defrosted risotto in a pan with a splash of hot stock or water, and stir gently over a medium heat for just long enough to distribute the heat.”And, says Randall, if Jill “really has to freeze leftover risotto”, he would urge her to turn it into arancini instead: “Those work quite well, because you’ve encased the cooked rice in flour, egg wash and breadcrumbs, so moisture doesn’t penetrate the grains.”Alternatively, Jill could shun the freezer altogether and simply turn her leftovers into another meal the next day, Randall says: “One of the great Milanese dishes isrisotto al salto, which is usually made with saffron risotto. Keep any leftovers in the fridge, then, when you’re ready to use it, get a hot pan, melt some butter in there – don’t let it brown, though – then tip in the risotto.” You want to pack that rice right down, so it gets into the edges of the pan and resembles a pancake. Leave to cook for five minutes – “Don’t touch it!” – and you’ll eventually get a lovely crust on the bottom of the rice. “Flip it over, again just like a pancake [or use a spatula to help, if need be] and cook for a further five minutes on the other side. You’ll end up with this lovely, crisp and slightly gooey risotto,” Randall says, “and that’s probably by far the best way to use up risotto leftovers.”And if Jill still wants to batch-cook,Poppy O’Toolesuggests a shift in mindset: “The kind of rice that you can freeze would be baked [basmati] rice,” says the author ofThe Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, namecheckinga spicy chicken numberthat appeared in Feast a few weeks back. “That freezes and reheats beautifully.” Of course, the freezer is a fan of plain rice, too: “That’s a better way to batch-cook rice,” O’Toole says. “Freezing and reheating risotto never truly works.”Got a culinary dilemma?
