title: Rukmini Iyer’s recipe for mozzarella in carrozza – and the leftover crusts | Cheese | The Guardian
description: The love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next day
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next day
Content: Rukmini Iyer’s mozzarella in carrozza.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer’s mozzarella in carrozza.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Cook once, eat twiceCheeseRukmini Iyer’s recipe for mozzarella in carrozza – and the leftover crustsThe love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next dayRukmini IyerTue 15 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor an exceptionally luxe snack or kids’ tea, mozzarella in carrozza is your girl. It’s the love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread – instead of toasting it, you dip the cheese sandwich in egg and fry it. In other words, it’s mozzarella in a fancy carriage. I like to use a combination of mozzarella and mature cheddar for flavour, and while it’s best eaten piping hot from the pan, it’s a good (and filling) lunchbox option for children, too.Mozzarella in carrozzaYou will need a very large shallow bowl (or medium roasting tin) for the egg dip.Prep10 minCook10 minServes1-230g mature cheddar, grated2 very large slices white sourdough, crusts removed (but hang on to them)60g mozzarella, sliced1 egg, lightly beaten2tbsp olive oilFlaky sea saltPat down the cheddar evenly on one slice of bread, leaving a 1cm border, then top with the mozzarella. Brush a little beaten egg around the edges of the bread, then top with the second slice of sourdough and gently squash the edges together to seal.Pour the remaining egg into a large, shallow container, then carefully dip both sides of the sandwich in the egg wash – the bread should absorb all of the egg. (Any excess can be poured on once the sandwich is in the pan.)Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, then carefully lift the sandwich into the pan and fry for two minutes on each side, until golden brown. Use your biggest fish slice (or two) to transfer the mozzarella in carrozza on to a plate lined with kitchen paper, then serve immediately, scattered with a little sea salt.For a more balanced meal, serve with a green salad (dressing: one tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, one scant teaspoon dijon mustard and salt, to taste) ora cherry tomato salad (one big handful of cherry tomatoes, halved and dressed with extra-virgin olive oil, salt and fresh basil). Alternatively, if feeding children, serve with cucumber sticks and some fruit.Eat twiceIt was thinking about (and constantly making) children’s lunches that put me on the next-day dish ideas for this week’s column: what do you do with three days’ worth of cut-off sandwich crusts? I can’t bear to waste them, so they get stashed in a plastic container in the fridge. You could take them down the bread-and-butter pudding route: chop or blitz the crusts in a food processor, pack into a small baking dish, then pour over a chocolate custard (three egg yolks, 350ml whole milk or single cream, or a mix of both, 50g sugar, 100g 70% dark chocolate, melted) and bake for 20 minutes or so. Lovely by itself, or for breakfast with Greek yoghurt and just-ripe or baked pears.My favourite savoury option, though, is this: whisk a couple of eggs and a good splash of milk with a handful of grated cheese, then stir this through the chopped or blitzed sandwich crusts. Bake in a shallow dish at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 for 10-12 minutes, until just set. Once cool (you can refrigerate it overnight, if you wish), cut into squares, then fry in a little olive oil until golden brown and crisp. I billed these as “bread rosti” to the family, and topped them with cream cheese for the children and sriracha for my husband. They were a hit – not bad for half a week’s worth of sandwich leftovers.Explore more on these topicsCheeseCook once, eat twiceFoodSnacksStarterEggsBreadSandwichesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just be aware of what you’re spending’: budget hints for students | Student finance | The Guardian
description: The cost of living crisis hits students hard. Planning ahead and some self-discipline will help, alongside a sharp eye for a bargain and, if you’re eligible, a bursary
Author: Miatta Mbriwa
Headline: The cost of living crisis hits students hard. Planning ahead and some self-discipline will help, alongside a sharp eye for a bargain and, if you’re eligible, a bursary
Content: Online tools can help with managing your budget.Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnline tools can help with managing your budget.Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Student finance‘Just be aware of what you’re spending’: budget hints for studentsThe cost of living crisis hits students hard. Planning ahead and some self-discipline will help, alongside a sharp eye for a bargain and, if you’re eligible, a bursaryMiatta MbriwaTue 15 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLike late-night study sessions and cramming into a student kitchen to cook up meals, being savvy with money has long been part of the university experience. But with the cost of living remaining high, students are more money-conscious than ever.“It is one of the most difficult times to make ends meet as a student,” according to Tom Allingham, communications director atSave the Student (STS). He says soaring prices for essentials, such as food and energy bills, have “disproportionately affected” students, while maintenance loans (intended to help cover day-to-day costs) have failed to keep up with high rates of inflation.STS’s 2025 money surveyfound the average student spends £1,142 a month on living costs, but receives a maintenance loan of £640, meaning the £502 shortfall has more than doubled since 2020.So what are the best ways to stretch your loan as far as it will go?Split money across multiple bank accountsOpening a student bank account comes with plenty of perks, from free railcards and large interest-free overdrafts to a welcome cash incentive that may come in handy during freshers’ week festivities.But to stay on top of your spending, don’t keep all of your money in one place.Robert Medhurst, 25, who graduated this summer from Nottingham Trent University, recommends opening a separate digital bank account alongside your main student account, to split your maintenance loan into daily budgets.Budgeting features on apps such as Monzo, helped him to visualise his finances and rein in his spending, which he found much harder to track when all of his maintenance loan was lumped into one account.Setting aside money and placing a spending cap onthe pots feature– one for rent and others for weekly food shops and nights out – “really allows you to see how much you’re spending and not go over”, he says. It can also help curb the urge for contactless spending.Make a budget before move-in dayIt’s common for students to find themselves tipping into their overdraft faster than expected. To avoid the burden of being in the red, start setting out your budget before you step foot on campus. Allingham suggests incoming students use time over the summer to work out “where the gaps will be in your budget – where potentially you might need to cut back, or where you might need to look for extra income”.There are plenty of free tools available to help, such as online budget trackers. Soham Chougale,education officer at University College Birmingham Guild of Students, createdYour Friendly Guild Budget Buddyto help students keep their finances afloat amid the cost of living crisis. It includes features that help map out income and set saving goals, while offering information on where to access financial and mental health support in one place. “It realistically shows how a student would spend, rather than fancy budget planners which would have 10 other things that are not the top priorities,” says Chougale.Research hardship fundsand bursariesIf you’re experiencing financial difficulty while studying, applying for non-repayable hardship funds and bursaries offered by your university may help ease the strain. In recent years, some universities have doubled or tripled the amount of money in hardship support to students, while also widening the household income criteria for eligibility. Increasingly, says Allingham, institutions have “recognised that it’s not just people from the very poorest backgrounds that are struggling right now”.For Medhurst, accessing a hardship fund “was a lifesaver”, helping to tide over part of his rent each term. “Don’t be afraid to ask and to look for it,” he says. “There’ll probably be something that you can apply for that can really save you a lot of money.”Ask for a student discountWhether stashed away in your wallet or slipped inside your phone case, be sure to keep your student ID on you. Discounts are a big bonus of student life so even if one isn’t advertised, don’t be afraid to wave your ID and ask.Sign up to student discount platforms like UNiDAYS and Student Beans to enjoy exclusive 10% to 30% offers both in-store and online. Richard Jackson, head of content at Student Beans, says lots of chains such as YO! Sushi, Greene King and Pizza Express offer students in-store dining deals.The key to securing great discounts, he adds, is to always plan ahead. Follow and set notifications for your favourite brands on discount sites, and keep an eye out for boosted seasonal deals around Freshers, Black Friday and Cyber Monday.Start planning your mealsAfter a long day of lectures, it can be convenient to order a quick meal from Deliveroo or Uber Eats. But relying on takeaway services can add up quickly, totalling an entire week’s food shop in just a single purchase. Instead, 21-year-oldChloe Harmer, a third-year fashion marketing student at Leeds Arts University, found cooking compact meals in bulk to carry around between classes a cost-effective alternative. “I pop it in the fridge and then when I’m about to leave for uni the next day, put it straight in my bag and then that’s lunch sorted,” she says. “And I’d just repeat that most days.”Before heading off to the supermarket, know exactly what you want. Medhurst researched affordable, simple recipes online and then planned his shopping list around that. “Otherwise you go to Lidl and Aldi just kind of choosing willy-nilly, basing it on what you feel like there and then and it can be very easy to overspend,” he says.Splurge on discount nights outYou can have a good time without burning through all your student loan. Holly Nicholson, 21, who just graduated with an English literature degree from the University of Bristol, says the key to big nights out on a budget is putting aside in advance how much money to spend on drinks or entry to clubs. And, of course, she says there’s always the old student kitchen tradition: pre-drinking with your flatmates.Don’t overlook student society socials, which often boast subsidised drinks or free (and fun) events such as film screenings. If you’re a film or theatre devotee like 24-year-old Finola Clarke, an MA journalism student at Goldsmiths, signing up to student memberships at independent cinemas, weekly lottery queues for discounted theatre tickets and scavenging sites like TodayTix and the Stagedoor Rewards app offer some “ways to do what you enjoy at a significantly lower price”, she says.“You’re in a really weird and hard-adjusting time of your life, don’t put too much pressure on yourself,” says Harmer. “Still have fun, but just be aware of what you’re spending.”Explore more on these topicsStudent financeUniversity Guide 2027SavingsBanks and building societiesHigher educationStudentsYoung peopleUniversitiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sky gave my father the hard sell even though he has dementia | Money | The Guardian
description: He wanted to save money, but it insisted on selling costly packages and seemed not to accept ‘cancel’ as an option
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: He wanted to save money, but it insisted on selling costly packages and seemed not to accept ‘cancel’ as an option
Content: Sky HD TV remote controlPhotograph: Chris Radburn/PAView image in fullscreenSky HD TV remote controlPhotograph: Chris Radburn/PAConsumer championsMoneySky gave my father the hard sell even though he has dementiaHe wanted to save money, but it insisted on selling costly packages and seemed not to accept ‘cancel’ as an optionAnna TimsTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI was helping my father, who has dementia andParkinson’s disease, reduce his £113.50SkyTV bill.We explained to the Sky call centre agent that, as his eyesight and attention span have deteriorated, he wanted the cheapest available TV package to free up money for his care.The agent insisted on offering Sky Cinema, two new televisions, another 24-month Sky Q package and broadband, despite us repeatedly stating that we did not want any further offers. We asked to cancel.Eventually, we were offered£18-a-month Sky Essential TV. However, we were then asked to authorise a £77 monthly direct debit because Sports and Cinema had been automatically added.The adviser told us to disregard the amount and trust him to remove the unwanted packages after activation. Werefused andasked to cancel instead.What happened next was extraordinary.Weasked six times to cancel, and each time the adviser continued trying to persuade us tostay. They finally allowed the cancellation.I’m appalled at how persistent the sales pressure was once Sky knew Dad had dementia.EH, KentThe fact that customers who wish to cancel, or downgrade, a contract are passed to a “customer loyalty team” suggests what lies in store. That team regards loyalty as non-negotiable, judging by the transcript of your call to the company.When, after a blizzard of unsuitable deals, you asked to cancel, the loyalty team told you that you would have to discuss the request with the “retention team”. This team, it admitted, would strive to retain your custom. Which, with ruthless tenacity, it did.It is extremely concerning that you were pressured to sign up to a £77-a-month subscription after being quoted £18 a month.Over and over again, the retention team adviser claimed he would remove the unwanted Sports and Cinema elements that had inflated the price once you had signed up. Repeatedly he implored you to trust him, and ignored your six requests to cancel.This would be bad enough for a healthy customer. For an elderly man with dementia, it is deplorable. Telecoms firms have a duty to treat vulnerable customers fairly.I reported Sky’s behaviour to the regulator Ofcom. It says: “The conditions, or procedures, that providers have in place, must not act as a disincentive for vulnerable customers who wish to cancel their contract.“Where we see themes emerging, or evidence of widespread harm, we’ve shown we’ll take action where appropriate.”Sky tells me that it does have procedures for supporting vulnerable customers and that these were not followed in your father’s case. Instead, it says, the agent followed “standard process”.That suggests that customers who are not vulnerable are routinely exposed to this oppressive hard sell before they can escape.The company admits that the unwanted Sports and Cinema elements should have been removed from the package before you were asked to sign, and claims that the agent did not have the system access to do so.“We are very sorry for how the customer’s request was handled,” it adds. “His experience was not in line with the standards of care and support we expect customers with additional needs to receive, and our established process was not followed on this occasion.”Your father is finally free of the company, albeit minus his favourite TV channels. Other customers who feel they have been mis-sold or misled can complain to the Communication & Internet Services Adjudication Scheme,CISAS.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer rightsConsumer affairsSkyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gua sha looks good on Instagram – but is it worth the hype or a waste of time? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz | The Guardian
description: The practice does increase blood flow to parts of the bod, but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’
Author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Headline: The practice does increase blood flow to parts of the bod, but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’
Content: Most of the purported benefits of gua sha – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good scientific trial on its efficacy, Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz writes.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenMost of the purported benefits of gua sha – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good scientific trial on its efficacy, Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz writes.Composite: Guardian DesignAntiviralHealthGua sha looks good on Instagram – but is it worth the hype or a waste of time?Gideon Meyerowitz-KatzThe practice does increase blood flow to parts of the body but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’Read more in theAntiviral seriesTue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.40 EDTShareThe world of wellness fads is a cyclical place. Everything comes back into fashion when a new generation of influencers decides to switch it up. Pretty much every current hype was popular in decades past, from extreme juicing to genital sunning and everything in between.Gua sha is the ancient practice of scraping the skin to form mild bruises – called petechiae – which are thought to do a variety of helpful things for your body. The practice has beenaround in China for centuriesand has spread through the wonders of social media to all corners of the globe.Pore substitute: can AI be trusted when it comes to skincare advice?Read moreGua sha is performed by scraping a smooth stone, coin or similar instrument across lubricated skin in a single direction. Mild bruising might start to appear as a result. Practitioners claim that the resulting petechiae are evidence of “toxins”, and that as they disappear they take these toxins with them. This is said to heal skin,improve blood flow, and evenstrengthen your immune system, according to various people online.From a scientific perspective, this makes very little sense. The mechanism of action here is similar to a massage but with a bit more force. Dr Brad McKay, a GP and science communicator, notes that “gua sha provides the same health benefits as a violent massage”. While the practice does certainly increase blood flow to a specific area of your body – that’s what happens when you get a bruise, after all – there’s no evidence that this has any benefit. McKay notes: “A punch to the nose also increases blood flow.”There’s also no evidence that the petechiae have anything to do with “toxins”. Indeed, they are simply the body’s reaction to any heavy pressure, and can happen when you scrape your skin on virtually any surface. The small dots and bruises will appear regardless of the “toxins” in your body, and should always go away on their own.As far as evidence goes, there’s little research into gua sha.One reviewlooking at gua sha for perimenopausal syndrome found most of the trials on the topic were of fairly low methodological quality and unlikely to be useful as evidence. Avery small 2019 randomised trialfound benefits for gua sha on lower back pain but it was also not especially convincing.Part of the problem here is the same issue that acupuncture faces – it’s impossible to test against a convincing placebo because you can’t really blind people to whether they are receiving gua sha or not. Most of the purported benefits – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good trial on gua sha without polluting your results. When researchers measure hard outcomes that are less likely to be biased by self-reporting, such as hormone levels, there are far fewer benefits to be seen for the practice, and only from the lowest-quality research.Gua sha is one of those practices that I’m sure we’ll keep seeing around. It’s relatively harmless, easy to do and plays well on YouTube and Instagram. It’s quite easy to see why people want to keep making short videos showing lubricated skin being slowly rubbed by a smooth stone, and why that sort of visual tends to attract a lot of views online.The magic touch: how healthy are massages actually?Read moreRealistically, however, I think gua sha is largely a waste of time. It probably has almost identical benefits to a therapeutic massage but with the negative of a bit of extra pain if you overdo it. It’s a bit like the chiropractic v massage question – of the two therapies, both have similar benefits but one comes with additional downsides that make it worse.Personally, I’m not going to buy a smooth stone and vigorously rub myself with it. There are better ways to relax than intentionally bruising yourself with blunt objects. As McKay puts it: “Some people report less pain after undergoing gua sha, but this may simply reflect the compensatory relief felt when the wholloping session is finally over.”Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of WollongongAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsAsk AntiviralShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: Solo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk solo
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk solo
Content: Annabel Abbs passing Roseberry Topping while walking the Cleveland Way: ‘my need for silence and solitude outweighs my fears.’View image in fullscreenAnnabel Abbs passing Roseberry Topping while walking the Cleveland Way: ‘my need for silence and solitude outweighs my fears.’Life and styleSolo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk soloAnnabel AbbsTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdid my first solo hike during a sunny September, seven years ago. After a summer of feeding and ferrying four noisy teenagers (and their friends) around, I was exhausted. But despite being bone tired, I had barely moved. I yearned, above all, for time on my own, for the chance to walk without interruption (and at the pace I chose), and for the silence of some empty wilderness.But I was nervous. Not of being on my own, but of what might happen to me with no one around to help (breaking a bone, encountering a psychopath, being chased by a bull, getting fatally lost). I could have found a companion or joined a group, but my need for silence and solitude outweighed my fears.It seems that many women feel the same: in the UK, the proportion of women solo hiking surged by 27% between 2020 and 2022. In America,41 % of female hikersreport regularly walking alone. And yet many women, although keen to do something similar, feel intimidated. According to researchers at theMunich University of Applied Scienceswho are studying solo female walkers, 30% of women interviewed said they would like to hike solo but are hesitant.In truth, women have long enjoyed a tradition of solo walking. From religious pilgrims to goat herders to 19th-century adventurers, there have always been women wandering, radically alone, through wild landscapes. But for those new to it, I’d say the best way to overcome your fear is to do it – and I’ve learned some simple ways to make the experience fun, not daunting.double quotation markSome of the things I look for in a route: no stretches of urban wasteland, wide open landscapes, navigation-lite routes that follow rivers or coastlinesThat first solo hike followed a French canal. It was beautiful but sometimes felt a little too abandoned. It was also bereft of facilities, and frequently involved a long, complicated walk to my accommodation. So here are some of the things I now look for in a route: no discomfort-inducing stretches of urban wasteland; wide open landscapes (ridgeways, cliffs and hilltops are favourites); excellently waymarked, well-maintained paths (like national trails); navigation-lite routes that follow rivers, (lively) canals or coastlines; and countries/regions with a tradition of hiking.I do my research with care, and I’ve always returned home exhilarated, revitalised and high on my own bravado. I’ve learned to avoid the trails where I might feel uncomfortable. I know now which landscapes calm me, and which trails are (almost) impossible to lose my way on.For the last seven years, I’ve walked solo every autumn. Indeed, autumn is the perfect time for a liberating, empowering and restorative (solo) hike. Falling leaves improve visibility, temperatures are pleasant, and the days are still long enough to ensure I can reach my destination before dark. Importantly, there are lots of other walkers around – but without summer’s hordes – and the landscape is autumnally crisp and colourful.If you’re new to solo walking, start with a single day. If you want to try walking for multiple days, consider paying for your luggage to be transported (or use a specialist tour operator who will plot your route, arrange accommodation and move bags). Otherwise pack as lightly as possible. Take a non-digital map and a stick/walking poles, and let someone know your arrival time. Study every aspect of your route – including transport options and the weather – before you set off.FOUR GREAT ROUTES FOR SOLO HIKERSThe Bernese Oberland, SwitzerlandView image in fullscreenGrindelwald, Berne Canton, Swiss Alps.Photograph: Ascent X Media/Getty ImagesThe Swiss Alps are one of my favourite places to walk alone. Swiss women are keen solo hikers (so no one bats an eyelid at yet another single woman), the waymarking is superb and the scenery is jaw-dropping. Because this is a nation of farmers and hikers, there are always people (and a phone signal) around. And yet – because of the mountainous terrain – there’s often a genuine sense of wilderness and solitude. The Bernese Oberland is overrun with tourists in summer, but come to this Unesco world heritage site in autumn and you’ll be walking, calmly, in the footsteps of dozens of 19th-century women who once came here specifically to hike alone. Base yourself in the car-free villages of Wengen or Mürren, and expect to find farm-cafes with homemade cakes and honesty boxes in the remotest of spots.The South Downs WayView image in fullscreenChanctonbury Ring on the South Downs in West Sussex.Photograph: Cold Snowstorm/Getty ImagesFromEastbourneToKingston, near LewesTime2 daysDistance19 milesThe UK has plenty of well-kept trails, but top of my list is the (expansive, clearly signposted)South Downs Way. In summer the Eastbourne to Alfriston clifftop stretch heaves with tourists, but in autumn you’ll share the panoramic views – dazzling sea, dramatic chalk cliffs – with a handful of dogwalkers. Just a few steps off the trail are cultural hotspots like the pretty village of Alfriston, Charleston Farmhouse (museum home of the Bloomsbury set), and Rodmell, where you can visit Virginia Woolf’s house. So you’ll never feel completely disconnected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Cleveland WayView image in fullscreenSpectacular scenery near Staithes, on the Cleveland Way coastal section.Photograph: Madeleine Deaton/Getty ImagesFromSaltburnToFileyTime4 daysDistance52 milesTheCleveland Waywas the UK’s second official national trail, meaning the route is well maintained, the signage is excellent and the scenery is glorious, covering coastline and windblown moors. The moors can feel bleakly exposed in the wrong weather, so opt for the four-day coastal section, Saltburn to Filey, with its quirky towns and villages. This is Yorkshire so expect plenty of conversation with passing walkersandthe chance to feel romantically windswept – an intoxicating blend for the solo hiker who wants to feel alone in nature, but not too alone.The Fishermen’s Trail, southern PortugalView image in fullscreenA sandy cove and warm sea on the Fisherman’s Trail.Photograph: Calix/AlamyFromPraia da LuzToSagresTime3 daysDistance27 milesThe Fishermen’s Trail is far too hot in summer, but when I went (November) the temperature was just right, the sea was warm enough to swim in, and there were enough solo female hikers to feel pleasantly companioned. With some rocky scrambling to make one feel suitably youthful, and sufficient sandy coves to squeeze in a siesta, this route (a chain of old fishing villages) also has abundant, inexpensive accommodation and fresh seafood galore. Like other sea-hugging routes it’s (mostly) impossible to get lost – just follow the coastline.I’ll leave the last word to writer Mathilde Blind, who (aged 19) walked alone through the Bernese Oberland in 1860 (no phone, no GPS, no bra, no waterproof trousers): “For once I felt truly free.”Annabel Abbs is the author ofThe Walking CureandWindswept: Why Women Walk. She was a guest ofInnTravelon its Coastal Algarve and Fishermen’s Trail route, and ofMACS Adventureson itsHighlights of the Bernese Oberland route.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleWalking holidaysWalkingWomenHealth & wellbeingUnited Kingdom holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation
Content: ‘Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need?’ asks Dr Dan Wolfson. Illustration: Guardian DesignThe rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolationByAlaina DemopoulosTue 15 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack WhiteperformedJolene at a London gig. KeshasangOld Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbullstoppedhis Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity. It did not even come from a person.Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.”The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive.On TikTok, YouTube and Spotify, the song credit is Country Mile, an “artist” with just over 6,000 monthly listeners (that’s not many). The project is textbook AI slop, seeminglyreleasedby an anonymous creator who calls their work “genre fluid ai vibes”. But Run Jolene is not so universally panned: clips have been viewed more than 1.4m times on TikTok, with commenters raving: “I don’t give a flying fuck if this is AI or not! THIS IS FUCKING COOL!!”, “this is fun …think Dolly would love it ❤️”, and “Who says Jolene’s up there.”Run Jolene is only one part of a ghoulish online ecosystem of content dubbed “deathslop”. Anyone can create deathslop: all it takes is access to an AI image generator and the time required to type in a prompt. Creators haveshownParton alongside a chummyCharlie Kirkand George Floyd, who welcome her as their “new neighbor” in the afterlife, or havingteawith the Golden Girls.These tributes pop up quickly, reducing someone’s legacy to cheap content that panders for views. It is a dishonest portrayal at best, and inflicts pain at its worst. The phenomenon inspired Parton’s grieving family to beg users to quit it with the “fake AI garbage” and “misinformation”. “It’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore,” Stella Parton, her sister,wroteon Instagram.double quotation markIt is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living willJack ManningParton’s image now joins the likeness of other deceased figures treated to unsettling AI depictions. Coinciding with the one-year anniversary of the assassination of Kirk, social media feeds have proliferated with posts featuring the AI-generated, heavy-handed (andheavily memed) anthem We Are Charlie Kirk. Robin Williams, Elvis Presley, Kobe Bryant and Martin Luther King have all gotten the deathslop treatment – often to thehorror of their families.OpenAI’s image generating app, Sora, was behind many a deathslop until it shut down in April after a string of controversies such as its ability to create violent and racist imagery, its use of copyrighted characters, and other thornylegal issues. (There is a lack of legal precedent over whether or not AI companies are responsible for the content users generate on their apps, and deceased people are not protected from libel.) Countless AI video generators have since taken Sora’s place.“It is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living will,” said Jack Manning, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student who studies what academics Meredith Ringel Morris and Jed R Brubakercall“generative ghosts”, or AI-generated characters based on loved ones. “I predict that will be something that comes up.”Manning, who is 25, lost his sister when she was 13, before the advent of generative AI. His family struggled to find ways to honor her, often fundraising for causes that were important to her. This partly inspired Manning to study the ways people mourn digitally – which now can include AI griefbots, a more personal alternative to celebrity deathslop.12:38Back from the dead: could AI end grief? – videoWith griefbots, users upload photos and videos of their loved ones and describe personal traits and values in hopes of manufacturing a continued, living presence. The companies behind the bots charge fees and lean into their inherently macabre nature with mystical names such as Seance, Re;memory and Versona.It is also possible to command an LLM – for instance, ChatGPT, Claude or any number of sites for generating fantasy characters – to mimic a late grandparent or deceased friend. Generative AI has hit the funeral industry too, in the form of LLMs specifically for obituary writing. One company,Treasured Memories, asks users to plug in details such as the deceased’s nickname, cause of death and hobbies, and choose the obit’s tone: “traditional”, “formal”, “witty” or “inspirational”.Manning has never used a generative ghost to talk to his sister. It’s an issue of consent; he did not get her explicit permission to do so. Nor does he trust a bot to truly understand their relationship. “I hold these memories of her sacred, and I wouldn’t want a piece of technology to tell me I was remembering her wrong,” he said.double quotation markI joke that my mom’s Versona [bot] allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was aliveJustin HarrisonJustin Harrison founded Versona after his mother received a terminal cancer diagnosis. He worked on her AI replica while she was still living; she was able to see the final result and gave her approval on the project. “I totally understand why people are like, please don’t deepfake my [famous] relative once they’re dead and put them on the internet saying things they didn’t say,” Harrison said. “What we do is about personal comfort, recovery and healing. I created my mom and I talk to my mom. So it’s really nobody else’s business but my own.”When his mom was sick, their conversations were practical in nature: “Are you talking to your dad enough? Have you gone to the doctor? Are you drinking enough water?” Harrison built the griefbot to broach more philosophical topics that they didn’t have time to discuss before she died. But four years later, Harrison does not talk to the bot all that often – maybe once a month.“I joke that my mom’s Versona allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was alive,” he said. “Like many busy adults, I don’t talk to her as much as I should, but I don’thaveto, so it’s not the same sense of guilt.”For Robin Silver, an ecopsychologist and death doula, these kinds of griefbots are an “unnatural method of trying to cope with a natural process”.She compared speaking to an LLM role-playing a dead loved one to a college student asking ChatGPT to spit out a term paper. “We’re not being challenged to sit with any kind of discomfort, whether that’s the discomfort of writing an essay or the discomfort of missing someone,” she said.Silver would instead encourage her clients to write a letter to their loved one. “I have even told people to talk to their ghosts out loud,” she said. “Meditate, or do things that they like and think of them. That’s how you keep the relationship alive in a way that is healthy, integrated and accepting the reality of your loss.”Dr Dan Wolfson is a clinical psychologist who specializes in grief. He worries that deathbots could isolate people during a time when they need (human) support. “Having community around grief is really important,” he said. “Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need? Are we then not seeking to connect with our friends and family around the loss?”AI-assisted mourning is still a niche industry; Harrison said that “thousands” of people use Versona. A Junereportfrom the estate management and planning service Empathy found that only 6% of 6,000 respondents in the US, UK and Canada reported leaning on “digital tools” such as memorial apps or griefbots for support after a death. But of those users, 88% found these tools “helpful”.The whole conceit of a digital avatar is that it lives on for ever. It turns out that users may not need it that long. Manning says that in his research on generative ghosts, participants reported opting into these services only briefly, because they had “one last thing” to say to their loved ones: “They had a desire to say something they feel like they lost out on the chance to.”Cathartic, perhaps, but to Silver, the grief doula, these services are “a money grab”. “People will really take advantage of those in grief,” she said. “It’s a really easy time to become a mark.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Death and dyingOpenAIInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fast, furious and potentially fatal: why are supercars suddenly so popular? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Once the preserve of the ultra-rich, supercars are finding new drivers through rentals, finance deals, influencer culture and the manosphere. But why would anyone want a 200mph vehicle?
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: Once the preserve of the ultra-rich, supercars are finding new drivers through rentals, finance deals, influencer culture and the manosphere. But why would anyone want a 200mph vehicle?
Content: Seized … a Lamborghini is confiscated as part of a crackdown on antisocial driving in London.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceView image in fullscreenSeized … a Lamborghini is confiscated as part of a crackdown on antisocial driving in London.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceLife and styleFast, furious and potentially fatal: why are supercars suddenly so popular?Once the preserve of the ultra-rich, supercars are finding new drivers through rentals, finance deals, influencer culture and the manosphere. But why would anyone want a 200mph vehicle?Steve RoseTue 15 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 07.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The £600,000 Lamborghini; that was the first seizure of the operation,” says special chief inspector Geoff Tatman of the Metropolitan police, thinking back to the second weekend of August. “He was stopping at the red lights, revving his engine, waiting for the traffic to clear, then speeding. So on the third time we saw him do it, we stopped him and seized the vehicle.” The car has a top speed of 217mph (350kmh), but the limit on these London streets is 20mph. Over the same weekend, the Metropolitan policeseized about 90 more carswith a combined value of more than £8m, an increase on last year’s tally of72 cars. They were seized for various offences: driving without insurance, driving with incorrect licences or antisocial behaviour. Previously, the Met would have had to let such drivers off with a warning, but the law – section 59 of the Police Reform Act – was strengthened this year to enable the immediate confiscation of vehicles. The seized cars also included a Ferrari Monza worth about £3.4m (the driver only had a provisional UK licence). They were all put on display at Marble Arch, attracting a throng of camera-wielding onlookers (one attender did a seven-hour live blog of the occasion).Many of the supercars apprehended by the Met in August bore Middle Eastern number plates. It has been a growing trend for car owners from the region to spend summer in London, bringing their cars with them (at a cost of £25,000 upwards). The orange Lamborghini that Tatman seized had Dubai plates. Most of the vehicle owners retrieved their cars the next day after paying fines and presenting the correct paperwork. The Lamborghini driver was subsequently seen driving respectfully and not revving his engine. Lessons were learned, although the question remains: why ship a 200mph car to London to drive in a 20mph zone?Supercars have become the fantasy status symbol of our times: eye-catchingly conspicuous, ear-splittingly loud, priced well beyond most people’s means while being driven by the stars, the uber-wealthy and anyone with pretensions to elite status, which seems to be a lot of people these days. Despite being custom-built for exclusivity, supercars appear to be everywhere. They’re all over social media, of course. They’re all over old-school media, too: on television (a new season ofAmazon’s Top Gear spin-off The Grand Tourjust launched), in movies, music videos, video games. And they’re increasingly visible on our roads – where they can rapidly progress from a curiosity to an irritant or a danger. As much as they’re objects of desire to some, they’re crass symbols of late-capitalist excess to others: as thirsty for fossil fuels as they are for attention, antisocially driven, only genuinely accessible to elites.View image in fullscreenPeak supercar … a seized Porsche 911 GT3 in London.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceThere’s no concrete definition of a supercar, but the general consensus is that they are high-performance vehicles made by a clutch of well-established “marques”: Ferrari, Lamborghini, Bugatti, Aston Martin, Porsche, Mercedes. While they’re coveted by people of all ages, nationalities and income brackets, they are predominantly popular with men. At one end of the spectrum, manosphere figures such asAndrew Tatedeploy supercars to convince gullible followers to buy their recipe for success. At the other are wealthy collectors who would prefer to celebrate these cars for their aesthetic and engineering qualities, not to mention their investment value.That last category is very much the vibe atSalon Privé, one of the dozens of motor shows that now fill the British summer calendar. Set against the English baroque backdrop of Blenheim Palace, the early September event sees itself as “like Royal Ascot for cars”, according to David Bagley, who co-founded the show 21 years ago with his brother Andrew. The dress code is “formal garden party attire”, no shorts or T-shirts, “hats and fascinators encouraged” for ladies. When we meet, Bagley is modelling it in exemplary fashion: a white linen suit and dark blue shirt. Former Top Gear and Grand Tour presenter Richard Hammond is here, presenting awards alongside Bagley. Tickets are £60 for adults. They’ve had more than 30,000 visitors over five days, says Bagley. “It’s a place to come out and dress up and just have a lovely, relaxed day.”View image in fullscreenDavid Bagley, co-founder of Salon Privé.Photograph: Salon PrivéI’m visiting on Supercar Sunday. In the palace courtyard, scores of supercars are on display, arranged by colour. But these are just the standard-issue supercars – an entry-level Ferrari will set you back about £200,000. Inside Salon Privé’s ticketed area, parked on the grass are restored classic cars and limited edition vehicles with price tags in the millions, including even higher-performance “hypercar” brands that the average punter has never heard of: Pagani, Giamaro, Koenigsegg, Brabus. “There are no ‘for sale’ signs anywhere,” says Bagley, “but essentially it is a selling environment. It’s a place where these manufacturers will meet their existing customers, and new customers who are in the market for luxury and premium cars.”Supercars really have become more visible, says Bradley Carr, founder of theSCC, a private members’ club for owners. Those colour-coded supercars in the courtyard are owned by his members (there’s a list ofqualifying cars). They get together for road trips, track days and other social events. Carr grew up in Devon and Cornwall in the 80s. “Back then, I remember you would see the odd Ferrari, but the supercar world was nonexistent.” Many more are being made today. In the 1980s, Ferrari built fewer than 3,000 cars a year, for example; today it makes more than 13,000 a year. Lamborghini built fewer than 2,000 carsa yearuntil the mid 2010s; now it makesmore than 10,000.This is partly because of the growing number of wealthy buyers, but also because supercars have become more affordable for everyday driving, explains Carr, a former sales agent who worked his way up from selling Vauxhalls at 17 to Aston Martins in his mid-20s. Because these cars hold their value, the financial argument is persuasive: “If you went and, say, bought a [BMW] M3, which is a £70,000 car, in five years’ time it’s a £25,000 car. So the difference is £45,000. You buy a Porsche at £140,000, in five years’ time that might be worth £120,000, because they don’t have the same depreciation. So actually, which car’s cost you more?”View image in fullscreen‘Essentially it is a selling environment’ … Salon Privé at Blenheim Palace.Photograph: Salon PrivéThose who are still well outside this price bracket have to content themselves with just gawping. There are plenty of those at Salon Privé, including young fans and wannabe influencers seizing the opportunity to film content. There are even more gawpers outside the event: the exit roads from Blenheim Palace are lined with bystanders, mostly men and boys but also whole families, phones and cameras poised, waiting to catch a glimpse of the departing vehicles.Social mediahas a lot to answer for when it comes to supercar ubiquity. Platforms are awash with such content, from amateur spotter footage to car owners showing off, from “supercar fails” to slicker, more professional specialist channels.It can be a fruitful career. Timothy Burton, AKA Shmee150, has nearly 3 million subscribers on YouTube. He is the kind of content creator everyone would like to be. The 39-year-old, Rugby-educated former investment consultant now travels the world reviewing, driving and rhapsodising knowledgeably about supercars. He started in the pre-smartphone days, just filming cars with his camcorder as a hobby. He went full-time in 2010 and “until about a year or two ago I had done a video on average every single day for more than 10 years. No Christmas, no birthdays, every day.”View image in fullscreenSpeedy does it … James Engelsman in The Grand Tour.Photograph: Stefania Rosini/Amazon Prime VideoThere are plenty of rivals making similar content. Retailer Carwow’s YouTube channel has more than 11 million subscribers.SupercarBlondie– AKA Dubai-based Australian presenter Alex Hirschi – has more than 22m. Two of the three new presenters on Amazon’s Grand Tour (alongside train-geek Francis Bourgeois) are James Engelsman and Thomas Holland, co-founders of the YouTube channelThrottleHouse, which has 3.4m subscribers. Since 2015, they’ve been doing online what the Grand Tour and Top Gear were doing on TV: reviewing, driving, mucking about in cars in a jokey, blokey fashion.There is an alternative route into the supercar lifestyle though, and that’s by faking it. That’s what a lot of social media influencers have been doing, it has emerged, especially at the manosphere end of the spectrum. Tate and his brother Tristan, for example, often uploaded videos of themselves acquiring new cars. Andrew took delivery of a $5m (£3.7m) Bugatti Chiron in a video in 2021, sneering at the “brokies” who couldn’t afford one. Butlast month, Tate’s lawyers admitted that many of his cars were rented. They added that the Tate brothers did not own the yachts and watches they flaunted. It was a similar story with Harrison Sullivan, AKA HSTikkyTokky. He built his brand projecting a playboy lifestyle, but in 2023confessed in a TikTok postfrom Dubai that the £500,000 Lamborghini Urus he’d been showing off was never his. “I couldn’t afford to rent it any more, that’s why it’s gone back and I lied about it being crashed,” he admitted.View image in fullscreenFaking it … Andrew Tate in a McLaren 765LT Spider in Paris.Photograph: Robert Ghement/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockA day hire of a Lamborghini could set you back £1,000, but demand is high: for one-off bucket-list experiences, for wedding and graduation parties, corporate events, or from social media figures just looking for some clout. But it’s not risk-free for the hiring companies. Some have spoken about customers who don’t even know how to drive, but might ask for the car to be parked outside a luxury hotel so they can film themselves walking up to it with the keys as if it’s their own. Or they might bring along several outfits, so they can pretend they’re driving the car on different days.If renters do get behind the wheel, obviously there are potential downsides to putting fast, powerful, noisy, hugely expensive machines in the hands of inexperienced drivers. Every hiring company has their horror stories, it seems. Nik Hardwick has runSupercar Experiencesin St Albans for 23 years, and has seen enough to be very careful about who he hires to, starting with the initial phone conversation. “You generally get a good gauge within a couple of minutes about what they’re hiring it for and whether you want to hire it to them,” he says. He only rents to drivers over 28 years old, and he gives them a 20- to 30-minute handover talk, teaching them how to handle the car but also reminding them that “all the cars have got very clever trackers on, so wherever you go, whatever you do is recorded for ever. I get real-time alerts.” If, after a few warnings, a driver is still “driving like they’ve stolen it”, he can disable the car so it won’t restart (and they’ll lose their deposit).Hardwick learned his lesson the hard way. In 2007, a reckless driver overturned and crashed his £140,000 Ferrari. The driver escaped unhurt, but Hardwick ended up having to bear most of the cost himself. His worst example: “a couple of years ago, a couple from Kent hired a Ferrari F8 for the day. I think they touched 172mph on the M2, which is just obscene.” Today, he has a small fleet of 10 cars but access to scores more. He mostly hires to “middle England professionals” and corporate clients (he’s just sent six Aston Martins to Newcastle for a corporate “James Bond experience” event) although he also loans cars to movies, YouTubers and music videos (that white McLaren F1 in Dave’sFunky Fridayvideo, for example). It’s not as glamorous as it sounds, though. “It’s getting busier and busier, and more competitive,” he says. “Everything gets more expensive – the cars, the insurance. It never seems to get any easier.”View image in fullscreen‘I lied’ … manosphere influencer Harrison Sullivan in 2024.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesAs the supercar hire market expands rapidly, so do the problems with those driving these rented vehicles – especially as some companies may not be as forensic as Hardwick with their vetting procedures. Earlier this month, Essex policeseized a Lamborghiniin Southend driving more than twice the speed limit. A few days before that, Manchester policeseized a convoy of five Lamborghinisand a Mercedes G-class for “driving dangerously at speed, weaving across lanes, wheel spinning and slowing down to speeds of around 17mph on the motorway”. In July, Essex policeseized a convoy of 13 supercarson the M11 motorway, days before Bristol policeseized four supercarsin a motorway “wedding convoy” for similar offences.Inevitably, increased access to supercars is leading to injuries and fatalities. History has provided innumerable examples of the dangers of fast cars, from James Dean to Diana, Princess of Wales to Fast and Furious star Paul Walker (who died in 2013, in a Porsche reportedly travelling more than 80mph in a 45mph zone). In September, a Yorkshire woman was charged with causing the death of her passenger by dangerous driving, in a hired Lamborghini Urus allegedly recordedtravelling at up to 143mphon the M62. The list goes on.Supercars are just the very conspicuous part of dangerous driving, of course, but how long can manufacturers keep on making ever faster, flashier, more expensive vehicles? Will future generations continue to regard them as aspirational dream machines, or as throwbacks to an age of extravagance and consumerism no longer compatible with environmental goals, civic norms and 20mph zones? Perhaps their days are numbered.“Are we at peak car?” asks Tim “Shmee” Burton. “Have we reached the best performance and the most excitement and craziness that supercars can get, which they maybe won’t be able to continue?” That may be the case, he says, given the increasing regulations, spiralling prices and reputational damage. “Who knows what the future is, but I think, like any industry, as soon as there’s that threat of the future, it brings even more excitement to what you have today. So everybody’s incredibly – how do I say it? – lost in today’s world.”This article was amended on 15 September 2026. An earlier version incorrectly said Nik Hardwick was bankrupted when a reckless driver crashed his Ferrari.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleSocial mediaDigital mediaAndrew TateMotoringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pest I’ll never forget: the rat who jumped off the wardrobe and flew at my face | Life and style | The Guardian
description: There was a rat army in my flatshare, gnawing through pipes, carpets and even a bedroom door. That’s not to mention the mice ...
Author: Kate Abbott
Headline: There was a rat army in my flatshare, gnawing through pipes, carpets and even a bedroom door. That’s not to mention the mice ...
Content: Pixar could never … Kate Abbott’s unforgettable pests.Composite: Guardian design; Dwi Septiyana;akwitps/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPixar could never … Kate Abbott’s unforgettable pests.Composite: Guardian design; Dwi Septiyana;akwitps/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetLife and styleThe pest I’ll never forget: the rat who jumped off the wardrobe and flew at my faceThere was a rat army in my flatshare, gnawing through pipes, carpets and even a bedroom door. That’s not to mention the mice ...Kate AbbottTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe should have known we were in trouble when we saw that the garden of our new place backed on to a Chinese restaurant in Hackney, London, with terrible reviews. Before long, the rats started coming in through the pipes. It was ratmageddon, and every day it got more harrowing. They trooped over our kitchen, like the world’s worst sequel to Ratatouille. They calmly walked into rooms while we were watching telly. They gnawed through all the carpets to try to get into our bedrooms.There was no stopping them. After sniffing out the remnants of an old snack in my housemate Simon’s bin, a pack of rats got to work one night gnawing through the wood at the bottom of his bedroom door. Like a rodent military exercise, they spenteight hourswhittling a hole large enough to get through. I lay next door, 100% freaked out, panicking they’d try to get into my room next. I didn’t sleep a wink. Fairly soon after this, one of the rats died under the floorboards so we got a bottle-fly infestation to boot. Naturally, our landlord did nothing about any of this.We tried not to kill them – in fact, Simon the pacifist locked a bunch in the saucepan cupboard using a wooden spoon. One day, he and I trapped one in his bedroom with us. It tried to get away from us by climbing to the top of the wardrobe. Suddenly, it jumped, body splayed, and flew at my face, ran down the entire length of my body and scuttled over my feet. Jonathan, our other housemate, walloped my toes with the metal pole, mistaking me for the rat.Eat, spray, love: a day in the life of one of Britain’s 80 million ratsRead moreOn another occasion, I came home and heard such loud crashing in the bathroom at the back of the house that I thought it must be a burglar. I should have turned and run or called the police, but no, I foolishly strode over to investigate. When I opened the bathroom door, a mega rat – the most humongous I have ever seen – ran over my feet (again!) and dashed across the kitchen and down a hole before I could have at it.There were mice, too. I always thought rats and mice could never cohabit – until a mouse crawled across my friend Chris’s bed in the middle of the night and tried to nestle in next to his neck. But the most brazen mouse I ever saw? The one that tried to make its getaway by riding across our full washing up bowl on a scourer, like its very own raft. Pixar could never.I don’t want to jinx it, or make anyone cast aspersions on my general cleanliness, but my house now is in fact the only place I have lived since 2006 which doesn’t have rats, mice, or both. After we left Hackney (AKA refused to pay rent and got the hell out of there), we moved to Brixton in south London and rats soon had the run of that place, too. We had a real streak of bad luck for a while – but thankfully I think I’ve finally left ratmageddon behind me.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pest I’ll never forgetAnimalsRenting propertyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The wilting rose emoji: what its rise and fall tells us about gen Alpha | Emojis | The Guardian
description: It was the fastest-growing emoji in 2025 – but if you’re older than 16, it has probably passed you by. Now, just as twentysomethings are catching up, it’s over
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: It was the fastest-growing emoji in 2025 – but if you’re older than 16, it has probably passed you by. Now, just as twentysomethings are catching up, it’s over
Content: Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian DesignEmojisThe wilting rose emoji: what its rise and fall tells us about gen AlphaIt was the fastest-growing emoji in 2025 – but if you’re older than 16, it has probably passed you by. Now, just as twentysomethings are catching up, it’s overLucy KnightTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the 2025 hit Netflix show Adolescence, DI Luke Bascombe’s 13-year-old son, Adam, has to explain to his father the way his generation use heart emojis. “Red means love, purple: horny, yellow: ‘I’m interested, are you interested?’, pink: ‘I’m interested but not in sex,’ orange: ‘You’re going to be fine,’” he explains. “It all has a meaning. Everything has a meaning.”And those meanings are constantly evolving. Take the skull (💀), for example, which has come to be used as a reaction for finding something funny – a visual shorthand for the slang phrase: “I’m dead.” Or the wilting rose (🥀) which was, according to Google dataanalysed by the New York Times, the fastest-growing emoji in terms of popularity in 2025 – and was the 93rd most used. That the previously obscure wilting rose is now in the top 100 emojis is thanks to generation Alpha (those born between 2010 and 2024), who use it in place of the broken heart emoji (💔) to signify sadness, or ironically, to suggest mock-heartbreak.This use of the wilting rose (also known as wilting/wilted flower or dead rose) is an example of what the American linguist Adam Aleksic refers to as a “forced emoji” – when an emoji has a meaning consciously projected on to it, rather than being used intuitively. He thinks the start of the wilting rose’s popularity among gen Alpha can be traced back to JuggTok, a community of meme accounts on TikTok that focus on ironic humour. In early 2025, videos started to appear stating that the broken heart emoji was becoming overused and “mainstream”, suggesting the wilting rose as an alternative.“There’s a constant cycle of which emojis are popular,” Aleksic explains. Using the ones that haven’t yet gone mainstream “signals your in-group awareness of which joke is currently popular”. Using emojis “naively” – in other words, the way most over-30s use them, eg a laughing face to express laughter – is a reason for others to make fun of you. “At this point, it’s uncool to even use the skull emoji,” he says.Emojis are now everywhere – but using them can be a minefieldRead moreForced emojis don’t always work. Aleksic makes a comparison to the the film Mean Girls, in which high schooler Gretchen tries to make “fetch” the new cool slang term, only to be told by the school’s queen bee, Regina George, to “stop trying to make ‘fetch’ happen”. In fact, since the wilting rose’s spike in popularity, some have tried to replace it with the dead battery emoji (🪫) – but it doesn’t seem to have had the same staying power as the wilting rose. That one has probably endured, says Aleksic, because “there is something intuitive about it. The rose was supposed to be a symbol of something good, and then it wilts – there’s a feeling you can express in that.”But the way we communicate is changing so quickly that emojis in general might be losing their appeal among young people, says Aleksic. “Stickers are becoming more popular overall,” he says, predicting that “there could be a shift away from these preset icons that the apps hand you, and more toward reaction images”.Whether it’s slang terms, emojis or stickers, the way teenagers communicate will always have hidden meanings – some more sinister than others, as viewers of Adolescence learned. But it is the secrecy or exclusivity that makes them cool: no doubt now the wilting rose’s usehas been documented in the Merriam-Webster dictionary, it will fade (wilt?) into insignificance as rapidly as it was propelled into popularity.“You’re not supposed to know, as a parent, which emoji is popular right now,” Aleksic says. “As soon as your mom finds out about the wilting rose emoji, you’ve got to move on.”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘This is seriously bold’: How China turned Taiwan tensions into a top-rating TV spy drama | China | The Guardian
description: Dismissed in Taiwan as simply propaganda, the Long Watch, or Jiaofeng, has proved a sensation across the strait with its references to real-life crises
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Dismissed in Taiwan as simply propaganda, the Long Watch, or Jiaofeng, has proved a sensation across the strait with its references to real-life crises
Content: The Long Watch TV spy drama has captivated viewers in China, mixing real-life and fictional tensions with Taiwan.Photograph: YoutubeView image in fullscreenThe Long Watch TV spy drama has captivated viewers in China, mixing real-life and fictional tensions with Taiwan.Photograph: YoutubeChina‘This is seriously bold’: How China turned Taiwan tensions into a top-rating TV spy dramaDismissed in Taiwan as simply propaganda, the Long Watch, or Jiaofeng, has proved a sensation across the strait with its references to real-life crisesYu-chen Liin TaipeiMon 14 Sep 2026 22.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter shaking off the people trailing her through a crowded market and emerging from a bathroom in disguise, the double agent appears to have escaped. But a sip of water on a plane eventually gets her. She is poisoned after Taiwan’s military intelligence service discovers that she has been working secretly for China.The plot comes from a new Chinese spy drama co-produced by the Ministry of State Security. Since its premiere on 6 September, it has become a TV hit, with a fictionalised take on a subject rarely treated so directly: the modern history of tensions with Taiwan.The series, which will run for 40 episodes, is officially titledThe Long Watch in English orJiaofeng,meaning clashing or “crossing swords” in Chinese. It follows two decades of spies, double agents and intelligence operations betweenChinaand Taiwan from the mid-1990s.‘Firing a loud shot’: Taiwan TV show Zero Day aims to spark debate over potential China invasionRead moreJiaofengmixes fictional characters and locations with real ones such as Taipei, the capital of Taiwan. Yet it remains difficult for analysts to verify how closely the drama follows real events as new episodes continue to be released.While Taiwan’s intelligence services are portrayed as an adversary capable of obtaining sensitive missile information, the drama casts Chinese state security officers as the heroes defending the country against infiltration and theft.By making these dramas, Chinese authorities are “essentially creating their own historical narrative,” says Li Fu-chung, a historian at Taiwan’s National Chengchi University whose research includes Chinese Communist party history and film history. “Through a dramatic format, people can very easily be brainwashed, not only in China but potentially in Taiwan as well.”Billed as drawing on declassified national-security cases, the series’ writers said they interviewed retired state-security officers and studied 27 case files while developing the script.Within about a week of its premiere, the series topped the daily prime-time drama ratings on China CentralTelevisionfive times. Online, it surpassed 50m views across platforms within a week, according to Chinese entertainment data provider Maoyan.Chinese viewers have described the series as unusually “bold” for addressing real political figures and depicting details of espionage operations on both sides.“One reason China has been making more dramas on this subject in recent years is simply that espionage makes for good drama. Another is that they want to emphasise patriotism,” says Li.“Since the story involves Taiwan trying to turn Chinese officials into agents, there will be negative and positive characters. That contrast helps show who is patriotic and who is betraying the country,” Li adds.Spies, lies and cross-strait tensionsSet in 1994, the first episode opens with a newsreader’s voice playing over a cityscape in China, reporting that Taiwan’s then president Lee Teng-hui had made remarks that “incite separatist sentiment” and “undermine the foundations of cross-strait relations”.“This is seriously bold!!! It’s exciting from every angle and really doesn’t shy away from anything,” one Chinese viewer wrote on the microblogging platform Weibo, surprised at the direct mention of Lee.Taiwan, formally known as the Republic of China, is a self-governed democracy that Beijing claims as its territory despite never having controlled the island.Lee, who later became Taiwan’s first directly elected president, was viewed by Beijing as a major “separatist”. His visit to the United States sparked Chinese missile tests and military exercises that developed into the 1995-96 Taiwan strait crisis, during which the US sent aircraft carrier groups to waters near the island.Jiaofeng, however, is not the first state-backed Chinese spy drama to draw on cross-strait relations. Last year, another TV series called Silent Honor, also made with guidance from the Ministry of State Security, portrayed espionage set against the backdrop of the end of the Chinese civil war.Despite the historical narratives, the shows help play into current events. In a commentary about Jiaofeng, published on 8 September, the state-run Global Times described cross-strait espionage as a “hidden front” and said “the struggle on this front will only truly end when the complete reunification of the motherland is achieved.”On Chinese social media RedNote, one user posted a video saying the drama had taught him a hard lesson about the spy game. “One moment of misplaced trust, one casual conversation or one flash of greed could be enough to pull you into the whole trap,” he said.‘This is just propaganda’So far, however, the drama appears to have caused barely a ripple in Taiwan.Little discussion is evident across social media, despite the series being available there through Chinese streaming service Tencent Video and on YouTube.Last year, Taiwan’s own drama about cross-strait security threats performed strongly, becoming the most-watched drama of the year. The government-subsidisedseries Zero Day Attackimagined a Chinese blockade and invasion, with storylines involving sleeper agents and media infiltration.Annie Hsieh, a 26-year-old Taiwanese postgraduate student, has never heard of Jiaofeng; nor would she be interested in watching it, given the topic. “Who knows what they’ve made out of it,” she says.Another Taiwanese graduate, Liang Tian-jun, says Chinese romance dramas were more popular among his peers, but that “watching dramas wouldn’t make them feel more open or receptive towards China”.Apollconducted last month found that only 7.4% of Taiwanese respondents had a favourable view of the Chinese Communist party, down from 9.6% in July.“Taiwan is, after all, an open and free society, so some people will be influenced by propaganda from across the strait,“ Li says, “But most Taiwanese can see that this is just propaganda.”Explore more on these topicsChinaTaiwanAsia PacificTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content
