title: ‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Drive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowing
Content: More than 13,000 Afrikaners have moved to the US as refugees since the first group arrived in May 2025.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA-EFEView image in fullscreenMore than 13,000 Afrikaners have moved to the US as refugees since the first group arrived in May 2025.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA-EFESouth Africa‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the USDrive to save thousands of Afrikaners from false claims of ‘white genocide’ appears to show signs of slowingRachel Savagein JohannesburgTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners fromSouth Africaas refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in SouthAfrica.After Trump’s February 2025executive orderannouncing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, thefirst group of 68 white South Africansarrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state departmentfigures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according toofficial data.View image in fullscreenThe first group of Afrikaners arrived in the US under Trump’s refugee programme in early May 2025.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesMeanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered afeeling among some white South Africansthat they are now the victims of racial discrimination.Theracist far righthas also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”View image in fullscreenDuring a meeting in May 2025, Donald Trump ambushed Cyril Ramaphosa with printed-out news articles supposedly pointing to a ‘white genocide’ in South Africa. In this image the US president is in fact holding up a photograph of Ebola victims being buried in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAPieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaUS foreign policyRefugeesRaceAfricaThe far rightTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow | Global development | The Guardian
description: Almost 3,500 people have died in outbreak and experts say more must be done to ensure Bundibugyo is under control
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Almost 3,500 people have died in outbreak and experts say more must be done to ensure Bundibugyo is under control
Content: Dr Papy Mafuta, medical director of Katwa hospital, washes his hands in chlorine after treating patients in North Kivu province, DRC.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersView image in fullscreenDr Papy Mafuta, medical director of Katwa hospital, washes his hands in chlorine after treating patients in North Kivu province, DRC.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersGlobal developmentEbola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slowAlmost 3,500 people have died in outbreak and experts say more must be done to ensure Bundibugyo is under controlSupported byAbout this contentProsper Heri Ngorora in GomaTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAuthorities in theDemocratic Republic of the Congohave announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of theBundibugyo variant of Ebola.“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.TheBundibugyo virus outbreak was declaredby Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common ZaireEbolavirus.View image in fullscreenChildren read an information poster about Ebola in Bunia, Ituri province, which is one of the areas of the DRC hardest hit by the outbreak.Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/ReutersAccording to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat is Ebola and why is the outbreak in DRC causing so much concern?Read moreHe warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.Early last month,Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but thatcontainment and contact tracing were still not effectiveenough.Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentGlobal healthEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricaInfectious diseasesMicrobiologynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Scandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidates
Content: André Mendonça and Alexandre de Moraes in Brasília, Brazil, on 2 September.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APView image in fullscreenAndré Mendonça and Alexandre de Moraes in Brasília, Brazil, on 2 September.Photograph: Eraldo Peres/APBrazilFerocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential electionScandal explodes as country’s election campaign peaks, with polls suggesting dead heat between candidatesTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroTue 15 Sep 2026 15.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pitsMoraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former presidentJair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealedan explosive police dossierrelating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. Inone text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique security and economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat | Canada | The Guardian
description: Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Prime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment Summit
Content: Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, speaks during the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersView image in fullscreenMark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, speaks during the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Carlos Osorio/ReutersCanadaCarney says Canada will pursue ‘unique security and economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spatPrime minister speaks of strengthening Canada’s economic and political ties to Europe at Canada Investment SummitLeyland Ceccoin Toronto andJennifer Rankinin StrasbourgTue 15 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inauguralCanadaInvestment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and theEuropean Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 whenCeta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for theMany vs the Moneycounter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s officeannouncednearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaMark CarneyEconomicsEconomic policyAmericasEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Panama canal traffic facing further cuts as drought from El Niño worsens | Panama canal | The Guardian
description: Planned daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes
Author: Mark Saunokonoko
Headline: Planned daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanes
Content: A Liberian-flagged container ship transits the Panama canal. A lack of rainfall linked to El Niño has affected the water levels in the canal, resulting in officials reducing daily vessel traffic.Photograph: Enea Lebrun/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Liberian-flagged container ship transits the Panama canal. A lack of rainfall linked to El Niño has affected the water levels in the canal, resulting in officials reducing daily vessel traffic.Photograph: Enea Lebrun/ReutersPanama canalPanama canal traffic facing further cuts as drought from El Niño worsensPlanned daily reductions will further choke one of the world’s most important shipping lanesMark Saunokonokowith Agence France-PresseMon 14 Sep 2026 22.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 17.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThePanama canalplans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.How Panama canal connects the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific OceanThe US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container shipreportedly paid about $4m(£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companiesscrambling to find alternative routes.El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year.Panama canal to reduce shipping as El Niño strikes vital routeRead moreFifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme.The extreme heat has taken many forms, fromunprecedented heatwaves in Europeto devastating drought in Sudan andtoxic smoke in Indonesia.More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it.Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.Explore more on these topicsPanama canalPanamaAmericasEl Niño southern oscillationDroughtShipping industryInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in Borneo | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: Critically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blaze
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: Critically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blaze
Content: An orangutan named Sampurna receives emergency treatment in the village of Kuala Satong after being rescued from wildfires in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersView image in fullscreenAn orangutan named Sampurna receives emergency treatment in the village of Kuala Satong after being rescued from wildfires in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersThe age of extinctionWildlifeIndonesian wildfires threaten leading orangutan research site in BorneoCritically endangered Bornean orangutans flee forests as staff at Cabang Panti work round the clock to stave off blazeThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentGloria DickieTue 15 Sep 2026 11.57 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWildfires in Indonesiaare sweeping through a critical research site for Bornean orangutans and are now threatening a celebrated research camp, home to one of the world’s longest-running studies of wild apes.In the past few days, the fires have burned within 200 metres of Rangkong research station, a satellite of Cabang Panti research station, which lies about four miles north in Gunung Palung national park.Hundreds of Bornean orangutans(Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species, live in the direct vicinity of the research stations, withmore than 2,500 thought to inhabit the park, many areas of which are now on fire. All three orangutan species are considered critically endangered.“Orangutans are fleeing from these forests. It’s just horrible,” said Prof Cheryl Knott, a biological anthropologist at Boston University who has been leading scientific research on orangutans at Cabang Panti for 32 years.In most cases, the fires were intentionally set to clear land, as is done every year on the island. But an extremely strong El Niño – a warming of sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean that disrupts global weather patterns –has fuelled exceptionally hot and dry conditions across the country, with fires easily escaping control as a result. In West Kalimantan province, some areas have gone months with little to no rainfall.View image in fullscreenField assistants fight fires near the Rangkong research station.Photograph: Jessica LamanScientists at Cabang Panti have collected decades’ worth of data on wild orangutans and their life histories, following some of the same individuals from birth to grandmotherhood. Research carried out at the site has helped to establish the orangutan reproduction cycle, finding that the apes only give birth once every eight years – the longest cycle of any mammal. “The long-term nature of this database and the detailed nature of the database is unparalleled,” Knott said.But the fires threaten to undo such continuous observations. At the rate the flames are moving, without intervention or large firebreaks, the fires will reach Cabang Panti in 20 days’ time, scientists said.“[Cabang Panti] protects what has been, until now, one of the only truly ecologically intact tracts of lowland tropical rainforest in Borneo,” said Prof Andrew Marshall, an anthropologist at the University of Michigan who ran an orangutan research project at the site from 2000 to 2020. “Without long-term, continuously collected field data, we cannot understand how tropical ecosystems are adapting to or suffering from global climate shifts.”In a desperate effort to save Rangkong research station, a team of more than 40 people – mostly field assistants, staff and local villagers – are fighting day and night to stave off the encroaching inferno. Recently, they constructed a firebreak and an improvised sprinkler system using a punctured hose line around the station to saturate the surrounding peat.View image in fullscreenBurnt forest near Palangka Raya, in Central Kalimantan province this week.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersOnce fire reaches a peat swamp, it can smoulder underground for months – even after surface flames have been extinguished. Keeping the peat wet is therefore a key defence.“The issue has surpassed any local organisation’s capacity,” said Caitlin O’Connell, deputy director of the Gunung Palung orangutan conservation programme. “We need large-scale water bombing and skilled firefighters.”Even if they manage to save the research station, it may be for nothing if the orangutans lose their home.“The orangutans need the forest,” Knott said. “If all we have left is the building, what are we studying if the orangutans are all gone, and the food they have is all gone? They can’t survive without that forest.”As solitary animals, orangutans require large ranges and live at low population densities. “You can’t just shove them all together in what remains of the forest,” Knott said.View image in fullscreenRescue workers prepare to transport a mother and baby orangutan named Raya and Rayu who were rescued from wildfires in East Kotawaringin, Central Kalimantan province.Photograph: Reina/AFP/Getty ImagesThose leading the on-the-ground fire response have already witnessed the impact on the apes. “Five orangutans from our long-term study population were observed fleeing the fire, some only metres from the flames,” said Wahyu Susanto, research director for Yayasan Palung, an Indonesian NGO that protects Bornean orangutans. “These are individuals that we have followed and studied for years.”Indonesian meteorologists predict an intense fire season persisting through October as climate forecasts point to a strengthening El Niño.“The hotspots are everywhere,” O’Connell said. “I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say that what we thought couldn’t burn could actually completely disappear if we’re looking at these dry conditions going on for months.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeThe age of extinctionIndonesiaEndangered speciesMammalsWildfiresAnimalsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Queenslanders’ rights to oppose mining projects ‘gutted’ by new laws, activists say | Queensland | The Guardian
description: As minister says process needs to be ‘streamlined’, Greens and Lock the Gate say the legislation is ‘corrupt’ and tears up environmental protections
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: As minister says process needs to be ‘streamlined’, Greens and Lock the Gate say the legislation is ‘corrupt’ and tears up environmental protections
Content: Delays to the expansion of the New Acland coal mine was cited by the resources minister to show the need for new laws.Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDelays to the expansion of the New Acland coal mine was cited by the resources minister to show the need for new laws.Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty ImagesQueenslandQueenslanders’ rights to oppose mining projects ‘gutted’ by new laws, activists sayAs minister says process needs to be ‘streamlined’, Greens and Lock the Gate say the legislation is ‘corrupt’ and tears up environmental protectionsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerTue 15 Sep 2026 19.39 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQueenslanders’ right to object to mining projects – including coal – would be “gutted” by new legislation that would ban opponents from being heard in court without the minister’s approval and then only if they owned a property within a 125km radius of the project.The Greens have called the move “corrupt” and community action group Lock the Gate Alliance said the state’s LNP government was “tearing up democratic and environmental protections just to make life easier for mining companies”.The state’s minister for natural resources, Dale Last, who tabled the legislation on Tuesday, said the bill was “about streamlining approvals and making faster decisions”.“Activists based thousands of kilometres away and green groups funded by foreign overseas entities are no longer eligible to have a say,” he said.“Objections received from a person or group outside the 125km boundary whose interests would not be affected will no longer be accepted.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailQueensland produces most of Australia’s coal and has the country’s second-largest mining industry, behind Western Australia. It is the most polluting state,due to its use of coal for energy.Under current law an objection to a mining project is automatically referred to the state’s land court for independent consideration.The legislation will amend that by giving the decision-maker the discretion whether or not to refer it on to the court.In the case of mining leases, the decision-maker is the resources minister. For environmental approvals, it is the director general of the environment department.View image in fullscreenQueensland minister for natural resources and mines, Dale Last.Photograph: Jono Searle/AAPAnthony Gough, acting director of Queensland Conservation Council, said that would mean the minister of the day could “pick and choose which community objections get heard in open court, and which mines get waved through without that scrutiny”.He said the bill “strips community members of their right to have their objection to damaging mining projects heard in court”.“The vast majority of objections are made by local groups and landholders to protect agricultural land as well as local bushland, native habitat or water resources. It was this process that led to the cessation of sand mining on World Heritage-listed K’gari [Fraser Island].“Queenslanders should be able to protect every inch of the state from inappropriate and invasive mining. They shouldn’t be denied that right simply because they live more than 125km away from a particular mine.”The government last year cancelled a months-long review of the laws dealing with objections to mining leases by theindependent Queensland Law Reform Commission, weeks before it would have released its findings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt replaced the review with one conducted by a cabinet subcommittee.Last told parliament objections were “one of the biggest hindrances on project timelines and delays” and the government was “laser focused on improving approval timeframes”.“You only need to look atthe debacle of the long-running legal battle that the New Acland coalmine expansionexperienced to understand that this process has to change,” he said.The legal battle against the mine lasted 11 years, and went all the way to the high court.A spokesperson for the OakeyCoalAction Alliance, a group of local farmers which litigated the case for 11 years, said the group had won its right to be heard at the high court.“As is evident now, King Coal also heard and had the Queensland Government change the laws so we could not win again,” the spokesperson said.“What the laws are designed to do is to stop anyone who understands we are in a climate crisis from objecting to putting more CO2 in the atmosphere.”Lock the Gate Alliance national coordinator, Ellen Roberts, said the government was “tearing up democratic and environmental protections just to make life easier for mining companies – it is following Campbell Newman’s playbook to the letter”.Queensland’s LNP government dramatically expanded objection rights against planning approvalsfor windfarmslast year, and recently passed legislation permitting the government tocompulsorily acquire land for coal mining.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandCoalMiningEnergyFossil fuelsQueensland politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labor accused of throwing creatives ‘under the bus’ with proposal to ease copyright protections for AI giants | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Compromise revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, meets Albanese ministers
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Compromise revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, meets Albanese ministers
Content: Independent senator David Pocock says any compromise Labor makes on copyright protections would put AI companies’ interests ahead of those of everyday Australians.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndependent senator David Pocock says any compromise Labor makes on copyright protections would put AI companies’ interests ahead of those of everyday Australians.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesAustralian politicsLabor accused of throwing creatives ‘under the bus’ with proposal to ease copyright protections for AI giantsCompromise revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, meets Albanese ministersFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniandCaitlin CassidyTue 15 Sep 2026 17.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Albanese government is considering giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as it pursues a compromise with US tech giants.The proposals were revealed as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator ofChatGPT, met with Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.The independent senatorDavid Pococksaid the compromise would throw protections for creatives and copyright holders “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.“It would mean putting AI companies’ interests over everyday Australians, giving AI companies access to all Australians’ content, unless they opt out,” Pocock said on Tuesday.“The burden should not fall on Australians to defend the rights they already hold over content they create and own and invest in.”The proposals were contained in a document Pocock described as screenshots of government’s consultation proposals, tabled in the Senate on Tuesday and titled “AI on Australian Terms”.AI companies have sought to train their models on content and data onlinebut cannot do so using Australian content due to local copyright rules.The document raises as a key issue the vast number of small individual creators of online content, for which voluntary deals with AI companies “is not realistic/possible”.It suggests requiring rights holders “digitally protect” their material if they do not want AI models trained on it – a proposal rights holders say is not feasible.Under one option it proposes, AI companies would gain the right to access and train models on any unprotected online material as long as they made deals with enough businesses.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereUnder another, AI companies would do deals with creatives’ rights holder organisations that give the access rights even if the content were made by someone who was not a member of the organisation that won the deal. A licence to access one category of material, such as music or text, would be extended to cover the many different small creators within that industry.Labor’s industry minister, Tim Ayres, had on Monday said the government’s forthcoming AI rules would “in no way” involve a reduction in copyright protection.The deputy prime ministerRichard Marles, said the federal government was “working at a pace” to respond to the issue of copyright, and maintained that the opportunity to work with US tech giants was a “significant moment for the country”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlbanese’s AI speech was a good start. Now Australia must confront these bigger questions | Julianne SchultzRead more“The opportunity for Australia economically is enormous in collaborating with frontier companies … and having frontier training occur in Australia,” he told the ABC’s 7.30 program on Tuesday evening.“We want to see this opportunity come to the country [but] it needs to come on terms which are in our national interests.”Marles confirmed that the federal government had spoken with tech companies in San Francisco in the past fortnight on the issue, adding: “I think this can be done.”Before the revelations on Tuesday afternoon, the Greens senatorSarah Hanson-Youngsaid the suggestions of a copyright compromise were “abhorrent”.“Every Australian deserves to get paid for the work that they make and the work that they do,” Hanson-Young said. “A weakening of the copyright laws letting big tech take the work of Australians for free, not have to pay for it, for their own profit.”Musicians, writers and artistslobbied againstweaker copyright laws this year after reports that AI companies were offering $50bn datacentre investments in exchange.The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, is running the government’s consultation with affected organisations.A spokesperson for Rowland on Tuesday said the government would ensure any future copyright changes delivered “meaningful control and fair compensation”.OpenAI’s vice-president for global policy, Ann O’Leary, met ministers and officials this week as the company considers investing in Australia.In an interview with The Australian newspaper about the prospect of training models here, O’Leary said: “Our company isn’t ready to have that conversation if we can’t get through the gating problem of the copyright barriers.”The newspaper reported the comments as an “ultimatum” that sought to “strong-arm” the government. Marles said the newspaper was “overstating” the comments. OpenAI has asked the paper to correct its headline and article.Andrew Charlton, the assistant technology minister, told News24 on Tuesday he hadn’t seen any ultimatum and he would reject one if it were issued.“We want to support Australian artists,” Charlton said. “We want to give them control over their work. We want to make sure they’re compensated, if they choose to have it used.“We’re not compromising them or trading them off. So if we lose some datacentres over this, so be it.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsLabor partyOpenAIDatacentres - AustraliaDavid PocockAI (artificial intelligence)ChatGPTnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pauline Hanson’s daughter Lee working for a NSW One Nation senator remotely from Tasmania without ministerial approval | One Nation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Lee Hanson also appears to be regularly campaigning for party during work hours, social media shows
Author: Sarah Martin
Headline: Exclusive: Lee Hanson also appears to be regularly campaigning for party during work hours, social media shows
Content: Pauline Hanson’s daughter Lee addresses a March for Australia rally in Hobart. She is earning up to $180,000 a year as a senior adviser to NSW One Nation senator Sean Bell.Illustration: Josh Agnew/Guardian designView image in fullscreenPauline Hanson’s daughter Lee addresses a March for Australia rally in Hobart. She is earning up to $180,000 a year as a senior adviser to NSW One Nation senator Sean Bell.Illustration: Josh Agnew/Guardian designThe Populist: Pauline Hanson's divided nationOne NationPauline Hanson’s daughter Lee working for a NSW One Nation senator remotely from Tasmania without ministerial approvalExclusive:Lee Hanson also appears to be regularly campaigning for party during work hours, social media showsListen to Guardian Australia’s podcastThe Populist hereGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah MartinSenior correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePauline Hanson’s daughter, Lee Hanson, has been working in Tasmania as a senior adviser to a New South Wales One Nation senator without the required ministerial approval, Guardian Australia can reveal.Under work base arrangements that apply to the staff of all MPs, a personal adviser such as Hanson can only be allowed to work in a location other than Canberra or the parliamentarian’s home base with approval from the special minister of state.View image in fullscreenPauline Hanson with Lee and her son Tony Zagorski at her home during vote counting for the 2004 federal election.Photograph: AAPBut Guardian Australia has learned that when Sean Bell appointed her as an adviser, he did not submit a request for an alternative work base arrangement as required under parliamentary rules.The revelations are included in the first episode ofThe Populist, the Guardian’s new podcast about One Nation.The Department of Finance approved a contract variation for Hanson to be reclassified from an electorate officer to a personal adviser, without going through the proper process.The PopulistThe Populist: Aeroplanes and bulldozers | Episode 1Sorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://audio.guim.co.uk/2026/09/13-33037-THE_POPULIST_E1_AB.mp300:00:0001:01:25The role pays between $150,000 and $180,000 a year, according to the latest enterprise agreement.Sources say the process was a departmental “stuff-up” that allowed Hanson’s work arrangements to take shape without the minister undertaking the required consideration of “special circumstances” for her employment in a different state.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereA Guardian Australia analysis of Hanson’s social media activity also shows that she appears to be regularly campaigning forOne Nationin Tasmania during work hours.If her activities are taking place without taking leave from her role, she would be in breach of the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, known as the Mops Act.Under the act, staff are employed to assist a parliamentarian to carry out their duties as an MP and “not for party political purposes”.View image in fullscreenThe Hansons in a photo from Lee Hanson’s Facebook pageDozens of social media posts and videos on Hanson’s page or One Nation Tasmania’s page in support of her bid to be elected as a senator for the state have been recorded or posted on her site during working hours.It is unclear whether she took leave to attend the events or undertake the campaign-related activities.Hanson has been spearheading the party’s expansion in the state, opening five new branches and claiming thousands of new members.Her Facebook accounts show that while there are almost daily posts about Tasmanian and party issues after work hours, there are many occasions when campaign activity takes place during normal business hours.This includes events that Hanson has attended as a One Nation representative.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce stayed at Gina Rinehart’s $20m mansion after One Nation fundraisersRead moreIn May she opened a new community centre in Longford for the organisation Rekindle. While she posted about the event after hours, the organisation had advertised that she was there during work hours for the ceremony.Hanson also spent a day at AgFest campaigning for the party, rockclimbing with Scouts Tasmania. “Great day meeting locals and enjoying everything AgFest has to offer,” she wrote.After another event, Hanson appears to have confused the day on which a meeting with the group Concerned Farmers Tasmania took place. A social media post for the One Nation Tasmania page on Saturday 16 May said: “Today, I had the pleasure of meeting with several deeply concerned Tasmanian farmers in Ross yesterday.”The Guardian has confirmed that the meeting took place on Friday 15 May.On 5 December last year, also a Friday, Hanson attended a networking event for businesswomen as a party representative, posting about the event with a One Nation authorisation.In February she posted about a “Tassie road trip” with her mother, showing the pair campaigning in regional Tasmania.View image in fullscreenThree of Pauline Hanson’s four children – Adam, Lee and Tony – outside a Brisbane prison after visiting their mother there in 2003. Hanson had been found guilty of electoral fraud but the conviction was later overturned.Photograph: Tony Phillips/EPAHanson has recorded multiple media interviews about One Nation’s success in Tasmania and posts letters and media releases about state issues.She is also a member of One Nation’s federal executive and oversees the party’s human resources management in parliament.An email obtained by the Guardian was sent to party staff in June announcing the appointment of staff to the MP David Farley’s office.“Please join me in extending a warm welcome to Nicki Waldron and Brenton Trott who have joined David Farley’s parliamentary office,” Hanson says from a party email address sent on a Tuesday afternoon at 2.20pm.“We are still recruiting the remaining positions within David’s office and will therefore make announcements of our new team members in due course.“Please share this with your teams to ensure nobody is missed.”One Nation and Lee Hanson did not reply to questions from Guardian Australia.Explore more on these topicsOne NationThe Populist: Pauline Hanson's divided nationAustralian politicsPauline HansonTasmaniaSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Top Democrat on House oversight panel investigating Trump Jr wedding party bankrolled by Russian oligarch | Donald Trump Jr | The Guardian
description: Robert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar Kremlev
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Robert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar Kremlev
Content: Robert Garcia speaks at a Texas Democratic party press conference before day two of the Republican national convention, on 10 September 2026.Photograph: Gabriela Passos/APView image in fullscreenRobert Garcia speaks at a Texas Democratic party press conference before day two of the Republican national convention, on 10 September 2026.Photograph: Gabriela Passos/APDonald Trump JrTop Democrat on House oversight panel investigating Trump Jr wedding party bankrolled by Russian oligarchRobert Garcia expresses concern over ‘any possible foreign entanglement’ between White House and Umar KremlevAriana BaioTue 15 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRobert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, is investigating potential ties between the White House and a Russian oligarch who paid for a portion of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding.In alettersent to Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, on Monday, Garcia expressed concern about “any possible foreign entanglement” between the president’s son and the oligarch,Umar Kremlev. Garcia asked Wiles to provide documents, records and communications between the White House and Trump Jr about Kremlev, among other requests.“As the son of PresidentDonald Trumpand the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter.Who is Umar Kremlev, the Russian oligarch who reportedly helped pay for Donald Trump Jr’s wedding?Read moreIn aseparate letteraddressed to Trump Jr, Garcia expressed similar worries and asked the president’s son to provide more details about his wedding events bankrolled by Kremlev, including: all dates of communication between Trump Jr and Kremlev, any communications Trump Jr may have had with the White House about Kremlev, financial records of purchases made by foreign nationals and a complete list of wedding gifts from foreign nationals.It came just hours afterProPublicarevealed that Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on wedding celebrations for Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, earlier this year. The couplealso confirmedKremlev’s financial involvement on Monday.“I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the US president said in a statement in response to the report.“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?”Garcia wrote on Xafter the ProPublica report was published.Garcia added: “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”Axioswas the first to report on Garcia’s letter.The investigation into Trump Jr’s wedding is part of the House oversight committee Democrats’ larger investigation into the ways the Trump family has allegedly enriched themselves since Trump took office last year.The Guardian reached out to Garcia’s office and the White House for further comment.Explore more on these topicsDonald Trump JrUS politicsDonald TrumpRussiaEuropeDemocratsHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter as Nato jets shoot down drone over Lithuania | Nato | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen says incidents ‘part of broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe’
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen says incidents ‘part of broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe’
Content: Lithuanian soldiers secure the area near Pratkunai village, Kaisiadorys district, on Tuesday, where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone early on Tuesday.Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/APView image in fullscreenLithuanian soldiers secure the area near Pratkunai village, Kaisiadorys district, on Tuesday, where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone early on Tuesday.Photograph: Mindaugas Kulbis/APNatoRussian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter as Nato jets shoot down drone over LithuaniaUrsula von der Leyen says incidents ‘part of broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe’Jon HenleyEurope correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 23.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Russian warship fired two emergency flares at a Danish helicopter in the Baltic Sea and an Italian Nato fighter jet shot down a drone carrying an explosive device overLithuaniain what the EU described as “reckless and dangerous” Russian behaviour.Poland also scrambled fighter jets “due to the activity of Russian jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory”, the day after Polish security forces retrieved a suspected Russian drone adrift in its waters.German authorities, meanwhile, were searching for more debris on Tuesday from a drone believed to have crashed on Monday near Lake Steinhude in the Hanover region, a little more than half a mile from the German Bundeswehr’s airbase in Wunstorf.The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the incidents inDenmarkand Lithuania were not isolated but “part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression and provocation against Europe testing our readiness and our resolve”. She added: “Russia will find our resolve only growing stronger.”The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, also condemned “reckless action fromRussiatowards Denmark’s military”, adding: “Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver.”Denmark’s armed forces said in a statement that one of its air force’s Fennec helicopters “was fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate” which was in international waters off southern Denmark.The frigate had fired “two flares towards the helicopter” on Monday, the military’s statement said. “One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter.”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Gitanas Nausėda, president of Lithuania; Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, and Kristen Michal, prime minister of Estonia, at the European Arctic summit in Rovaniemi, Finland on Monday.Photograph: Jouni Porsanger/ReutersNo warning or radio contact was given before the flares were fired and they came within “a matter ​of metres” of the helicopter, the Danish defence minister, Jeppe ‌Bruus, said. He said the ‌helicopter had been following standard procedures to photograph the vessel, an operation carried out “many times” in the past.The Danish foreign minister, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, said on Tuesday he had summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident. “Russia is gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour,” he said.“This is completely unacceptable and could have put human lives at risk. That is something we cannot accept,” he said.The Danish straits are the main sea route in and out ​of the Baltic Sea for commercial ​and military shipping.Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, said it was “not the first time” Danish helicopters had “carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships”, accusing this one of “provocative actions” against the Russian frigate.MapThe Lithuanian president, Gitanas Nausėda, said early on Tuesday a drone “that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed byNatofighter jets”, adding: “With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region.”The drone fell near the village of Pratkūnai, about 60 miles (100km) west of the capital, Vilnius, and near the Kaunas reservoir, and had most likely entered the country’s airspace form Belarus, Lithuania’s national crisis management centre said.The centre’s head, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, told LRT public radio the drone had remained in Lithuanian airspace for about 30 minutes and had flown along the outskirts of populated areas before being intercepted.Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, said it “most probably” came from Russia and his Lithuanian counterpart, Robertas Kaunas, said an explosive device had been “discovered and subsequently neutralised” during a search of the site, near a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant.Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Nato allies had been informed about the incident and discussions were under way “both in the EU and Nato, because it is obvious that we all still have a lot of homework to do”.Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – all of which are Nato members and share a border with Russia – have regularly reported drone incursions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. A Nato fightershot downa Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May.European officials have said Russia has been diverting Ukrainian drones meant to strike industrial facilities and oil terminals in the St Petersburg region on the Gulf of Finland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenContractors work along the railway line in Holten, the Netherlands, after trains were halted.Photograph: Vincent Jannink/EPAPoland said early on Tuesday it had launched “aviation operations” in its airspace because Russian jet-powered drones were “conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory”. The operations were “preventive” and concluded without any violation of Polish airspace being observed, it later said.They came after the country’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said on Monday that the military had located ⁠and recovered a Russian drone from the Baltic Sea near the ​beach in Rusinowo, close ‌to the coastal town of Jarosławiec.Poland’s prime minister, ​Donald Tusk, has ​repeatedly said Nato countries ​should expect an increase in provocations from Moscow.A ​Russian drone hit ‌a passenger ​trainon ​Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, shortly after the former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other foreign diplomats had used the same line.View image in fullscreenTV picture of a suspected Russian drone lying on a Baltic Sea beach after it was retrieved by the Polish military on Monday.Photograph: AFPTV/TVN/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the Netherlands, train services were severely disrupted by deliberate ⁠acts of sabotage in more than 30 places around the country, the national rail infrastructure operator said, adding that it was not yet known who was responsible.The Dutch rail infrastructure operator, ProRail, said lengths of steel pipe had been “deliberately” attached to railway tracks in more than 30 locations, mainly in ⁠rural areas in the middle and the east of the country.“We are classifying this as ​sabotage of railway infrastructure,” ‌a ProRail spokesperson, Joke ‌van der Cruysen, said.All trains in the vicinity of the track blockages were halted, while there were also serious disruptions elsewhere, including to international services ‌to Germany.The ​Dutch intelligence agency, AIVD, said it was investigating the incidents, which were uncovered hours before King Willem-Alexander opened a ‌new session of parliament on Tuesday with a speech setting out the government’s 2027 budget plans.Angry farmers set hay bales and tyres alight alongside several main roads later on Tuesday, forcing authorities to ​close them and seriously affecting traffic. The militant Farmers Defence Force said it was not responsible for the railway sabotage, but could not rule out farmers taking action individually.Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this reportThis article was amended on 15 September 2026. Kęstutis Budrys is Lithuania’s foreign minister, not defence minister as stated in an earlier version.Explore more on these topicsNatoDenmarkLithuaniaRussiaPolandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countries | Jaguar Land Rover | The Guardian
description: Carmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament drive
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Carmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament drive
Content: Jaguar Land Rover said the new Defenders were ‘exceptionally robust and versatile’.Photograph: Jaguar Land RoverView image in fullscreenJaguar Land Rover said the new Defenders were ‘exceptionally robust and versatile’.Photograph: Jaguar Land RoverJaguar Land RoverJaguar Land Rover in talks to sell Defender to Nato countriesCarmaker builds on relationship with British armed forces by seeking to cash in on Europe’s rearmament driveJulia KolleweTue 15 Sep 2026 07.35 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 03.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJaguar Land Rover is in talks with Nato countries about selling them the newly revamped Defender military vehicle, as the UK-based carmaker seeks to tap into Europe’s defence spending boom.It is also among carmakersbidding for a UK defence ministry contract worth £900mto replace an ageing fleet of Land Roversthat have been out of production since 2016, competing with General Motors and the UK’s Ineos Automotive, which builds the Grenadier 4x4 for the civilian market.JLR, owned by India’s Tata Motors, has set up a new Defender defence division to explore new partnerships to supply vehicles for people and equipment transportation to defence sectors around the world.The carmaker is trying to expand beyond its relationship with the British armed forces to exploit a spending boom by Nato countries racing to rearm, as it faces weaker demand elsewhere coupled with higher costs.JLR insisted that the move, which was first reported by the Financial Times, was not related to itsplanned 4,000 job cuts globally, as part of an effort to save £1.7bn. It is slashing costs as it struggles with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a damaging cyber-attack last year.As he unveiled three new variants of the Defender Wolf Series II, the next-generation military vehicle, Patrick McGillycuddy, the Defender managing director, said: “Through our newly established Defender defence division, we will offer Defender Wolf Series II to defence organisations worldwide, while also bidding for the UK Ministry of Defence light mobility vehicle tender.”He said the new 4x4s were “exceptionally robust and versatile”, and added that their lightweight aluminium monocoque (French for “single shell”) construction, with a stiffer body structure, means they can be adapted to the “wide range of roles and operational requirements demanded by military organisations”.He said: “It is a modern successor to the world-famous Defender Wolf and Land Rovers that have served the British armed forces for more than 70 years.” The new Defender series is designed and engineered in the UK, with engines built in Wolverhampton.JLR also wants to break into the $80bn (£59bn) US pickup truck market with a local version of its Defender vehicle. The Defender pickup will be built in the US through a joint venture with the Chrysler carmaker, Stellantis, the Sunday Times reported at the weekend. JLR declined to comment on this.It is the most high-profile UK carmaker to pivot the newly booming defence sector as manufacturers grapple with atransition to electric vehiclesand rising competition from Chinese rivals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast week, Volkswagen struck a deal to sell its Osnabrück factory to Israel’s Aurelius Capital and VW’s ⁠second-biggest shareholder, its home state of Lower Saxony, in a move labour officials said could save about 1,400 of the site’s 1,800 jobs. The site would switch production from cars to heavy-duty trucks that carry anti-missile systems for the maker of Israel’s Iron Dome, Arrow ‌and David’s ⁠Sling air and missile defence systems.“These plans involve the potential manufacture of systems and components for air defence systems for Germany andEurope,” Volkswagen said, adding the cooperation could pave the way for further such deals.Renault is repurposing part of its Le Mans chassis plant in western France to make up to 600 drones a month for the French ministry of defence.Explore more on these topicsJaguar Land RoverAutomotive industryDefence policyManufacturing sectorEuropeMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild
Content: The site of what Iranian media said was a US strike on a home where a wedding celebration was being held on 1 September, in Kuhestak, southern Iran.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APView image in fullscreenThe site of what Iranian media said was a US strike on a home where a wedding celebration was being held on 1 September, in Kuhestak, southern Iran.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APUS-Israel war on IranIran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report findsDamaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuildJoseph GedeonandAndrew Rothin WashingtonTue 15 Sep 2026 17.47 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe war inIranhas cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls.Theeconomic reportcomes a day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn, and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”.The Pentagon’s report did not address an internal Pentagon investigation into the Minab school strike on the first day of the war, which killed 156 people, including 120 children. Critics have accused the Pentagon of burying the results of the investigation that would show negligence by the Pentagon in how it compiled targeting data for the initial strikes.The new $38bn estimate in the CBO report, which is some of the first public accounting of the cost of the war in Iran, was requested by the Democratic congressman Brendan Boyle, the ranking member of the House budget committee. It also found that Iranian strikes had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
