And it estimated that the cost would grow $3bn for every additional month the conflict continues, depending on its intensity, while noting that the war has driven up inflation.Much of that cost has come from missile defenses. Fending off Iranian ballistic missiles and drones has consumed such a large share of the US stockpile of Patriot, Thaad and navy interceptors that the CBO said rebuilding it “would probably take at least five years, even if production was increased”.In a White House statement responding to reports of the shortage, Donald Trump said the US had “far more munitions than anyone in the world” and “far more than we need”. Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, separately dismissed a CNN report on the depleted stockpiles as “not true” in August.graphicAccording to the CBO report, the shortage would be “especially problematic” in a hypothetical clash over Taiwan, because of the need for interceptors to engage “large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles”. China maintains such an arsenal and is expanding it, the report noted, and any US-China conflict over Taiwan would likely require far more interceptors, deployed far more quickly, than the campaign against Iran has.Munitions have been the single largest driver of the Pentagon’s costs overall, CBO found: $21.7bn to replace weapons expended so far, of which $13.1bn went toward missile defense interceptors alone. The office also put a price on damage to American aircraft and equipment, including a destroyed Thaad radar system, and said it was forced to build its estimates largely from public reporting because the Pentagon did not respond to its requests for information.The report also found that increased energy costs, due in large part to the disruption of oil shipments through the strait of Hormuz, have increased inflation by half a percentage point compared with previous estimates. Brent crude jumped from $64 a barrel before the fighting to $103 at its peak, and CBO projects the war will leave inflation running 0.5 percentage points higher than expected by early 2027, with short-term interest rates already about 0.2 points higher than they otherwise would have been.It also said that the war had led to the “large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years”.In June the White House requested $87.6bn in supplemental funding, of which $67.1bn was earmarked for the Pentagon. Once funding the CBO judged unrelated to combat operations is stripped out (including money for cybersecurity, drones and classified programs), $42.3bn of the Pentagon’s request appears tied to the Iran conflict, about 10% above CBO’s estimate. The request included $12.1bn for classified programs CBO could not examine – a far larger share of secret funding than in past war supplementals.CBO further added that it still cannot estimate the cost of repairing bomb-damaged US bases, nor any future diplomatic and foreign aid costs tied to the war.Explore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranUS militaryTrump administrationUS defence spendingMiddle East and north AfricaIranUS national securitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Estimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab strait
Content: Displaced Yemenis at a shelter north of Aden in southern Yemen. Thousands have been forced to flee their homes as fighting in the country intensifies.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDisplaced Yemenis at a shelter north of Aden in southern Yemen. Thousands have been forced to flee their homes as fighting in the country intensifies.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthis threaten more Saudi strikes as UN warns of humanitarian crisis in YemenEstimated 100,000 Yemenis displaced amid renewed fighting as Qatar sounds alarm over Bab al-Mandab straitPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorTue 15 Sep 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSaudi cities faced the threat of a second day of Houthi attacks as fighting acrossYemenled the UN to warn of a humanitarian crisis with 100,000 Yemenis already displaced.As oil prices remained well over $100 (£74) a barrel,Qatarwarned of a catastrophe if the Iran-backed Houthi militants won full control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway at the bottom of the Red Sea dominating the key naval route to Asia. The strait has become vital to Saudi crude oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.An emergency meeting of the UN security council in New York heard repeated calls for Houthi forces to show restraint. In a sign thatIranis still seeking a broader solution, its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, travelled to Beijing to discuss China’s possible role in solving the related strait of Hormuz dispute.The future of the strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime and which the US and Iran are now mounting blockades of – is the diplomatic key to unlocking the conflict between the US and Iran, and to a lesser extent the related conflict betweenSaudi Arabiaand the Houthis.Oil prices rose sharply after Reuters reported that ⁠loadings at Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Red ⁠Sea port ​of Yanbu had ⁠been suspended, citing shipping industry sources. The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose nearly 3% to $108 a barrel.Prices have risen this week after the ⁠world’s biggest ​crude ‌oil exporter, Saudi Aramco, ‌closed its East-West ‌pipelinedue to an attack by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. Aramco had increased ⁠use of the ​Yanbu terminal since the start of theUS-Israel war on Iranin late February.View image in fullscreenA screen grab from a Houthi video released earlier this week purporting to show militants on an armoured personnel carrier during an offensive near Yemen’s Red Sea city of Mocha.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPAQatar, acting as a mediator in the Iran war, is still trying to revive a postponed meeting planned for Monday between Iran and most Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The planned talks in Oman were delayed at the insistence of Saudi Arabia in protest at what it regarded as Iranian-inspired Houthi attacks on Saudi cities.The Houthis had claimed responsibility for a new “large-scale” attack using “dozens of ballistic missiles and drones” againstKing Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, southern Saudi Arabia, on Monday. Air raid sirens were activated in six governorates including Jeddah on Tuesday. The warnings were lifted relatively quickly, but reflect an unprecedented new state of insecurity across Saudi Arabia.The Oman meeting had been organised with the intention of reaching a regional agreement on an authorised route for commercial shipping through the strait of Hormuz. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, spoke withOman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday amid US concern that Oman will cede excessive control of the waterway to Iran.View image in fullscreenA shipping vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast in the Bab al-Mandab strait. Qatar has warned a blockade of the waterway could have a significant impact on world trade.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe prospect of the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits both being under the long-term control of anti-western forces would be a significant strategic reversal for the US and Europe.The Qatar foreign ministry official Ibrahim al-Hashmi told reporters: “The world is suffering enough with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandab into that equation.” He added that the closure of the southern entrance to the Red Sea would be “catastrophic for the entire world … and we are already seeing the consequences”.The strait of Hormuz remained largely closed for commercial traffic on Monday and Tuesday, with a Qatar ship disabled by Iran and only four ships recorded as crossing the strait on Monday compared with a prewar average of about 130 ships.So far Donald Trump has rejected Saudi pleas to join the fight to drive theHouthisback north up the coast of the Red Sea. Houthi leaders have also spoken to the US vice-president, JD Vance, reassuring the White House that their forces are seeking only to hinder Saudi-owned shipping, and that their overall goal is to end what they regard as a Saudi blockade of Houthi-controlled areas. The Houthis have signed a ceasefire agreement with the US, but are still subject to US sanctions.The UK is unlikely to offer direct military, as opposed to political, support to Saudi Arabia unless there is a clear instruction from Washington to do so. Inside Yemen the next military engagement is likely to focus on the city of Marib where Saudi air raids have been trying to weaken Houthi formations.Yemen’s ministry of foreign affairs and expatriates said: “If the world wants stability and calm in the region, it must tell the Saudis: enough interference in the Yemeni affair.”Rather than giving direct military help, western governments are providing intelligence, including targeting advice as well as strategic help in the task of trying to integrate the disparate anti-Houthi forces in Yemen.A map of Yemen annotated with details of locations of military actions that have taken place in September 2026.Houthi forces have been advancing in recent days amid a new offensive.But Maysaa Shuja al-Deen from the Sana’a Center thinktank said: “Any renewed military campaign must be accompanied by a serious reassessment of past mistakes, meaningful reform of the Yemeni government, stronger coordination among anti-Houthi forces, and a more balanced relationship between Yemeni actors and their regional partners.”She added: “In many cases, the Saudis choose Yemeni figures who are weak, easily manipulated, and willing to follow their orders. If they instead chose competent, strong actors who could implement a shared agenda, they would also gain the respect of other competent Yemeni figures.“This approach contrasts with the Iranian and Emirati models, which have generally given their local allies more room to manoeuvre while building relationships around specific objectives and clearer mandates.”Due to the weakness of the UN-recognised government in Yemen, various militias with different ideological or regional loyalties operate alongside the official national army. Together on paper, the number of anti-Houthi forces could reach as many as 500,000 troops but in practice not all these forces cooperate or are willing to fight outside their area.Saudi Arabia gives support to Yemen’s Homeland Shield Forces while the United Arab Emirates had backed both the 80,000-strong Southern Transitional Council’s Giants Brigade and a 20,000-strong force led by Tareq Saleh. But the UAE, after backing separatist forces in the south, has now pulled out of Yemen.Explore more on these topicsYemenSaudi ArabiaStrait of HormuzQatarMiddle East and north AfricaUnited NationsHouthisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors | Movies | The Guardian
description: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Content: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesMovies‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsBacking comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treasonCatherine Shoardin London andLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemTue 15 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.The 80-minute documentarywon the special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.View image in fullscreenJonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at theBologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreTricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home wastargetedby a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position cameunder threatafterseveral prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stageat the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including fromIsrael, rallied around Tuttle.View image in fullscreenLaura Poitras in Venice last week.Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty ImagesIn Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers havesigneda petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.“The facts about the mass killing of civilians inNAZAhave been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.View image in fullscreenNo Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesShe called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists inGazaand has normalised the murder of journalists.”Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”British film industry veterans offering their support include directorRichard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip OltermannExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm industryKen LoachRichard EyreNAZAGazaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts say | Ethical foreign policy | The Guardian
description: More than 130 sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlements
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: More than 130 sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlements
Content: A new residential neighbourhood under construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on 9 September in the West Bank.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA new residential neighbourhood under construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on 9 September in the West Bank.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesEthical foreign policyUK sanctions on Israel ‘fall far short’ of its obligations, legal experts sayMore than 130 sign letter to PM saying international law requires further measures to stop illegal settlementsHaroon SiddiqueandGeneva AbdulTue 15 Sep 2026 07.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 130 legal experts, including 18 king’s counsel (KCs), have written to Andy Burnham saying that sanctions on Israeli settlements “fall far short” of Britain’s obligations under the international court of justice’s (ICJ’s) finding that the occupation is unlawful.The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last weekannounced an import ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in Palestineand other measures. Signatories to the letter to the prime minister, including the leading lawyers Michael Mansfield KC and Imran Khan KC, and the former lord justice of appeal Alan Moses, say it is not enough.In a 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ, which is the UN’s top court,ordered Israel to end the occupation “as rapidly as possible”and said other countries were under an obligation not to recognise the occupation as lawful nor aid or assist it.The letter, sent on Tuesday, says the ICJ’s findings have “not had an impact on Israel’s apartheid practice” and, while the UK sanctions are “a necessary corrective”, they are “improperly narrow” when compared with sanctions on Russia, which are not limited to economic activity in occupied Ukrainian territory but apply to wider economic structures supporting the unlawful conduct.It says: “We ask it to commit to further and more rigorous measures to ensure that no part of the UK’s economic relationship with Israel continues to sustain the illegal occupation itself, and the settlements and other serious violations of fundamental rules of international law perpetrated through its conduct, and to build on this to adopt robust coercive measures to seek to bring all these serious violations of international law, and the practices they sustain, including, fundamentally, the occupation itself, to an end.”The letter, also signed by legal academics, calls for a range of additional measures including a full arms embargo on Israel. When announcing the sanctions,Miliband accused Israel of ethnic cleansingin the West Bank, and the signatories sayarticle 6(3) of the arms trade treatyprohibits transfers of arms where a state has knowledge of such a crime.The sanctions were announced after escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank and an Israeli tender was issued for 1,200 homes in theE1 settlement, east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.The signatories want extension of the sanctions to cover insurance, accountancy services and digital infrastructure as well as public confirmation that no UK public body, pension scheme or sovereign fund holds settlement investments.One of the letter’s signatories and drafters, Ralph Wilde, a professor of international law at University College London, welcomed the UK’s recent recognition of Israel’s occupation of theWest Bankas unlawful as an “important shift”, but said it fell short in its focus on the settlements and settlers.“The elephant in the room is the illegality of the occupation itself,” said Wilde, who acted as senior counsel and legal adviser to the Arab League in the case before the ICJ. “It’s not just simply the settlements and the abuse of treatment and the genocide, which of course are also wrong, it’s Israel’s very presence.”He added: “There’s a mismatch between saying Israel’s very presence there is illegal, but then only focusing on the question of the settlers and the settlements. If the problem is with the settlements themselves, then the problem is with the state that establishes them.”A government spokesperson said: “This is the biggest reset in the UK’s approach to protecting and securing the two-state solution in a generation. We have shown our commitment to international law and our refusal to be bystanders to further suffering.“We have taken concrete action, supported accountability, pledged to galvanise the international community and acted with our partners across the globe.”In response to the sanctions, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”.Explore more on these topicsEthical foreign policyInternational court of justiceIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaInternational lawIsrael-Gaza warEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthis seize strategic Red Sea islands as analysts warn of impending oil crunch | Houthis | The Guardian
description: The Yemen militant group captured the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, new the chokepoint of Bab al-Mandab strait
Author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
Headline: The Yemen militant group captured the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, new the chokepoint of Bab al-Mandab strait
Content: A commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab, where Houthi militants have seized new islands, further threatening the world’s oil supply.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab, where Houthi militants have seized new islands, further threatening the world’s oil supply.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesHouthisHouthis seize strategic Red Sea islands as analysts warn of impending oil crunchThe militant group in Yemen captured the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, near the chokepoint of the Bab al-Mandab straitJonathan YerushalmyTue 15 Sep 2026 00.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 01.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s Houthi militants have seized two strategic islands in the Red Sea, reinforcing the Iran-backed group’s ability to control a key shipping route, as concerns mount that the world is facing a new oil supply crisis.The seizure of the islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish is the latest in the militant group’s swift advance across Yemen’s Red Sea coast, after the capture of theport of Mokha and Perim islandin the Bab al-Mandab strait.The islands lie 160km north of the strait which is a chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the open ocean andSaudi Arabia’s key Asian markets.The speed of the Houthis’ advance has left Yemen’s Saudi-backed government trying to claw back territory captured by the militants in recent days, while Riyadh grapples withattacks on a critical oil pipelineby Iran-allied militants in Iraq.Threats from Houthis have leftSaudi Arabiaon high alert, with air alerts flashing across the country daily, while a series of attacks carried out by the militant group using ballistic missiles and drones wounded 13 civilians on Monday.The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stakeRead moreNearly 94,000 people in Yemen have fled their homes since fighting between the Houthis and government forcesescalated this month, the International Organization for Migration said on Monday. About 200 schools have been converted to shelters in south-western Yemen to absorb an influx of families, the International Rescue Committee said.More than 2,000 people have reportedly fled across the sea into Djibouti. The Houthi advance puts them just 32km from a US military base in the tiny country on the Horn of Africa, on the other side of the Bab al-Mandab strait.Red Sea MapOn Monday, experts warned that the closure of Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which has been vital for Riyadh to move oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will further pile pressure on its shipments and global oil supplies. Officials have estimated it could take weeks to fully repair it.“The big question for traders right now is ​the duration of the east-west ‌outage. Any prolonged ​disruption and the associated supply ​loss could easily push prices to the next level higher,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.Research company Rystad Energy said on Monday that since late August, an average 2.6m to 4m barrels of oil a day moved through the pipeline and out of the port of Yanbu – a volume it said was now at risk of “disappearing from the market”.Janiv Shah, vice-president of oil markets for Rystad Energy, noted the recent jump in Brent prices proved the market was already responding to “a significant loss of supply”. Saudi inventories could sustain exports in the coming days, but that could “change quickly,” Shah added.On Tuesday morning, Brent crude oil rose 1.17% to $106.92 a barrel. The average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, as theIranwar, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, squeezed supply.The Houthi leadership has said it is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked ships. Supplies from Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of oil, are vital to economies in Africa and Asia, which rely on oil imports from the Middle East and have been hit hardest by the disruption in trade.Experts say the stock buffers that existed in the system earlier this year, shielding the world from the worst effects of an oil shock by limiting price increases, have now largely disappeared.Since the war began in February, countries have released some crude stockpiles to the market, ⁠and the US also lifted restrictions on oil stored on ships floating at sea from countries ​under sanctions. Those buffers have now ‌been “played out”, Chevron CEO Mike ⁠Wirth said on Friday.“It’s harder to envision a scenario ‌where prices soften and quickly,” he said. “I think the risks remain to the upside over the next few months.“Explore more on these topicsHouthisYemenMiddle East and north AfricaSaudi ArabiaUS-Israel war on IranOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Imran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned father | Imran Khan | The Guardian
description: Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Kasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim Munir
Content: Sulaiman (left) and Kasim Khan say they have not been allowed to speak to their father for more than six months.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/The Times/News LicensingView image in fullscreenSulaiman (left) and Kasim Khan say they have not been allowed to speak to their father for more than six months.Photograph: Vicki Couchman/The Times/News LicensingImran KhanImran Khan’s sons accuse Pakistani army chief of vendetta against imprisoned fatherKasim and Sulaiman Khan tell Guardian they believe ex-PM is being ‘slowly killed’ by harsh treatment, driven by Asim MunirHannah Ellis-Petersenin Delhi andShah Meer Balochin IslamabadTue 15 Sep 2026 07.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sons ofImran Khanhave accused Pakistan’s powerful army chief of a “personal vendetta” against the incarcerated former prime minister and expressed fears their father is being “slowly killed” in jail, as international pressure mounts over his prison conditions.Kasim Khan, 27, and Sulaiman Khan, 29, have become strong advocates for the release of their father, who has been held in Adiala prison in Rawalpindi since his arrest in 2023, and is serving a14-year sentence on corruption charges.They have not been allowed to speak to Khan for more than six months and have been prevented from travelling from the UK toPakistanto lobby for his release.On Wednesday, the supreme court will rule on a case alleging the Pakistan government has been in contempt of court by denying Khan private hospital treatment for a worsening eye condition and preventing family from visiting him or speaking with him in jail for more than six months, in violation of a court order. Khan is being held in solitary confinement, in a cell alleged to be 6ft by 8ft.View image in fullscreenImran Khan outside court in Lahore after a hearing in February 2023.Photograph: Mohsin Raza/ReutersLater this month, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) – the political party Khan founded in 1996, four years after retiring from international cricket – is planning a nationwide march demanding his release.Speaking to the Guardian from London, Khan’s sons – from his first marriage to Jemima Goldsmith – said they were “deeply, deeply concerned” about their father’s health, and that the conditions he was being kept in amounted to “a form of mental and physical torture”.“The reality is that he is locked in a tiny 6x8ft cell without human contact,” said Sulaiman. “He hasn’t been allowed new books for months and he’s not been allowed to see or speak to his family or a neutral doctor. He has an eye condition which was neglected for months and has meant he’s probably almost lost sight in one eye.”Late last month, Sky Sportsaired an interview with Khasim and Sulaimanduring its coverage of a test match between England and Pakistan. The Pakistan Cricket Board, which has close links to the government and whose chair is also the interior minister,made a formal complaint to Sky Sportsafter the broadcast and the Pakistani team threatened to refuse to return to the field after the lunch break.“It shows how out of touch they are with the rest of the world, that they thought they could silence media like they do at home,” Sulaiman said of the complaint. “It just exposed them for the authoritarian regime that they are.”The UN has said Khan’s prolonged detention violates international law and the UN’s special rapporteur on torture said his solitary confinement and detention conditions could amount to psychological torture.Sulaiman said the family had been told their father, 73, had also been diagnosed with high blood pressure. “More than anything, we just want to speak to him and make sure he’s OK,” he said.Khan’s sons said they were particularly concerned that the “cruel” treatment was being driven by a “personal grudge” by Asim Munir, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces and army chief.View image in fullscreenAsim Munir praying after laying a wreath on the martyrs’ monument during a ceremony in Rawalpindi last year.Photograph: APWhen Khan was the prime minister, he unceremoniously demoted Munir, and thebad blood between them was well known. When Munir was made army chief in 2022, the persecution of Khan increased notably.“It’s very clear this is being driven by personal grudge and that’s one of the reasons he’s being treated so harshly, on the orders of Asim Munir,” said Sulaiman.Munir’s powers expanded over the past yearas he established himself as a close ally of Donald Trump, who referred to him as “my favourite field marshal”.Last month, the supreme court ruled that Khan should be taken to a private hospital for treatment for a blood clot in his retinal vein, believed to have destroyed 85% of the sight in his right eye because of a prolonged lack of medical attention.Khan was instead taken briefly to a government hospital, where he was given several injections and ruled fit to return to prison, prompting outrage from his family and political party.“There’s still been no light shed on our father’s real condition from an unbiased, neutral physician,” said Kasim. “We believe they’re trying to slowly kill him in there. Just as soon as there’s less pressure, we are sure they will put even harsher restrictions on him and try to finish him off.“The one with the real vendetta here is the army chief Asim Munir.”Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran Khan – podcastRead moreIn a statement, the Pakistan government called the allegations around Khan “fake propaganda” and said he was being kept in adequate conditions, with access to home-cooked food, nuts, bottled water, exercise equipment, family visits and regular medical examinations.“The government of Pakistan categorically rejects allegations that the convicted prisoner is being subjected to punitive solitary confinement, cruelty or deprivation,” the statement said.It was widely acknowledged that Khancame to power in 2018with the backing of Pakistan’s military, widely referred to as the “establishment”, which has long held an oversized role in the country’s governance. Khan had promised to build a “naya Pakistan” (new Pakistan), which would end corruption and follow the rule of law. However, his time in power was plagued by allegations of corruption,press censorshipand persecution of his opponents.He wastoppled in 2022after falling out with his military benefactors. He then began a campaign calling for the generals to be kept out of government.By 2023, as his accusations against the military grew, Khan turned from alleged persecutor tothe persecuted. He was arrested and charged with more than 100 crimes, including alleged corruption and sedition, which he claims are trumped up to keep him out of power.Despite his toppling and imprisonment, Khan still remains popular. “They want to do everything they can to sideline him and disappear him from public life,” Kasim said.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf display a poster of Imran Khan at a rally in February on the second anniversary of the 2024 general elections, which the party alleges were rigged.Photograph: Bilawal Arbab/EPASulaiman said that while it was “clear the establishment think they can get away with it without any kind of repercussions”, it was also evident the government had been rattled by international coverage of Khan’s case.Khan’s sons said that while they were keen to travel to Pakistan, their visas had still not been granted more than nine months after applying.They emphasised they had no interest in entering politics in Pakistan or leading Khan’s PTI party in his absence.“We definitely don’t want to get involved in politics in Pakistan in the long term,” said Sulaiman. “Our father always said that one of the biggest problems with Pakistani politics is this dynastic nepotism; that power’s been held by just two families for the last 40 years. It’s a sign of what’s wrong with the political system in Pakistan.”Speculation has abounded on whether Khan would strike a deal with the military to secure his release. Khan’s closest aide, Zulfi Bukhari, said: “There is only one deal Khan would ever accept: the restoration of democracy, the rule of law and the people’s mandate in Pakistan. If they’re genuinely willing to do that, then fine – let’s talk.”Kasim and Sulaiman said they did not believe Khan would give up his politics to secure his release. “He’s a very single-minded person,” said Kasim. “I don’t think there’s a chance that he’d ever give it up.”Explore more on these topicsImran KhanPakistanSouth and central AsiaSolitary confinementnewsShareReuse this content

title: What would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer? | World news | The Guardian
description: After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viral
Content: A view of Mumbai.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAView image in fullscreenA view of Mumbai.Photograph: Divyakant Solanki/EPAThis Is IndiaWorld newsWhat would it take to make India’s cities better – and safer?After a five-storey building collapsed in Delhi, focus is on how urban areas can adapt to growing populations. Plus, Ahmedabad’s ace newspaper delivery driver goes viralDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 15 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is nevernotunder construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke aboutthe collapse of a five-storey buildingin Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier,the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died ina fire at another building.As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by theTimes of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.The collapse inDelhihas prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated,seasonal floodingis common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.View image in fullscreenThe problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking, believe some experts.Photograph: DB Pictures/AlamySo, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”View image in fullscreenPeople vacate buildings marked for demolition in Satya Niketan after the collapse of a five-storey building.Photograph: Vishal Kapoor/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high courthas directed authoritiesto inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenXi Jinping, far right, with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and India’s Narendra Modi at this year’s Brics summit.Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/EPANew Delhi declaration| TheBrics summitheld in New Delhi over the weekend adopted a declaration with Iran and the United Arab Emirates agreeing to a late-stage compromise onthe languageabout the war in the Middle East. Chinese president, Xi Jinping, who visited India for the first time in almost seven years, announced that China would helm the group’s presidency for the next year.Political donations| An investigation by theBBC’s Shubhangi Misraclaimed that six unrecognised political parties registered in Gujarat received donations of £132m (Rs 1,700 crore) in 2023-24, higher than the income of national parties excluding the BJP. Despite fielding few candidates and evidence of little political activity, the high amounts expose glaring gaps in oversight of political finances.Women’s health support| Two south Indian states, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, have recently announced policies aimed at supporting women through perimenopause and menopause. Karnataka plans to introducea women’s health programmethat will integrate menopause into the public health system. Tamil Nadu will assessthe physical and mental health needs of perimenopausal women.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCalling all emerging writers| Applications are open for South Asia Speaks, a wonderful platform for emerging writers from the region offering free, year-long mentorship and resources to develop a book-length project. The deadline is 30 September –find out more and apply here.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenPoet Parag Pawan’s book.This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar(@amitavawriter), whose latest book,The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet namedParag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenUmar Khalid, who has spent six years in an Indian jail without trial.2,192That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published inThe Quint. Earlier this year, inhis first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”Vibe checkView image in fullscreenWorld’s fastest paper delivery service? Ayan Shaikh at work in Ahmedabad.Photograph: InstagramAs more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspaperswith serious swaggave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rivalJasprit Bumrah.Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaMumbaiDelhiNarendra ModiBricsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: About 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers | Carers | The Guardian
description: More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: More than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK says
Content: The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianCarersAbout 1,500 Britons a day quitting their jobs to become unpaid carersMore than a million people have left work to look after loved ones in the past two years, Carers UK saysPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorTue 15 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 1,500 Britons a day are quitting their jobs to become unpaid carers, as they try to balance their vulnerable relatives’ growing care needs with declining access to state-funded social care services.Research estimates that more than a million people have left the workplace to look after ageing, ill and disabled loved ones in the past two years, highlighting the social challenges caused by UK’s rapidly changing demographic profile.Unpaid caring is now a “widespread social and economic reality” for UK households, it says, with one in five employees – equivalent to 6.7 million people – facing career and financial sacrifices as they juggle paid work and care for family or friends.Over a fifth of those surveyed (22%) had reduced their job hours to juggle work and care, with over a third (34%) working less than eight hours a week. Around one in 10 carers said they had turned down promotions or taken on lower-paid roles to stay in work.Emily Holzhausen, the director of policy atCarersUK, said: “These figures represent real people who have had to make difficult decisions about their careers, their financial security and their futures due to the pressures of balancing work and care.”Carers UK, which published the report, called on government to strengthen employment rights for unpaid carers, including introducing a statutory entitlement to 10 days’ annual paid carer’s leave for employees.It urged Louise Casey’s independentreview of adult social care, expected to report in the next few months, to recommend policy changes putting carers at the centre of a reformed system, by making it easier for carers to combine work and unpaid care.Midwife Jacqui Hylton, aged 58, gave up her 30-year NHS career to become a full-time carer two years ago when her then 86-year-old mother Winnie’s health took a serious turn for the worse.Hylton moved from Hertfordshire to Leeds to live with Winnie and become her full-time carer. But she is frustrated that her professional skills are going to waste when the NHS faces a midwife shortage.Caring will make it harder for her to return to midwifery as she is unable to work the required number of hours a year to maintain her professional accreditation. Enhanced respite allowance would potentially enable her to keep her hand in at work.“I don’t regret caring for my mum. But financially I’m worse off, my pension will be less than it should have been. It’s lonely at times and its extremely hard work – harder than working in the NHS,” she said.The surge in unpaid carers reflects both an ageing population and a rise in children and working age adults with disabilities or long-term health conditions. Around one in five (20%) of UK adults, equivalent to 11 million people, report unpaid care duties.As well as affecting carers’ finances, careers and wellbeing, the report estimates the doubling in the number of people quitting paid work to care over the past seven years comes at an annual £37bn economic cost to the UK.A government spokesperson said: “Unpaid carers make an extraordinary contribution to families, our communities and the economy, and I would like to personally thank Carers UK for their invaluable work in supporting unpaid carers and championing the issues they face every day.“We want to ensure there are good jobs for carers who want to work alongside managing their caring responsibilities. This is why we are exploring how best to support unpaid carers through our review of employment rights.”Explore more on these topicsCarersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigation | Metropolitan police | The Guardian
description: PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: PC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police station
Content: Panorama’s investigation followed seven months of undercover filming.Photograph: Mark Thomas/AlamyView image in fullscreenPanorama’s investigation followed seven months of undercover filming.Photograph: Mark Thomas/AlamyMetropolitan policeThirteenth Met police officer sacked after undercover BBC investigationPC Mason O’Connor dismissed following Panorama film showing misogyny and racism at London police stationYassin El-MouddenTue 15 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 13th servingMetropolitan policeofficer has been dismissed in relation to an undercover BBC investigation into misogyny and racism at Charing Cross police station.PC Mason O’Connor was found to have committed discreditable conduct and breached professional behaviour standards, linked to a comment he made towards a female colleague, according to the Met.ThePanorama investigation aired in October 2025and followed seven months of undercover filming. It included footage of officers calling for immigrants to be shot and boasting about using violence against suspects.On Tuesday, a disciplinary panel heard that O’Connor told a female colleague in October 2024 that he “hope[d] you get raped on your way to Waterloo”, while he was off-duty in a pub.The incident was reported as part of a witness appeal and “proactive wider investigation” launched after the broadcast of the Panorama film.At the time, the Met police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said the footage was “vile to watch” and featured “incontrovertible evidence” that would enable the fast-tracking of misconduct hearings.O’Connor’s sacking comes a few weeks after the dismissal of PC Lloyd Hunter, who was found to have made comments that trivialised the use of force and suggested that he would enjoy using force against members of the public. Hunter also said he “hated” homeless people.Commander Simon Messinger, from the Met’s professionalism department, said: “Two more officers have now been dismissed for their appalling comments and attitudes.“I hope this sends a very clear message about the standards we expect from all our officers and the Met’s determination to improve our culture across the organisation.“We continue to support the ongoing IOPC [Independent Office forPoliceConduct] investigation.”The IOPC confirmed that investigations were continuing against 15 other officers or police staff and that misconduct had been identified from footage provided by theBBCwhich had not been included in the Panorama broadcast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA gross misconduct hearing is scheduled for later this month over comments made by a detention officer regarding the treatment of people being held in police custody.Amanda Rowe, the IOPC’s director of engagement, said: “This is one of our largest ever investigations in terms of the number of officers investigated, and the sheer number of fast-tracked disciplinary proceedings show how seriously the IOPC and the Met, who held the misconduct hearings, are treating this matter.”Both O’Connor and Hunter will be barred from rejoining the police force.Explore more on these topicsMetropolitan policeBBCLondonPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Britons of all ethnicities feel racial inequality is worsening, study shows | Race | The Guardian
description: Nearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Nearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past year
Content: The British Future poll found that racial or nationality prejudice was most common in public spaces.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe British Future poll found that racial or nationality prejudice was most common in public spaces.Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/ReutersRaceBritons of all ethnicities feel racial inequality is worsening, study showsNearly half of minority ethnic respondents in a poll say they have faced prejudice over the past yearGeneva AbdulTue 15 Sep 2026 18.47 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany Britons feel inequality is worsening and that discrimination has become more common, according to a thinktank study.The report by British Future has found that people across ethnic groups believe racial equality is worsening in Britain. One in six people are from minority ethnic backgrounds.“Most ethnic minorities in Britain feel there was a positive change against racism in our lifetimes yet now fear that progress being reversed,” said the thinktank’s director, Sunder Katwala.The research found nearly half of ethnic minority respondents had faced racial or nationality prejudice over the past year, with the problem notably higher among those aged 18 to 24. Prejudice was most often reported in public spaces, followed by on social media and in the workplace.The research found that 62% of ethnic minority Britons saw racial inequality as a serious problem, a view supported by 57% of the white population.White respondents were less likely to see structural barriers in education, work and public services and more likely to believe minority communities received equal or preferential treatment.The report, part of a three-year study funded by theNuffield Foundation, found a growing polarisation over perceptions that minorities received preferential treatment.Among white respondents, 37% felt ethnic minorities were treated better than white British people, while 33% disagreed. Among ethnic minorities, 23% agreed and 48% disagreed.The report found divisions by age and politics were deeper than those relating to ethnicity. “In both the white and ethnic minority surveys, gaps between rich and poor are seen as the most important divide impacting the UK,” the report said.The research was driven by two online surveys of 2,009 white adults and 3,014 ethnic minority adults between 30 March and 29 April. It was supplemented by information from 12 focus groups.The study noted a difference within ethnic minority attitudes, finding Black respondents were frequently more positive about the UK making progress on racial equality. By contrast, Bangladeshi and Pakistani heritage respondents were found to be more pessimistic, with heightened anxiety seemingly linked to the 2024 riots.“Women, particularly ethnic minority women, are also more pessimistic than men throughout,” the report said.The study found that ethnic minority Britons would like to see more effort to promote equal pay and tackle disparities in essential services and unequal treatment in media reporting.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis was brought into “sharp focus”, the report said, by the intense media scrutiny onJason Arday, a Cambridge University professor who died at his London home after allegations of plagiarism.The report, which criticised successive governments for having “rarely held” a sustained focus on race, laid out 10 recommendations for the government, including challenging zero-sum thinking, supporting grassroots activities and pushing the watchdog Ofcom on compliance against online racism.Overall, it found low trust among political parties. While the Green party and Labour led narrowly in terms of treating people of different backgrounds fairly (+15 and +13 in net trust scores respectively), Reform UK had a net score of -31 (16% trust/47% distrust).Katwala said leaders should “counter the sense of a zero-sum contest over race equality: that fairness for ethnic minorities comes at the expense of the white majority, or vice versa”.He added: “The antidote to that is to pursue a broad and proactive fairness agenda – with the confidence and tools to tackle racism and discrimination where it is most needed.”Explore more on these topicsRaceInequalitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Search under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playground | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: More than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss
Content: Noah is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey.Photograph: Family Handout/Suffolk Police/PAView image in fullscreenNoah is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey.Photograph: Family Handout/Suffolk Police/PASuffolkSearch under way for three-year-old boy missing from Suffolk playgroundMore than 100 people reported to have joined search for Noah, who is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing lossYassin El-MouddenTue 15 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice are urging people to check their gardens and sheds for a three-year-old boy who went missing on Tuesday during a visit to a playground near the Suffolk-Essex border.The boy, named Noah, was last seen at 3pm in Merriam Close in Brantham, near Manningtree, before being separated from a relative. Officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah was reported to have run down an alleyway near the playground towards a housing estate.He is described as white, with curly ginger hair and was wearing shorts, white trainers and a white T-shirt featuring an illustration of the TV character Bluey. Police also confirmed that Noah is autistic, non-verbal and has partial hearing loss.The BBC reported that more than 100 people had joined in the search efforts by Tuesday evening and that train services between Manningtree and Ipswich were running at reduced speed while searches continued.Police have cordoned off the alleyway and there were reports of door-to-door inquiries in the area.A spokesperson for Suffolk constabulary said late on Tuesday: “Emergency services are currently in Brantham conducting searches. Residents in the area are asked to check their gardens, sheds and outbuildings.”A coastguard helicopter was also seen circling the village, which is near the estuary of the River Stour, and there were reports of sightings of drones flying overhead.Anyone who believes that they have seen Noah is being asked tocontact Suffolk police, quoting CAD 203 of 15 September.Explore more on these topicsSuffolknewsShareReuse this content

title: Air pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggests | Air pollution | The Guardian
description: Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Analysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide
Content: Researchers at Queen’s University Belfast say environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies.Photograph: Tomasz Trybus/AlamyView image in fullscreenResearchers at Queen’s University Belfast say environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies.Photograph: Tomasz Trybus/AlamyAir pollutionAir pollution linked to higher suicide risk, international research suggestsAnalysis of 29 studies highlights potentially heightened danger from small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxideAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentTue 15 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAir pollution is associated with anincreased risk of suicideand suicidal thoughts, according to research.Environmental pollution is known to beassociated with poorer mental healthbut its role in suicide risk is less well understood. Scientists at Queen’s University Belfast examined whether air, noise, light, and water pollution could influence the risk of death by suicide and suicidal behaviours.Their meta analysis of 29 studies found that exposure to airborne small particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide were linked to a heightened risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation.Narrative analysis of a further 16 studies suggested that some other air pollutants such as sulphur dioxide and ozone, as well as noise pollution, were also associated with a higher suicide risk. However, evidence for light and water pollution was inconclusive.The authors said the findings, published in the Journal of Epidemiology and CommunityHealth, suggested that environmental pollution could be considered in suicide prevention strategies and that suicide prevention should also be viewed as a public health issue.“These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they said.“Integrating environmental health into mental health policy, through cross-sectoral collaboration, pollution reduction strategies, and targeted public health interventions, could play a vital role in reducing suicide risk and improving overall population mental wellbeing.”Air pollution from ships may be more harmful than road traffic emissions, port study findsRead moreBut other experts expressed caution about the findings. Dr Jess Moody, the senior research and evidence manager at Samaritans, said: “While the reasons for suicide are complex, evidence shows that a variety of factors can impact suicide risk and we must not ignore the environments we live in, particularly inequalities around living conditions. Samaritans welcomes research that helps awareness of how suicide links to wider public health concerns.”Dr Jon Van Niekerk, the chair of the general adult faculty at the Royal College of Psychiatrists, said the research suggested some forms of air pollution may be associated with a small increase in suicidal behaviour but it did not establish that air pollution itself caused suicidal thoughts or attempts.He added: “Air pollution is closely associated with other factors which we know can influence mental health, including socioeconomic deprivation, urban living, physical health and housing.“The study provides further population-level support for reducing harmful air pollution, though the findings should not be seen as supporting individual suicide risk prediction or suggesting that pollution reduction alone could be a suicide prevention measure.”Dr Rosie Cornish, a senior research fellow in epidemiology and health data science at the University of Bristol, said there were many factors associated with higher levels of air pollution as well as increased risk of suicide.“If air pollution is not actually a cause of increased risk of suicide then reducing pollution will not help to prevent suicide. The authors do not acknowledge this when drawing their conclusions.”Dr Stephen Burgess, a professor of biostatistics at the University of Cambridge, said: “This study confuses two fundamentally different concepts: causation and association.“There are many other factors that could potentially explain the associations observed. For example, areas with higher levels of pollution may differ in other ways that affect suicide risk.“This research finds factors that are associated with increased suicide risk, but further research is needed to claim that the factors identified are causes of increased risk.”More than 720,000 people globallydie by suicide each year. It is the third leading cause of death among 15– to 29-year-olds, according to the World Health Organization.In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsAir pollutionMental healthHealthMedical researchnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sleeping teen and camper wounded as Colorado bear attacks reach record high | Colorado | The Guardian
description: Bears came through bedroom window and swiped tent at campground, causing scratch marks and puncture wound
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Bears came through bedroom window and swiped tent at campground, causing scratch marks and puncture wound
Content: There have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado.Photograph: Pete Lomchid/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado.Photograph: Pete Lomchid/Getty ImagesColoradoSleeping teen and camper wounded as Colorado bear attacks reach record highBears came through bedroom window and swiped tent at campground, causing scratch marks and puncture woundUwa Ede-OsifoTue 15 Sep 2026 19.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 19.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA black bear burst through aColoradoteenage girl’s window and scratched her, days after a bear also bit a camper in the state, according to wildlife officials.On Friday, a woman at a campground in south-west Colorado heard a growl and felt something hit her outdoors tent,accordingto a news release.She was treated for a puncture wound on her arm – consistent with a black bear bite – authorities said. Wildlife officers found claw marks on her tent and recovered several dark hairs.“The bite in this incident was more likely an act of surprise than aggression,” said Monte Vista area wildlife manager Rick Basagoitia, adding that the area had “no history of conflict or damage”.Two days later, a bear opened a cracked window, tore the screen off and entered the bedroom of a sleeping 17-year-old girl. The girl was roused by the animal’s presence and hid under her blankets. The bear’s paw struck her stomach, leaving three scratch marks, according to authorities.“The woman is very lucky she had multiple blankets covering her when the bear swiped her,” said district wildlife manager Luke Clancy.There have been 10 reported bear attacks on humans this year in Colorado, a number officials have described as unprecedented.A statewide drought has squeezed the food supply of black bears, who mostly eat berries, fruits and insects, officials say.The bears, who seek up to 20,000 calories per day as they prepare to hibernate during the colder months, have sought out new food sources in human residences.Nationwide, there has also been arisein bear-human conflicts. In August, a bear broke into a New Mexico man’s home andmauledhim to death, marking a rare fatal attack for the state.Wildlife officials have urged the public to secure their trash and to lock windows, doors, garages and vehicles.Explore more on these topicsColoradoAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a success | US economy | The Guardian
description: On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041%, even as investors wary Iran war fallout
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: On Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041%, even as investors wary Iran war fallout
Content: Scott Bessent testifies at a hearing on the state of the international financial system on Capitol Hill in Washington DC, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenScott Bessent testifies at a hearing on the state of the international financial system on Capitol Hill in Washington DC, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Roberto Schmidt/AFP/Getty ImagesUS economyUS treasury secretary hails government’s bond buyback a successOn Tuesday, the 10-year treasury rate yield reached a 19-year high at 5.041%, even as investors wary Iran war falloutLauren Arataniin New YorkTue 15 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, claimed the government’s massive buyback of US bonds was a success.The claim came as the 10-year treasury yield reached a 19-year high on Tuesday, increasing pressure on interest rates as the Federal Reserve weighs another hike to see off rising inflation.US treasury yields, or the rate of return that investors receive when a bond matures, underpins the rates of other loans such as mortgage, car payments and credit card debt. On Tuesday, the yield rate for the 10-year treasury reached 5.041%, the highest level since 2007.The treasury yield rises when demand for bonds goes down. Though the US bond market is typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, investors have been wary of the effect the war in Iran is having on energy prices. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, hit $108 a barrel last week for the first time since May.US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-offRead moreWhen bond yields started to rise in August, the US treasury announced it would triple its buyback of government debt, going from $2bn to $6bn in an effort to bring down bond yields.Though the yields have continued to rise since, Bessent told Congress on Tuesday the operations are “the two most successful treasury auctions that we’ve had in 20 years”.“Since President Trump has come in, (the US bond market) has been the best-performing bond market in the developing world,” Bessent said.Earlier in August, the US government also stepped in to prop up the Japanese yen, a move that was seen as an effort to protect the Japanese government, a major holder of US bonds. Bessent told Congress the effort was a way for the US to signal support for Japanese policies.The Trump administration has been doing its best to fight against growing concerns over high inflation as the war in Iran continues, which is expected to have a major effect on the upcoming midterm election.
