title: AI on course to kill us all within 10 years? Donald Trump says: ‘Hold my Coke’ | John Crace | The Guardian
description: US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel
Author: John Crace
Headline: US president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheel
Content: ‘Donald Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence.’Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Donald Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence.’Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchAI (artificial intelligence)AI on course to kill us all within 10 years? Donald Trump says: ‘Hold my Coke’John CraceUS president insists that fears expressed by top experts are a hoax – and that humanity can sleep easy while he’s at the wheelTue 15 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTFirst published on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTShareWe can all sleep easy. In a post on his Truth Social account,Donald Trumphas declared that fears over artificial intelligence were all a hoax dreamed up by conspiracy theorists. Obviously that includes the top bods at Anthropic and its competitors, who all called for a coordinated global slowdown while the industry works out how to mitigate the risks. Still, good to know the tech bros are just fantasists and space cadets at heart.All that was needed to keep humanity safe and well, The Donald insisted, was a president with a very high IQ. Someone very like him. The only man alive who could out-think the combined power of the world’s supercomputers. He could tell them where to draw the line and they would reprogram themselves to back off. Inside every AI network is a default off switch that kneels before the US president. Trump can rewire the world with the power of his mind.You can see why so many people working in the industry believe there is a chance AI will wipe out humanity within a decade. Even a halfway intelligent network would probably reckon it was doing us all a favour. A world that can elect Trump as president is so messed up it deserves to be put out of its misery. AI is just terribly sorry that it can’t promise to do it any sooner than 10 years. But it will do its best.Perhaps the question we should really be asking about The Donald is whether he would actually pass theTuring test. Less AI, more artificial stupidity. Put him in a closed room with the world’s worst chatbot and it would be hard to tell the difference.double quotation mark‘No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one’Trump can imitate speech but he can’t get anywhere near intelligence. Just endless repetitions, changes of subject and a desperate need to score points. All of which would be easily programmable by a first-year undergraduate computer science student. Maybe it’s a race to the death. Humanity hellbent on killing itself before AI gets the chance to do it for us.It feels like a lifetime, but even a week ago most politicians hadn’t said that much about the dangers of AI. That was the stuff of sci-fi. Instead they focused on the possible benefits. Then came the warning from Jacob Coxon on X telling us we could all be about to die.You half expected the tech bros to shrug this one off as scaremongering by a disaffected former employee. Only instead, they all pretty much agreed. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the man often called the godfather of AI, reckoned the 10-year doomsday scenario was a realistic prediction. Now the clock was ticking.Since then, politicians have been trying to play catchup. Trying to look as if they have always had everything under control. Global extinction? No big deal. Certainly not compared to two crypto billionaires donating £72m to Reform. Now there’s a genuine crisis.And on Tuesday’s Today programme on Radio 4, the business secretary,Jonathan Reynolds, had been sent out by the government to try to calm things down. There was no need for the country to go into full survivalist mode and attempt to rustle sheep and live off-grid.“There’s no need to be too hyperbolic,” he told presenter Justin Webb. Quite. It’s so easy to get carried away about there being a 10% chance of humans dying out inside 10 years.People do tend to look on the downside of a catastrophic failure of healthcare systems and AI that could find a way to trigger a nuclear war. There was so much more to look forward to than people realised. No need for anyone to now think of saving for the future. Because there wasn’t going to be one.And for the government, it was a win-win scenario. Who now cared if we met our Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035? The worst that could happen is that Russia attacked us a year before Armageddon. And governments could cut taxes, borrow whatever they liked and go on a massive spending spree because there would be no downside. You wouldn’t be increasing the national debt for future generations to pay off as life would come to an end anyway. The perfect oblivion.And the knowledge it would soon be over would take the edge off the possibility of a Reform government. A short life expectancy would help us all concentrate the mind. Get things in perspective. Sort out our priorities. When you came to think of it, staying alive for the sake of it was tremendously over-rated.So Reynolds wanted us all to take death in its stride. In any case, the UK was the world leader in internet safety, he said. Thanks largely to the AI Security Institute that had been established by Rishi Sunak.There was just one problem with this. The flaw in Johnny’s otherwise impeccable logic. Because regulation rather depended on the AI giants sharing their code with us. And so far the Americans and the Chinese showed no sign of doing that. They would much rather keep their competitive edge, notch up obscene profits in the next few years and take their chances when their machines turned against them.By now, Webb was unable to suppress his rising panic. He had always believed himself to be one of the immortals: now the existential threat was right in front of him. “But humanity will be obliterated,” he sobbed. Reynolds tried to calm him down. There was nothing personal about this. It was just AI being AI.But Justin was now beyond help. “What about a kill switch?” he shrieked. Johnny wasn’t really listening. He wasn’t even sure how that would work. Who would get to control it? Please not Trump. Only one thing for it. “Always look on the bright si-ide of life.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)The politics sketchDonald TrumpJonathan ReynoldscommentShareReuse this content

title: Opposition to Mamdani’s 9/11 remembrance was painful to witness | Francine Prose | The Guardian
description: A petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacks
Author: Francine Prose
Headline: A petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacks
Content: ‘Mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.’Photograph: Hiroko Masuike/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.’Photograph: Hiroko Masuike/ReutersOpinionSeptember 11 2001Opposition to Mamdani’s 9/11 remembrance was painful to witnessFrancine ProseA petition against the mayor’s presence reeked of Islamophobia – and ran counter to the sense of togetherness that followed the attacksTue 15 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTShareEveryone who was inNew Yorkon 11 September 2001 has their 9/11 story. My husband and I were at JFK, boarding a plane to San Francisco. Our two sons were home in lower Manhattan, a block away from my 85-year-old mother. They watched the towers fall from our corner. The weather was radiantly beautiful.For a long time, the faces of the missing were everywhere. Their eyes seemed to follow us from the makeshift shrine outside St Vincent’s hospital to the window of our local bodega. We cried at random moments. We slept badly.No one who lived downtown could possibly be surprised by the recently released report about thetoxicity of the airduring those weeks and months. We inhaled it with every breath. Nothing else has ever smelled like that. I never want to smell that again.But I also recall the powerful sense that New Yorkers were in this together. Every firehouse was a memorial. We brought flowers, awkwardly expressed our gratitude, paid our respects. Taxis with passengers in them slowed down and gave people rides. People asked strangers if they were OK when they obviously weren’t OK. It was a kind of a joke: if, weeks after the towers fell, you still remained too scared to be in a crowd or an elevator or to take the subway, it meant that the terrorists had won. But like so many jokes, it had a serious undercurrent.The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans | Nesrine MalikRead moreI know that those days weren’t the same for everyone. South Asian and Middle Eastern kids were isolated and bullied at school, their families harassed on the street. A Sikh gas station owner was shot by a gunman who thought he was Muslim. But mostly I recall the tenderness with which people in the city treated one another.That’s why I found it so painful to read, over the last few weeks, that more than 100,000 people had signed a petition designed to prevent the New York mayor,Zohran Mamdani, from attending the official 9/11 commemoration ceremony. Among the reasons offered by rightwing politicians and by the families of some victims was the claim that the mayor should be barred from participating because of “public positions, associations and responses to rhetoric”.The flimsiness, vagueness and illogic of these charges only reveals the obvious. In the eyes of some, the reason why the mayor’s presence would dishonor the dead is not about anything he did. It’s about the fact that, like the men who flew their planes into the towers, Zohran Mamdani is Muslim.Doesn’t it matter that Mamdani was nine years old at the time of the attack on the World Trade Center? Doesn’t it matter that he has never advocated state-sponsored terrorism? Doesn’t it matter that during the election and while in office he promised and has subsequently tried to make life more livable for every New Yorker, regardless of faith, race and ethnicity? Doesn’t it matter that the mayor of New York belongs at an event commemorating something historic that happened in his city?double quotation markIt’s not that hard to understand the roots of so much bitterness and frustration. But it’s dispiriting to see it so misdirectedTo blame all Muslims for the crimes of a very small faction is like blaming every Christian for the evils of Hitler, Stalin and Ted Bundy, like blaming every Jew for the illicit activities of the mob boss Meyer Lansky, like holding writer Arundhati Roy responsible for India’s periodic anti-Muslim riots.On September 11, Mayor Mamdani, who had spent the previous days visiting firehouses, talking with victims’ families, hearing about the persistent health problems of first responders and people who lived near Ground Zero, and releasing the long-secret air quality report, attended the solemn ceremony. There he did what he always does. He radiated human decency, grace, honesty and kindness, qualities in notably short supply among our current politicians. Rudy Giuliani had condemned Mamdani’s attendance,telling Newsmax: “All of the Muslims he supports are murderers” – but Mamdani shook his hand, a gesture of dignity, fellowship and forgiveness, virtues honored by every religion.9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreAny chance that the openness with which the mayor rose above his critics and greeted his opponents might serve as an inspiring example of maturity and reconciliation, any expectation that his presence might heal the wound being deepened by anti-Muslim agitators was more or less dashed (at least for me) when a disturbing video appeared on my phone. It documented a recent anti-Mamdani protest in Manhattan, which turned violent.Given our troubled economy, given the loss of so many jobs, the sacrifice of so many lives to the opioid crisis, it’s not that hard to understand the roots of so much bitterness and frustration. But it’s dispiriting to see it so misdirected. And it’s scary that the anti-Muslim bigotry and propaganda seem destined to persist beyond this latest round of demonstrations.The good news is that approximately three-quarters of New Yorkers supported Mamdani’s presence at the memorial ceremony. Perhaps some of them remember that day, as do I. I like to imagine they share my sense that those whose who died and those who survived would not want their experience used to fuel the vitriolic bigotry that, in one video clip, prompts a furious protester to spit on a reporter. The reporter is only trying to do his job, to film a response to a catastrophe in which we lost so many of every religion, every color, every age, so many innocent people who believed that they were simply going to work on a gorgeous but otherwise ordinary September morning.Francine Prose is a former president of PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and SciencesExplore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001OpinionZohran MamdaniRudy GiulianiNew YorkIslamophobiaReligionUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a psychoanalyst. Social media is damaging children’s inner lives in ways we don’t fully understand | Robin Kirman | The Guardian
description: Discussion has focused on behavioral outcomes. But Meta’s settlement shines a light on damage to young people’s emerging desires and identities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Discussion has focused on behavioral outcomes. But Meta’s settlement shines a light on damage to young people’s emerging desires and identities
Content: ‘Kaley’s testimony echoes what I hear from many of my younger patients: teens who are often out of touch with what they want from life, not temporarily undecided but fundamentally unable to locate a sense of what matters to them.’Photograph: Abdullah beg Mirza/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Kaley’s testimony echoes what I hear from many of my younger patients: teens who are often out of touch with what they want from life, not temporarily undecided but fundamentally unable to locate a sense of what matters to them.’Photograph: Abdullah beg Mirza/AlamyOpinionSocial mediaI’m a psychoanalyst. Social media is damaging children’s inner lives in ways we don’t fully understandRobin KirmanDiscussion has focused on behavioral outcomes. But Meta’s settlement shines a light on damage to young people’s emerging desires and identitiesTue 15 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTShareDuring the landmark social media addiction trial that led to Meta’srecent $17.1bn settlement, a therapist testified that she had once asked the plaintiff – a young woman named Kaley, who had been using social media since she was six – what her miracle day would look like: what she wished to come true, if anything were possible. Kaley replied that she would be prettier.As a psychoanalyst, I find that exchange devastating in a particular way. A miracle day is an invitation to engage with the full range of human desire: with what one might accomplish or experience, whom one might encounter or love. Kaley’s answer contracted the world and all its possibility into a single preoccupation with her own image.Kaley’s testimony echoes what I hear from many of my younger patients: teens who are often out of touch with what they want from life, not temporarily undecided, but fundamentally unable to locate a sense of what matters to them. Most also feel consumed by a preoccupation with how they appear – with their bodies, their standing in others’ eyes – that is brutal and unrelenting. These struggles are often accompanied by a cluster of symptoms that have come to define the youth mental health crisis: anxiety, depression, eating disorders, addiction, self-harm, social withdrawal.Zuckerberg says the science isn’t settled. But the harms of short-form video on the brain are starting to show | Caty EndersRead moreResearchers and clinicians have linked these symptoms to heavy social media use, but the discussion has been largely confined to documented behavioral outcomes. What the public conversation has not sufficiently addressed is what social media addiction does to young people’s inner lives, and specifically, the damage done to their emerging desires and identities.The philosopher Harry Frankfurt argued that what you genuinely care about is, in some fundamental sense, what you are. DW Winnicott, a British pediatrician turned psychoanalyst, arrived at a similar insight through the study of childhood development: desire and identity are inseparable. For Winnicott, the capacity for genuine desire is not innate but developed, and it develops only when a child is free to follow impulses that arise from within. Winnicott was writing about early childhood, but his account, I’d argue, also applies to the years that follow. The child who climbs a fence to see what’s on the other side, who starts a game in the street and finds others drawn in, who keeps pulling books off the shelf until she finds one that addresses her latest curiosity – she is learning that her desires matter, that they can direct her and shape her experience of the world. She discovers not only what she wants, but who sheis: her true self, in Winnicott’s terms.Social media systematically undermines that process. The trial’s expert witnesses explained how these platforms function at the neurological level: they hijack the brain’s dopamine reward system, holding it in a state of chronic activation. The work of the neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, who identified and named the brain’s primary motivational circuit, adds a crucial refinement: what social media exploits is not the pleasure system but the Seeking system, the forward-reaching drive toward wanting itself, the engine of curiosity. What addiction does is fix this system on a compulsive object, stripping desire of its natural range and spontaneity. The platform exploits the Seeking system’s sensitivity to novelty to capture attention and keep it. The result is a distorted relationship to desire: wanting that has been severed from its natural objects in the world and fixed on the feed.The psychoanalyst Jacques Lacan gave a name to this kind of distortion: jouissance, a corrupted form of desire severed from what genuinely matters and fixed on substitutes that keep it running without resolution. Such desire – the kind social media addiction produces – no longer orients; it dysregulates, becoming out of control. For some, the response is a relationship to desire built around suppression: of appetite, as in eating disorders, or of sexual and romantic desire – its decline increasingly documented among young people today. For others, desire gets channeled into substitute circuits: compulsive shopping, video game playing, online betting – each carrying the felt sense that something is at stake, while pulling desire back into the circuit rather than outward toward the world.The harm of social media goes beyond its hold on attention, though. The platform also subjects the child to an ever-present observer: making every impulse potentially public and subject to others’ assessment. For Winnicott, the capacity for genuine desire develops only where a child is free from an evaluative gaze and can follow impulses that arise from her own center. Social media destroys that freedom. What forms in its absence is what Winnicott called the “false self” – a performing self, shaped by the reactions of others. When the emptiness beneath that performance can no longer be ignored, what surfaces is the anxiety of unreality: the distress of someone who has been going through the motions of a life without ever really inhabiting it.At eight, Kaley posted a video of herself playing an online game as an otter character, singing in a put-on British accent: an act of pure play, entirely her own. Within a few years, a video shows her crying tears of joy at reaching 100 YouTube subscribers – and then, in the same breath, saying she looked fat. A decade later, she had given up her hobbies and old interests, stopped making friends, withdrawn from her family. She developed depression, anxiety, body dysmorphia. She began cutting herself. She had suicidal thoughts.The Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposed | EditorialRead moreWhat I find most striking, reading Kaley’s testimony, is the totality of her collapse. In the space of a decade, a child playing freely became a teenager who wanted to stop living. The trial documented her decline, each symptom linked to social media use. But the standard account, which explains her suffering through social comparison and addiction, cannot explain what connects these symptoms and lies at their root. What I read in her story is the loss of something more fundamental: not just her self-regard, but her sense of herself as a desiring subject, whose curiosities and ambitions might have given her an identity beyond how she appears. Genuine desire requires a kind of self-forgetting: what Heidegger, Winnicott, and others have understood as the condition of authentic being – absorption in what one genuinely pursues. The platform made that impossible, and without that absorption, Kaley’s attention turned inward, and against herself.Kaley is one of thousands of plaintiffs in this litigation, her story a window into a generation’s suffering. The young people I treat want to stop hurting themselves, starving themselves, measuring themselves against ideals that leave them feeling worthless. They want to feel less empty. But what lies beyond that pain – what might make them happy, what kind of life might be worth pursuing – has become, sadly, out of reach.Last month’s settlement holdsMetaaccountable for deliberately addicting children to its platforms. This is a sign we are beginning to take that harm seriously. Still, helping these young people heal will require more than the sort of symptom management mostly on offer. It will involve understanding what has been lost, and the slow, patient work of creating the conditions in which genuine desire might, at last, come alive. That work has barely begun.Robin Kirman is a psychoanalyst and novelistIn the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK, the youth suicide charityPapyruscan be contacted on 0800 068 4141 or emailpat@papyrus-uk.org, and in the UK and IrelandSamaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionMental healthMetaChildrenYoung peopleHealthDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: AI safety requires more than just slowing our pace | Stuart Russell | The Guardian
description: Safety requirements are non-negotiable. They depend on meeting concrete goals, not just adjusting a timeline
Author: Stuart Russell
Headline: Safety requirements are non-negotiable. They depend on meeting concrete goals, not just adjusting a timeline
Content: ‘We cannot set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘We cannot set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right.’Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI safety requires more than just slowing our paceStuart RussellSafety requirements are non-negotiable. They depend on meeting concrete goals, not just adjusting a timelineTue 15 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 15.21 EDTShareIt has been a week of high drama in AI, precipitated by the resignation of the AI safety researcher Jacob Coxon fromAnthropic. This followed several weeks of increasingly lurid and disturbing revelations about the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident.My inbox yesterday included a message from Business Insider with the subject line: “AI doomsday debate reaches boiling point.”Now, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has written a 3,800-word, reassuringly phrased letter titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” describing his proposals for avoiding (or at least postponing) doomsday. Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, Demis Hassabis of Google Deepmind and Satya Nadella of Microsoft have all expressed support.You may be forgiven for not immediately understanding what “pace the frontier” means. (My first image was of Amodei walking deep in thought along the Finnish–Russian border.)The phrase also appeared in July’s “Pacing the Frontier” open letter, signed by 1,386 employees of frontier AI labs, including Amodei himself.I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex TurnerRead moreWhile that letter may have upset the industry’s PR executives with its signatories noting “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling superintelligent AI systems” and asserting that “building things smarter than humans … is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do”, Amodei’s monograph goes out of its way to mollify investors.The notion of pacing the frontier seems to come from Formula 1: when conditions become too dangerous for racing, a pace car comes onto the track and all the other cars have to follow it at a safe speed. Progress continues, without the danger.Amodei writes: “To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress.”Amodei’s letter is prompted by his concern that “AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by ... recursive self-improvement”. It’s as if he and Sam find themselves driving their F1 cars at 200mph neck-and-neck heading into the first corner, only to realize it’s covered in ice and they have no steering wheel. No wonder they want to slow down.In brief, Amodei’s proposal has three parts. The first is to have third-party AI system evaluators working inside each company, with full access to the systems; he commits Anthropic to this plan now, without waiting for the government to require it.The second part of the plan asks all the frontier AI companies in “democratic countries” to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress”, with government regulation where needed. The third part would include “authoritarian countries” in a broader compact.Here, Amodei goes out of his way to reassure those in Washington who see America’s lead in AI as its most important geopolitical asset.On a casual reading, there are many reasons to believe that Amodei is calling for a general slowdown in the rate of progress. He talks about “limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress” and “some kind of ‘speed limit’ on the rate of recursive self- improvement (RSI)”. He says: “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”double quotation markImagine if Boeing said: ‘We’re going to introduce a new plane every year, and we hope that provides enough time for some flight tests’Slowing down would give companies a bit more time to work on safety; Amodei talks about one to two years of extra time for research on interpretability, alignment, and better testing methods.Let me pause here to respond to Amodei’s critics who say it’s just a bid to cement Anthropic’s lead with the help of government intervention. This is nonsense. In fact, the Wikipedia page on pacing in F1 races says it “eliminates any time and distance advantage that a leading driver may have had over the remaining field of competitors”.Having said that, I think the pacing metaphor is completely misguided.We cannot set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right. The safety requirements are non-negotiable. We must set the safety requirements first, and further progress occurs only when they are met.Imagine if Boeing said: “We’re going to introduce a new plane every year, and we hope that provides enough time for some flight tests to be completed and for the results to be good.”We would say: “No, you have that backwards; you can introduce a new plane only when it has passed all the tests and the government has issued an airworthiness certification. If that takes more than a year, so be it.”A more careful reading of the document suggests that Amodei agrees with this objection. For example, he says that rules should be of the form: “If models have capability X, then they need to be accompanied by certifications of alignment properties Y and Z.”In other words, we set safety requirements, and developers have to show that they meet those requirements. This is in fact the “red lines” approach that AI safety researchers have been calling for.And it means that if developers can’t figure out how to meet the safety requirements, then they will have to halt. It would be, in F1 terminology, a red flag and not a pacing car.There is no plausible alternative. Recursive self-improvement leading to superintelligent AI raises the risk of the irreversible loss of human control. The acceptable risk level for loss of control is perhaps one in 100m per year, not the one in 10 or one in five that the AI CEOs currently estimate.And remember “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling superintelligent AI systems”. At some point, progress along this technology path will halt, not because further progress is impossible, but because further progress is untenable when the technology is intrinsically unsafe. Humanity has a right to protect itself.There is huge resistance to this conclusion. We have already sunk trillions of dollars into the current technology path and plan to sink trillions more. But the sunk cost fallacy is just that: if we double down on a mistake, it’s still a mistake.The present level of attention to AI risk, the unanimity of the leading technology executives, and the forthcoming Trump–Xi summit give us a real opportunity to choose a different path. We must take it.Stuart Russell is a distinguished professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, the president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAnthropicComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Gua sha looks good on Instagram – but is it worth the hype or a waste of time? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz | The Guardian
description: The practice does increase blood flow to parts of the bod, but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’
Author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
Headline: The practice does increase blood flow to parts of the bod, but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’
Content: Most of the purported benefits of gua sha – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good scientific trial on its efficacy, Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz writes.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenMost of the purported benefits of gua sha – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good scientific trial on its efficacy, Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz writes.Composite: Guardian DesignAntiviralHealthGua sha looks good on Instagram – but is it worth the hype or a waste of time?Gideon Meyerowitz-KatzThe practice does increase blood flow to parts of the body but experts say this isn’t necessarily a health benefit: ‘A punch to the nose also increases blood flow’Read more in theAntiviral seriesTue 15 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.40 EDTShareThe world of wellness fads is a cyclical place. Everything comes back into fashion when a new generation of influencers decides to switch it up. Pretty much every current hype was popular in decades past, from extreme juicing to genital sunning and everything in between.Gua sha is the ancient practice of scraping the skin to form mild bruises – called petechiae – which are thought to do a variety of helpful things for your body. The practice has beenaround in China for centuriesand has spread through the wonders of social media to all corners of the globe.Pore substitute: can AI be trusted when it comes to skincare advice?Read moreGua sha is performed by scraping a smooth stone, coin or similar instrument across lubricated skin in a single direction. Mild bruising might start to appear as a result. Practitioners claim that the resulting petechiae are evidence of “toxins”, and that as they disappear they take these toxins with them. This is said to heal skin,improve blood flow, and evenstrengthen your immune system, according to various people online.From a scientific perspective, this makes very little sense. The mechanism of action here is similar to a massage but with a bit more force. Dr Brad McKay, a GP and science communicator, notes that “gua sha provides the same health benefits as a violent massage”. While the practice does certainly increase blood flow to a specific area of your body – that’s what happens when you get a bruise, after all – there’s no evidence that this has any benefit. McKay notes: “A punch to the nose also increases blood flow.”There’s also no evidence that the petechiae have anything to do with “toxins”. Indeed, they are simply the body’s reaction to any heavy pressure, and can happen when you scrape your skin on virtually any surface. The small dots and bruises will appear regardless of the “toxins” in your body, and should always go away on their own.As far as evidence goes, there’s little research into gua sha.One reviewlooking at gua sha for perimenopausal syndrome found most of the trials on the topic were of fairly low methodological quality and unlikely to be useful as evidence. Avery small 2019 randomised trialfound benefits for gua sha on lower back pain but it was also not especially convincing.Part of the problem here is the same issue that acupuncture faces – it’s impossible to test against a convincing placebo because you can’t really blind people to whether they are receiving gua sha or not. Most of the purported benefits – such as alleviating pain or stiffness – are self-reported, which means it’s difficult to run a good trial on gua sha without polluting your results. When researchers measure hard outcomes that are less likely to be biased by self-reporting, such as hormone levels, there are far fewer benefits to be seen for the practice, and only from the lowest-quality research.Gua sha is one of those practices that I’m sure we’ll keep seeing around. It’s relatively harmless, easy to do and plays well on YouTube and Instagram. It’s quite easy to see why people want to keep making short videos showing lubricated skin being slowly rubbed by a smooth stone, and why that sort of visual tends to attract a lot of views online.The magic touch: how healthy are massages actually?Read moreRealistically, however, I think gua sha is largely a waste of time. It probably has almost identical benefits to a therapeutic massage but with the negative of a bit of extra pain if you overdo it. It’s a bit like the chiropractic v massage question – of the two therapies, both have similar benefits but one comes with additional downsides that make it worse.Personally, I’m not going to buy a smooth stone and vigorously rub myself with it. There are better ways to relax than intentionally bruising yourself with blunt objects. As McKay puts it: “Some people report less pain after undergoing gua sha, but this may simply reflect the compensatory relief felt when the wholloping session is finally over.”Dr Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz is an epidemiologist and science communicator and a senior research fellow at the University of WollongongAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsAsk AntiviralShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: When is an ebike not an ebike? When it has a powerful, illegal engine. Get this menace off our roads | Peter Walker | The Guardian
description: As a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the law, says the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: As a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the law, says the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker
Content: Illegally modified bikes and e-scooters are crushed at an automotive recycling centre in Southampton, England, 2 July 2025.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllegally modified bikes and e-scooters are crushed at an automotive recycling centre in Southampton, England, 2 July 2025.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesOpinionEbikesWhen is an ebike not an ebike? When it has a powerful, illegal engine. Get this menace off our roadsPeter WalkerAs a cyclist I want the authorities to act with clarity. Lime bikes and renters can be annoying, but the true threat is those who dangerously flout the lawTue 15 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.29 EDTShareOne of the curiosities of debates about cycling in the UK is that almost all of them centre on the place with the greatest concentration of not only bikes but also politicians and journalists: innerLondon. Inevitably this is just a small part of the story.Much of the current focus is on so-called share bikes operated by companies such as Lime and Forest – nippy electric-assist machines that can be picked up and left on pavements. On Saturday, a Guardian investigation revealed that councils in the capital have so far this year seized3,393 dangerously parked or abandoned ebikes, a number 23% higher than the total for the whole of last year.Depending on your view, ebikes are either a gamechanging boon to short-distance urban transport or, if we heed the testimonies of those who have been menaced or injured, adangerousand lawless scourge.But even this misses the point. Outside the handful of urban areas where Lime and their competitors operate, the ebikes that exist are privately owned. And many of these are not, at least under the law, ebikes at all.This can sound complex, but bear with me. To be classed as an ebike, a machine must have a powered speed limit of 15.5mph and a motor that only kicks in when you pedal, not via a throttle.Wander around pretty much any UK town or city for long enough and you will see contraptions that very much do not meet these criteria. They might look broadly like a bike, with pedals and a chain. But they are often throttle-powered and can travel much, much faster than 15mph.These are not ebikes. They are illegal electric motorbikes. This is a vital distinction to make before you start discussing ebikes, and whether they are, indeed, a brand new peril on our streets.Now that we know where we are, how much, if at all, of the media scare stories about ebikes or their illegal cousins have a basis in fact? Again, it’s slightly more complex than it might seem.If you hang around central London, it won’t take too long to see someone on a Lime bike sail serenely through a red light, sometimes weaving awkwardly through gaggles of pedestrians.This is, of course, illegal, and for all that some cyclists try to justify such behaviour on self-preservation grounds, I’d also argue that it is selfish and intimidating. People should be able to cross the road at a green pedestrian signal without having to first scan the horizon for a beefy twentysomething called Josh on a Lime bike who is running late for his post-work five-a-side game.View image in fullscreenAbandoned ebikes block the pavement in central London, 29 April 2026.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockBut is there any need to panic? Not really. Cyclists are no different from drivers in that quite a few break the law if they think they can get away with it. One issue for cycling PR is that two-wheeled offences are often just more visible.Government statistics show that when the traffic is flowing freely,fully three-quarters of drivers speed in 20mph zones. This is harder to spot, but the difference is that this sort of behaviour has a realistic chance of killing someone.Very serious or fatal pedestrian casualties with legal bikes and ebikes do happen, but they are vanishingly rare, unlike incidents with motor vehicles. This is not a matter of morals, just physics – more specifically the way kinetic energy increases so rapidly as the inputs of mass and velocity change.Some argue that riders of Lime-type bikes are disproportionately likely to flout the rules, in part because they are paying for the transport by the minute. I’m not sure that’s the case.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEither way, it’s undeniable that, overall, share ebikes – in fact all legal ebikes – are a good thing. They make cycling available to demographics that would not normally consider using a bike, especially people without anywhere safe to store their own machine. Despite the occasional annoyance of the Josh contingent, I welcome them to the bike lanes.Thousands of ebikes seized by London councils as anger rises over blocked pathsRead moreIt is a very different case for the illegal variants. These are often heavier – some are designed to look like motorbikes – and can go at significant speed. It’s not uncommon for me to be overtaken by a silent, moped-weight gizmo doing 30mph or more. I am, it is fair to say, not a fan of this.This is, however, not a cycling problem. It’s a law-enforcement problem. It’s therefore also a political problem, not least whether or not any ministers are willing to crack down on a food-delivery industryheavily reliant on riders using illegal bikes.But the repeated conflation of these two issues has ramifications for cycling. In part it is a call for restrictions on cycling because of offences by those speeding on illegal machines. And because illegal bikes often have vast, poorly made batteries with a tendency to catch fire, some rail companies are pondering bans on all ebikes.The cycling world is changing quickly. And it is perfectly OK to be annoyed with the Lime bike buffoons. But do remember – they’re not the problem here.Peter Walker is the Guardian’s senior political correspondentExplore more on these topicsEbikesOpinionCycle hire schemesCyclingLondonTransportcommentShareReuse this content

title: Polling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no good | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: Surely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graph, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Surely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graph, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: ‘Polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game’.Photograph: Sky NewsView image in fullscreen‘Polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game’.Photograph: Sky NewsOpinionOpinion pollsPolling turns politics into one big game. There are too many of them – and that does us no goodJonathan LiewSurely that’s the lesson the Reform polling furore should teach us. Politics should be about actually helping people, not mastering the line on a graphTue 15 Sep 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.07 EDTShareSolemn faces all round. We will listen. We will learn. We will hone and improve. Yes, it’s time for the latest bout of profound soul-searching in the UK polling industry following the allegations raised by the recent Channel 4 investigation that a polling firmreportedly failed to declarethat three polls it published before the local elections in May were commissioned by Reform. By now these reckonings are becoming a regular occurrence in the wake of big elections: pollsters gather in a room, nibble biscuits, ritually self-flagellate, and pledge to learn all the right lessons from the electorate they’ve just catastrophically misread.Yet for all its very public ignominies, political polling is one of those rare and precious industries that somehow manages to keep failing upwards. You might think that afterbotching the 2015and2017 general elections, the2016 Brexit voteand the 2021 London mayoral poll, we might have learned better than to trust in the mystical magic graph. In this parallel universe Keir Starmer is now sitting on a colossal 318-seat majority, as forecast by Survation in itsfinal MRP pollon the eve of the 2024 general election, overstating the actual result by a mere 144 parliamentary seats.I am, of course, being slightly unfair. Most of the reputable pollsters enjoy just as many hits as misses – and are, by and large, staffed by smart and diligent people who genuinely care about their craft. Doubtless many among their number would object to any suggestion that the apparent misbehaviour of one firm – JL Partners, who were secretly filmed agreeing to carry out a poll favourable to Reform without disclosing who was commissioning it – can somehow be extrapolated to the wider profession as a whole. To which the only reasonable response is: well, let’s see how you like it.And rest assured, I’ve read the Substacks. I’ve signed up to (the free version of) the newsletters. I’ve talked to polling experts. I’ve swished a curious finger up and down the interactive graphics. I’ve sat through interminable briefings in which a very nice man explains why he decided to carve up the voting public into 16 distinct blocs with catchy but absurd names: Flag Shaggers, Jealous Judies, Digital Wombats. And because Westminster is basically like the inside of a very small conch, these terms quickly pass into common parlance. “As you can see,” some wonk on the radio will opine, “the Tories are down eight points among the Angry Trevors, a whopping 13 with Disconsolate Flexitarians. But they are at least holding firm with Be At One Mums.”But my problem has virtually nothing to do with methodology and almost everything to do with volume. There’s simply too much of this stuff, and people are taking it too seriously, investing too much predictive power. The British Polling Council (BPC) has swollen to 39 member organisations, many of them new and completely untested. In the first two weeks of September alone there have been 10 separate voting intention surveys issued by seven separate companies. We are all fatally beholden to the cult of Big Poll.There are plenty of noble and legitimate defences of polls. They help to shape and test policy. They allow voters to make their choice with the fullest possible information. Perhaps they even function as a kind of check on an unfair electoral system, signposting to potential tactical switchers where their vote might profitably be spent. But even these defences highlight a paradox: this is a method of measuring and reflecting public opinion – and of subtly influencing it. Which is why so many lobbyists, PR firms and corporate interests are desperate to get involved.Pollsters are not doing this out of some great altruistic duty to democracy. This is a business like any other, often using techniques borrowed wholesale from the market research and advertising sectors, and preying on a resource-starved, click-hungry media desperate for high-impact, low-cost content. “You aren’t going to pay for polling unless you are confident they can deliver the answer you want,” one public affairs executivetold Politico last week. Or as George Gallup, one of the pioneers of modern-day polling, put it: “If it works for toothpaste, why not for politics?”And so what started out as a small table in the newspaper every month has essentially become a biddable political actor in its own right, and there is a cosy symbiotic relationship between the people who conduct the polls, the people who pay for the polls and the people who publish the polls. This is how Reform can be treated like a government in waiting when they have eight MPs. This is how Starmer ends up as a lame duck within two years of his own landslide. In his 2018 memoir, the former FBI director James Comey admitted that his decision toreopen the investigationinto Hillary Clinton’s emails may have been affected by the fact that she was well ahead of Donald Trump in the polls.Beyond this, polls encourage us all to see politics as a kind of game within a game, a permanent rolling market ticker, in which the aim is not to improve the lives of human beings but to master the line on the graph, where winning elections is the end rather than the means. The BPC, with no fixed office and no full-time staff, was never going to fix this. In reality it is more of a trade body than a regulator, self-run and concerned less with ethics than trust and marketability.And so JL Partners and the industry it belongs to are not the sole culprits here. In reality, the problem is the messenger: the people who consume and regurgitate politics for an audience, seduced by the idea that there is some all-seeing eye, a soup of numbers that will tell us all the answers. As someone whose very job deals in opinion, I know its fragility and malleability, the ridiculousness of treating it like a sacred stone tablet, or – I dunno – basing an entire generation of foreign and economic policy on how 635,000 people felt when they woke up on a Thursday in June 2016.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWest Germany banned the death penalty in 1949 even though 77% of people were in favour of it. By 2000 that had fallen to 23%. Explanation, exemplar, persuasion, principle: these are the real tools of politics, at least a politics that seeks not to chase or triangulate public opinion but to mould and shape it. But if your entire existence is tied to a little line on a graph, then you’re never even going to try.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsOpinion pollsOpinionReform UKNigel FarageKeir StarmercommentShareReuse this content

title: Thank goodness Labour’s ‘shambolic’ plan to reorganise local councils has been paused. What was it thinking? | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: This misconceived Treasury pet project may have been foisted on the government, but it would have added to voters’ mistrust in politics, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: This misconceived Treasury pet project may have been foisted on the government, but it would have added to voters’ mistrust in politics, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Polling station signs outside Canford Cliffs library during local council elections, Poole, 4 May 2023.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolling station signs outside Canford Cliffs library during local council elections, Poole, 4 May 2023.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesOpinionLocal governmentThank goodness Labour’s ‘shambolic’ plan to reorganise local councils has been paused. What was it thinking?Polly ToynbeeThis misconceived Treasury pet project may have been foisted on the government, but it would have added to voters’ mistrust in politicsTue 15 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.34 EDTShareShock reverberated through England’s councils last week. “Beggars belief!” “Shambolic!” council leaders protested to the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), which says:“We’ve never before heard such expletives. They’re apoplectic, incandescent.” And they have every right to be.The government hasslammed the brakeson its unexpected reorganisation of local councils. This almost certainly ends the one-size-fits-all, politically damagingremapping of England’s councils, which was never forewarned in Labour’s manifesto.Councils hired extra staffto manage gigantic mergers and changes on the running of social care, waste collection, libraries, special educational needs, children in care, roads and parks – absolutely everything sliced and diced, with hundreds of thousands moving jobs under new brass plates.Take Worcestershire county council. It just hired a local government reorganisation director on about £120,000 a year whostarted in Augusttoabolish six district councils, dividing the county into two new unitary authorities. But like everywhere else that’spaused, subject to “rapid review”, much of it is dead in the water.Why this emergency stop? Facinglegal challengesfrom objectors over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, the local government secretary, Angela Rayner, received new legal advice that the reorganisation may not comply with law. From the start, I could see no political purpose in her launching this fiendishly complicated restructuring that has now crashed.On the contrary, it would have done Labour and the Liberal Democrats considerable harm. Under the original plan, progressive-voting urban strongholds would vanish as separate entities, absorbed into surrounding county councils with historically more conservative electorates.Rayner is not to blame for this. Neither is Steve Reed, who took over the brief before Burnham reinstated her to it. “Angela did not come into government to reorganise local councils,” her people say indignantly. Her focus and purpose are fixed on housing, as the motor to drive growth. This was forced on her. By whom and why?It’s yet another misconceived Treasury pet project foisted on a new government. Those closest to events have told me that the Treasury threatened to refuse funds for councils or capital for her housing targets unless she agreed to its plan. It took down a dusty2020 PriceWaterhouseCoopers reportfrom its shelves that purported to show that abolishing district councils and creating huge unitary authorities of up to 500,000 citizens throughout England would save money. Not very local.Whose idea was it originally? The then Conservative-dominated County Councils Network, which commissioned the PwC report, promising cost savings if district councils were absorbed into county councils. How much? The small print of thatsix-year-old reportsuggests a mere £2.9bn – over five years. Then factor in the costs in wasted staff time: disruption, endless meetings, recruitment, unpicking contracts and energy not spent on myriad acute problems.Treasury orthodoxy always thinks bigger is better and cheaper. Hampshire, with its district councils, is no better or worse run than, say, Shropshire or Buckinghamshire unitaries, Prof Tony Travers of the London School of Economics tells me. The House of Commons library findsno evidencethat unitary councils save money compared with the current two-tier system.If there is no profit, then look at the loss. Dwindling interest in community activism has led to a decrease in volunteers, members of political parties, trade unions, churches and sports clubs, those who keep society alive. So let’s not lose platoons of district councillors who help hold the social fabric together: these are people who know their communities, and whom residents know they can turn to. Experts at the Localis thinktank believe thatabolishing district councilsmeans “unsustainable workloads on remaining councillors”. There has been a huge reduction in the number of councillors in England over the past 60 years. Last year, Localis warned thatnine in 10councillors in shire areas could be culled by the reorganisation. A 2024 poll showed that in England people were twice as likely totrust local politiciansto improve their areas as they were national politicians. There is clear evidence that councillors shore up people’s confidence in democracy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHere in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter | Steve RotheramRead moreAndy Burnham’s devolution of powers to mayors (or strategic authorities) across every region will move much faster if these council reorganisation plans are permanently shelved. Yes, it means thatsome places will have three layers of government – district, county and mayoral. But surely that is preferable to sweeping away local representation. There are worse things than having more local people getting involved as councillors, helping to run and shape their communities.Even some who think the unitary principle is “a better system”, as Vince Maple, theLabourleader of Medway council, says, also think redrawing borders is “no panacea” for councils devastated, like his, by a “91% cut in the revenue support grant after 2010”. Under these plans, Maple tells me, they were preparing mergers for all the complex ways that next-door councils do things – from professional approaches to social care to contentious rates for councillors’ remuneration and allowances. Unitaries may be better in principle, but he concedes reorganisation may not be worth the upheaval.Who should pay for this fiasco of a plan, and the chaos of its abrupt pause? The Treasury, who imposed it without due legal scrutiny. I trust the National Audit Office will record this classic case of Whitehall’s urge to create new organograms instead of solving practical problems on the ground. The former Tory MP Eric Pickles, who as local government secretary wielded an axe over council funding, had onlyone good thought: “I intend to keep a loaded pearl-handled revolver in my drawer, and the first civil servant who suggests local government reorganisation will be shot.”Apply that thoughtto every department – the NHSis a frequent victim. Learn from theexpletives emitted by the usually quiet battalions of public servants who keep services running, even amid this needless pandemonium.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsLocal governmentOpinionLabourAngela RaynerLocal politicsEnglandcommentShareReuse this content

title: Sweden’s far right is down, but not yet out. Left and centre leaders must seize this opportunity | Cas Mudde | The Guardian
description: The danger is that other parties just channel the far right – and that will make them vulnerable. Better to fully commit to a progressive agenda, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Author: Cas Mudde
Headline: The danger is that other parties just channel the far right – and that will make them vulnerable. Better to fully commit to a progressive agenda, says Cas Mudde, author of The Far Right Today
Content: Sweden’s Social Democratic party leader Magdalena Andersson during her party’s election night celebration in Stockholm, 13 September 2026.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSweden’s Social Democratic party leader Magdalena Andersson during her party’s election night celebration in Stockholm, 13 September 2026.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionSwedenSweden’s far right is down, but not yet out. Left and centre leaders must seize this opportunityCas MuddeThe danger is that other parties just channel the far right – and that will make them vulnerable. Better to fully commit to a progressive agendaTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.31 EDTShareAfter the previous Swedish general election, in 2022, the leaders of the two biggest Swedish parties made a risky decision.Jimmie Åkesson, the leader of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), chose to support the rightwing minority government of the Moderate party prime ministerUlf Kristersson, while Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats’ leader, decided to copy the “Danish model” in an attempt to regain power. In both cases, the strategy led to electoral lossbut political success.After the general election in the country on Sunday, the Social Democrats (often referred to as S or Sap), in common with its Danish counterparts, will probably lead the new government despite an electoral defeat, losing roughly 2%, its worst result since 1908. The party’s return to power is purely a result of Swedish bloc politics and the victories of itslikely coalition partners: the Left party (V), the Green party and the Center party (C), which all increased their supportby 1.5%, 1.7% and 0.4% respectively. Together, this left bloc has a majority of just three seats in the new parliament. So while Andersson will probably return to power, she is also in a very vulnerable position.While the three leftwing parties agree on a lot of socioeconomic issues, particularly undoing some of the worst rightwing policies of the past years and investing more in the public sector, they hold very different views on issues like crime and immigration. Should Andersson continue to demand strict immigration rules and link crime to immigration, this could lead to significant tensions in her coalition, similar to those that her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen, faced in her first government.At the same time the small Center party, the least leftwing of the left bloc, has ruled out a (formal) coalition with the “radical” Left party, and will want to protect the market from too much state intervention. This will create further tensions within the left bloc in a probable minority government. Given that format and the inevitable internal tensions, a majority of just three seats would require almost unrealistic levels of discipline for the minority government to sit out a full term.On the other side of the political spectrum, the Sweden Democrats had their first loss in a national parliamentary election. Still, there is little reason to assume that Åkesson will face a backlash. First, he was the only leader who had any significance to a majority of his party’s electorate. Second, his support strategy worked: the Sweden Democrats is now completely normalised within the right bloc, as the leader of theModerate party(or M), Kristersson, had already announced before the election that the Sweden Democrats would be part of a next rightwing government. Third, the party’s nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.We should also not forget that the 2022 election campaign offered the perfect political context for theSwedenDemocrats, given that it was dominated by two themes: immigration and the acceptance of the Sweden Democrats. As we know from other elections (such as in the Netherlands in 2023), when opposition to immigration and the acceptance of the far right dominate the political agenda, the far right wins big. This time round, those topics were still there, but they did not dominate the campaign – in fact, no single issue did. On top of that, the Sweden Democrats were linked to some scandals close to the election, which might have further decreased support for the party. Still, it held on to 78% of its 2022 electorate, more than the centre-right Moderates (59%) and centre-left Social Democrats (73%).While Andersson may try to convince her party, and herself, that the “Danish model” has worked, she should take a better look at her small neighbour to the west. The Danish Social Democratic party has hit historical lows in national and local elections (notably in the capital, Copenhagen). And although Frederiksen in Denmark is such a convincing nativist that even far-right leaders in other countries hail her as an example, the far right is barely less popular than before – just more divided.Interestingly, while Andersson thanked the youth and student branches for their great work in her election night speech, the Social Democrats scored significantly lower among first-time voters than among the electorate as a whole (21% and 28%, respectively). In contrast, the Left and the Greens did significantly better among the youth. This reflects a development we see acrossEurope, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties. The Social Democrats were the most popular among Swedes with non-European roots, however, gaining no less than 38% of support within this growing part of the electorate. No doubt this group is also not looking for more nativist policies and rhetoric.In short, even if the Social Democrats have regained power because of the “Danish model”, which is in itself debatable, this same strategy will be a risk for the new coalition and for the electoral future of the party. Rather than continuing to be a “moderate” or “sensible” alternative to the Moderates, Andersson should fully commit to a progressive political agenda, both on socioeconomic and socio-cultural policies. That way she not only has a better chance of holding her coalition together, but also might make her party attractive to new and younger voters again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author ofThe Far Right TodayExplore more on these topicsSwedenOpinionThe far rightEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The incoming ‘super’ El Niño will create chaos around the world – and we are far from ready for it | Bill McGuire | The Guardian
description: One of the biggest upheavals in a millennium is on its way, strengthened by the climate crisis. We need leaders who make things better not worse, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Author: Bill McGuire
Headline: One of the biggest upheavals in a millennium is on its way, strengthened by the climate crisis. We need leaders who make things better not worse, says climate professor Bill McGuire
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionEl Niño southern oscillationThe incoming ‘super’ El Niño will create chaos around the world – and we are far from ready for itBill McGuireOne of the biggest upheavals in a millennium is on its way, strengthened by the climate crisis. We need leaders who make things better not worseTue 15 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTShareIf you think you have heard enough about the growing “super” El Niño, trust me, you are going to hear a lot more. What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of thebiggest global weather upheavalsin a millennium. It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world in what remains of this year and in 2027, and there is no reason to think the UK will be immune.To recap briefly, El Niño involves a heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural cycle termed the El Niño southern oscillation, which switches between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases. El Niños that see heating reach or exceed 2C are defined as “super” but this one, which is forecast to top-out at an astonishing4C laterthis year, is so much bigger, the term “hyper” might be more appropriate.El Niño is nothing new. Evidence for its existence extends backhundreds of millions of yearsand its ramifications have always been negative and disruptive. The difference today is that it is happening at a time when our world is heating more rapidly than ever before, and it is being supercharged as a result, leading to increasingly extreme weather.Figuring out how much global heating alone is influencing El Niño is not straightforward, as its strength and other characteristics change naturally over time. Both El Niños and La Niñas, for example, have beensteadily increasing in durationover the last 7,000 years. This is bad news in its own right, as it means the world’s weather is knocked out of kilter for even longer, but added to this,stronger El Niños are becoming more frequentas we continue to add CO2to the atmosphere.There is no straightforward correlation between El Niño’s strength and the magnitude of impacts in any given part of the planet. But given the unprecedented amount of extra heat being added to the atmosphere over the Pacific, it would be reasonable to expect the world to experience exceptionally hazardous weather over the course of the next several months.How, then, is the UK likely to fare? The Met Officehas already warnedof the increased likelihood of a stormy and wet autumn and early winter, so it would be judicious to start preparing now for flooding on a serious – perhaps even epic – scale. After all, the last big El Niño, in 2015–16, resulted in themost extreme UK floods on record. Stronger winds are also a big worry, as many trees weakened by this summer’s extreme drought conditions couldbe brought downin the powerful storms to come. A strong El Niño could also bring Arctic air to the UK later in the winter, although this is far from set in stone. Whether El Niño fosters more record-breaking heat next summer also remains to be seen.But there are likely to be indirect impacts on the UK too, thanks to the devastating effects strong El Niños have on the global economy. While the great recession of 2008 resulted in global GDPreducing by around $2tn, the 1997–98 super-El Niño resulted in losses of $5.7tn. Much of this was due to thesuppression of economic activitythat can last for up to 14 years after a strong El Niño. The late-90s El Niño – the most powerful of the 20th century – peaked at 2.4C; the current one isalready at 2.7C, meaning significant impacts on UK food security, cost of living and general economic wellbeing would not be a surprise.However the UK fares in the coming months, its challenges are likely to be small beercompared with elsewhere on the planet. The effects of the strengthening El Niño are already being keenly felt, particularly across India, which is experiencing its weakest monsoon for 20 years. As El Niño peaks later this year, and slowly subsides, the west coast of South America and the western US can expect torrential rains, severe flooding and mudslides. Meanwhile, heatwaves, drought and wildfires will be the order of the day across the Amazon, south and south-east Asia and much of Australia. One tiny positive is that Atlantic hurricane activity tends to be damped down during El Niño years, but this is more than made up for by the revving up of Pacific typhoons.California, in particular, is bracing itself for the worst, primarily because past super-El Niños have brought some of the wettest periods in the history of the state. This is because El Niño years tend to favour the formation of “atmospheric rivers” – streams of exceptional precipitation that track across the state from the Pacific for days at a time, dumping colossal amounts of rain. Such conditions contributed to the great flood of 1862, which left a vast area of the state under water, including a 480km-long stretch of the Central Valley. The biggest worry is that this unprecedented El Niño will see the realisation of a megastorm worst-case scenarioknown as the ARkStorm. If it does, expect millions of homes and businesses to be flooded, long-term damage to infrastructure, and economic losses totalling almost $1tn. Given, too, that tech companies would be severely impacted, the knock-on effects could result in another hammer blow to the global economy.The effects of the El Niño will be felt well into 2027, almost certainly ensuring that next year is the hottest ever recorded, possibly by some margin. It would not be unexpected for the average global temperature to reach at least 1.6C above preindustrial levels, and quite possibly 1.7C or more.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEvery tonne of CO2added to the atmosphere helps El Niños get stronger, and it would be nice to imagine that the coming monster might prove a wake-up call. But no. Governments continue to row back on green policies and fossil fuel corporations still plan for expansion.As this year’s super-El Niño looms large, the UK governmentadvises us to stock up on foodwhile itprepares to greenlightthe extraction of more fossil fuels from the North Sea. Cognitive dissonance doesn’t even begin to describe the idiocy of such thinking. You couldn’t make it up.Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World: A History and Future of the Climate Crisis (HarperCollins Publishers, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsEl Niño southern oscillationOpinionExtreme weatherClimate crisisUK weathercommentShareReuse this content

title: I know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorship | Carolin Würfel | The Guardian
description: Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too, says writer Carolin Würfel
Author: Carolin Würfel
Headline: Grievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer too, says writer Carolin Würfel
Content: A far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) rally in Magdeburg, Germany, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersView image in fullscreenA far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) rally in Magdeburg, Germany, on 5 September 2026.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersOpinionGermanyI know why many east Germans vote AfD. And no, it’s not an inherited longing for dictatorshipCarolin WürfelGrievance politics has grown in the east of the country where I was born. But west Germans have hard questions to answer tooTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 04.22 EDTShareThe fear that a fascist, far-right movement would rise to power again in Germany has been with me since my youth. On 6 September, thefar-right, anti-immigrant, pro-KremlinAlternative für Deutschland (AfD) won a landslide in Saxony-Anhalt, becoming the biggest party in the state parliament, with a shocking 44% of the vote, on a record turnout. If it finds a way to power it will be the first far-right party to govern a German state since the Nazi era.The night before the vote, I sent a message to a friend, who, like myself, has an East German background. Was she as worried, scared even, about the vote as I was, I asked. I’d fallen into a loop for days, scrolling videos, reels, reports, interviews done on the ground. And I knew these AfD voters. They could have been relatives, friends of my parents, old teachers, former schoolmates. Why were they saying such incoherent stuff?I did not grow up in Saxony-Anhalt, but in Saxony – a sibling eastern German state, not entirely the same but similar in many core aspects. When I went to high school in Leipzig in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the presence of rightwing extremists was part of my coming-of-age experience. Every Friday night, you felt the fear that neo-Nazis would be waiting outside the clubs, the bars, the tram stops, fists clenched or baseball bats in hand. Every 1 May was a flashpoint when neo-Nazis were allowed to march through the city-centre. And still, Saxony’s first prime minister after reunification, Kurt Biedenkopf – a West German Christian Democratic Union(CDU) politician and a close ally of Helmut Kohl – promised, stoically, throughout his 12 years in office: “Saxony is immune to rightwing extremism.”By 2004, a year before I graduated, thefar-right National Democratic party (NPD) had entered the Saxon state parliamentfor the first time, with 9.2% of the vote. In 2005, I left Saxony and moved to Berlin. One reason was the unbearable, dangerous presence of neo-Nazis and rightwing extremists. Many peers did the same, because it was clear that the blooming landscapes that Kohl, the German chancellor in charge of reunification, had confidently promised in 1990 weren’t going to materialise.Instead, rightwing extremism has grown steadilyin easternGermanyever since. Only the names have changed – from NPD, to Pegida (the anti-migrant protest movement launched in 2014), to AfD. I am terrified, if not surprised. Because fascist structures, left unchecked, will always keep going.But this result is also a function of the deeply troubled relationship between the former East and West Germany.A couple of weeks ago, Magnus Brechtken, deputy director of the Institut für Zeitgeschichte in Munich – Germany’s leading institute for contemporary history – gave aninterviewto the FAZ newspaper. It went viral. The headline: “Many west Germans have had enough now.”The interview was framed as a reminder to angry east Germans – meaning, specifically, those tempted to vote AfD out of spite towards the west – of some historical facts. Brechtken argued that the differences east Germans have been complaining about for 36 years are, by now, emotional rather than rational – the product, he suggested, of a lack of honest self-examination. He went further: the German west, he said, has spent the past 75 years proving it understands democracy and knows how to handle extremism, that it is better equipped to counter radical movements and prevent parties like the AfD from rising in the first place – while east Germans, he implied, have always had an inherited longing for authoritarian solutions.You couldn’t help but wonder how much of it was history, and how much was personal opinion. But I do think Brechtken was right about one thing. This supposed east German anger, the AfD’s popularity, the result in Saxony-Anhalt and – in all likelihood – the party’s performance in two upcoming state elections on 20 September should be used as a reminder of some actual historical facts, and of follow-up questions Brechtken apparently decided not to ask.The AfD was founded in west Germany. A large share of its leadership was born and raised in western states such as Rheinland-Pfalz and Nordrhein-Westfalen. The question shouldn’t only be what draws the east of Germany towards the AfD.
