It’s just as much: what draws a certain kind of west German towards building a party like this one, pushing it, and choosing the east as the place to make it grow?I believe the west German states – which officially claimed to have carried out denazification after 1945, and prided themselves on the culture of remembrance, or “coming to terms” with the Nazi past – need to look, just as urgently as the east German states, at why this fascination with fascism keeps recurring. And why, by now, are there no working structures against the rise of right-extremist movements, parties and agendas – but somehow still a system that lets them flourish?View image in fullscreenPeople from East and West Berlin climbing on the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate, Berlin, Germany in 1989.Photograph: imageBROKER/AlamyIt’s also worth asking whether a party like the AfD went east only because east Germans are more susceptible – or because the visible inequalities there are excellent material to organise around.In 1989, a lot of east Germans had hoped for something between socialism and capitalism. Reunification wasn’t necessarily the preferred option. What followed felt, to many, badly mishandled – too fast, laws and decisions imposed rather than negotiated. And then there was theTreuhand– the agency put in charge of privatising the former GDR’s entire state-owned economy. In the process of reunification,94% of East German companieswere taken over by West German or international investors. Six per cent stayed with the people of East Germany. Six per cent. Approximatelytwo million jobswere eliminated in the east.In the autumn and winter of 1990-91, people took to the streets again – not against their own government’s repression this time, but against the perceived occupier: West Germany. They demanded new elections, a renegotiation of the agreements that had left millions empty-handed and jobless,as unemployment in the east skyrocketed.Detlev Karsten Rohwedder, head of the Treuhand and the key figure in overhauling the former East Germany, was asked in an interview back then by a TV host: “If it doesn’t get better, aren’t you afraid there might be another revolution in East Germany?”In those years, the former East Germany was treated like a child that had to follow the laws and orders of its wiser western counterpart – a parent. Now, that child is all grown. But it remembers the experience – and quite possibly holds on to it too tightly. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s man in Saxony-Anhalt, was born the same year as reunification.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund poses for pictures with a supporter as he campaigns in Saxony-Anhalt, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersOne of his main promises is to take back control. Maybe you could say that what happened in Saxony-Anhalt went beyond a question of control and was driven by the desire for a sort of revenge. The east, finally, daring to say to the overpowering west: enough. Or as Siegmund at his first victory press conference said, the result showed that the people of Saxony-Anhalt wouldn’t be “patronised” any longer. With this he was tapping into something almost visceral. The remark also clarified for me something about the motives of the countless potential AfD voters I had listened to over the past weeks and months. Most of them don’t actually read or know what’s in the AfD’s programme. And they don’t seem to care. What won people over was simpler: I hear you. I see you. Yes, you have every right to be unhappy.Throughout the campaign, Siegmund travelled the entire state and threw parties: free sausages, free beer, dancing, music and maybe for some, it felt like the return of community. Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic | Jörg LauRead moreWhat many have not realised yetis that the AfD won’t improve life in east Germany. But that was never the point. It gave people attention in exchange for a vote.And for now, that was what counted most.Because the AfD is bigger than east versus west. It was built by west Germans, carried by east Germans, and now it strives for power across the country. Its programme runs on ideas Germany once needed a war and total defeat to bury: racism, the belief in superiority and a hierarchy of who really belongs, contempt for who doesn’t, a hunger for enemies dressed up as pride. That’s not a regional problem. It’s a national one, and it should frighten every single German citizen.A vote for the AfD is a vote for that same set of beliefs. Whatever anger, disappointment, or legitimate demand to finally be seen or heard got bundled in alongside it.In April 1932, the Nazi party became the strongest party in the state election in the region that now makes up Saxony-Anhalt, with 40.7% of the vote, and formed, with coalition partners, the first Nazi-led state government in Germany. Whatever happens next, it will be hard to say we didn’t know.Carolin Würfel is a writer, screenwriter and journalistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightEuropean UnionEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s summer emergency was a dire warning for Australia. What can be learned before it’s too late? | Nick Rowley | The Guardian
description: Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined
Content: ‘We treat bushfire as a seasonal certainty,’ writes Nick Rowley. ‘It is time we treated heat the same way: by preparing early, coordinating well and protecting people before the next heatwave reaches a street near you.’Photograph: Little Yarra CFA/PR HANDOUTView image in fullscreen‘We treat bushfire as a seasonal certainty,’ writes Nick Rowley. ‘It is time we treated heat the same way: by preparing early, coordinating well and protecting people before the next heatwave reaches a street near you.’Photograph: Little Yarra CFA/PR HANDOUTOpinionExtreme weatherEurope’s summer emergency was a dire warning for Australia. What can be learned before it’s too late?Nick RowleyBetween 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combinedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 14 Sep 2026 21.36 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 03.38 EDTShareBack in April 2004, in the shadow of the previous European summer, I started work at Downing Street advising the British prime minister on climate change. The 2003 heatwave had killed an estimated 70,000 people across Europe. Many were older people, in homes and neighbourhoods ill-equipped for prolonged heat.In May this year, I walked through Bordeaux with my 83-year-old mother-in-law in 38C heat. I saw how quickly heat changes the terms of ordinary life. Streets emptied. Shade became essential. The question was not simply the temperature, but whether people could work, sleep or remain safely at home.That was the European spring. By summer, 42,000 hectares around Gironde and Arcachon surrounding the city had burned. France experienced its worst fires since 1949.Extreme high temperatures double young people’s risk of mental health admissions, Australian research showsRead moreIn June, during the Tour de Suisse, the Italian champion cyclist Elisa Longo Borghini suffered heatstroke. She struggled afterwards to remember the final climb. If extreme heat can overwhelm an elite athlete, we should understand the danger it presents to us all.Europe’s warning is relevant to every Australian city.Extreme heat is not merely uncomfortable weather. Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined. Yet it remains under-recognised because it leaves little visible destruction and its effects are often recorded as heart, kidney or respiratory illness rather than heat itself.And risk is not evenly shared. Older people, particularly those living alone, people with chronic illness, outdoor workers and people in poorly cooled homes are more exposed. As we age, our ability to sense heat, sweat effectively and regulate body temperature can diminish, while thirst can become a less reliable prompt. Staying hydrated must be a habit throughout a hot day, not an afterthought when work is finished.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThis has cultural as well as policy implications. We should challenge the idea that a cold beer is enough to manage the impact of hard physical labour in dangerous heat. Or its quieter twin: the carer skipping her own break to help someone else. Nagging your older relatives and checking on neighbours could save a life.Australians understand seasonal preparation. We do it for bushfires. Governments plan, agencies coordinate, volunteers are mobilised and communities are encouraged to act before danger arrives.We should bring the same mindset to extreme heat.The risk is not confined to bushland at the edge of our cities. It may be a hot top-floor apartment, a home with no shade or breeze, or a worksite. It affects the postcodes of Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth differently, but is now a national test of whether our homes, cities and services are ready for the climate we have.Here in New South Wales, the state government and its agencies have recognised heat as a growing risk and strengthened arrangements for declared heatwaves, including clearer roles and updated warnings.The government can build on these foundations. OurHeat Stress Spotlight Reportidentifies a critical gap. NSW has improved its response once a heatwave is declared, but dangerous heat does not always meet a formal threshold. Isolated very hot days and heat combined with high humidity can be dangerous too. Emergency arrangements must be complemented by a coordinated, annual system of preparation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe believe NSW Health can lead a seasonal heat plan through the hotter months. It could help agencies prepare, ensure warnings are clear and trusted, and direct support to those at greatest risk. Exposure to extreme heat can also be reduced through cooler housing, better shade and tree cover, stronger thermal protections for renters and social and Aboriginal housing tenants, and effective workplace heat plans.BoM forecasts strong El Niño and warns climate change could amplify effects on AustraliaRead moreNSW also needs consistent public data on heat-related illness and deaths. If we cannot see the burden clearly, we cannot judge whether our responses reach those who need it to prevent avoidable harm.Responding to hotter summers is work government cannot do alone.Resilient Sydneyhas helped place heat resilience on the public agenda, including through theGreater Sydney Heat Smart City Plan.Sweltering Citieshas made the everyday reality of heat in homes, streets and suburbs impossible to ignore, especially for people least able to avoid it. Their work deserves recognition. It also shows why state government, councils, health services, employers and community organisations need to work together.Bushfires have flames. Floods leave visible damage. Extreme heat acts silently, accumulating in homes, streets and bodies over days and nights. By the time it becomes visible in emergency departments or mortality figures, the opportunity to prevent much of the harm has passed.We treat bushfire as a seasonal certainty. It is time we treated heat the same way: by preparing early, coordinating well and protecting people before the next heatwave reaches a street near you.Nick Rowley is chair of the NSW Net Zero CommissionExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directors | Movies | The Guardian
description: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Backing comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treason
Content: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham at this year’s Venice film festival where they won the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesMovies‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsBacking comes after Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor were threatened with having their citizenship revoked and accused of treasonCatherine Shoardin London andLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemTue 15 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFilm industry heavyweights across the globe have expressed solidarity with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the Oscar-winning Israeli directors of documentary NAZA, who have been threatened with having their citizenship revoked by Israel’s culture minister, who accused them of “treason against the state”.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym euphemistically used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. It includes interviews with 24 Israeli military or intelligence soldiers and officers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombard Gaza, resulting in the mass killing of Palestinian civilians.The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025.The 80-minute documentarywon the special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record. On Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.View image in fullscreenJonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham and James Wilson in Venice.Photograph: Stefano Rellandini/AFP/Getty Images“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.Representatives for Venice, or the jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal, have not yet commented on these threats, but the artistic director of the Telluride film festival – widely acknowledged as the foremost Oscars launchpad – was swift to voice her outrage.“Documentary film-makers are among the best long-form journalists working and critical to our understanding of the world,” said Julie Huntsinger. “To even threaten their citizenship standing is unacceptable. This should be condemned by any thinking human.”Her words were echoed by the heads of the Locarno film festival, who said they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ right to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal. Artistic and journalistic freedom are the very foundation of what cinema can be: a space for dialogue which engages critically with the world we live in.”They added that they “reaffirm our support for film-makers who ask difficult questions and help us reflect”.NAZA will screen at the San Sebastián film festival next week. In a statement, its festival directors said the film “exposes the systematic genocide of the Palestinian people by the Israeli government” and that they stand “in solidarity” with the film’s makers as well as “the Palestinian people”. The documentary will show at theBologna film festival tonight, before its North American premiere, at the New York film festival, later this month.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead moreTricia Tuttle, director of the Berlin film festival, said: “Artists must be free to critically examine the world. Films can provoke discussion, disagreement and criticism, but in a democratic society, the response to art must be dialogue and scrutiny, not intimidation or punishment by the state. Our team at the Berlinale stands with Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and all artists who exercise these rights.”Abraham and Szor won the documentary Oscar in 2025 for No Other Land, about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, alongside their Palestinian co-directors Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal. That film premiered at Berlin the previous year, where it won a prize. Following this victory, Abraham’s family home wastargetedby a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he told the Guardian last week. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”Earlier this year, Tuttle’s position cameunder threatafterseveral prize winners condemned Israel’s actions against Palestinians from the stageat the closing night awards gala. In the wake of this, the German culture minister, Wolfram Weimer, convened a crisis meeting as the Bild tabloid reported Tuttle was to be fired over giving “hate speech” an airing. In response, hundreds of prominent film-makers worldwide, including fromIsrael, rallied around Tuttle.View image in fullscreenLaura Poitras in Venice last week.Photograph: Alessandra Benedetti/Corbis/Getty ImagesIn Israel, more than 1,500 film-makers havesigneda petition in support of the directors, and refuting the accusation that they have sought to damage the country’s image internationally.Signatories include film-makers Liran Atzmor, one of the petition’s initiators, Nadav Lapid, Orna Ben Dor, Netalie Braun, Rani Blair, Hagai Levi, Shai Carmeli-Pollak and Shlomi Elkabetz.The petition calls on those who support freedom of expression and artistic freedom to stand in solidarity with Abraham and Szor.“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented campaign of vilification and incitement against the film’s creators,” it says, warning that the rhetoric was moving increasingly close to “effectively sanctioning violence” and posed a physical threat to their lives.So far the Academy of Motion Pictures and Sciences has not commented on the situation in which its recent winners find themselves. However, previous recipients of the documentary award have done so.Laura Poitras, who won the documentary Oscar in 2015 for Citizenfour, about the WikiLeaks whistleblower Edward Snowden, defended the film’s factual credentials.“The facts about the mass killing of civilians inNAZAhave been reported by the Guardian in dozens of rigorously fact-checked articles, and every assertion in the film is based on multiple sources,” said Poitras, who acted as a consultant on NAZA.View image in fullscreenNo Other Land co-director Hamdan Ballal with his Oscar in March 2025, shortly after he had been attacked by Israeli settlers at his home, in his village of Susya in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP/Getty ImagesShe called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide. They are also familiar – my reporting with the Guardian on the National Security Authority’s illegal global mass surveillance was met with similar denials and attacks by the US government.“Despite the alarming nature of these current threats, it is important to emphasise that Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists inGazaand has normalised the murder of journalists.”Meanwhile Nan Goldin, the US photographer and activist who worked with Poitras on the 2022 Oscar-nominated documentary All the Beauty and Bloodshed, said she applauded NAZA’s directors “for their enormous courage in presenting a film that shows irrefutable proof of Israel’s war crimes at their own great risk.”British film industry veterans offering their support include directorRichard Eyre, who said he was “beyond shocked by anything that the Israeli government does”, and the novelist and screenwriter Hanif Kureishi, who called the pair “both brave and admirable, standing up to state oppression, steadfast in their pursuit of the truth”.Israeli attacks in Gaza since 2023 have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, and injured more than 174,000 others, together representing more than 10% of Gaza’s prewar population. Israel launched its war after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, when more than 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken to Gaza by militants. The majority of the dead and hostages were civilians.Additional reporting by Andrew Pulver and Philip OltermannExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm industryKen LoachRichard EyreNAZAGazaIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spy | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: She has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: She has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?
Content: ‘I played one match for Wales then thought: I’ve done that’ … Aimee-Ffion Edwards.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I played one match for Wales then thought: I’ve done that’ … Aimee-Ffion Edwards.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTelevision & radioInterview‘I’m fearless. I was in a boys’ rugby team’: Slow Horses’ Aimee-Ffion Edwards on playing a cocaine-snorting spyDonna FergusonShe has played rugby for Wales, is putting a Welsh spin on Princess Leia and is returning to TV screens as Shirley, the explosive, traumatised MI5 agent. Why is Edwards so drawn to liars, crooks and sneaks?Tue 15 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a moment, just before Aimee-Ffion Edwards jumped off a nightclub balcony inSlow Horses, when she had to lie to herself about what she was about to do. “It was quite hard,” says the actor. “You basically tell yourself, ‘You’re not jumping.’ Obviously, you know you’re harnessed in, but you’re also going, ‘This is mad! This is mad! This is mad!’”She laughs. “I couldn’t feel my fingers for a second. I was like, ‘Huwwaah!’” She sucks in her breath, then says: “But there were 200 people stood there watching. You’re like, ‘Well, I gotta do it.’”In the scene that we see, though, Shirley Dander – the tough, traumatised, cocaine-snorting MI5 agent Edwards plays – does not hesitate, leaping from the balcony to land on a suspect. That collision (on a stuntman) was no soft landing either and, at 38, Edwards knew she’d feel it the next day. And yet she jumped off the balcony “five or six times” during filming. “I played rugby in a boys’ team,” she explains, “and I think I have a fearlessness that comes from that. It’s quite instinctive.”double quotation markMy biggest achievement? I was an answer on Pointless!Edwards is wearing an elegant sleeveless blouse, smart navy trousers and gold hoop earrings. She does not, as she sits there sipping a flat white in London’s Soho Hotel, look much like a rugby player. Yet, with some pride, she reveals that her childhood dream was to play rugby forWales, where she was born and raised. “That was all I cared about. And I did! I played one match for Wales. Then I was like, ‘I’ve done that. I think I’m going to do some acting.’”View image in fullscreen‘There’s so much to play’ … with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/Apple TV+Edwards, a fluent Welsh speaker, still lives in Newport. She had a paper round there until she was 19 and grew up the middle child of five. “I have a strong sense of being part of a pack,” she says. The actor regularly commutes to London (“it’s so close – an hour and 35 minutes on a good train”) and finds it refreshing to be able to play a British spy with her authentic Welsh accent, pleased Shirley’s Welshness is not a talking point in the hit show.“Nobody ever mentions it,” she says. “And I think that’s really important. It’s good to normalise it. We hear northern and other accents all the time, but Welsh accents have been underrepresented.” Except, she adds, in comedy roles. “Like there’s a novelty aspect to being Welsh – like it’s some sort of kooky thing. It’s really not.”Before Slow Horses, which follows a ragtag bunch of reject MI5 agents who are presumed to be inept despite usually saving the day, Edwards had to fake a Brummie accent as the opportunistic criminal Esme Shelby inPeaky Blinders, and adopt a southern one as manipulative Elizabeth Barton, the “Holy Maid of Kent” in Wolf Hall.But as Shirley, and especially as Richard Burton’s older sister Cis in the 2025 film Mr Burton, she has increasingly been able to lean into her Welsh identity. And now she is voicing Princess Leia in the first-ever Welsh language-dub of 1977 blockbuster Star Wars. Due to be broadcast in Wales on Christmas Day, its Han Solo will be voiced by Matthew Rhys. So is she a fan? “Oh my God, I was pinching myself. That was so surreal, being in a booth, watching the film and lip-syncing I was going, ‘I don’t know how I got here, but I’m here – and I’mherefor it.’ It was amazing. And it’s brilliant the Welsh language dub is happening. I’d be excited even if I wasn’t in it.”View image in fullscreenLooking for contradictions … as Esme Shelby in Peaky Blinders.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/BBC/Caryn Mandabach Productions Ltd.In season six of Slow Horses, about to launch on Apple TV, Shirley’s anger and grief about the death of her colleague Marcus, played by Kadiff Kirwan, keeps bubbling to the surface. This grief is, to some extent, genuine: “I found it really hard when Marcus died, especially coming in for season five, because it was quite a lonely experience.”She and Kirwan were “partners in crime”, she says. “That unique relationship between Shirley and Marcus – it was purely platonic, but with a lot of love, a lot of frustration, a lot of projecting each other’s nonsense back at each other.” At the same time, his death has helped her to develop Shirley’s character emotionally. “There’s so much to play.”As a strong, dangerous woman whose physical bravery and moral courage is undermined by her emotional cowardice, explosive temper and penchant for violence, Shirley is “liberating” to play. “I love that she’s scrappy,” says Edwards. “There’s so much negative energy in her and she doesn’t know what to do with it. She can’t communicate it properly.”View image in fullscreen‘I love making things with wood’ … if she ever gave up acting, Edwards would get a dog and become a carpenter.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianEdwards – whose first major role was as Sketch, the stalker in teen dramaSkins– looks for contradictions in the women she plays, which may explain why she is so good at humanising liars, criminals and sneaks. “I’m fascinated by people’s strengths,” she says, “and the mechanisms we have to protect ourselves when we feel vulnerable.” Shirley, she says, gives off a “stench” of “Try it – come and get it” when she walks into a room. “But I understand why she is like she is. I keep trying to pick at those threads, to expose them a little bit.”Gary Oldman, who plays the chain-smoking, whisky-drinking, rarely washing boss Jackson Lamb, is the joker of the cast. “He loves making people laugh. He’s always got an anecdote, a tale to tell. He’s very silly and funny – a fun father figure.”In her spare time, Edwards exercises a lot, mainly swimming and running, because team sports are a problem. “The nature of this work means you can’t commit,” she says, adding that she also enjoys making furniture in her garage. If she ever gave up acting and working far from home, she’d like to get a dog and become a carpenter. “I love making things with wood.”Social media doesn’t interest her much. “I’m here for YouTube videos about carpentry, but I don’t know why anyone would ever be interested in what I had for breakfast.” She prefers to keep her personal life private, to protect her family and those she loves. And perhaps as a result, even though strangers often smile at her like they know her, they rarely identify who she is, even in Newport. “They think we went to school together or I work in the corner shop, rather than know me off the telly.”This suits her. No actor, she says, ever regrets someone appreciating their work. “If they do, they should quit.” But she feels lucky she gets to live “a normal life” in her home town, where no one bothers her. “I’ll tell you what my biggest achievement is: so many people messaged me one day, because I was once an answer on Pointless.”The question on the TV quizshow was: name a famous Edwards. “Which is ironic, because nobody knew who I was.” She beams. “What a contradiction.”Slow Horses series six launches on Apple TV tomorrow.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTelevisionSlow HorsesPeaky BlindersDramaTV crime dramaThrillersinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favourites | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print cover
Author: Daniel Dylan Wray
Headline: From a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print cover
Content: Cover stars … clockwise from top left: Cosmopolitan, Frieze, Colors, Bloomberg Businesssweek, S&M Sniper, the Cornhill MagazineView image in fullscreenCover stars … clockwise from top left: Cosmopolitan, Frieze, Colors, Bloomberg Businesssweek, S&M Sniper, the Cornhill MagazineArt and design‘Every magazine cover needs to seduce’: designers pick their favouritesFrom a timeless portrait of Lana Del Rey to an alternative guide to the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, experts unpick what makes an enduring, shocking, or alluring print coverDaniel Dylan WrayTue 15 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘We need to rethink what a successful magazine looks like,” says Steve Watson, founder of the subscription magazine club Stack. “It doesn’t make sense to compare the magazines of today to those of the 1960s when many people still didn’t have colour televisions. Print magazines are no longer the best way of reaching lots of people quickly and cheaply but they are still really great at engaging deeply with readers, providing an opportunity to slow down and absorb information. They provide us with an alternative way of seeing the world.”Watson, along with a group of editors, publishers, designers, historians and academics, will be discussing the varying roles and functions that magazines have played over the years duringa one-day event at the forthcoming London design festival. In contrast to the doom and gloom we often hear about the print industry, he remains upbeat about the humble mag’s future. “The truth is there are brilliant new magazines launching all the time,” he says.And with every new title comes new opportunities for bold, innovative and eye-popping cover design. Here, industry experts – including many taking part in theLondon design festivalevent – pick out their favourite magazine cover designs and tell us why they find them so enduring …Photograph: Wyndham Lewis Memorial TrustBlast, issue 1,1914Scott King, ex-art director for i-D magazine and former creative director for SleazenationBlast was published a month before Britain entered the first world war. It was an anti-petit-bourgeois rant against the professional classes. It features lines such as “Curse abysmal inexcusable middle class” and “The britannic aesthete – cream of the snobbish earth”. It was – for want of a less gratuitous expression, given when it was published – a call to arms. It was punk 60 years before punk was invented. In fact, Blast often reads exactly like a Fall song [the band’s singer Mark E Smith was a huge fan], with the artist and editor Wyndham Lewis piecing together phrases into a collage of barely focused loathing: “Blast the amateur, sciolast, art-pimp, journalist, self man, no-organ man.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Million PublishingS&M Sniper, issue 5, 1984Meara Sharma, senior editor of ElasticThis is a fetish magazine but it does what I think every magazine cover needs to do: seduce. It’s luring a reader in, tickling the senses, giving a flavour of what’s inside, but also tantalising whoever’s passing by. This does a great job of fulfilling that mandate of seduction. The art itself is this incredible photorealistic airbrushed painting by Yosuke Onishi, an amazing Japanese artist who featured in every issue. So the artist gets to play, but you get this lovely consistency and distinct look, and it becomes unmistakably that magazine. It’s so lush, visceral and delicious. The lips are dripping and they feel like they’re bursting out of the page.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Benetton GroupColors,issue 90, 2014Steve Watson, founder of StackmagazinesThis is the last issue of Colors ever published and it was edited by Patrick Waterhouse, who I think is a genius. This was the year of the World Cup in Brazil, so they did a survival guide to football but they took a completely different view. There’s stuff in here about refugee and amputee teams and artists who change the shape of the football pitch to explore what it would do to the game. It’s full of of nice little symmetries and links: it’s issue 90 and a football match is 90 minutes long, and the cover has got this gold foil on it that references football cards. It’s loads of fun, but also really clever.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Retro AdArchives/Hearst/AlamyCosmopolitan debut UK issue, 1972Dr Sharon Maxwell Magnus, media historian and principal lecturer inmasscommunications at the University of HertfordshireCosmopolitan was different from anything that went before it. Other women’s magazines in the UK, at the time, focused on domestic life, family, cooking, recipes, and were very homely. This was for women not bound by marriage and children, and who can, and are, having sex before or outside marriages. The cover is a brilliant partnership between design and words. It’s daring but not so daring that newsagents aren’t going to stock it. It was a revolutionary moment for the magazine industry and it sold 350,000 copies by lunchtime on its first day.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Life Magazine/The Life Picture CollectionLifemagazine: Faces of the American Dead in Vietnam, 1969Jaap Biemans, art director at VolkskrantmagazineThis cover is like a slap in the face. You have the image of a face, just like you see on thousands of covers, but when you read the headline you get goosebumps everywhere. It’s the maximum of emotion with minimal elements. It’s a great execution by cropping the face and, design-wise, it’s the most simple cover you can make but it’s got such an impact. When you look at normal covers about war, you see heroic poses, grieving people, flags, explosions, battlefields. But on this one, you don’t see any of that, but it fires into your mind and heart like an arrow.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Smith, Elder & CoCornhill, December 1865Tony Quinn, magazine historian and founder of MagforumThe people behind this cover were all working at the top of their trade. It was edited by William Makepeace Thackeray and engraved by WJ Linton, while designer Godfrey Sykes was working at the time on the architectural decoration for the V&A Museum. Cornhill was named after a street that had a market where they brought in agricultural products, so Sykes interprets Cornhill via the manufacturing of corn: each roundel shows a stage of making it. Everything about this cover has a story behind it. It also changed the way that names were invented for magazines – within about 40 years there were dozens of magazines named after streets in London, from Pall Mall to the Strand.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: BloombergBloomberg Businessweek, 2 May, 2016Alice Sherwin and Harry Bennett, founders of Studio Ground FloorDesigner Tracy Ma’s run for Bloomberg Businessweek was unbelievable – as her work continues to be. For us, this is a particular standout, because it both embodies her editorial approach to the periodical and taps into something we love in design: everyday visual language. Typographically, systematically and spatially, Tracy draws on familiar visual cues, the design that comes to exist without designer’s involvement, and subverts them. That way, people are drawn in and then shown something surprisingly new. In this case, it’s super self-aware. Kitsch and boring. It’s sublime design and a capsule for the time, helping its audience better understand the issue at hand through creative choices.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: New York MediaNew Yorkmagazine, Lindsay Lohan as Marilyn Monroe, 2008Charlie Baker,editor of the FenceI was 19, living in New York, and remember being struck by this. I think this was the last era when you could do a cover that would be a little bit daring, bold, and put it out into the ecosystem as a way of getting readers to buy it. It was like a last great show of what covers can do. I think it’s good for tasteful erotic things to be in mainstream culture but I don’t think you could do something like that now.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Frieze PublishingFrieze, issue 134, 2010Frith Kerr, art director at Studio FrithI love this. It’s an instinctive, joyful response to something poetic made from the very ordinary: a sock, a foot and a logotype. The image is so concise that the magazine becomes an artwork – an egalitarian one that you can afford.Artshould not only be for the super-rich.The scale is important, as is the sharp yellow of the logotype. The graphic simplicity poses a question. It is a visual idea. Questions are much more potent than answers as they engage and form relationships. Visual communication is all about creating relationships. A good magazine cover, like this, will instantly do that.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Crystal Ball MediaInterviewmagazine, Lana Del Rey, 2023Jeremy Leslie, founder of magCultureThis cover really struck a chord. The photoshoot by Nadia Lee Cohen is timeless, this could have been the 1950s or 70s. It’s a fabulous portrait of a woman that was really of that moment. It sold out and became hugely in demand. I visit universities for talks and there’s a box of magazines I take with me and my copy of that went missing at one. It’s easy to go back and find classic covers from, say, the 1960s but that was a different time. It’s interesting seeing how today a cover can still punch above its weight and deliver something that’s an iconic cultural moment.Reading Magazines: 300 Years of Magazine Evolutionis at London design festival, 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designLondon design festivalDesignArtMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin David | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Her father was Laurie Lee, her mother the Bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape painting
Author: Alice Fisher
Headline: Her father was Laurie Lee, her mother the Bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape painting
Content: Her own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity … Untitled (Green Landscape), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistView image in fullscreenHer own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity … Untitled (Green Landscape), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistArt and design‘She went to her studio every day and no one was allowed near it’: the glorious nature paintings of Yasmin DavidHer father was Laurie Lee, her mother the bohemian Lorna Garman, and the full extent of her talent wasn’t apparent until after her death. A revelatory exhibition places David at the heart of British landscape paintingAlice FisherTue 15 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Clio David was growing up, her mother’s studio was off-limits. The wooden outbuilding where her mother, Yasmin, went to paint was in the apple orchards that surrounded her childhood home in southDevon. It had once been a dormitory for the students of Dartington Hall, a progressive school where Clio’s father taught during the 1960s.View image in fullscreenYasmin with her father, Laurie Lee, West Sussex, 1940.Photograph: Estate of Yasmin David“It was somewhere she went every day to paint and work, and no one was allowed near it,” says Clio. “The walls of our house were covered in her paintings, but the studio was a private place.”Yasmin’s own family had celebrated and nurtured creativity. Her mother, Lorna, was one of theGarman siblings, a free-spirited family whose friendships and love affairs connected everyone fromPeggy GuggenheimtoVita Sackville-West. Lorna married Ernest Wishart, a wealthy communist who co-founded socialist publishing houseLawrence & Wishart, but she was also Lucian Freud’s lover and the subject of a number of his paintings before the painter met and married Lorna’s niece, Kitty. When she was 19, Yasmin discovered that her biological father was writerLaurie Lee. He dedicated his 1944 book of poetry, The Sun My Monument, to her mother and to “Y”. Yasmin found out that her name was chosen because a capital letter Y resembles two conjoined Ls – to symbolise Laurie and Lorna’s relationship.View image in fullscreenUntitled (Waterfall 2), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistBut Yasmin quit London and art school at 23, moving to rural Devon with her husbandJulian David, who became a Jungian analyst. She lived onLuscombe farmfor much of the rest of her life, and the full extent of her painting talent was only discovered after her death. Clio was going through her mother’s possessions, and opened a cupboard to find more than 200 canvases and 550 works on paper neatly stacked inside – luminous, brooding pictures of the area’s moorland, woods and rivers, with the wild landscape lit by spectral sunlight. There was also a wealth of poetry, nature writing and touching letters from Yasmin’s father.A selection of these pieces were shown alongside the paintings in a memorial show at theNew Art Gallery Walsall in 2021. The gallery had been built by Lorna’s sister, Kathleen Garman, to showcase work by her husband, sculptor Jacob Epstein.Untitled (Luscombe 1962), by Yasmin David.Photograph: Courtesy of the ArtistThis month, Yasmin’s work is in a new solo show that focuses on her contribution to British landscape painting. The Nature of Light, featuring more than 40 works on canvas alongside drawings, sketches, notebooks and photographs, is at theThelma Hulbert Gallery in Honiton, about 40 miles from Yasmin’s home in Luscombe.Curator Gemma Girvan says: “Presenting Yasmin’s works here brings them full circle, reconnecting them to the place which inspired them. Yasmin lived and worked on the edge of Dartmoor and many of the landscapes she painted will be instantly recognisable to our local audiences. We hope this exhibition will encourage wider debate about the many talented female artists whose work remains under-recognised including our gallery’s namesake,Thelma Hulbert.”Art historian Sophie Hatchwell, who is giving a talk on Yasmin’s work during the run of the show, says that it “sits in comparison with that ofJoan Eardley,Barbara DelaneyandGillian Ayres. It offers a way into thinking about the British landscape outside the traditional patriarchal framework as a territory to be conquered.”The British art world, confronting its long history of institutional bias and sexism, is now reconsidering the importance of female art inspired by nature. The Courtauld gallery in London ran the exhibitionA View of One’s Own: Landscapes by British Women Artiststhis spring, and artists as disparate as Cuban sculptorAna Mendietaand British printmakerAngie Lewinhave major shows either on or scheduled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPortrait of Yasmin David in 1972.Photograph: Estate of Yasmin DavidClio David, a documentary film-maker based in London, is now sharing her mother’s work with academics at the Courtauld Institute to ensure Yasmin’s contribution to the landscape genre is recognised. “She was one of the few women working in landscape during the latter part of the 20th century, and I want to place her archive within that period of art history.”Yasmin’s art is unique, but her background undeniably is, too. And raising the profile of her work would also change the picture of a family where typically women supported the men in their creative endeavours. Clio is all too aware of this: “I want to show her work as her family history is largely dominated by male artists and writers –Laurie Lee, Lucian Freud, Jacob Epstein, Roy Campbell, Michael Wishart. She was a female artist from a very well-connected family, but working outside the art establishment on a farm in the middle of the countryside, about as far from the Colony Rooms as you could get. I want her work as an artist to be recognised and celebrated.”Yasmin David: The Nature of Light is atThelma Hulbert Gallery, Honiton, until 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsArt and designPaintingPoetryLaurie LeeArtDevonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No one could stand in the way of this juggernaut! The biggest shocks from the Emmy awards | Television | The Guardian
description: There were plenty of upsets, and one show in particular failed terribly. But the night was rightfully dominated by Matthew Rhys and the genuinely scary, genuinely hilarious Widow’s Bay
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: There were plenty of upsets, and one show in particular failed terribly. But the night was rightfully dominated by Matthew Rhys and the genuinely scary, genuinely hilarious Widow’s Bay
Content: His face in one scene alone was a worthy winner … Widows Bay.Photograph: AppleView image in fullscreenHis face in one scene alone was a worthy winner … Widows Bay.Photograph: AppleTelevisionNo one could stand in the way of this juggernaut! The biggest shocks from the Emmy awardsThere were plenty of upsets, and one show in particular failed terribly. But the night was rightfully dominated by Matthew Rhys and the genuinely scary, genuinely hilarious Widow’s BayStuart HeritageTue 15 Sep 2026 04.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo tell the story of how Hacks performed at last night’s Emmys, you have to acknowledge both its incredible success and its terrible failure. The first is undeniable. Last night, Jean Smart won lead actress in a comedy series yet again. This meant that every time Hacks brought out a new season, Smart won the same award for it. This makes her the first woman to ever win an Emmy for every season of a programme’s run. It’s a history-making achievement, and thoroughly well earned.The flipside of that, however, is that this is all Hacks won last night. One Emmy is better than many shows can even hope to dream of, but the reality is that Hacks swaggered into the Emmys with a record 24 nominations – the most ever for a comedy in a single year – and had the momentum of a huge farewell narrative behind it. But it only ended up winning one for Jean Smart and a Creative Arts Emmy for picture editing. In other words, last night Hacks lost 22 Emmys.View image in fullscreenA historic achievement … Jean Smart in Hacks.Photograph: SkyThis isn’t a complete surprise. My long-held theory about Hacks is that while lots of people enjoyed it, it was always a bit of a protest vote. The show’s big year – 2024, when it finally won outstanding comedy series – came when the industry was tying itself in knots trying to decide whether The Bear should qualify as a comedy or not. Hacks was the biggest immediately identifiable comedy in a weak field at the time, so that’s where the votes went. In other words, it primarily won because nobody wanted The Bear to win.Emmys 2026: Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic winsRead moreSince then, shows that are easier to love came along. Seth Rogen’sThe Studio– same subject matter but more pointed, more technically ambitious and funnier – swept the board last year, and this time around it was the turn ofWidow’s Bay. Did Hacks deserve better? Perhaps. In its final season, Hannah Einbinder was allowed to play more notes than she did in the year that she won. Either way, all involved have to be fairly disappointed this morning.Then again, who’d stand in the way of a juggernaut like Widow’s Bay? A genuinely funny, genuinely scary comedy-horror, Widow’s Bay won a grand total of 14 Emmys this year. There are seven comedy awards presented during the televised ceremony, and Widow’s Bay won six of them; outstanding comedy series, lead actor in a comedy, supporting actor in a comedy, supporting actress in a comedy, writing for a comedy and directing for a comedy. Obviously Jean Smart won the seventh for Hacks, but it’s worth pointing out that Widow’s Bay didn’t field a nominee in that category.Emmys 2026: the full list of winnersRead moreNone of this will come as a surprise if you’ve actually seen the show. However, one surprise might come in the form of Matthew Rhys. His win for Widow’s Bay was never in question – in one episode he pulled a face of surprise that probably could have won an Emmy by itself – but the interesting thing is that he also won lead actor in a limited or anthology series or movie forThe Beast in Me.That was a much harder fought category, and the frontrunner was always thought to be Oscar Isaac for the second season of Beef. One working theory here is that his work on Widow’s Bay was so extraordinary that the affection for him spilled over into an entirely different show. Either way, Rhys has now become the first actor to win lead actor Emmys in comedy, drama and limited series.View image in fullscreenCertainly came as a shock … Allison Janney in The Diplomat.Photograph: Clifton Prescod/NetflixElsewhere there were plenty of smaller upsets. Allison Janney winning best supporting actress in a drama forThe Diplomatcertainly came as a shock, especially since The Pitt’s Katherine LaNasa had such a powerhouse year. Same for Sally Field, who won an award for Remarkably Bright Creatures ahead of Carey Mulligan, who was tremendous in Beef. Stephen Root’s win for Widow’s Bay meant that Harrison Ford remains Emmyless, which is extraordinary given both Ford’s age and the Emmy predilection for handing awards to the most famous people who turn up on the night.View image in fullscreenShould have won years ago … Rhea Seehorn in Pluribus.Photograph: Apple TV+But let’s end with one happy surprise.Rhea Seehorn, a woman who for years has been the textbook Emmy snubee, finally won something forPluribus. Should she have won in previous years for her work on Better Call Saul? Yes, several times over. But her work on Pluribus was undeniable; scared and angry and for much of the season the only identifiable human on screen. It was a truly well deserved win, and let’s hope it is repeated when Pluribus comes back, even if the speed at which Vince Gilligan works means we might all be too old to appreciate it by then.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionEmmys 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: Benedict Cumberbatch on his Earth-saving eco film: ‘We are in the last grab of the extraction era’ | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: From Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venison
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: From Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venison
Content: ‘Nature can be monetised to be protected’ … Cumberbatch in How to Live on Earth.Photograph: Conor McDonnellView image in fullscreen‘Nature can be monetised to be protected’ … Cumberbatch in How to Live on Earth.Photograph: Conor McDonnellDocumentary filmsInterviewBenedict Cumberbatch on his Earth-saving eco film: ‘We are in the last grab of the extraction era’Helena HortonFrom Obama’s chef to a big cat obsessive, the actor has gathered experts from all over the world for a film about how to heal our besieged planet. He talks about naysayers, elephant tusks – and the wonders of venisonTue 15 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenedict Cumberbatch is dreading stepping outside. He’s speaking to me from his air-conditioned hotel room in Soho at the peak of the summer heat. Few doubt that climate breakdown was a major cause of those scorchers, with nature, farming and water supplies all placed under huge strain. By midsummer,according to a report co-authored by the Met Office, there were 2,700 excess deaths in England and Wales due to the searing heat.But for Cumberbatch, in a bittersweet way, the record-breaking temperatures have come at a good time. The actor has been on a tour to promote his new documentary, How to Live on Earth. “The irony is not lost on anyone,” he says. “We’re living in the results of climate breakdown so stepping outside is – literally – a call to action.”double quotation mark‘I walk my dog on the heath. I cycle, use public transport – and I’m a wild-water nut’His film launches on YouTube this month and the actor hopes it is a “blueprint” for how we interact with our besieged planet in the future. It features Cumberbatch delivering monologues from the cavernous halls of the Natural History Museum in London, in between short films showing how activists, scientists and even chefs are learning a “new way to live on Earth” – one that could stop humanity damaging it.Cumberbatch has spent the last two decades trying to reframe his relationship with the planet: he’s tried to live more gently on Earth and became vegan. However, this was a problem during the shooting of The Courier, in which he plays captured British spy Greville Wynne, who languishes in a Russian jail. “They said, ‘You can’t have any fibre in the last two weeks. You need to eat lean meat.’ And I was like, ‘I’m vegan!’”View image in fullscreen‘You should think about eating a little bit of meat now’ … Cumberbatch in The Courier.Photograph: Liam Daniel/APNo fibre for two weeks must have been tough on the bowels? “Yes, it was, but it was much less than what the character I was portraying went through, because it was a true story.” Although he went straight back on the vegetables, the extreme diet caused his blood sugar to plummet and he became unwell. “People were saying, ‘You should think about eating a little bit of meat now, because your body doesn’t really work under these conditions – you’ve lost so much weight.’”Now, Cumberbatch tries to source the meat he does eat ethically, opting for venison, which in the UK needs to be culled as the country has an overpopulation of deer. But his experience on The Courier is just one way that working in films can challenge even the most committed eco-campaigner. Cumberbatch works with theGreen Ridermovement, which asks actors to make cutting pollution and emissions during filming a condition of taking part.“What we’re trying to push towards is where it becomes contractual,” he says. “We’re working with Disney at the moment – their Avengers project in the UK. So yeah, it’s scaling up – and everyone I speak to about it in my community is on board.”So, he’s ditched veganism, but would he get a private jet? “No,” he says, but adds the caveat: “We just waste our energy if we’re naysaying and calling people hypocrites. The fashion industry is a bigger polluter than aviation, and the food industry massively. That’s all of us, that’s everyone.” Not just movie stars.View image in fullscreen‘A lot of the work we do just isn’t widely seen’ … snow leopard expert Dan O’Neill in the rainforest.Photograph: Open Planet StudiosThe 50-year-old has long been an environmental campaigner. He visited the Extinction Rebellion protests in 2019 and has been dismayed by the recent government crackdowns on climate protests, with long sentences given to people who have blocked roads and smashed windows for the cause. “We should have the right in a democracy to peaceful action, even if it is direct action,” he says.Cumberbatch is keen to highlight the film’s positive message and, unlike most environmental documentaries, it does (almost) have a happy ending. It follows some remarkable people, from Indigenous activists trying to protect salmon from a dam, to Barack Obama’s former White House chef who is experimenting with alternative proteins. The message is that there are alternatives out there, and that nature can heal if humans stop hurting it.One of the film’s most striking characters is Dan O’Neill, a biologist who studies big cats and spends weeks at a time in the depths of rainforests to study the creatures who live there. He’s hopelessly in love with nature and that comes across in the film. “I always work in remote places,” he says. “A lot of the work we do just isn’t seen by wide audiences. People in Mongolia often have never seen a snow leopard, for example. I am so proud How to Live on Earth is going on YouTube – as people who live in these remote places can see it. It democratises our message for the entire world. Indigenous communities will see themselves represented.”In one scene, O’Neill is being whisked away from the rainforest in a car, and he turns on his phone to finally receive messages from friends and family after a long stretch without signal. But his dopamine hit turns to frustration as he is barraged with notifications and he ends up missing the seclusion of the forest. “That happens every time,” he laughs. “It is so weird that we are addicted to this little device. The ability to communicate with my family even from remote parts of the world is powerful. But the second you get your phone, you realise you don’t want it.”Many of us have a similar love-hate relationship with our phones and Cumberbatch is no exception. “For about half a year,” he says, “I haven’t brought myself to look at the tally of unanswered WhatsApps and emails. It’s just thousands. I can’t deal with it.” He talks disparagingly of “swiping left, clickbait, all the rest of it”.View image in fullscreen‘We’re making cutting emissions a condition of taking part in a film’ … in Avengers: Infinity War.Photograph: Chuck Zlotnick/APJonnie Hughes, the film’s joint producer, says many of its participants work in far-flung corners of the globe. “Some people,” he says, “just cast themselves because they’re incredible individuals who have done something amazing and they can get across all the emotion and the excitement we should all be feeling, because it’s too easy to feel gloomy when we see what’s going on.”Cumberbatch and company discuss some blue-sky thinking in the documentary, which to the jaded viewer could seem unrealistic. The conclusion is that the trees in rainforests should be viewed as more valuable than the gold underneath them – which may be true in some moral sense, but is it going to happen in today’s economic system?double quotation markWe don’t want to foster extraction – nor all the other nasty things of populism and nationalism“Nature that’s alive is actually far more valuable to us than dead nature,” Cumberbatch says. “So an elephant’s tusk is not worth as much as the elephant alive, in terms of what it brings to the savannah, to make the savannah work as an ecosystem. It’s how you create a new financial model whereby people can invest as shareholders in nature and that nature – which has done all this work for us for free – can actually be monetised to be protected, actually get paid.”His view is refreshingly optimistic and he says he truly believes humans can save the planet: “Hopefully, what we’re seeing now in this last grab for the extractive industries is that we actually don’t want to foster that, nor all the other nasty things of populism and nationalism.”How to Live on Earth review – Benedict Cumberbatch exudes positivity in response to the climate crisisRead moreAlthough the documentary takes us to remote places, such as the Amazon, it also instructs the viewer to seek out nature at home and nurture it in cities. Where he lives, in Hampstead, London, Cumberbatch is in touch with nature almost daily, primarily through swimming in the ponds on the heath. “I am a bit of a wild-water nut,” he declares. “I also walk on the heath. I have a dog and I cycle and take public transport when I go into town.”O’Neill is doing the same thing when he’s home, across town in Walthamstow. Although there aren’t any snow leopards, he’s managed to find nature: “We have Walthamstow wetlands, which are one of the most important in Europe. I have learned so much. I make sure I spend so much more time in nature in London now.”Cumberbatch hopes to incorporate the message of the film into his daily life. “As a child, you have that sense of wonderment, which we do sadly lose. There’s a lot to knock it throughout our evolution as humans. So hold on to that – and realise how precious it all is.”How to Live on Earth is on YouTube from 20 SeptemberThis article was amended on 15 September 2026. An earlier version described Jonnie Hughes as the film’s director. He is in fact a producer. Also, a reference to filming in Alaska was made in error.Explore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsBenedict CumberbatchNature documentariesClimate crisisConservationEnvironmental activismEthical and green livinginterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The cauldron was already bubbling …’ Green Lung, Druidess and the return of folk horror to British heavy metal | Metal | The Guardian
description: Playing a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of way
Author: Michael Hann
Headline: Playing a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of way
Content: ‘Metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades’ … Green Lung, with Tom Templar centre.Photograph: Andy FordView image in fullscreen‘Metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades’ … Green Lung, with Tom Templar centre.Photograph: Andy FordMetal‘The cauldron was already bubbling …’ Green Lung, Druidess and the return of folk horror to British heavy metalPlaying a sound rooted in 80s bands such as Witchfinder General and Pagan Altar, metal bands are once again gravitating towards dark folklore – but in a ‘Glastonbury crystal shop’ kind of wayMichael HannTue 15 Sep 2026 06.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBehind Tom Templar’s shoulder as we talk over video call is a poster forThe Wicker Man, the 1973 cult folk-horror film set on a remote Scottish island, whose sunniness conceals – inevitably – a dark secret. It’s fitting, because Templar is the singer of Green Lung, the breakout British metal band who immerse themselves in British mythology. The forthcoming Necropolitan, their fourth album devoted to the folklore of the isles, takes its inspiration from the “Magnificent Seven” London cemeteries built in the 1830s and 40s, and from the Necropolis railway, which transported the dead out of the city. No generic demons here: this is metal in the spirit of Fairport Convention as much as Black Sabbath.“My big thesis is that heavy metal has become a form of folk music in the past couple of decades,” says Templar. “They’re both riff-based, circling around similar tropes, and about reinventing what has gone before.Metaleven feels like a folk movement, in the way it’s full of festivals no one else has heard of. There’s such a thriving ecosystem.” Green Lung have certainly been nourished by it: at this year’s Desertfest in London, their T-shirts felt like an unofficial uniform.UK black metal has experienced this folkloric crossover, with bands such as Old Corpse Road, Winterfylleth and Wodensthrone, and Shonagh Brown, singer of Newcastle folk-horror-metallers Druidess, has also noticed the evolution. “Metal had quite a Hammer horror focus, and that’s great when times are good,” she says. “When people are comfortable they seek escapism in the less comfortable. But people spend so much time in front of screens and want to shift towards the natural world, and the folk traditions connect with that.”View image in fullscreen‘People want to shift towards the natural world’ … Druidess.Photograph: Idene RoozbayaniGreen Lung and Druidess don’t just write about the past; they sound like it. There’s plenty of Black Sabbath in both, but lots moreDeep Purple, especially in the prevalence of organ. It is more hard rock than metal: words are sung to be heard, melody matters. It’s music that reveres its history, both cult and occult. That big, rich sound, Brown, says fits their sense of past. “This kind of music is from an analog time.”Though its sound is rooted in the 70s, the two bands that planted the seed of this microgenre were active in the early 80s, though it would take years for either to be recognised. Hailing from Stourbridge, Witchfinder General released two albums that were best known at the time for their cover images, one of them showing a Page 3 model being “murdered” in a churchyard. Only later were they credited as the birth of UK doom metal. Their folk-horror claim lies largely in a song sharing the band name, one inspired by the 1968 horror film starring Vincent Price, extremely loosely based on the life of Matthew Hopkins in the English civil war. “I’m coming to get you / I’m coming to take you away!” howled singer Zeeb Parkes. “You witches are evil, you worship the devil / So listen to what I say!”They were trying to sound like Sabbath in a world that wanted velocity, guitarist Phil Cope told me in 2020: “Witchfinder tried to keep the music slow and heavy. But it didn’t really work because the majority of people were moving with the times and they liked that fast music, and we got left behind.”The other original totems, south London’s Pagan Altar, are more obscure – even in their own time. All that existed was one self-released set of demos, which was gradually reissued in various forms, though a whole catalogue of songs written during the band’s initial existence were later recorded for the Mythical & Magical album. Dance of the Druids, had it been released first time around, might have spoiled one of Spın̈al Tap’s most famous songs: “This ritual of the druids has been the saviour of mankind / Unknown to them the price was paid by personal sacrifice.”But in the absence of much music to hear, word spread of their legend: that they had built their studio on a site where witches were burned in Brockley in south London; occasional hauntings, including one by a woman in black who disappeared through the floor; and that they allegedly recreated satanic rituals onstage. “Being a strange and uncovered relic heightened their appeal, because it felt like you were discovering something arcane,” says Nick Ruskell of metal bible Kerrang! (who also moonlights as Necroskull, singer/guitarist of folk-horror-adjacent doom band Witchsorrow).It may be those legends that have made Pagan Altar guitarist Alan Jones reluctant to talk, citing bad experiences with the press, until he agreed to answer questions via email.Their interest in the occult came from their singer, Alan’s dad Terry. “I’d been playing in bands with my dad since I was 11, in 1973,” he writes. “All through the 1970s there was a lot of interest in the occult and folk, and my dad’s lyrics reflected the time.”Interestingly, as well as metal bands, Jones cites folk acts Steeleye Span, Renaissance and Pentangle, all of whom summoned English mythology. And it ties with something Fenriz of legendary Norwegian black metal band Darkthrone told me in 2021 about the rise of occultism in early 80s metal: “One had it from the 60s; the cauldron was already bubbling with Coven, Black Widow, Black Sabbath. Combine that with a lot of folk-rock that didn’t exactly feel Christian but pagan as hell – yes, I get an anti-Christian vibe from Steeleye Span. There, I’ve said it – and top it off with some Vincent Price movies.” It’s your one-pot recipe.But that raises the question: given the status of, say, Fairport Convention’s Liege & Lief, and its thematic relation to this stuff, why don’t we get more metal covers of folk music?“It’s funny you mention Liege & Lief,” says Green Lung’s Templar. “My girlfriend’s dad just gave me that record: ‘You’ll like this!’” Templar’s connection to the English past came not from those records, as it had for musicians 30 or more years older. “I grew up in rural Norfolk. There was very little to do in a hamlet of 400 people, and that was good for the imagination. I’d go round secondhand bookshops, looking for books about ufology or folkloric myths and legends. The horror came in at 16, when I started watching Evil Dead and Dawn of the Dead.”He also credits Julian Cope for spurring interest in the ancient. “He was someone who made me think this stuff was cool as a kid growing up in Norfolk, where you live without a musical context – we didn’t have a Sheffield or a Manchester nearby.”Why does he think British bands, and English bands in particular, have not embraced folklore fully, given its role in European metal? Well, he says, there’s the fact that some Nazi bands in Europe have co-opted folklore (Green Lung sell anti-Nazi merch), though he, Ruskell and Brown, all make it plain that they’ve seen no sign of that in the UK. “I don’t see an interest in British folk history as having been colonised by Nazis,” Templar says. “If anything, it’s associated with new-agey, travelling people. Of course, you don’t want to be associated with a Reform vision of Britain, but this is more Glastonbury crystal shop.”There’s also an innately British reason for resisting folklore. “Folk culture in the UK has often been depicted in a very twee way, and there are always going to be moments where it will be cheesy. But you can’t get to the good stuff if you don’t have a bit of bravery around that.”Necropolitan by Green Lung is released via Nuclear Blast on 11 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsMetalPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Debut review – Julianne Moore is a thrill in Jesse Eisenberg’s oddball comedy | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musical
Author: Richard Lawson
Headline: Riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musical
Content: Julianne Moore in a scene from The Debut.Photograph: Matt Infante/A24/APView image in fullscreenJulianne Moore in a scene from The Debut.Photograph: Matt Infante/A24/APFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewThe Debut review – Julianne Moore is a thrill in Jesse Eisenberg’s oddball comedyToronto film festival:riotous lead performance holds together third movie from actor turned film-maker, about a housewife who joins a local musicalRichard Lawsonin TorontoTue 15 Sep 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJesse Eisenberg’s last two directorial efforts – the prickly comedyWhen You Finish Saving the Worldand the slightly softerA Real Pain– are small films rooted in the real world. They have their little idiosyncrasies, their bits of cinematic flair, but they keep their feet grounded in the here and now. For his third film, Eisenberg has said goodbye to all that (or most of that) and run headlong at the surreal and the absurd, borrowing from Charlie Kaufman and other oddballs to tell a small story in a big way.Elsinore review – Andrew Scott is astonishing as Ian Charleson in devastating Aids dramaRead moreThe Debut is about a repressed housewife, Mona (Julianne Moore), who decides to audition for a role in a community theater production of a musical called Nosy Neighbors, one of those gassy Manhattan trifles that were so ubiquitous on Broadway a half century ago. Mona’s kids are about to fly the nest, and her husband barely seems to notice her when she’s standing right next to him. So why not have a little creative adventure?From that setup, Eisenberg could have gone to the obvious place, staging a sweet dramedy about a humble act of artistic expression opening Mona’s eyes to all the possibility of life outside her little bubble. He does do that, in part, but he also wants to take things to a darker place. The film gradually morphs into a study of actorly obsession and vanity, as Mona takes the Stanislavksi-esque teachings of the play’s director, Jerry (Paul Giamatti, doing his wearily charming thing), to extremes perhaps not seen since Black Swan. That’s a clever idea: a director watching in horror as the monster he’s created threatens to lay waste to his production.The trouble is, none of this, not the nice story of blossoming passion, nor the acidic satire of pretentious artistes, unfolds in an environment that looks and feels anything like the dimension all of us are currently living in. Eisenberg has unrooted the film in time – there is lots of 1980s decor, but some more modern clothing; we see nary a cellphone, but there is no other specific period detail – and has his characters behave in archly cartoonish fashion.A movie needn’t be situated in plain reality, of course. But Eisenberg is inconsistent in his quirky abstraction. The Debut toggles too frequently between recognizable humanity and the mores and attitudes of whatever other-place Eisenberg has invented. Which undercuts both the parody and the pathos; without a reliable reference point, it’s hard to know what, exactly, we are meant to think and feel about anything happening on screen. Or, rather, it’s hard to connect to the sentiment that, I’m surmising, Eisenberg is trying to get across: a wry and bleary appreciation for the thrill and risk and silliness and beauty of making art.Still, it is fascinating to watch Eisenberg expand his purview like this, taking a swing at the grand and busy techniques of marquee film-makers like Kaufman, like Ari Aster, like Alejandro González Iñárritu. He shows an aptitude for ornate visuals, his camera ceaselessly moving as we are whisked around the theater and down the grimier avenues of Mona’s curious journey outside of herself. Eisenberg sets a quick pace early on and manages to sustain that energy for the duration. By the end of the picture, we really do feel that we’ve traveled somewhere, that all of the film’s relentless motion and noise has given us some kind of full-bodied experience.But I suspect none of that would be possible without the invaluable presence of Julianne Moore, enjoying one of the most substantial, dynamic film roles she’s had in a long time. She attacks each scene with the breakneck vigor that first endeared her to audiences, in 1990s films like Boogie Nights and Magnolia. And she’s often a riot, knowing just how to make Mona’s mounting melodrama and histrionics funny without tipping it all into hammy slapstick. It’s a thrilling performance, even when Eisenberg seems to have lost his hold on the reins. Maybe there’s a kind of accidental tribute in that, a director finding the right leading lady to hold things together until the production rights itself.Oh, and Moore can sing! Which I guess we sort of knew from her turn in the grisly film adaptation of Dear Evan Hansen. She fares far better here. The music in The Debut will be one of its nerdy selling points, for theater geeks eager to kick the tires of this made-up musical and assess whether it’s credible as a show that could have once existed. Eisenberg wrote the songs himself, and I think they mostly pass the test. Though, what does it ultimately matter, when the film takes place nowhere and at no time in particular? Nothing needs to add up, really, because the film is forever inventing its own rules.That does get frustrating as The Debut unfolds; true investment proves difficult when what we’re watching could arbitrarily change shape at any moment. But at least there is Moore to rely on, whipping up a floridly tragicomic storm. She once again reminds us of her boggling range and tenacity, reaching for things that many other actors might timidly think well beyond their grasp. It’s become a trite word to use about acting, but Moore’s work in the film is at times downright fearless. She careens toward embarrassment, courts the wreckage of a bold choice flopping, and somehow comes up shining. Not every actor can do that – but, as any wannabe thespian with a dream can tell you, man is it fun to try.The Debut is screening at theToronto film festivaland will be released in US cinemas on 11 December, in Australia on 25 December and in the UK on 15 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalJulianne MooreJesse EisenbergComedy filmsPaul GiamattiComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: New Order keyboardist Gillian Gilbert announces she is ‘living with cancer’ | New Order | The Guardian
description: Musician clarified her own health status after concerns were raised by interview with husband and bandmate Stephen Morris earlier this month
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
