Headline: Musician clarified her own health status after concerns were raised by interview with husband and bandmate Stephen Morris earlier this month
Content: Gillian Gilbert performing in 2023.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsView image in fullscreenGillian Gilbert performing in 2023.Photograph: Lorne Thomson/RedfernsNew OrderNew Order keyboardist Gillian Gilbert announces she is ‘living with cancer’Musician clarified her own health status after concerns were raised by interview with husband and bandmate Stephen Morris earlier this monthBen Beaumont-ThomasTue 15 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGillian Gilbert, keyboardist withNew Order, has announced she is again having treatment for cancer.The 65-year-old musician announced the news on Instagram, as a response to an interview her husband and New Order bandmate, drummer Stephen Morris, gave to Rolling Stone earlier this month. Morris had said: “I’ve got a bit of a health problem at the minute, which precludes leaving the country for any length of time … it’s pretty serious.”Gilbert wrote: “I would like to gently clarify a misunderstanding from the interview, in the course of which comments were misinterpreted leading people to believe that Stephen is seriously ill. Thankfully, he is well. It is in fact me, who like many other people, is living with cancer. We completely understand how the misunderstanding arose and simply wanted to ensure that the correct information was shared.”She thanked everyone who had shared “kind words and well wishes”, and said she would “appreciate some privacy as I continue with my treatment”.Gilbert has been part of New Order since almost the very beginning of the band, after they formed out of Joy Division in the wake of the death of that band’s frontman Ian Curtis. Morris, with frontman Bernard Sumner and bassist Peter Hook, played one tour before recruiting Gilbert on keyboards and guitar.“It seemed like a dream, really,”she said in 2023. “A dream come true. I was a bit daunted because they were obviously songwriting, and I couldn’t play keyboards at all, and I thought I’d just play guitar. But they said, ‘Well, we’ve got some keyboard parts.’ So, I got my sister’s Bontempi organ out.”She then performed and co-wrote on every New Order album between their debut Movement and 2001’s Get Ready, before taking a decade-long hiatus from the group to focus on looking after her and Morris’s children, including daughter Grace who had become physically disabled after an illness.Gilbert was successfully treated for breast cancer in 2007. She later returned to the touring lineup and contributed to the band’s most recent album,2015’s Music Complete.New Order are due to tour South America in November, with Gilbert and Morris replaced by touring musicians in the lineup. The band will also be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in the same month.Explore more on these topicsNew OrderPop and rockCancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Matthew Rhys’s alma mater pays tribute to ‘loyal pupil’ and Welsh language devotee | Matthew Rhys | The Guardian
description: Actor, who made history at the Emmys, thanked the ‘great and the good people of Wales’ for nurturing his talent
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Actor, who made history at the Emmys, thanked the ‘great and the good people of Wales’ for nurturing his talent
Content: Matthew Rhys, who grew up in Whitchurch, Cardiff, is still in contact with his former school.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatthew Rhys, who grew up in Whitchurch, Cardiff, is still in contact with his former school.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesMatthew RhysMatthew Rhys’s alma mater pays tribute to ‘loyal pupil’ and Welsh language devoteeActor, who made history at the Emmys, thanked the ‘great and the good people of Wales’ for nurturing his talentCaroline DaviesTue 15 Sep 2026 11.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Matthew Rhysmade history as the first actor ever to win two best lead Emmy awards in one night,he paid tribute to his roots.“To the great and good people ofWales, who were as much a nurturer as anyone else,” said the proud Welshman now living in New York, “We are a small but mighty nation”. “Diolch yn fawr iawn,” he added, meaning “thank you very much” in Welsh.Rhys, 51, who won best lead for the supernatural Apple comedy Widow’s Bay, and the psychological Netflix thriller The Beast in Me, trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art (Rada), one of the UK’s most prestigious drama schools. Growing up in Whitchurch, Cardiff, he was inspired by Welsh film heroes Richard Burton and Anthony Hopkins.But the seeds of his undoubted talent were truly sown at his Welsh-speaking schools – Ysgol Melin Gruffydd and Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Glantaf – where he received not just an “excellent education, but “lots of drama and school performances”, he has said.A fellow pupil, BBC’s Morning Live host Gethin Jones, has recalled the pair performing together in an Elvis show at Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Glantaf, when Rhys was 17. “In the Welsh language there’s no ‘v’ so we all walked around in these shirts that said ‘Elfis’,” Jones told viewers.“[Rhys] was a remarkable talent, even then,” the school’s current headteacher, Matthew Evans, told the Guardian. Former staff remember how he was “able to enthuse an audience and the cast around him”.The Hollywood star remains in contact with the school, whose alumni also include the fellow actor and friendIoan Gruffudd. Rhys took time to talk to pupils during Covid, said Evans, and he joined in a virtual farewell for his former music and drama teacher. “He’s a very loyal former pupil,” he said.“He’s very proud of his Welsh language skills. He also commends his upbringing in Welsh cultural activities, like the Eisteddfod, as a great stepping stone for his career. From a very young age, pupils take part in ensembles, all kinds of choirs, and that has given him, obviously, such a fabulous start in life. Also a love for the theatre and performing.”Rhys, whose partner Keri Russell was also nominated for her lead role in Netflix drama the Diplomat, has said that seeing Burton and Hopkins “up there on screen made me believe that my own ludicrous hopes could one day become real. They were proof that it was possible for people from Wales to get a foothold in the industry.”View image in fullscreenMatthew Rhys and Keri Russell.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesToday he has his own enviable haul of awards – 10 wins and 58 nominations according to IMDb – including another Emmy in 2018 for The Americans. His stellar career has included roles as diverse as gay lawyer Kevin Walker in the US series Brothers & Sisters, to Welsh poet Dylan Thomas in The Edge of Love.Success was not guaranteed and, even when it came, was punctuated with periods of drought, which is why he has been keen to give back. He is an ambassador for Into Film Cymru, which helps educators teach film as part of the curriculum for Wales.It is “as much down to luck as talent,” he has said. After The Graduate – he starred as Benjamin Braddock at the Gielgud Theatre in London in 2000 – he didn’t work for a year. “And it was touch and go whether I’d carry on.” He considered other professions outside the industry, including joining the British army.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEven after success there have been hiccups – a botched James Bond audition for one – and he still found himself out of work for long periods of time, which “keeps you humble”.Perhaps that is why, on learning of his double Emmy nomination this year, the Welsh pessimist in him said: “Well, this is it, this is the height of it all, it’s downhill from now on,” he told Wales Online ahead of Monday’s ceremony.There is not much time for celebrating his Emmys in a packed diary. Rhys has a second series of Widow’s Bay to film in 2027, he is back to the UK soon for the BBC drama Dragon Slayers as the the former Sunday Times editor Harry Evans, and he is about to take Mark Jenkins’s one-man play Playing Burton off-Broadway. He is the Welsh language voice of Han Solo in Star Wars: A New Hope due to air on S4C this Christmas.He may be enjoying his status as undisputed king of American TV, but can he claim the Welsh crown too? Speaking of his friend and former Hollywood flatmate, the actor-director Michael Sheen, Rhys has said there is no “real rivalry”, despite “constant humiliation”.“I always know whatever it is I think I’m doing well at, Sheen’s always like, ‘Oh, well, I’ve just taken over the Welsh National Theatre,’” he told Wales Online. “So, you always know it’s like whatever you’re doing, times it by 10, and that’s what Sheen’s probably doing.”Explore more on these topicsMatthew RhysEmmys 2026Awards and prizesWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emmys 2026: Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic wins | Emmys | The Guardian
description: Rhys becomes first actor to win lead acting awards for different shows in the same night, while Hacks’ Smart is the first woman to win for every season of a show
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Rhys becomes first actor to win lead acting awards for different shows in the same night, while Hacks’ Smart is the first woman to win for every season of a show
Content: 2:11Emmys 2026: Matthew Rhys makes history with double win – videoEmmysEmmys 2026: Widow’s Bay dominates as Matthew Rhys and Jean Smart land historic winsRhys becomes first actor to win lead acting awards for different shows in the same night, while Hacks’ Smart is the first woman to win for every season of a showEmmys 2026: red carpet looks and outfits at TV’s biggest night – in picturesIn the Hacks v Widow’s Bay Emmys battle, it’s we – the audience – who are the real winnersEmmys live blog: as it happenedEmmy winners: the full listSian CainMon 14 Sep 2026 23.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthew Rhys has become the first actor in 78 years of Emmys history to win multiple lead actor awards for performances in different shows in the same year, forWidow’s BayandThe Beast in Me.No one could stand in the way of this juggernaut! The biggest shocks from the Emmy awardsRead moreThe 51-year-old Welsh actor won outstanding lead actor in a comedy for Apple TV’s Widow’s Bay and outstanding lead actor in a limited series for his role in Netflix’s The Beast in Me at the ceremony on Monday night. With his 2018 win of outstanding lead actor in a drama for The Americans, he is the first male performer to win all three lead acting categories.During his speech for his Widow’s Bay win, Rhys thanked “the great and good people of Wales, who were as much a nurturer as anyone else. We are a small but mighty nation. This is incredible.”“I am slightly giddy and a little bit dizzy,” he told media after his historic win. “I genuinely can’t believe it. I hope to reflect on it tomorrow. At the moment, I genuinely can’t quite believe what has happened.”He said he had not expected he would win for The Beast in Me: “That was such a shock, as I am sure you could tell from the rambling speech I gave … a vomit of a speech.”Widow’s Bay dominated the ceremony in Los Angeles’ Peacock Theater, winning 14 of 19 nominations, including best comedy series, supporting actress in a comedy for Kate O’Flynn, supporting actor for Stephen Root, as well as best writing for its creator, Katie Dippold, and best director for Hiro Murai.View image in fullscreenThe Pitt star Noah Wyle with his second consecutive Emmy for outstanding actor in a drama.Photograph: Rob Latour/ShutterstockIn other categories,The Pittwon outstanding drama series and outstanding lead actor in a drama for Noah Wyle. The medical drama lead this year’s nominee tally with 25, winning six.Wyle, the first drama actor to win consecutiveEmmyssince Bryan Cranston on Breaking Bad, spoke about his roots. “I grew up in LA,” he said. “I’m a Hollywood kid. I was raised on a television, and movie theaters were my place of worship. This is all I’ve ever wanted to do, and this is the only club I’ve ever wanted to join. Thank you for accepting me.”Emmys 2026: red carpet looks and outfits at TV’s biggest night – in picturesRead moreJean Smart and Alison Janney both won their eighth acting Emmys, tying for the most acting Emmy wins with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman. Janney won best supporting actress forThe Diplomat, while Smart won her fifth outstanding lead actress in a comedy Emmy for her performance as Deborah Vance in the fifth and final season ofHacks, becoming the first woman to win an Emmy for every season of a show.View image in fullscreenJean Smart with her fifth Emmy for Hacks, and eighth overall acting Emmy.Photograph: Alberto Rodriguez/Deadline/Getty ImagesIn the drama categories, Rhea Seehorn won best lead actress forPluribus, her first Emmy win, while Tom Pelphrey won best supporting actor forTask, in a category stacked with actors from The Pitt.DTF St Louisdominated the limited or anthology series categories with seven wins, including best series, supporting actor for David Harbour and supporting actress for Linda Cardellini.Emmys 2026: the full list of winnersRead moreAfter the controversial cancellation ofThe Late Show, Stephen Colbert won the Emmy for a variety show for the show’s final season. Colbert thanked “the over 200 people” who worked on the show over a decade – and used his speech to spruik their talents. “Hire them,” he told the room. “They will make your day better and your lives easier.”The ceremony was relatively light on politics compared with previous years. Accepting best writing in a drama for Pluribus, the show’s creator,Vince Gilligan, described the show as set in a world “in which everybody gets along – that’s so sci-fi. But think about it: there’s nothing weirder than our current reality.”“We will never agree on everything, but we can treat each other with respect,” he said, “and we can stop listening to a relative few who think that is for suckers.”0:37Macaulay Culkin pays tribute to his Home Alone on-screen mother Catherine O’Hara - videoThe Pitt’s creator, R Scott Gemmill, while accepting the best drama award, told the room: “It is so hard to tell what is real and what we can believe any more, which makes telling honest stories about real human struggles so much more important than ever. What you do, it changes people’s lives.”Nominated shows that came away empty-handed during the ceremony included Shrinking, A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, Beef, Margo’s Got Money Troubles, Abbott Elementary and Paradise.Explore more on these topicsEmmysAwards and prizesEmmys 2026US televisionUS television industryTelevisionTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Venice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victory | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Mathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrive
Content: Mathilde Arcel poses with the Volpi Cup at the awards ceremony on Saturday in Venice.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenMathilde Arcel poses with the Volpi Cup at the awards ceremony on Saturday in Venice.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersVenice film festivalVenice best actress winner says she signed on at Danish job centre days before her victoryMathilde Arcel, who won the Volpi Cup on Saturday for her role in Golden Lion winner Woman Unknown, said job offers have now begun to arrivePhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorTue 15 Sep 2026 06.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe winner of this year’s best actress prize at theVenice film festivalhas revealed that she is on unemployment benefits and had to fly to back to Copenhagen to report to the job centre before receiving her award.On Saturday night, Danish actor Mathilde Arcel won the prestigious Volpi Cup for her first leading role in a feature film, May el-Toukhy’s post-second world war drama Woman Unknown, which alsowon the Golden Lion awardfor best film.Jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal said the judges had been able to relax Venice rules around not awarding more than one prize per film because the vote for Arcel had been unanimous.Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love and NAZARead moreAfter her triumph, the 30-year-old actor revealed in interviews with Danish media that she had returned toDenmarkafter her film’s premiere to sign on at the job centre, as she is on unemployment benefits when not working on films. She then returned to the Lido after being told it would be wise to be present at the awards gala.In the UK, actors’ trade union Equity said in a2023 reportthat 63% of its members have been in receipt of social security at some point in their life.Set in the direct aftermath of the Nazi occupation of Denmark, Woman Unknown tells the story of Marie, a young housemaid and nanny who is about to marry her widowed industrialist employer.But a chance encounter with an old schoolfriend threatens to reveal a shameful secret, exposing Marie to the retributive hounding of female “horizontal collaborators” who had intimate relations with German soldiers.At Venice, Arcel drew wide critical praise for the contained inner anguish she brings to the role of Marie. “Mathilde is going to blow our socks off,” Gyllenhaal said in a press conference after the awards ceremony.The actor said her agent had received several calls with new job offers since she scooped the Volpi Cup, the male version of which went to Hollywood veteran John Malkovich. “There are a lot of calls and a lot of interest from abroad and things like that, and we need to talk about what’s going to happen,” she told Danish broadcaster DR.Speaking in Venice on Saturday night, Arcel joked that her ultimate dream would be to play a part in one long-running British TV detective drama she was particularly fond of. “I really want to keep on working and meet some new artists”, she said. “I’m looking so much forward to what the future will bring, perhaps even a role in Midsomer Murders”.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalUnemploymentAwards and prizesDenmarkEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: it’s the final chapter of the landmark 7 Up series | Television | The Guardian
description: Oscar-winner Asif Kapadia takes the reins for a last catchup with the 70-year-olds. Plus: a year in the life of Gemma Collins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hannah Verdier
Headline: Oscar-winner Asif Kapadia takes the reins for a last catchup with the 70-year-olds. Plus: a year in the life of Gemma Collins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Tugs the heartstrings … the cast of 70 Up.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVView image in fullscreenTugs the heartstrings … the cast of 70 Up.Photograph: MultiStory Media/ITVTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: it’s the final chapter of the landmark 7 Up seriesOscar-winner Asif Kapadia takes the reins for a last catchup with the 70-year-olds. Plus: a year in the life of Gemma Collins. Here’s what to watch this eveningHannah Verdier,Graeme Virtue,Hollie RichardsonandPhil HarrisonTue 15 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google70 Up9pm, ITV1Asif Kapadia directs the final instalment of the long-running documentary (it first aired in 1964) and it does all its subjects – and their loyal viewers – proud. Meeting the now 70-year-olds again tugs at the existential heartstrings and some, such as cheeky dreamer Tony, have stayed close to their childhood selves, whereas the more mellow John worries about how he has been portrayed.Hannah VerdierRace Against the Tide7.30pm, BBC TwoThe upbeat sand-carving competition reaches its semi-final, as good a reason as any for host Iain Stirling to dress up as a Baywatch lifeguard. He gives the remaining four teams six hours to construct the tallest sculpture they can. It’s a high-risk, high-reward challenge … but who will be left standing?Graeme VirtueThe Great British Sewing Bee: The Final8pm, BBC OneBeth is perfectly precise with patterns. Emma’s garments are packed with character. Anna’s love of costume has won her seven transformation challenges. Who will be this year’s champion? The last tasks include a cummerbund and bow tie, a beach club outfit made out of gala table linen, and a showstopper for the Sewing Bee’s version of the Met Gala.Hollie RichardsonGemma Collins: Everything. All at Once9pm, Sky OneView image in fullscreenBringing the GC spirit … Gemma Collins: Everything. All at Once.Photograph: Sky UK Ltd/PAIt’s been 15 years since the GC introduced herself to the world on Towie. But this documentary series is the most personal look we’ve had – and it follows what Collins calls “the toughest year of my life”. From receiving hate mail to her mother’s illness, starting an IVF journey and her fiance’s addiction issues, it’s certainly a bumpy and emotional time. But there’s always some GC spirit to get by with.HRCelebrity MasterChef9pm, BBC OneIt’s finals week in the kitchen and that means a few surprises. It’s off to Crufts for a slightly bizarre challenge: Michelin-starred chef Tom Shepherd has designed a doggy-style menu (including a bone-shaped dessert), which the finalists must cook. Then, back to base for a meal that evokes a favourite holiday.Phil HarrisonThe Royals: Time to Go?9pm, Channel 4The percentage of people in the UK in favour of abolishing the royal family is at a high, according to this report. John Humphrys – a royal sceptic, who had encounters with the queen – speaks to those for and against the monarchy.HRLive sportInternational T20cricket: England v Sri Lanka, 6pm, Sky Sports Main EventFirst T20 in the three-match series.EFL Carabao Cup: Liverpool v Tottenham, 7pm, Sky Sports Main EventOn Wednesday, Man United play Brighton at 8pm (ITV1 at 7.30pm).Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Rouse by China Miéville review – a mighty achievement from the ‘new weird’ author | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Twenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousness
Author: Stuart Kelly
Headline: Twenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousness
Content: Stylistic bravado … China Miéville.Photograph: Barney CokelissView image in fullscreenStylistic bravado … China Miéville.Photograph: Barney CokelissBook of the dayFictionReviewThe Rouse by China Miéville review – a mighty achievement from the ‘new weird’ authorTwenty years in the writing, this paranormal epic of cold war espionage and family tragedy is a quantum leap in terms of ambition and moral seriousnessStuart KellyTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina Miéville’s epic new novel is presented as being “20 years in the making”. It is quite a testament to how extravagant – even Stakhanovite – his imagination is that during that period he also produced six novels (includingThe City & the CityandThe Book of Elsewhere, co-written with Keanu Reeves), two novellas, two series of graphic novels, a children’s book, a volume of short stories and two works of nonfiction, on theOctober Revolutionand the Communist Manifesto.It does not mean that these works were, as Graham Greene called The Third Man and Our Man in Havana, “entertainments” –Embassytown, to my mind, is the best translation of deconstructionist philosophy into science fiction – but certainly The Rouse is a quantum jump in terms of ambition, moral seriousness and stylistic bravado. It means that rather than classifying Miéville with “the new weird” or “speculative fantasy”, he ought to be compared to Roberto Bolaño or Mircea Cărtărescu. This new novel is equally maximalist, dense, disorienting and discomfiting, reflecting how surreal our reality seems to have become.Readers acquainted with Miéville’s other work might be disconcerted by the first hundred pages: broadly speaking, they are social realism. We are in 1970s London and Maur, short for Maureen, gets pregnant and decides to keep the baby. Ewan grows up reading Rupert Bear and Starlord comics, watching Steptoe and Son and Rentaghost, and having Chinese takeaways with obligatory background racism. It is canny rather than uncanny, with the exception of a cameo from the truly odd 80s comedian Roy Jay doing his “slither-spook” routine, possibly on The Bob Monkhouse Show. (Now an internet meme, it is unforgettable and queasily sinister – and on YouTube.) Eventually Ewan, at a loss in many ways, decides to join the army. Then Miéville drops the bombshell just before the 100th page: Ewan dies, supposedly by suicide, at an army base. “Now everything is codas,” thinks Maur, and in capital letters we get THE END. The novel – all epilogue – now begins, for more than a thousand pages.The descriptions of Maur’s grief are phenomenal. “After a long time she came to believe what she knew, which was that this would never unhappen. So she did the bargaining. Just for a moment. I understand he won’t come back but I need everything to stop for just a second … What I need is I just need a moment when this isn’t all there is. That’s all I’m asking. To have anything else, or nothing, in my head. All I’m asking is just let me have one single minute ever again when he isn’t dead.”Maur, it transpires, is not the only grieving parent with a connection to Shackingham Barracks, and she finds a support network for those who are similarly bereaved. There seems to have been a spate of suicides, rather like theDeepcut controversy; something is being covered up.She falls in with an investigative journalist, Jock; a fellow bereaved parent, Cybill; and eventually a renegade ex-army operative named Stallo. At the very beginning of the book, the young Maur is warned by her father to “stay out of the dead’s business”. She doesn’t understand the import of his words, thinking, comically, he just means not becoming an undertaker.double quotation markThe Rouse is affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frighteningThe Rouse is the name of the army’s bugle call, played to call soldiers to their duties and also after the Last Post. Here it is a code for more than that: the stirrings are supernatural. The scales will fall from Maur’s eyes about the extent of the deep state’s paranormal interests.Her narrative, however, is held in counterpoint to the story of Allardyce, a soldier with a background in the more eldritch side of the armed forces. His experiences are vastly wide-ranging, from Malaya to Kenya, Akhalkalaki and the Falklands; and with both untrustworthy American allies and cabals of USSR and Chinese counterparts. This global reach is not mere exoticism: not only is Miéville concerned with the geopolitical in the broadest sense, here he holds it in parallel with the “radical democracy of death”, the “revolutionarinessof death”. Why is the military concerned with haunting and the afterlife? I don’t want to give away too much, but somehow death and the dead are an exploitable resource and a radical alternative at the same time. This being Miéville, even those “freed” from life and suffering are prey to capitalist forms of commodification and exploitation: the final twist is genius. The links between Allardyce’s schemes and the quest of Maur and increasingly Stallo are seeded cunningly and have a “rightness” in the reveal – notable in a book obsessed with “not rightness”.Linguistically, the novel is a riot. The name of Cybill harks to Sibyl, the Greek prophetess; Maur sounds like the Frenchmort. Miéville’s prose has always been baroque and esoteric, and here it is combined with slang and period detail perfectly. It has its own idiolect – one character, the spiky backrooms scientist Dr Croome, coins “inodus” as an opposite to “exodus”, commenting that “the efficacy of words is wildly overstated, most especially by those who work with them”. She opines that she “always foundgast,gæst, and particularlygōstto be so close to the dread unsayable as to be ridiculous” – but by not giving an obvious infodump of, for example, phenomena the soldiers nickname “lesprys” (derived froml’esprit de corpsbut conjuring something almost fey), the book keeps its corner-of-the-eye shimmer. The prefix “un” is used as a leitmotif: unsee, unwritten, undone, unopened. It is negation on the level of the sentence.In a sly aside, there is praise for John le Carré, whose version of the world of spooks is less paranormal than Miéville’s. Their books share the shabbiness of cold war espionage, and an ambience of regret for the days of simple us v them situations, but also the capacity to keep the reader guessing about the true affiliation and trustworthiness of the characters. That is just the tip of references, with Miéville’s capacious knowledge of the weird canon on display: there can’t be many novels that nod to Lord Kilmarnock’s 1903 Ferelith. Along with the “found texts” and concrete poems at the end of chapters there is enough here to sate the hungriest of readers. The Rouse is affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening. “Life,” as Miéville writes, “is just a prologue to a ghost story.” This is a novel destined for a rich afterlife.The Rouse by China Mieville (Pan Macmillan, £35). title: Legend of Destruction review – starry voices grace animated telling of the Jewish revolt against the Romans | Movies | The Guardian
description: Eight years in the making, the innovative film uses painted still images – it’s like being read a graphic novel by a cast including Oscar Isaac, Evangeline Lilly and Elliott Gould
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Eight years in the making, the innovative film uses painted still images – it’s like being read a graphic novel by a cast including Oscar Isaac, Evangeline Lilly and Elliott Gould
Content: Resistance … Berenice of Cilicia, voiced by Evangeline Lilly, in Legend of DestructionPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenResistance … Berenice of Cilicia, voiced by Evangeline Lilly, in Legend of DestructionPhotograph: PRMoviesReviewLegend of Destruction review – starry voices grace animated telling of the Jewish revolt against the RomansEight years in the making, the innovative film uses painted still images – it’s like being read a graphic novel by a cast including Oscar Isaac, Evangeline Lilly and Elliott GouldLeslie FelperinTue 15 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Israeli animated film has been largely hanging around in limbo since it was finished in 2021 after taking eight years to complete – though this may or may not be due to the international opprobrium thatIsraelhas attracted in the intervening period. It’s actually a rather fascinating film, if oddly told and a bit severe. Legend of Destruction isn’t about the current conflict, taking place as it does in the first century, 66 years after the birth of Christ – although of course, if you squint a bit, parallels with current events are there to be discerned. Revolutions fracture from within, hegemons topple due to their own greedy self-destruction, and in the end ordinary people are the ones who suffer and die as cities burn. Fill in the blanks as you see fit.Cleaving pretty closely to the known facts as recorded by Flavius Josephus’ The Jewish War and the Talmud, the script by director Gidi Dar and Shuli Rand recounts how Jewish resistance rose up in Judea, particularly in Jerusalem, against the occupying Romans and the reigning Jewish elite, including the Temple’s high priests and queen Berenice of Cilicia (Evangeline Lilly), over excessive taxation. Our protagonist narrator is ordinary schlemiel Ben Batich (voiced in this English language version by Oscar Isaac), who becomes a leader of one faction after he snaps and can no longer agree with the pleas for patience and tolerance from his mother (Marilu Henner) and rabbi uncle Yohanan ben Zakkai (Elliott Gould).Riots in the streets bring early victories, but Batich and his followers eventually fall out with rival anti-Roman revolutionaries led by Simon Bar Giora (Billy Zane) and others, in such a way that might make some viewers involuntarily think of Monty Python’s Life of Brian. Either way, it all ends with the Second Temple of Jerusalem in flames, Ben Batich and his family starving, and Rome ready to repress further once they get their own house in order (back home in Italy the emperor Nero has been killed and the peasants are revolting). What’s thrillingly persuasive about this rendition of history is that no one mentions Christianity here – it just wasn’t that much of a thing at this point in time, outside a few scattered followers of Christ kicking around and trying to get a new religion off the ground.The whole story is told through still digital pictures by David Polonsky and Michael Faust that look sometimes like oil paintings and sometimes like pastel, full of energy and movement. Inspired apparently by Chris Marker’s immortal photograph-based short La Jetée, there’s almost no movement, until the end when the film-makers break out a tiny bit of stutter animation to drive home the final point.The end result is like having a very fancy graphic novel read to you by a cast of big-name actors. It’s innovative, for sure, but arguably not a direction many others are likely to take as it seems so static – but you have to admire Dar’s audacity for trying it.Legend of Destruction is on digital platforms from 15 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmPeriod and historical filmsIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaOscar IsaacreviewsShareReuse this content

title: James McNeill Whistler review – painter’s work shines through attention-grabbing life story | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his art
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: The latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his art
Content: Proto-modern … Arrangement in Grey and Black No 1, Portrait of the Artist's Mother by James McNeill Whistler.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesView image in fullscreenProto-modern … Arrangement in Grey and Black No 1, Portrait of the Artist's Mother by James McNeill Whistler.Photograph: Bridgeman ImagesMoviesReviewJames McNeill Whistler review – painter’s work shines through attention-grabbing life storyThe latest Exhibition on Screen documentary does a good job balancing the famous scandals with the subtle brilliance of his artAndrew PulverTue 15 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTimed to coincide withTate Britain’s impressive gallery show– which closes at the end of September, so you haven’t long if you’ve missed it so far – this latest from the Exhibition on Screen strand does a fine job in outlining the ins and outs, and ups and downs of this still somewhat divisive artist who, Whistler’s Mother notwithstanding, is still probably most famous for winning a farthing in damagesin his “flinging a pot of paint” libel actionagainst John Ruskin. The film assembles the customary lineup of notables including the Tate’s Carol Jacobi, critic Rachel Campbell-Johnston and art historian Stephen Calloway, the latter of whom’s dandyish attire and Colonel Sanders goatee suggests he has very much bought into the Whistler aesthetic.In fact, as all the interviewees are keen to point out, Whistler’s self-constructed persona, always with an eye to making a splash, is as significant an element of his artistic presence as the art itself – even if, as I can’t be alone in thinking, there’s something fundamentally irritating about his southern-genteel attudinising even at a century and a half’s distance. Be that as it may, the film gets to grips with Whistler’s instinctive brilliance as an artist, his natural flair for boundary-pushing and forward-thinking idealism. The big life episodes – his arrival in London, painting his mother, the brouhaha over thePeacock Room, the court case and subsequent bankruptcy – are recounted, but there is impressive detail on the actual art: from the dynamics behind hisbrooding Wapping pictureto the temper tantrums (not his) that made Harmony in Grey and Green, his portrait of the eight-year-old Cicely Alexander so distinctive. And while Whistler’s dealings with the women in his life wouldn’t exactly pass modern-era scrutiny, his pictures of them are genuinely brilliant, with especial attention given to awonderfully tender sketch of his wife Beatrix, terminally ill in a hotel bedroom.The only downside is that, so delicate and subtle is his work, Whistler’s shimmering proto-modern visions are perhaps let down a little by pointing a camera at them; it’s hardly the film-maker’s fault but they just don’t jump out of the screen as they do in the gallery. Nevertheless, the film itself is an excellent primer to one of the greats, whose richness of artistic achievement appears to be getting the comprehensive attention it deserves.James McNeill Whistler is in UK and Irish cinemas from 15 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPaintingArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Premature review – sunny charm provides screwball energy for surprise-pregnancy comedy | Movies | The Guardian
description: First-time director Kevin Walls creates a film sweet-natured enough to cancel out some comedy misfires as flatmates Eilidh and Cameron prepare for parenthood
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: First-time director Kevin Walls creates a film sweet-natured enough to cancel out some comedy misfires as flatmates Eilidh and Cameron prepare for parenthood
Content: Skew-whiff … Elle Watson and James Rottger in Premature.Photograph: Sonorous FilmsView image in fullscreenSkew-whiff … Elle Watson and James Rottger in Premature.Photograph: Sonorous FilmsMoviesReviewPremature review – sunny charm provides screwball energy for surprise-pregnancy comedyFirst-time director Kevin Walls creates a film sweet-natured enough to cancel out some comedy misfires as flatmates Eilidh and Cameron prepare for parenthoodCath ClarkeTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe pram in the hallway is the enemy of good art,or so the famous quote goes. This sunny Scottish comedy, made on a minuscule budget, deals with the bit before the pram, when an art school dropout in her 20s gets unexpectedly up the duff. It’s directed by first-timer Kevin Walls, who gives his film the screwball-ish energy of things being skew-whiffly the wrong way round; a couple are going on their first date at three months pregnant, having a baby at an age most people are putting it off to establish their careers. It’s sweet-natured with just about enough charm to cancel out a couple of thunderously awful comedy moments.Elle Watson is artist Eilidh, who works as a barista in a museum cafe. She has a friends-with-benefits setup with her flatmate Cameron (James Rottger); he has a job in finance and, after two degrees, a mountain of student debt and years in a mind-numbing entry-level position, he’s finally lined up an interview for his dream job. It would be crazy to have the baby, but Eilidh doesn’t take the abortion tablets. She can’t give Cameron a coherent reason why not; fair enough, it’s her decision, a gut feeling. Walls sensibly doesn’t go anywhere near the pro-choice/anti-abortion debate.But it is a shame his script seems to naturally click more with Cameron’s point of view as he agonises about how a baby will impact his career. Eilidh cheerfully breezes through pregnancy – though inexplicably she turns mumzilla in one scene, demanding that Cameron help her break into a house to steal a secondhand cot, wearing tights over their heads. It’s a scene that reduces the film’s IQ and likability by about 10%. Elsewhere, there are some moments of gentleness, like Cameron’s lovely dad and his no-nonsense wisdom. “Life doesn’t give two shits about your plans, son.”Premature is in UK and Irish cinemas from 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsRomance filmsChildbirthComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: She was the Royal Ballet’s first ‘young choreographer’ – Charlotte Edmonds’ next 10 years show how dance is changing | Dance | The Guardian
description: As a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directions
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: As a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directions
Content: The challenge is ‘making a living while still being creatively intact’ … Charlotte Edmonds.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellView image in fullscreenThe challenge is ‘making a living while still being creatively intact’ … Charlotte Edmonds.Photograph: Camilla GreenwellDanceShe was the Royal Ballet’s first ‘young choreographer’ – Charlotte Edmonds’ next 10 years show how dance is changingAs a teenager, Edmonds had a three-year residency at the Royal Opera House. Her eclectic career – creating NFTs, adverts and films as well as for the stage – reveals a precarious industry moving in new directionsLyndsey WinshipTue 15 Sep 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 06.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the age of 18,Charlotte Edmondswas such apromising choreographer(“astonishing”, in the words of the Observer) that the Royal Ballet invented a whole new job for her. As the company’s “young choreographer”, she spent three years learning everything she could at one of the world’s biggest dance institutions. “It’s mad to think that happened,” she says, a decade on.With that kind of start, you’d expect Edmonds’ career to have followed a predictable narrative, choreographing for the big ballet brands, maybe setting up her own company. But that’s not exactly how it’s gone. Her eclectic portfolio reflects how the dance industry has changed and become ever more precarious, but also expanded in uncharted directions. She has indeed made short works for a number of European ballet companies, but she’s spent more time recently making films, music videos and adverts for the likes of Budweiser and Nike, as well as advocating for artists with dyslexia and launching her own video series,Cameo, in which she interviews female and non-binary choreographers to counter a lack of representation.I ask her to tell me about the practical challenges of making a career in choreography. “I would say, ‘Ohh,’” Edmonds laughs. “It’s really fucking tough. It’s really, really hard to get things going. It was hard back then but it feels even tougher now. Because of Covid, funding cuts, cost of living …” She will have conversions with Arts Council England, she says, during which they remark: “‘This is a project that would have been funded 10 years ago.’ And it’s frustrating for them because there’s only a certain amount of resources.” She goes online to apply for smaller grant funds, “and on the website it says, ‘We’re closing our doors for this year and rethinking how to structure our grants.’”Nevertheless, Edmonds says, “When you do something you love, it’s so consuming.” The challenge is “making a living while still being creatively intact. It’s such a juggling act and that can really take a mental toll.” Everyone has had to diversify – some of Edmonds’ colleagues have become intimacy coordinators; Edmonds does movement direction for singers, recently with Lola Young on a TV appearance (there was no dancing; Edmonds’ job was to help Young navigate the set and cameras, hone the “intention” and emotion of the performance, and even to be “a support system” for a jet-lagged singer).There’s a boom in dance online, with brands making arty short films instead of straight ads andold songs going viral with new dance routines. Edmonds has also experimented with digital art. Amid the flush of excitement over NFTs in 2021, she created several works with the artist Brendan Dawes for Sotheby’s. “With that Sotheby’s exhibition, I remember going into the rehearsal room thinking, am I going to suddenly walk out a millionaire? ‘No’ was the answer. But we could all dream,” she smiles. “The making of the NFT itself was really interesting. It was fascinating where choreography could go and how it could be utilised.”Edmonds is endlessly curious, and entrepreneurial. You have to be a hustler in this business, yes? “Yeah, but not in a Wolf of Wall Street way,” she says. “In a really conscious, intentional sense.” Getting an email just offering you a gig is rare (“Oh my gosh, that literally feels like the lottery”), and you have to make your own opportunities. In the early days Edmonds got a £15,000 Arts Council grant to make an ambitious project, the filmSink or Swim, featuring Royal Ballet principal Francesca Hayward in a giant water tank. She raised another £5,000 herself. It took her a year to raise the money and she didn’t pay herself a fee.View image in fullscreenLukas Bjørneboe Braendsrød, Mica Bradbury, Gina Storm-Jensen and Reece Clarke in Meta by Charlotte Edmonds at the Clore Studio, Royal Opera House, in 2016.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThese days, at 29, she has to think more seriously about supporting herself. “There are so many social pressures,” she says. And then she starts two or three different sentences before saying, “You can see I’m whirring away about the conversations I have with myself about sticking to it. People do step away [from dance] to have stability, have a family; all these elements that naturally creep up as you get older.” For those who choose to leave, even when it’s a profession you’ve been training in your whole life, “it’s not a failure”, she says. “It is a choice of what’s right for you in life.”For Edmonds, though, the drive and passion for choreography she had as a teenager is still strong. I watch her in a studio at London Contemporary Dance School where she’s rehearsing a group of students forher new film, Ladette, examining 90s gender roles. (Edmonds was only a baby in the 90s, but the theme is in sync with the current nostalgia for all things pre-smartphone.) A mass of 43 bodies move with a powerful pulse, shifting from sharp, blunt stamps and jutting shoulders to snakey and molten movement. Edmonds works out steps and shapes on her own body and shares them with the dancers, her classical and contemporary training now shot through with street and club dance influences. She’s in her element in the studio, and it’s still her ambition to make major works for large ballet companies. “I really want to make live work in the UK,” she says. “I’ve been planning and writing and curating ideas that are close to my heart and I’d love to see them take off.” Watch this space.Explore more on these topicsDanceRoyal BalletDigital artSocial mediaBalletDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pre-Existing Condition review – Lupita Nyong’o is phenomenal in domestic abuse drama | US theater | The Guardian
description: The Oscar-winning actor transfixes in Marin Ireland’s masterfully nuanced play about a woman reeling from a toxic relationship
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The Oscar-winning actor transfixes in Marin Ireland’s masterfully nuanced play about a woman reeling from a toxic relationship
Content: Lupita Nyong'o in Pre-Existing Condition.Photograph: Jessica KourkounisView image in fullscreenLupita Nyong'o in Pre-Existing Condition.Photograph: Jessica KourkounisUS theaterReviewPre-Existing Condition review – Lupita Nyong’o is phenomenal in domestic abuse dramaGreenwich House Theater, New YorkThe Oscar-winning actor transfixes in Marin Ireland’s masterfully nuanced play about a woman reeling from a toxic relationshipJuan A RamírezMon 14 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 08.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParadoxically, the more stars step into the lead role inPre-Existing Condition, the more the brilliance of Marin Ireland’s domestic abuse play takes center stage. Not that it ever suffered from a lack of acting talent – when it premiered in 2024, at New York’s tiny Connelly Theater Upstairs, it countedTatiana Maslany,Edie Falcoand Deirdre O’Connell among the actors who played its central character in quick succession, for only a few weeks each. And this return engagement, at the larger Greenwich House Theater across town, kicks off withLupita Nyong’o, before making way for Phillipa Soo, Susannah Flood, Hari Nef, Falco again and Whitney White.‘The myth is constantly being told’: creating a live album on stage as tribute to New YorkRead moreIt’s a straightforward conceit, perfectly calibrated for a 75-minute run time. A woman (whom the script refers to as A, currently played by Nyong’o) is dealing with the aftermath of a breakup triggered by her partner hitting her. When we meet her, someone (perhaps a lawyer, or a therapist) is laying out the reality of her situation: even with the deep pockets required to go to court, it’s been seven months since the incident, it happened across state lines and she never called the police. “You have to be ready for a fight,” she tells A. “Which, just from our short time with each other, I can already tell that you’re not.”From there, people appear in A’s life as if through a haze. Three performers (Greg Keller, Dael Orlandersmith and Sarah Steele, all perfect) play a series of friends, relatives and social workers. Some are empathetic group counselors, trained to be helpful. Others, like one of the former couple’s mutual friends, wishes A would just move on.Characters might define who they are midway through a scene. But as played by the rotating trio, and with even well-meaning acquaintances capable of uttering something unwittingly devastating, anyone who walks into A’s life registers as a stranger. Director Maria Dizzia blurs transitions by having characters linger as Isabella Byrd’s lighting shifts, and the next scene begins before we’ve realized the current one has ended. (Cate McCrea’s set and Enver Chakartash’s costumes are aptly nondescript.)View image in fullscreenSarah Steele, Lupita Nyong’o and Dael Orlandersmith in Pre-Existing Condition.Photograph: Jessica KourkounisThe result is an atmosphere of confusion, matching A’s destabilized self. Ireland’s script places her on a gently upward trajectory, but is clear about the reality that healing is hardly linear. She’s based it on her own experience with domestic violence: her ex, the actor Scott Shepherd, struck Ireland while they were rehearsing a play in London in 2012.There’s anger and vengefulness and displaced blame, as well as sharp, well-researched and clearly lived observations of the impossible situations into which women are placed. The title refers to how certain US states, as late as 2010, classified domestic violence as a way for insurance companies to deny victims coverage. A counselor at one point notes that children are the main reason women do, and don’t, leave violent situations – a chilling “damned if you do” reality.Hollywood encore: how ‘pro-shot’ Broadway shows became a major draw on the big screenRead moreBut it’s the levity and cautious optimism of the piece that best comes across. Flowing through the all-around excellent work is a real sense of care, of a team of women coming together to share a wave of communal honesty.That’s in part because Ireland and Dizzia are best known as actors, which instinctively makes our lizard brains wonder why they’ve stepped out of the box into which we’ve put them. And the wide range in lead casting (across age, race, artistic milieu), which Ireland’s script encourages to explore “being a shared experience”, is both practically ingenious and thematically profound.Though both are excellent, Nyong’o could not be further from Falco, whom I saw in the role two years ago – in terms of acting, temperament, appearance and familiarity. That a critic could be so stunned by different actors succeeding in the same role should typically be grounds for dismissal, but there’s a humbling quality to Ireland’s play, as beautifully directed by Dizzia, that both highlights and dismantles differences – of what’s in the text and beyond, and of who’s in the room on any given night, onstage or off, and how they might react.Nyong’o’s inherent youthfulness and regality renders her somewhat of an entitled millennial, rocked by the first bad thing to ever happen to her. It’s leagues away from Falco’s humiliation at being put through this at a later stage in life. Both, the script demands and Ireland knows, must confront that shame.During A’s too-soon attempts at dating, Nyong’o goes for a flirty, almost hypersexual approach, and I tried to remember how Falco played the scenes. I wondered how Nef or White would take to them. How would – does – anyone? Ireland’s play, while it can’t be a roadmap, is a tightly designed, gorgeously felt blueprint.At Greenwich House Theater,New York, with a rotating cast until 8 January 2027Explore more on these topicsUS theaterLupita Nyong'oEdie FalcoNew YorkTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Solo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk solo
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk solo
Content: Annabel Abbs passing Roseberry Topping while walking the Cleveland Way: ‘my need for silence and solitude outweighs my fears.’View image in fullscreenAnnabel Abbs passing Roseberry Topping while walking the Cleveland Way: ‘my need for silence and solitude outweighs my fears.’Life and styleSolo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’Hiking alone in the countryside can be joyous, but for women it can sometimes feel unnerving. Here’s how to enjoy it safely, plus four stunning routes to walk soloAnnabel AbbsTue 15 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdid my first solo hike during a sunny September, seven years ago. After a summer of feeding and ferrying four noisy teenagers (and their friends) around, I was exhausted. But despite being bone tired, I had barely moved. I yearned, above all, for time on my own, for the chance to walk without interruption (and at the pace I chose), and for the silence of some empty wilderness.But I was nervous. Not of being on my own, but of what might happen to me with no one around to help (breaking a bone, encountering a psychopath, being chased by a bull, getting fatally lost). I could have found a companion or joined a group, but my need for silence and solitude outweighed my fears.It seems that many women feel the same: in the UK, the proportion of women solo hiking surged by 27% between 2020 and 2022. In America,41 % of female hikersreport regularly walking alone. And yet many women, although keen to do something similar, feel intimidated. According to researchers at theMunich University of Applied Scienceswho are studying solo female walkers, 30% of women interviewed said they would like to hike solo but are hesitant.In truth, women have long enjoyed a tradition of solo walking. From religious pilgrims to goat herders to 19th-century adventurers, there have always been women wandering, radically alone, through wild landscapes. But for those new to it, I’d say the best way to overcome your fear is to do it – and I’ve learned some simple ways to make the experience fun, not daunting.double quotation markSome of the things I look for in a route: no stretches of urban wasteland, wide open landscapes, navigation-lite routes that follow rivers or coastlinesThat first solo hike followed a French canal. It was beautiful but sometimes felt a little too abandoned. It was also bereft of facilities, and frequently involved a long, complicated walk to my accommodation. So here are some of the things I now look for in a route: no discomfort-inducing stretches of urban wasteland; wide open landscapes (ridgeways, cliffs and hilltops are favourites); excellently waymarked, well-maintained paths (like national trails); navigation-lite routes that follow rivers, (lively) canals or coastlines; and countries/regions with a tradition of hiking.I do my research with care, and I’ve always returned home exhilarated, revitalised and high on my own bravado. I’ve learned to avoid the trails where I might feel uncomfortable. I know now which landscapes calm me, and which trails are (almost) impossible to lose my way on.For the last seven years, I’ve walked solo every autumn. Indeed, autumn is the perfect time for a liberating, empowering and restorative (solo) hike. Falling leaves improve visibility, temperatures are pleasant, and the days are still long enough to ensure I can reach my destination before dark. Importantly, there are lots of other walkers around – but without summer’s hordes – and the landscape is autumnally crisp and colourful.If you’re new to solo walking, start with a single day. If you want to try walking for multiple days, consider paying for your luggage to be transported (or use a specialist tour operator who will plot your route, arrange accommodation and move bags). Otherwise pack as lightly as possible. Take a non-digital map and a stick/walking poles, and let someone know your arrival time. Study every aspect of your route – including transport options and the weather – before you set off.FOUR GREAT ROUTES FOR SOLO HIKERSThe Bernese Oberland, SwitzerlandView image in fullscreenGrindelwald, Berne Canton, Swiss Alps.Photograph: Ascent X Media/Getty ImagesThe Swiss Alps are one of my favourite places to walk alone. Swiss women are keen solo hikers (so no one bats an eyelid at yet another single woman), the waymarking is superb and the scenery is jaw-dropping. Because this is a nation of farmers and hikers, there are always people (and a phone signal) around. And yet – because of the mountainous terrain – there’s often a genuine sense of wilderness and solitude. The Bernese Oberland is overrun with tourists in summer, but come to this Unesco world heritage site in autumn and you’ll be walking, calmly, in the footsteps of dozens of 19th-century women who once came here specifically to hike alone. Base yourself in the car-free villages of Wengen or Mürren, and expect to find farm-cafes with homemade cakes and honesty boxes in the remotest of spots.The South Downs WayView image in fullscreenChanctonbury Ring on the South Downs in West Sussex.Photograph: Cold Snowstorm/Getty ImagesFromEastbourneToKingston, near LewesTime2 daysDistance19 milesThe UK has plenty of well-kept trails, but top of my list is the (expansive, clearly signposted)South Downs Way. In summer the Eastbourne to Alfriston clifftop stretch heaves with tourists, but in autumn you’ll share the panoramic views – dazzling sea, dramatic chalk cliffs – with a handful of dogwalkers. Just a few steps off the trail are cultural hotspots like the pretty village of Alfriston, Charleston Farmhouse (museum home of the Bloomsbury set), and Rodmell, where you can visit Virginia Woolf’s house. So you’ll never feel completely disconnected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Cleveland WayView image in fullscreenSpectacular scenery near Staithes, on the Cleveland Way coastal section.Photograph: Madeleine Deaton/Getty ImagesFromSaltburnToFileyTime4 daysDistance52 milesTheCleveland Waywas the UK’s second official national trail, meaning the route is well maintained, the signage is excellent and the scenery is glorious, covering coastline and windblown moors. The moors can feel bleakly exposed in the wrong weather, so opt for the four-day coastal section, Saltburn to Filey, with its quirky towns and villages. This is Yorkshire so expect plenty of conversation with passing walkersandthe chance to feel romantically windswept – an intoxicating blend for the solo hiker who wants to feel alone in nature, but not too alone.The Fishermen’s Trail, southern PortugalView image in fullscreenA sandy cove and warm sea on the Fisherman’s Trail.Photograph: Calix/AlamyFromPraia da LuzToSagresTime3 daysDistance27 milesThe Fishermen’s Trail is far too hot in summer, but when I went (November) the temperature was just right, the sea was warm enough to swim in, and there were enough solo female hikers to feel pleasantly companioned. With some rocky scrambling to make one feel suitably youthful, and sufficient sandy coves to squeeze in a siesta, this route (a chain of old fishing villages) also has abundant, inexpensive accommodation and fresh seafood galore. Like other sea-hugging routes it’s (mostly) impossible to get lost – just follow the coastline.I’ll leave the last word to writer Mathilde Blind, who (aged 19) walked alone through the Bernese Oberland in 1860 (no phone, no GPS, no bra, no waterproof trousers): “For once I felt truly free.”Annabel Abbs is the author ofThe Walking CureandWindswept: Why Women Walk. title: Can you freeze leftover risotto?  | Rice | The Guardian
description: It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if you must, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mush
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if you must, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mush
Content: Felicity Cloake’s perfect risotto and the not-soggyarancinishe made out of the leftovers.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food styling: Kitty Coles. Prop styling: Jemima Hetherington and Kitty Coles. Food assistant: Jo Jackson. Photo assistant: Liam Desbois.View image in fullscreenFelicity Cloake’s perfect risotto and the not-soggyarancinishe made out of the leftovers.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food styling: Kitty Coles. Prop styling: Jemima Hetherington and Kitty Coles. Food assistant: Jo Jackson. Photo assistant: Liam Desbois.Kitchen aideRiceCan you freeze leftover risotto?It’s probably not a good idea to freeze cooked risotto rice, but if youmust, we have three experts who can tell you how to minimise the mushAnna BerrillTue 15 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI have tried various ways to reheat risotto after freezing, but it always turns into a gloopy, starchy, unappetising mess. What am I doing wrong?Jill, by email“Freezing risotto will be a bit of a disaster,” says Theo Randall, chef/patron atTheo Randall Cucina Italiana at the Intercontinentalin London, “and it doesn’t really work.” The reason for this is that the cooked rice absorbs all the moisture while it’s defrosting, resulting in, well, Jill’s gloopy mess.It’s also possible her risotto was overcooked to begin with, says Sue Quinn, author ofCheese Please. “Softer grains mean more leached starch, which leaves less leeway for further cooking without it going sticky and pasty.” Then there’s the question of reheating that defrosted rice for too long: “That can over-soften the already-cooked rice,” adds Quinn, so you have to do it “quickly and only until it’s piping hot”.The reality, however, is that “freezing, thawing and reheating rice will make it squishier whatever you do”, Quinn says, but “if that’s the way Jill rolls”, her best bet is to get that defrosted risotto in the microwave, sprinkle it with a little water or stock, cover loosely, then reheat on high in one-minute intervals, stirring in between, until it’s hot all the way through. “To do this on the hob, put the defrosted risotto in a pan with a splash of hot stock or water, and stir gently over a medium heat for just long enough to distribute the heat.”And, says Randall, if Jill “really has to freeze leftover risotto”, he would urge her to turn it into arancini instead: “Those work quite well, because you’ve encased the cooked rice in flour, egg wash and breadcrumbs, so moisture doesn’t penetrate the grains.”Alternatively, Jill could shun the freezer altogether and simply turn her leftovers into another meal the next day, Randall says: “One of the great Milanese dishes isrisotto al salto, which is usually made with saffron risotto. Keep any leftovers in the fridge, then, when you’re ready to use it, get a hot pan, melt some butter in there – don’t let it brown, though – then tip in the risotto.” You want to pack that rice right down, so it gets into the edges of the pan and resembles a pancake. Leave to cook for five minutes – “Don’t touch it!” – and you’ll eventually get a lovely crust on the bottom of the rice. “Flip it over, again just like a pancake [or use a spatula to help, if need be] and cook for a further five minutes on the other side. You’ll end up with this lovely, crisp and slightly gooey risotto,” Randall says, “and that’s probably by far the best way to use up risotto leftovers.”And if Jill still wants to batch-cook,Poppy O’Toolesuggests a shift in mindset: “The kind of rice that you can freeze would be baked [basmati] rice,” says the author ofThe Actually Delicious Batch Cookbook, namecheckinga spicy chicken numberthat appeared in Feast a few weeks back. “That freezes and reheats beautifully.” Of course, the freezer is a fan of plain rice, too: “That’s a better way to batch-cook rice,” O’Toole says. “Freezing and reheating risotto never truly works.”Got a culinary dilemma? title: Rukmini Iyer’s recipe for mozzarella in carrozza – and the leftover crusts | Cheese | The Guardian
description: The love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next day
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next day
Content: Rukmini Iyer’s mozzarella in carrozza.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenRukmini Iyer’s mozzarella in carrozza.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Cook once, eat twiceCheeseRukmini Iyer’s recipe for mozzarella in carrozza – and the leftover crustsThe love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread, this fried sandwich makes for an elevated snack or kids’ tea – and the leftover crusts give you ‘bread rosti’ the next dayRukmini IyerTue 15 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor an exceptionally luxe snack or kids’ tea, mozzarella in carrozza is your girl. It’s the love child of a cheese toastie and eggy bread – instead of toasting it, you dip the cheese sandwich in egg and fry it. In other words, it’s mozzarella in a fancy carriage. I like to use a combination of mozzarella and mature cheddar for flavour, and while it’s best eaten piping hot from the pan, it’s a good (and filling) lunchbox option for children, too.Mozzarella in carrozzaYou will need a very large shallow bowl (or medium roasting tin) for the egg dip.Prep10 minCook10 minServes1-230g mature cheddar, grated2 very large slices white sourdough, crusts removed (but hang on to them)60g mozzarella, sliced1 egg, lightly beaten2tbsp olive oilFlaky sea saltPat down the cheddar evenly on one slice of bread, leaving a 1cm border, then top with the mozzarella. Brush a little beaten egg around the edges of the bread, then top with the second slice of sourdough and gently squash the edges together to seal.Pour the remaining egg into a large, shallow container, then carefully dip both sides of the sandwich in the egg wash – the bread should absorb all of the egg. (Any excess can be poured on once the sandwich is in the pan.)Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, then carefully lift the sandwich into the pan and fry for two minutes on each side, until golden brown. Use your biggest fish slice (or two) to transfer the mozzarella in carrozza on to a plate lined with kitchen paper, then serve immediately, scattered with a little sea salt.For a more balanced meal, serve with a green salad (dressing: one tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, one scant teaspoon dijon mustard and salt, to taste) ora cherry tomato salad (one big handful of cherry tomatoes, halved and dressed with extra-virgin olive oil, salt and fresh basil). Alternatively, if feeding children, serve with cucumber sticks and some fruit.Eat twiceIt was thinking about (and constantly making) children’s lunches that put me on the next-day dish ideas for this week’s column: what do you do with three days’ worth of cut-off sandwich crusts? I can’t bear to waste them, so they get stashed in a plastic container in the fridge. You could take them down the bread-and-butter pudding route: chop or blitz the crusts in a food processor, pack into a small baking dish, then pour over a chocolate custard (three egg yolks, 350ml whole milk or single cream, or a mix of both, 50g sugar, 100g 70% dark chocolate, melted) and bake for 20 minutes or so. Lovely by itself, or for breakfast with Greek yoghurt and just-ripe or baked pears.My favourite savoury option, though, is this: whisk a couple of eggs and a good splash of milk with a handful of grated cheese, then stir this through the chopped or blitzed sandwich crusts. Bake in a shallow dish at 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 for 10-12 minutes, until just set. Once cool (you can refrigerate it overnight, if you wish), cut into squares, then fry in a little olive oil until golden brown and crisp. I billed these as “bread rosti” to the family, and topped them with cream cheese for the children and sriracha for my husband. They were a hit – not bad for half a week’s worth of sandwich leftovers.Explore more on these topicsCheeseCook once, eat twiceFoodSnacksStarterEggsBreadSandwichesrecipesShareReuse this content
